en: The *Combined Commentary on the Brahma’s Net Sūtra*, titled “The Arising of the Great Brahma’s Net Sūtra, Chapter on the Mind-Ground”: How magnificent is the teaching of this sūtra! It points directly to the profound source of true nature and definitively demonstrates the beginning and end of wondrous cultivation.
It regards both precepts and vehicles with equal urgency, and encompasses both sudden and gradual approaches simultaneously. Regarding its fundamental and manifested aspects:

It opens up both horizontally and vertically, encompassing the profound essentials of the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. In terms of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), it is complete in both phenomena and principle;
it grasps the grand outline of the five periods and eight teachings. Although the text transmits only a single chapter, its meaning truly unifies and penetrates the entire sutra.

Reflecting upon the time of the Great Master Zhiyi, the faculties of people were still sharp; therefore, after he had extensively propagated the dharma-gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, he composed only this commentary on the lower fascicle concerning the precepts.

While the Master was thoroughly versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka—its text being concise yet its meaning vast—it was easier for him to point it out to those of his own day who were clear in the Vinaya, but more difficult to awaken those of the present time who are ignorant of the Vinaya. [This task remains] a thousandfold...
Many years have passed since this secret scripture was completed. My preceptor, Master Lianchi, was the first to follow it and reveal its hidden depths;
his sincere resolve to save the age is truly inconceivable. However, because he specialized exclusively in the Pure Land teachings, his mastery of the Vinaya studies was somewhat sparse.
Consequently, there remain many points of uncertainty within the commentary (*yishu*). Furthermore, although the lower fascicle has been circulated, the upper...

The scroll has not yet been fully opened and expounded. Alas! How could the Great Beings who rely on the four reliances harbor any stinginess regarding the Dharma? It is simply that the karmic conditions of sentient beings are meager;

few are able to encounter such a rare gateway to the Dharma. Since my youth, I, Zhi Xu, have revered the study of principle and have taken it as my own responsibility to uphold the lineage of the Way of the sages and worthies of a thousand ages.
Yet, I lament that my hindrances are deep and my wisdom inferior, often causing me to cling to the teachings of the East (Confucianism).
He had slandered the Western Region (India). Later, upon hearing the preface to the *Zizhi lu* and reading the discourse on "Innate Awareness and Quiescent Response," he first conceived faith.
Subsequently, having heard the *Original Vows of Kṣitigarbha* and listened to the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, he resolutely sought to transcend the mundane world.

Thereupon, he resolved to practice Chan meditation. He left home to travel as a wandering monk (*paryaṭaka*). Although he experienced several moments of awakening and understanding, alas, there was no foreseeable time for his realization to be perfected.

Relying on a single point of shame and the correct cause, he dared not rashly assume the burden [of enlightenment] or give rise to *adhimāna* (arrogance), lest he follow in the footsteps of those who have recently fallen into the trap of great falsehoods. Thus, reflecting that his past karmic roots were weak, he felt he must also...

He cultivated himself by combining the precepts with the teachings. First, he followed the ancient masters and eminent Dharma teachers to study the methods of the precepts according to the legacy of Master Yuanlian.
Next, he delved into such works as the *Fahua xuanyi* and the *Mohe zhiguan*, privately studying the doctrinal and contemplative systems of the Tiantai school.
Regarding the *Vinaya-piṭaka*, he read it through three times in detail; as for the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, he took it as his daily recitation.
Consequently, the doubts that had remained unresolved in the *Fayi* were suddenly dispelled like melting ice.

Even the passages in the first fascicle where the ancient meanings were profound and obscure—those which people of former times claimed could not be read as coherent sentences—now had their wondrous purport clearly manifest before me.
I therefore intended to compose a combined commentary to supplement the deficiencies of my predecessors; yet, although this aspiration arose, obstacles were manifold for six or seven years.
I have come, yet my journey has been long and my purpose unfulfilled. Last year, taking a severe illness as a potent medicine, I finally realized my original aspiration to enter the mountains.
Just as I was beginning this path, Master Fang arrived from the region of Min, carrying his staff to seek me out for the sake of his late teacher, Master Xiaoman Quan.
"I request that you preach this sutra to provide merit for the deceased's peace in the afterlife. Furthermore, there were two or three like-minded companions who joyfully desired to hear it.
Consequently, I exerted myself despite my illness to expound upon it; before I realized it, the lotus of my mind had blossomed and the spring of its meaning gushed forth.

I hurriedly took up my brush to record it as it came, resulting in one volume of *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and seven volumes of commentary. Once the commentary was completed, I composed a preface detailing its origins and development.

I address those who come after: although I dare not claim that the mental power of an ordinary person can truly surpass that of former sages, I have long possessed subtle causes, and having recited [the scriptures] for a long time throughout half my life, it is not that I have failed to gain some insight from among a thousand considerations.

Therefore, regarding the contemplation of principles and the investigation of phenomena, I do not begrudge pointing each one out in detail; this is truly intended to assist those who seek understanding and those who practice with earnest devotion.
This is but a half-sleeved garment. Future readers should not, out of concern for its prolixity, treat it with disdain or neglect.
It may be appropriate to regard it as a raft-like metaphor once both understanding and practice have become perfectly complete.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Zhi Xu on the first *poṣadha* day of the latter summer retreat in the previous Dingshu year,
within the Fanwang Chamber at Jiuzi Biéfēng.
Re-carved by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Shen Shūzhǔn on the eighth day of the fourth month in the Bingchen year of the Kangxi era.

Regarding the preface to the rules for carving [the woodblocks]: in the past, the sutras and their commentaries were necessarily printed on separate lines. First, it was out of a sense of not daring to conflate the commentary with the sutra; secondly...
The textual meanings of the sutras and their commentaries each possess their own internal logic and continuity; they should not be interrupted or interspersed with extraneous matter.

Because those of later generations have dull faculties, it is difficult for them to read and compare these texts side by side. Consequently, the masters of our tradition have repeatedly sought to synthesize and harmonize them accordingly.
Although my skillful efforts were directed toward beginners and my compassionate heart was most earnest, there remain many instances where the text has been fragmented or confused.

Now, wishing to preserve the ancient format, yet fearing that future generations might again fragment and rearrange it, I have instead conformed to the needs of the times by combining the sūtra with its commentary.
The sūtra text is written flush left (in the top margin), while the commentary and the topical headings are indented one character to the right. Thus ends the fascicle.
The initial *yuanqi* (causal origin) is also indented by one character. This is done to demonstrate respect for the Buddha’s words and to ensure they are not confused with other material.
Since the ancients did not allow commentaries (*shu*) to be mixed with the sūtras, there are even instances where every single word and phrase is treated in this manner.
Regarding "sections" (*ke*): since a section is itself a commentary (*shu*), it serves to clarify and explain the purport of the sutra; therefore, one does not weary of its detail.
Those who compile [the text] likewise divide it into sections word by word and phrase by phrase, to the point that the sutra text becomes nearly unreadable—this is truly lamentable.
Furthermore, in the Dharma-ending age, people’s faculties are dull and they mostly fear excessive subdivision; for this reason, I have now ceased [doing so].
The major sections (da-ke) are established, while all other minor sections (zi-ke) are treated with brevity.
Should there be one or two that cannot be omitted, they are presented within the commentary (shu), ensuring that the scriptural text does not become fragmented or disjointed.
In the writings of the ancients, there was often much refutation and establishment; for instance, works such as the *Xuanyi xuantan* (Profound Meaning:

A Preliminary Discourse) invariably first presented the old interpretations before proceeding to provide a definitive judgment. Although there are one or two commentaries on the upper scroll of this present sutra, they are insufficient for circulation.

As for the lower scroll, there exists only the single work titled *Yishu fayin* (Commentary on the Meaning: Unveiling the Hidden); while it contains many omissions and deficiencies, [it remains our primary resource].
Errors are few. Even if there are one or two discrepancies, I shall no longer distinguish between right and wrong or long and short;

I will simply provide a straightforward explanation based on principle alone. If you wish to know in detail the similarities and differences between ancient and modern views, please consult the *Yishu fayin* (Unveiling the Hidden Meanings of the Commentary) by comparing them side-by-side, and you will naturally come to understand them.
Regarding the gravity of the offenses associated with the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*), each is fundamentally based upon the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and vinayas.
Only after deep reflection, meticulous discernment, and the harmonious integration and thorough mastery of these sources did I venture to compose this work.

I have striven to ensure that the language is concise yet the meaning is exhaustive, without daring to include even a single word or character based on my own private conjecture. However, this does not follow the method of the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*, which treats each section individually.
I have merely indicated from where these were derived. Should you not believe this, I request that you examine the entire Tripitaka with great proficiency;
thereafter, please discern what I have failed to include and grant me your corrections. I look forward to this deeply.
Although the Mahāyāna Vinaya is the ultimate source and standard for all codes of discipline, because it is common to all seven classes of practitioners,
the names and definitions of the five categories and seven groups of offenses pertaining to bhikṣus must still be kept concealed and not explicitly taught.
This is because Bodhisattva bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs should naturally study the *Vinayamātṛkā* and the essential points of the Vinaya.
The entire Tibetan Canon already contains the names and meanings of these chapters and sections; there is no need to explain them further here.
Whether one is a bodhisattva śrāmaṇera or a bodhisattva upāsaka, it is sufficient to practice and study according to this.
Furthermore, the names and meanings of the *pien-zu* (the Vinaya sections) are not even within the scope of what one ought to know;
by no means should one seek prior knowledge of them, lest one incur the grave offense of stealing the Dharma. Let the wise and enlightened take this to heart and exercise caution.
The Combined Commentary on the "Bodhisattva Grounds Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Annotated by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Zhixu of Gusu, Ming Dynasty.
Compiled by the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Wēnlíng Dàofǎng. △ The text is divided into three parts.
From the beginning of the chapter to “What kind of light is it? consists of nine lines of scripture; this constitutes the Section on the Emission of Light.
From “At that time, Śākyamuni raised up the great assembly” to the end of the lower scroll, [the section] titled “Mind and Mind.”

To receive and uphold this with reverence and joy constitutes the section on the "Correctly Revealed Dharma Gate," which extends from the passage where Śākyamuni Buddha speaks of the "Superior Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury" at the beginning of the volume until the end of the scroll. This includes eight lines of prose and fourteen lines of verse.
It constitutes the section on "Circulation for the Benefit of the World. Although this is but one chapter among the sixty-two chapters, it comprises both the introduction and the circulation.
Within this entire *Vaipulya* sūtra, this single chapter alone clearly exhibits the three divisions. First, the emission of light that initiates [the discourse] is divided into three parts:

first, the general indication of the time and place of the Dharma assembly; second, Śākyamuni’s emission of light to alert the assembly; and third, the Bodhisattvas’ emission of light to assemble and inquire.
Regarding the first—the general indication of the time and place of the Dharma assembly—there are further two sections: first, clarifying the time, place, and presiding host.
The Companion. Regarding the Dharma-gate taught by the two fingers:
first, at that time, Śākyamuni Buddha was in the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara within the realm of the Fourth Dhyāna.

Together with immeasurable Great Brahma Kings and an unspeakably unspeakable multitude of Bodhisattvas, the general prefaces of all sutras fully possess the sixfold accomplishment. This is a separate circulation of a single chapter, which briefly lacks the [sections on] faith and hearing;
for the two meanings of faith and hearing are found in the first chapter, as their principle permeates the entire sutra. Now, only these [sections] are set forth.

There are four aspects. At that time—these two words establish the accomplishment of the time. Śākyamuni establishes the accomplishment of the principal [teacher]. The stage of the fourth dhyāna establishes the accomplishment of the place.
The Brahmā Bodhisattva establishes the accomplishment of the retinue. Since the principal and the retinue are simultaneous and in the same place, they must hear the sublime Dharma.
Having heard the sublime Dharma, they must believe and understand it according to the principle. Although the text explicitly indicates these points:
Fourth: The meaning comprises six aspects. Regarding the phrase "at that time" (*tadā*), time has no substantial reality; its duration—whether long or short—is merely a matter of the mind.

It is designated as "that time" based on the harmonious union of teacher and disciple, and the perfect correspondence between the capacity of the audience and the teaching. Regarding the phrase "Śākyamuni Buddha":
This is the title of my original teacher, endowed with myriad virtues. Since the Buddha possesses immeasurable virtues, he must have immeasurable names;
however, for now, we shall refer to him by the clan name of his manifested birth in this land and the appellation bestowed upon him by his father, the King, which all people together invoke.
In the Sanskrit language, *Śākya* is translated here as "Capable Benevolence" (*Néng-rén*), also as "Capable Confucianism" (*Néng-rú*), and also as "Straight Forest" (*Zhí-lín*).
This is his clan name. In the Sanskrit language, *Munī* is translated as "Silent Stillness" (*Jímò*).

Because when the Bodhisattva was a crown prince, he personally attended a great assembly of the Śākya clan and the entire Śākya multitude remained silent, his father the King established this title for him. When the clan name and the personal title are joined together, [it forms the full name].
Regarding the establishment of this auspicious title, the explanation based on its essential meaning is as follows: because of his profound stillness, he does not abide in saṃsāra;
because of his supreme capability, he does not abide in nirvāṇa. The union of compassion and wisdom is what is termed "Great Enlightenment.

As for his taking up residence in the stage of the fourth dhyāna: the Dharmakāya is neither localized nor non-localized; yet, for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests a dwelling place. Some say that this is termed "abiding" only temporarily.
"Long-term abiding" (*jūju*) is a partial designation; "long-term" is also called "remaining" (*zai*), and "temporary" is also called "abiding.

Although the characters for "remaining" and "abiding" differ, their meanings are firmly established. Here, the meaning is explained according to "abiding. The Buddha has four types of abiding: first, the celestial abiding (*devasthāna*);

second, the Brahma abiding (*brahmasthāna*); third, the noble abiding (*āryasthāna*); and fourth, the Buddha abiding (*buddhasthāna*). The five precepts and the ten wholesome paths are called the celestial abiding.

The four dhyānas and eight samādhis, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, are called the Brahma-abodes. Precept, concentration, wisdom, and liberation are called the Noble Abodes.
The Śūraṅgama-samādhi, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, and other such dharmas are called the Buddha-abodes.
Amidst the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—one never departs from all these Dharma-gates. One should employ the Celestial Abode in accordance with desire.
Regarding the realms and capacities: the Brahma-abode corresponds to the capacities of those in the form and formless realms; the Noble-abode corresponds to the capacities of the three vehicles;
and the Buddha-abode corresponds to the capacity of the one vehicle. The Buddha is the one who dwells, and the four dharmas are that in which he dwells.

Furthermore, these four dharmas are the means by which he dwells, and the celestial palaces of the deva kings are the places where he dwells. Because he gathers sentient beings through these four dharmas, he manifests the existence of a dwelling place.
Abiding is fundamentally non-abiding. It is not like ordinary people who abide according to karma within non-abiding.

The fourth dhyāna is called "the ground" because, among the nine grounds of the triple world, it is the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness. Since the Buddha dwells here, he should be considered to abide in the Brahma-abodes;
however, his intention lies in opening the gate of the Ground of Mind to lead all beings to see their fundamental source—this is true abiding.
Regarding the Buddha’s dwelling: Maheśvara—translated here as "Great Sovereign" (Dà Zìzài)—resides in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven and serves as the lord of the trichiliocosm;
he is also called the Great Brahmā King. Within a single trichiliocosm, there is only one such king;
the mention here of "immeasurable" [kings] refers to those who have gathered from other directions. For the meaning of "bodhisattva," see the *Xuányì* (Profound Meaning).
"Inexpressible-inexpressible" is the designation for the ultimate great number. The Great Brahmā constitutes the assembly of those born of different origins;

the Bodhisattvas constitute the assembly of those born of the same origin. Whether of different or the same origin, they are all those who have long heard the Great Teaching, have perfected the great faculties, and are worthy to hear this Great Dharma—it is precisely these who are present in this great assembly.
Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: "the slightest movement of thought" (*jier you xin*).
This mind being identical in essence with all sentient beings is named Śākya.
This mind’s original nature being empty and quiescent is named Muni. This mind being inherently numinous and awakened is named Buddha.
This mind being inherently equal and pure is named the Stage of the Four Dhyānas. This mind being originally sovereign and unattached is named Maheśvara.
The Palace of Śūra. This mind, which possesses all distinct qualities of purity, is named the Immeasurable Great Brahmā King.
This mind, which possesses all undifferentiated wisdom that is inexhaustible, is named the Ineffable-Ineffable Multitude of Bodhisattvas.
△ Second, the Dharma-gate expounded by the two fingers:
the Exposition of the Mind-Ground Dharma-Gate as taught by Vairocana Buddha in the Lotus-Womb World.
The ocean-like assembly gathers like clouds, desiring to hear the Great Dharma. He demonstrates it according to their capacities, with the intent that they return to the source. Such is the mind.

The Dharma-gate of the Grounds was originally taught by Vairocana Buddha. Now, the primary deity, Pure and Full (Jingman), resides within the Lotus-Womb World (Padmagarbha-lokadhātu) and proclaims it for the sake of the assembly, so that they may know its origin. This serves as a preliminary introduction for the subsequent acts of receiving, honoring, and paying homage.
Although this Flower Treasury (Huazang) is called a land of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*), it is said to be the manifestation of the Dharma-body bestowing retribution; its essence is...

This is precisely the *Sāmbhogikakāya* (Peaceful Light). The principle-nature of the Peaceful Light becomes manifest by relying upon the *vipākaphala* (retribution-body). To point it out in this way is precisely intended to lead people toward self-awakening.
Regarding the "interpretation through contemplating the mind": the essence of this mind is undefiled and possesses wondrous cause and effect;
thus, it is called the "Lotus. This mind is firm, solid, lofty, and eminent; among all phenomena, its Middle Way is called the "Pedestal. This mind is vast...

Because it contains the names of all phenomena, it is called a "Treasury" (*garbha*). This mind is called "World" (*loka*) because it extends vertically through time; it is called "Realm" (*dhātu*) because it pervades horizontally across space.

This mind is called "Pure" (*viśuddha*) because it is free from faults and severed from non-virtue; it is called "Full" (*pūrṇa*) because it possesses virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Because this one mind universally encompasses and illustrates all minds, it is called "Exposition" (*nirdeśa*).
Because all phenomena gather and arise within this mind, it is called "Mind" (*citta*); because all phenomena rely upon and are sustained by this mind, it is called "Ground" (*bhūmi*).

This mind, being capable of serving as a standard and support, is called "Dharma" (the Teaching). This mind, which pervades all phenomena, is called the "Gate. This brief explanation of the general outline is thus;
the details will not be further elaborated below, as they can be understood through one's own reflection.
△ Second, Śākyamuni emits light to awaken the assembly.
At that time, Śākyamuni’s body emitted rays of wisdom-light. From this palace of the Heavenly King, the light shone as far as the Lotus-womb World-realm (*padmagarbhalokadhātu*).
Within all those worlds, all sentient beings looked at one another and were filled with joy and gladness.
Though they rejoiced, they were unable to know this light—what its cause was and what its conditions—and thus all conceived doubts;
immeasurable devas and humans likewise conceived doubts.
Previously, the world of the lotus pedestal and the dharma-gate taught by the primary deity Śākyamuni were revealed.
Fearing that people might not believe this, he again emitted light that thoroughly illuminated that realm, so that they might awaken to their original source.
As for "wisdom-light" (prajñā-āloka), because form and mind are non-dual, bodily radiance is itself wisdom-light. That which is called "knowledge and the locus of knowledge" is all termed *prajñā*.

As for the statement that "the illumination extends even to the Flower Treasury World" (*Huazang*), this is because the fundamental and the phenomenal are non-dual; thus, it is able to illuminate the entirety of the ocean of the Dharma-realm.

Regarding "mutually beholding with joy," this is because the essence of the sentient being and the Buddha are identical; therefore, one does not perceive the ease with which they are perfumed by each other.

"Unknown as to what cause and what condition" means that the cause of the original source-ground of the mind is not yet known, nor is the condition for opening up the provisional traces to reveal the fundamental reality.
"All give rise to doubts" means that sentient beings have long remained mired in delusion, while devas and humans merely uphold the provisional traces;
therefore, it is difficult for them to attain sudden enlightenment.
△ Third: The Emission of Light and the Gathering for Inquiry by the Bodhisattvas.
At that time, from within the assembly, the Bodhisattva Lord of Profound Penetration and Flower-Light arose from the Great Adornment Flower Radiance Samādhi.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he emitted light the color of white clouds of vajra; this light illuminated all worlds. Within them—
All the bodhisattvas gathered together; with one mind but different voices, they asked about this light: "What are the characteristics of this light?

Since the assembly had given rise to doubt, it was necessary for them to attain awakening. If not through an appropriate occasion, who could serve as the requester to reveal the [Buddha's] true identity? Thus, he manifested his trace.

To reveal the fundamental source is none other than the inconceivable great cause and condition; therefore, he must emit light to awaken and assemble the ocean-like assembly to collectively pose the question.

The Bodhisattva named Xuántōnghuāguāng (Profound Penetration Flower Light) is so called because "xuán" (profound) refers to subtle penetration, which signifies the title encompassing both cause and fruit;
"huā" (flower) symbolizes practice, while "guāng" (light) symbolizes wisdom. Through this practice and this wisdom, one attains Buddhahood.

Because it is the fundamental source, it is called the "Master. In its profundity (*xuan*), both the Flower and the Light are profound, for the nature of wisdom and practice is exceedingly subtle and wondrous.
In its pervasiveness (*tong*), both the Flower and the Light are pervasive, for the dharma of wisdom and practice permeates cause and effect. In the Sanskrit language, this is called *samādhi*.
This is translated as "right concentration. As for the samādhi in which he abides being named "Great Ornamentation Flower Radiance":
this activity of wisdom arises in accordance with the nature [of reality] and, in turn, adorns that very nature; therefore, it is called "great. Regarding "by the Buddha’s spiritual power":
he abides in his fundamental samādhi, touches the Buddha’s light, and thereby emerges from meditative absorption; subsequently, relying on the Buddha’s power, he emits light to summon the assembly.
The light emitted is called "Vajra-White-Cloud-Colored. It is named "Vajra" because it is ultimately firm and solid, signifying the virtue of the Dharmakāya.
It is called "white" because it is pure and free from blemish, signifying the virtue of Prajñā. It is the gathering place of myriad virtues.
It is named "Cloud," signifying the virtue of liberation. Furthermore, these three virtues are all firm; these three virtues are all without flaw;

these three virtues are all the gathering of the Dharma. This radiance is entirely the secret treasury of the three virtues, which all Bodhisattvas throughout every world-world-system cultivate and realize together;
therefore, being illumined by it, they all come to this assembly. With one mind, yet distinct...
The question regarding "this light" refers back to the causes, conditions, and characteristics of the light previously emitted by the Buddha.
Next, the formal presentation of the Dharma-gate has two parts: first, Śākyamuni explains the *Cittabhūmi* (Mind-Ground) Dharma;

second, Śākyamuni proclaims the Bodhisattva Precepts. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the question and answer that designate the title; second, the formal exposition of its meaning and intent; third, the entrustment.
The Broad Dissemination. This section has two parts: first, Śākyamuni poses the question; second, Vairocana provides the answer. The first part also has two sections:
first, gathering the assembly to behold the source; second, having the assembly request the Dharma. Now, the first [of these].
At that time, Śākyamuni immediately lifted up the great assembly of this world and returned to the Lotus-Womb Treasury World (*padmagarbhalokadhātu*).

There, within a palace of hundreds of millions of billions of purple-gold adamant light, he beheld Vairocana Buddha seated upon a majestic throne of hundreds of millions of billions of lotuses, radiating brilliant light.
Then Śākyamuni and the entire great assembly simultaneously paid homage to Vairocana.
That Buddha’s foot has already descended [upon this land].
The Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*) is the world of the original source; it is like returning to one's former office. Thus, it is said that he has "returned.

Although light was previously emitted that illuminated this realm through and through, the great assembly merely perceived it from afar by receiving its radiance, never having personally trodden upon it. Now, for the first time, they face it directly.

Revering the Honored One, one knows that the provisional manifestation (*jaku*) and the fundamental reality (*hon*) are not separate; by performing a single prostration, one truly symbolizes the merging of the provisional with the fundamental.
△ Second, requesting the Dharma for the sake of the assembly.

Śākyamuni Buddha said: "In this world, for what causes and conditions do all sentient beings, both on the earth and in space, attain the ten stages of the Bodhisattva path and achieve the fruit of Buddhahood?
What are their characteristics? This shall be explained extensively according to the 'Chapter on the Source of Buddha-nature,' which broadly inquires into the seeds of all Bodhisattvas."

Since he had previously emitted light on two occasions to stir their doubts and incite them to inquire, the assembly now requests that he again explain the profound meaning of the causes and conditions, so that each may hear it directly from the Buddha himself.

As for "the earth, space, and all sentient beings," this refers to the five destinies; specifically, the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven constitute the sentient beings who dwell upon the earth.

The remaining four heavens of the desire realm, as well as those of the form and formless realms, are the beings who dwell in space. All these sentient beings shall eventually attain the fruit of Buddhahood;
it is only that they do not yet know by what causes and conditions this will occur. The ten stages (*bhūmi*) constitute the partial fruit, while the Buddha constitutes the full fruit.
The realization of this must necessarily rely upon causes and conditions, and whether cause or fruit, there must be its respective characteristics. Now...
This is merely a direct and concise inquiry. Were it to be asked in detail, it would be exactly as presented in the "Chapter on the Source of Buddha-nature.
These words belong to the compilers, who point forward to that entire scripture; all subsequent instances follow this pattern.
△ Second, Vairocana’s response in two parts: first, the response by manifesting through meditative concentration; second, the response by admonishing the listeners.
Now, the first:
At that time, Vairocana Buddha was filled with great joy; he manifested the light-body of empty space, the fundamental source of his nature, as the attainment of Buddhahood.
The Samādhi of the Permanently Abiding Dharmakāya was manifested to the great assembly.
Regarding the fact that he first demonstrated it through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) before expounding the Dharma-gate, there are briefly three meanings:
first, to reveal the essence of the Dharma, showing that this Dharma-gate cannot be proclaimed by means of language or written characters, but is solely the domain of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
Regarding the "sphere" (*viṣaya*): since the Buddha has personally realized this Dharma, he is constantly in meditative absorption; how could there be any entering or exiting?

Its very essence is suchness; how could it be hidden or manifest? It is only because sentient beings have long been immersed in the net of delusion that [the Buddha], through his great compassion of same-essence (*samatā-karuṇā*), employs inconceivable, nature-conforming skillful means (*upāya*) to enlighten them. Therefore, it is called "manifestation. Second.
This is to accord with the causes and conditions of the *siddhānta*. There are some sentient beings who obtain the four benefits upon hearing the Dharma being preached;
there are also some sentient beings who obtain the four benefits upon seeing [the Buddha] enter meditative concentration. Therefore, it is necessary to demonstrate through concentration.
Thirdly, it is to reveal that whether the Tathāgata speaks or remains silent, everything is nothing other than the wondrous Way; all the Buddha-activities he performs are entirely [efficacious].
"Emptiness. First, he indicates it through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), thereby making known that this Dharma does not cling to verbal designations.
Then, he answers with words, thereby making known that this Dharma does not fall into obscure realization. Both appearance and sound constitute the substance of the teaching;

yet, regarding this samādhi being called "the essence of the nature of the light of emptiness," emptiness is vast and devoid of even the slightest speck of dust, while light universally illumines all phenomena.

The *dhātu* (element/realm) is, in its essential nature, the true source of the real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). It is merely another name for the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*).
This secret treasury is primordially complete within all sentient beings as the true cause for attaining Buddhahood.

The Buddhas and Tathāgatas have ultimately and perfectly realized it, thereby achieving the supreme fruit of eternal abiding. Now, I present this whole and unadorned; I shall directly enable [all beings to realize it].
The assembly shall immediately perceive the characteristics of both cause and effect; this may indeed be called direct, straightforward, and incisive.
△ Second, the admonition to listen followed by the answer, in two parts: first, the admonition to cultivate the three types of wisdom; second, the detailed response to the questions. Now...
First: O sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! Contemplate well and practice accordingly.

Although the Buddha-dharma is subtle and wondrous, it cannot be realized without wisdom. Though there are many forms of sublime realization, they are all fully encompassed within the three types of wisdom. If one does not listen attentively...

If one does not examine thoroughly, the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) will not arise. If one reflects improperly, the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) will not arise. If one does not practice with diligence, the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) will not arise.
The wisdom born of hearing resides in names; the wisdom born of reflection resides in contemplative practice; the wisdom born of cultivation resides in the stage of semblance.

By means of the wisdom born of hearing, one attains the subduing of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*). By means of the wisdom born of reflection, one attains the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). By means of the wisdom born of cultivation...

Because of wisdom, one attains the opening of the secret treasury. This is still explained according to the sequential [development]. If one speaks in accordance with the nature [of reality], the three types of wisdom are simultaneously present within a single mind.

△ Next, the detailed response to the questions has two parts: first, a general response concerning the cause and effect, the origin and the manifestation; second, a comprehensive exposition of the ground of the mind.
Regarding the names and characteristics, there are four sections in the first part: first, clarifying the cause; second, clarifying the fruit; third, manifesting traces from the source;
and fourth, returning the traces to the source. This is the first.
"I have practiced the Mind-Ground for a hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Taking this as the cause and taking my own body as the witness, I clarify that this is the true Dharma-gate of my own practice. Regarding the Sanskrit term *asaṃkhyeya*, this is translated here as "innumerable.
It does not say "three *asaṃkhyeyas*" but rather "a hundred *asaṃkhyeyas*" because it is intended for those outside the [Three] Realms.
The Capacity. One must know that the ground of practice (*bhūmi*) is thus vast and remote.
△ Second, clarifying the fruition:

First, having abandoned the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment and is named Vairocana, dwelling in the Lotus Flower Terrace Repository World (*padmagarbhalokadhātu*).
In the ocean [of the Dharma], when the ignorance of arising-characteristics is forever exhausted, it is called "the first abandonment of the state of an ordinary person.

When the fruit-virtue is ultimately perfected and consummate, it is called "attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. "Equal" means illuminating both extremes simultaneously; "Perfect" means accords with and realizes the Middle Way. Regarding the ten...
The title [of the Buddha] is precisely that of the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha). "Vairocana" translates here as "Pure and Full.

Like the moon on a clear night, all dark marks are entirely purified and the essence of light is perfectly complete; this title is established based on his virtues and is the supreme designation for the ultimate union of retributive wisdom with the Dharma.
As for "dwelling in the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury World-Ocean," this refers to the Land of Real Retribution Free from Obstructions.
The fruit of retribution manifested by all Buddhas accords with reality; therein, form and mind are non-dual, and the primary and secondary environments are interpenetrating.
Furthermore, this world manifests through the nature of the sentient beings' minds and abides in reliance upon that very nature of their minds.

This nature of the sentient beings' minds is called the "Lotus," for it remains unstained despite being in the mire. Cause and effect are simultaneous, arising from the wondrousness of this mind-nature.
Because it is like a lotus, it causes the world to be like a lotus as well. This very nature of mind is the ultimate source of all phenomena, and is therefore called the "pedestal" (*maṇḍala*).
It contains an infinite network of lands, and is therefore called the "treasury" (*garbha*). It extends vertically without beginning or end, and is therefore called "worlds" (*loka*).

It spans horizontally across all directions, and is therefore called "realms" (*dhātu*). It is profound, vast, and inconceivable, and is therefore called the "ocean" (*samudra*). Ultimately, it accords with...
Because they are joined together, it is called "abiding.
△ Third, descending from the fundamental to the manifested traces:
the pedestal is all-encompassing and possesses a thousand petals; each petal is one world, thus constituting a thousand worlds. I manifest as a thousand [bodies].

Śākyamuni presides over a thousand-world system. Subsequently, regarding a single-leaf world-system, there are further ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion suns and moons, ten billion sets of four continents, and ten billion Jambudvīpas.
Within these, ten billion Śākyamuni Bodhisattvas sit beneath ten billion bodhi trees, each expounding upon the *Bodhisattva-citta-bhūmi* that you have asked about. As for the rest...
The nine hundred and ninety-nine Śākyamunis each manifest a thousand times ten billion Śākyamunis, and it is likewise so for all of them.

As for the "thousand petals" that encompass them, this circle represents the thousand dharmas; its specific correspondence to the second stage is briefly as clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
Regarding the "thousand Śākyamunis," this refers to what is correctly explained in the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith): their manifestation in the world from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

The "intermediate supreme body" refers to that which is perceived by those of intermediate capacity, appearing as an inferior yet superior *nirmāṇakāya*. Regarding the term "basis" (*ju*), it carries the meaning of universally encompassing and guiding through transformation.
As for "ten billion" (*baiyi*): one hundred million is a "billion" (*yi*); together they constitute the number of ten million times ten million, which is the domain of a great trichiliocosm.
Sumeru—here translated as "Wondrous High"—is composed of four precious substances and resides [at the center].
Amidst the great oceans of the four continents, it is narrow at the base and broad at the top;
its summit is the dwelling place of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, and its waist is encircled by the sun and moon, as explained in detail in the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World).
Jambudvīpa is one of the four continents, located to the south of Mount Sumeru, and is the place where all Buddhas manifest their births. On this continent there is a great tree named Jambudvīpa.
It is so named because it is not found on other continents; it is also called Jambudvīpa.
As for the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, while he was first seated beneath the Bodhi tree and had not yet manifested his attainment of Buddhahood, he was still called a Bodhisattva.

His manifestation of transformations within hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of worlds signifies his vast gathering of all sentient beings according to their capacities and his skillful application of expedient means, as elucidated in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Spontaneously, there exists inconceivable karma capable of manifesting throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings;

this is the "inferior response" (劣應) manifested among humans, which is what is perceived by those whose capacities are obscured. Each [response] manifests as a thousand, a hundred, or ten billion Śākyamunis—the character "thousand" (千) is likely a scribal error for "ten" (十), as when calculated together they total a thousand, a hundred, or ten billion.
△ Fourth, tracing the manifestations back to the source.
The Thousand-Petal Upper Buddha is my transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis are the transformation bodies of those thousand Śākyamunis.
I am their fundamental source, named Vairocana Buddha.
From the fundamental source descending into its manifestations, they are non-different yet different; by subsuming these manifestations back into the source, they are different yet non-different.

Pointing toward these two layers of transformation, one returns to the single reality. This is precisely intended so that each person may awaken to their own original source, the enlightened nature, which is fundamentally pure and perfect.
△ Second, the detailed exposition of the names and characteristics of the Mind-Ground has two parts: first, the formal enumeration of the forty dharma-gates;
second, the concluding demonstration of the signs of the fruit of entry. Now, for the first:
At that time, in the Lotus-Pedestal Treasury World, Vairocana Buddha extensively answered and addressed the thousand Śākyas and the hundred thousand [bodhisattvas].

The Chapter on the Dharma of the Ground of Mind Asked by a Billion Śākyas: "O Buddhas, you should know that within the stage of firm faith and patience (*adhimukti-kṣānti*), there are ten minds directed toward the fruit of the ten stages of departure (*daśa-prasthāna-citta*):
first, the mind of relinquishment; second, the mind of precept; third, the mind of patience; fourth, the mind of diligence; fifth, the mind of concentration;

sixth, the mind of wisdom; seventh, the mind of aspiration; eighth, the mind of protection; ninth, the mind of joy; and tenth, the mind of the summit (*mūrdhan*). O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten..."

Within the stage of firm acceptance of the Dharma for those who have set out on the path, there are ten types of cultivated mental orientations toward the fruit: first, the mind of loving-kindness; second, the mind of compassion;

third, the mind of sympathetic joy; fourth, the mind of equanimity; fifth, the mind of generosity; sixth, the mind of pleasant speech; seventh, the mind of beneficial action; eighth, the mind of concordance;

ninth, the mind of meditative concentration; and tenth, the mind of wisdom. O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten cultivated mental orientations, one enters the ten [aspects] of firm cultivation of patience.
The adamantine mind directed toward the fruit consists of ten aspects: first, the mind of faith; second, the mind of mindfulness; third, the mind of dedication; fourth, the mind of penetration;
fifth, the upright mind; sixth, the non-regressive mind; seventh, the Mahāyāna mind; eighth, the signless mind; ninth, the wisdom mind; and tenth, the indestructible mind.

O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten adamantine minds, one enters into the firm and holy patience (*kṣānti*). This leads to the fruition of the ten stages (*bhūmi*): first, the stage of the equality of the nature of reality;
second, the stage of excellent wisdom of the nature of reality; third, the stage of luminosity of the nature of reality; fourth, the stage of the flame of suchness of the nature of reality;

fifth, the stage of the illumination of wisdom of the nature of reality; sixth, the stage of flower-light of the nature of reality; seventh, the stage of fulfillment of the nature of reality... [and so forth].
The eighth is the Ground of the Buddha’s Roar; the ninth is the Ground of the Flower Adornment of Essential Nature; and the tenth is the Ground of Entering the Buddha-realm.
As for the "Patience of Firm Faith," one looks up to and believes in the principle of the Middle Way Buddha-nature from the stage of the external ordinary person;
by cultivating this with firmness, one attains Patience and thus realizes the Stage of Progression. Regarding the "Mind of Progression," it is the entry from the conventional into emptiness.
These develop the path leading toward the attainment of Bodhi. Regarding "orientation toward the fruit," each and every mind is oriented toward the fruit of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, within each individual mind, both meanings of "orientation toward the fruit" and "the fruit itself" are present: "entering" is called orientation, while "abiding in the stage" is called the fruit, as in the case of the four fruits and four orientations.
These ten minds are themselves the ten pāramitās, and they are also the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
Gate: Profoundly penetrating the dharma of emptiness, one cultivates the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*). These ten perfections are all dharma-gates of signlessness (*animitta*):

protection is the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*); joy is the perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*); and the crown is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). As for those instances where the sequence differs slightly from the general path, each has its own specific significance;
one must not adhere to them dogmatically. Furthermore, all ten *pāramitās* nurture and develop wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*).
The meaning of the adamantine firmness is entirely a dharma-gate of essential nature;
yet, it is merely called "setting forth" (prasthāna) because, within the stage of provisional understanding, one speaks from the perspective of the mind arising while fundamentally having no abiding.

As for "firm dharma-patience" (dṛḍha-dharma-kṣānti), by cultivating firmness based on the dharma of setting forth, one attains patience and thereby realizes the stage of nourishment (puṣṭi). Nourishment...
The mind emerges from emptiness and enters into the provisional, nourishing wholesome dharmas through the illusion-like samādhi.

This is precisely the four immeasurables and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). Concentration subsumes the immeasurables, while wisdom subsumes the means of integration; it is also the dharma-gate of the ten practices.

Furthermore, the sublime concentration of the four immeasurables and the sublime wisdom of the four means of integration both possess the development and progression toward the meaning of adamantine solidity. All of these are likewise...
Regarding the dharma-gate of the essential nature (*dharmatā*), it is referred to here simply as "nurturing" (*poṣaṇa*).

This is stated from the perspective of the stage of provisional understanding, speaking of the mind that is constantly arising while being non-abiding. As for "firmly cultivating patience," one cultivates the nurturing mind so that patience becomes firmly established.
This is the realization of the stage of Vajra. As for the "Vajra-mind," it refers to practicing Madhyamaka to subdue ignorance; like a vajra, it is indestructible.
This name and meaning of this mind closely resembles the Ten Faiths of the Perfect Teaching (*Yuanjia*), and it is also the dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications (*Daśapariṇāmanā*).
Furthermore, faith and the other stages all possess the significance of setting forth and nurturing, and they are all its essential nature.

Regarding this Dharma gate, it is simply called "Vajra" because, within the stage of semblance-understanding, one speaks of "non-abiding as the arising of the mind" and "the arising of the mind as non-abiding.
As for "firm noble patience," within the Vajra-mind, one cultivates the noble Dharma through the contemplation of the Middle Way;
by giving rise to true wisdom and severing [delusions], one achieves firm patience and thereby realizes the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
One cuts off the ten heavy obstacles and realizes the ten true suchnesses (*tathatā*).

Like the great earth, which bears all things, one abandons the state of an ordinary person and enters the state of a sage, suddenly becoming identical with the Buddha-body and clearly perceiving the Buddha-nature; therefore, each stage is called the "Stage of Essential Nature" (*tixing-di*).
This is largely similar in meaning to the common ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), though the names differ significantly and will be explained later. Furthermore, the ten...
Each stage (*bhūmi*) possesses the meaning of "setting forth," "nurturing," and "vajra. Yet, it is simply called the "stage of essence" (*tattva-bhūmi*).

This is because the preceding [classification] was based on analogous understanding and practice, and thus each stage was termed a "mind" (*citta*); whereas this [classification] is based on realizing the truth and treading upon reality, and thus every mind is termed a "stage."

△ Second, the summary indicating the signs of attaining entry into the fruit, which has two parts: first, realization through one's own person; second, the transfer of this to sentient beings. Now, the first:
these forty dharma-gates were practiced by me when I was formerly a bodhisattva; they are the root source for entering the fruit of Buddhahood.
If the Perfectly Awakened One is like a tree, this Dharma is like its root; if the Perfectly Awakened One is like the ocean, this Dharma is like its source.
That which the Buddha first cultivated is certainly not erroneous.
△ Second, the entrustment to sentient beings:

All such sentient beings enter the ten stages of the adamantine path of development and advancement, realizing the fruit to be attained—unconditioned, signless, great fulfillment, and eternally abiding.
They become fully perfected in the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, the dharma-body, and the wisdom-body.
Only by entering the forty dharma-gates, such as the stages of entry and departure (*prasthāna*), can one realize the fruit of future attainment.

This clearly demonstrates that although the principle is inherently complete (*prakṛti-sampad*), the mind must rely on cultivation for its realization; thus, one must not engage in lofty talk regarding the rational nature while giving rise to false pride.

"Unconditioned and signless" means the eternal exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*). "Greatly fulfilled" means the perfect culmination of the myriad virtues. "Permanently abiding" means unchanging and...
It is "transmigratory" because its power is not shared with others and is thus fully perfected; it is "eternally abiding" because the Dharma-body is fully perfected;
and it is "unconditioned and signless" because the Wisdom-body is fully perfected. Furthermore, the unconditioned is the virtue of the sovereign self, and the signless is the virtue of purity.
Great fulfillment is the virtue of bliss; eternal abiding is the virtue of permanence. Power, the unshared [qualities], and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are signless (*animitta*).

Great fulfillment, eternal abiding, and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) are also unconditioned and signless. Great fulfillment, eternal abiding, and the Wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) are also unconditioned.
It is signless (*animitta*), great fulfillment (*mahāpūrṇa*), and eternally abiding (*nitya*). Each of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) possesses these four virtues (*catur-guṇa*).
△ Second, the formal exposition of the meaning and intent has two parts: first, the Bodhisattva’s inquiry into the meaning; second, Śākyamuni’s detailed response. Now, the first part.

At that time, in the Lotus-Womb World (*Padmagarbhalokadhātu*), Vairocana Buddha—upon his majestic and great radiant throne, the Buddha atop the thousand-petaled lotus, the hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, and all the Buddhas of every world—had a bodhisattva seated among them named King Flower-Light Great Wisdom Radiance Bodhisattva.
Rising from his seat, he addressed Vairocana Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One!"

The Buddha has briefly expounded above the characteristics and aspects of the ten stages of setting forth (*prasthāna*), the ten stages of nurturing (*puṣṭi*), the ten adamantine stages (*vajra-bhūmi*), and the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Within each of these meanings, they are not yet fully understood; we only pray that you will explain them, we only pray that you will explain them.
This has already been clarified within the "Chapter on the Hundred Contemplations of the Tathāgata" in the *Sūtra of the Supreme and Ultimate Adamantine Treasure-Treasury of All-Knowledge*.
That the Bodhisattva initiates the inquiry within the great assemblies of all Buddhas is precisely because he belongs to the specific capacity of those to be taught.
"Flower-Light King" (Huaguangwang) signifies the meaning of being the master of flower-light; "Great Wisdom Radiance" (Dazhiming) signifies the meaning of profound penetration.

In the preceding text, the emission of light to gather the assembly represents the arising of wondrous practice from fundamental wisdom; therefore, he is named the Master of Profound Penetration and Flower-Light.

This text addresses the meaning of practice and cultivation, indicating that by relying on sublime conduct one proceeds toward Great Enlightenment; therefore, it is titled "The King of Flower Radiance, the Great Wisdom Light.
△ Second, Śākyamuni’s detailed response has four parts: first, clarifying the ten stages of setting forth; second, clarifying the ten stages of nurturing; third, clarifying... [text continues].

The Ten Vajras. The Four Clarifications explain the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). Regarding the first three [of the four], the first is a general inquiry, the second is a detailed explanation, and the third is a concluding reference. Now, for the first:
At that time, Vairocana Buddha said, "O Thousand Buddhas, listen attentively! As for what you previously asked regarding the meaning of 'setting forth' (*prasthāna*):"
As for the section on the "Middle": the reason for addressing only the thousand Buddhas is that this is the unsurpassed Dharma-gate originally practiced by the Tathāgata;
therefore, he causes the thousand Buddhas to successively transmit it to one another. The meaning of "setting out" (*prasthāna*) is briefly explained as before. This [refers to] the ten *pāramitās*.
Honey. The mind and mind are developed and opened, tending toward the True Path; this is called the "Ten Tendencies" (*daśa-prasthāna*).

Specifically, one mind corresponds to one dwelling (*vihāra*); in the perfect sense, one dwells upon and cultivates this mind at every stage, until it reaches fulfillment in the Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*).
Now, for the sake of convenience, I shall provide an explanation based on the entry from the conventional into emptiness (*śūnyatā*). For those of sharp faculties, having already seen emptiness—
One also perceives non-emptiness. Because one perceives non-emptiness, one develops the aspiration to realize the wondrous True Truth (*tattva*).

This truth is itself the Middle Way and is also itself the Conventional. The three truths are perfectly interfused and inconceivable. Within a single mind are all minds; within all minds is a single mind.
This principle is revealed in each of the ten sections of this text; readers must awaken to it well.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the ten [stages], from the first, the Mind of Renunciation, to the tenth, the Mind of the Summit. Now, the first:
O Sons of the Buddha, one renounces everything—kingdoms, cities, towns, fields, houses, gold, silver, bright pearls, sons, daughters, and even one’s own body.
All conditioned things are entirely relinquished; the unconditioned is signless. The notions of self, person, knower, and viewer are merely provisional aggregations.
The agent who constructs the view of self [is absent]; the twelve links of dependent origination have no union and no dispersal, and there is no experiencer.

The twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the five aggregates—all these aspects of a unified whole—are devoid of the marks of self or what belongs to self; all phenomena are provisionally established. Whether internal...
Regarding all phenomena and all external phenomena, neither abandoning nor grasping them, the bodhisattva at that time is said to have the contemplation of the illusory assembly manifest before him;
thus, with a mind of relinquishment, he enters the samādhi of emptiness.
"Those who are sons of the Buddha" are so named because they succeed to the family enterprise of the Buddha and shall tread the path to the Buddha’s station.

"Relinquishing everything" is a general heading for the cultivation of relinquishment (*tyāga*); it refers to relinquishing internal and external things, even unto relinquishing attachment to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*).

Regarding "kingdoms" and below, he first clarifies the relinquishing of internal and external things; regarding "unconditioned" and below, he next clarifies the relinquishing of attachment to self and phenomena, meaning that one should simply contemplate...
The principle of the unconditioned and signless is to thoroughly understand that all notions of self, person, knowledge, and views are merely provisional aggregations.
Those non-Buddhists falsely reckon in a sovereign creator, an agent, and the view of a spiritual self (*pudgala*);

even the two vehicles falsely reckon in the twelve links of dependent origination as real dharmas. In reality, these conditions do not truly conjoin; dependent origination itself is without conjunction.
Even in cessation there is no dispersal, nor is there anyone who undergoes union or dispersal.

Generally speaking, all phenomena such as the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*)—which ordinary beings conceive of as a unified whole—are fundamentally devoid of the characteristics of a self or what belongs to a self;
they are merely dharmas established through conventional designation. Therefore, if one [examines] all internal [phenomena]...
Regarding phenomena: all external phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, and thus there is no need to abandon them; they are fundamentally non-existent, and thus they cannot be accepted.

This is the transition from the conventional to the empty, termed "contemplation in accord with the conventional. When this contemplation manifests before one, one spontaneously enters the Samādhi of Emptiness.

This may also be specifically correlated with the Stage of Arousing the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*); because one discards delusion, it is called the "mind of relinquishment," and because one gives rise to the Real...

Therefore, it is called the Stage of Resolving the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*). Furthermore, "arousing the truth" (*satya-utpāda*) carries the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*vyatireka*), while "arousing within" (*madhya-utpāda*) carries the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*).

"Not accepting any phenomena" (*sarva-dharma-anupādāna*) is the negation of the conventional while illuminating the true; "not abandoning any phenomena" (*sarva-dharma-aparityāga*) is the negation of the true while illuminating the conventional.

Moreover, "not accepting" is the simultaneous negation of both, and "not abandoning" is the simultaneous illumination of both. This simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination constitutes the Middle Way in its full clarity.
However. △ Second, the Mind of Precepts.

If, O Sons of the Buddha, precepts were not non-precepts, there would be no one who receives them; the ten wholesome precepts would have no teacher to preach them, and [one would merely] deceive and steal.

Up to and including wrong views: the absence of accumulation consists of kindness, goodness, purity, uprightness, correctness, reality, right view, equanimity, joy, and so forth. These are the essential natures of the ten precepts.
They restrain the eight inversions; they are free from all [defiled] natures; they are the single path of purity.
The single character "precept" (*śīla*) designates the essence of non-action (*avijñapti*). This precept of non-action eternally transcends the two extremes and accords with the Middle Way.
The phrase "not [mere] precepts" clarifies first the transcendence of existence (*bhava*). The phrase "benevolent and kind" clarifies next the transcendence of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

The phrase "restraining and controlling" concludes by clarifying its virtuous function. Regarding "not [mere] precepts": this refers to the heterodox precepts of external paths (*tīrthika*) and the precepts maintained by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who grasp at signs; though these are wholesome...
These various forms of misconduct are all not the correct gateway for entering the Path; therefore, they are called "non-precepts" (*aśīla*).
Now, the essence of the Bodhisattva precepts is not the same as the non-precepts of ordinary worldlings or outsiders, because it thoroughly realizes that there is no recipient [of the precepts].

Although this Dharma of the ten wholesome precepts has been transmitted from teacher to teacher, in reality, there is no teacher who can speak this Dharma. That which is called the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) is [merely a designation].
Is it the precepts? Is it the *ācārya* who is the precepts? Or even the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* that is the precepts?
Furthermore, those ten unwholesome dharmas, such as deceit and theft which are the opposites [of the precepts], are likewise fundamentally without accumulation.

These unwholesome dharmas do not arise of themselves, do not arise from another, do not arise from both together, and do not arise without cause. Moreover, when they have not yet arisen, they have no place of storage; yet when they wish to arise...
It has no place from which it comes; in its very arising, it has no place where it abides; once arisen, it has no place to which it goes. Thus, the *dharmatā* is fundamentally free from defilement.
Yet, within this *dharmatā*, there are inherently present all the virtues of nature, such as benevolence (*maitrī*) and goodness (*śubha*), which constitute the essential nature of the ten precepts.
That is to say: benevolence is the essential nature of the precept against killing; goodness is the essential nature of the precept against stealing; purity is...
Non-lust is the essential nature of non-duality; straightforwardness is the essential nature of non-divisive speech; correctness is the essential nature of non-abusive speech;
truthfulness is the essential nature of non-falsehood and non-frivolous speech; right view is the essential nature of non-delusion;
relinquishment is the essential nature of non-greed; and joy is the essential nature of non-anger. That which restrains the eight inversions is the state of being free from all inherent natures.
This is the absence of sensation up to the absence of origination. It can suppress the four inversions of ordinary beings and non-Buddhists;
it is the single path of purity, which is the essential nature of benevolence and goodness. It can suppress the four inversions of the two vehicles.

For ordinary beings and non-Buddhists, regardless of whether they observe unwholesome or wholesome precepts, all give rise to grasping and attachment: they reckon the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, and the non-self as self.

They cling to a self and, regarding the impure as pure, thus bring about the causes and effects of outflows (*sāsrava*). Although the followers of the Two Vehicles have realized the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*), they do not penetrate the essence of the nature;
they constantly take the permanent to be impermanent, pleasure to be suffering, the self to be non-self, and the pure to be impure.

Therefore, at the time of entering *nirvāṇa*, the precepts and virtues are accordingly abandoned. In the Mahāyāna, cultivation arises from the nature (*prakṛti*); the entirety of cultivation resides within the nature.
It takes the qualities of the nature as its foundational substance and takes non-conceptual form (*akṛtakarūpa*) as its essential body.

From the initial reception [of the precepts] up to the attainment of the Buddha-body, they are neither destroyed nor lost; one spontaneously ceases evil and practices good. The qualities of the nature are themselves the *dharmakāya*. There is no...

The manifestation of form (*rūpakāya*) is the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is the ultimate form of all Buddhas. Within the context of the moral discipline (*vinaya*), there is inherently the principle of gathering sentient beings;
this refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sāmbhogakāya*. Furthermore, this mind of preceptual restraint can also serve as a specific antidote for those abiding on the stages (*bhūmi*).
Here, the "stages" are that which is to be remedied, while the precepts are the remedy.
△ Third, the Mind of Patience.
O Disciples of the Buddha, patience possesses the essence-nature of the wisdom of signlessness. All things are empty; this is the patience of emptiness.

The patience toward all places is called the patience of the practice of non-arising. Attaining it in all places is called the patience regarding suffering as such. Each and every one of the immeasurable practices is named patience. There is none.

There is no receiving of blows, nor of staffs or weapons; all states of anger are simply suchness (*tathatā*). There is not even a single truth, nor a single mark (*lakṣaṇa*), nor the absence of marks, nor the presence of the mark of non-existence, nor that which is not the mark of mind.
It is the mark of the unconditioned object; it is established, abiding, moving, and ceasing; it is self and person; it is bondage and liberation.
The suchness of all phenomena is the characteristic of patience, which is ungraspable.

That which has the nature of wisdom characterized by existence and non-existence refers to the three patiences of a bodhisattva; all of these take the wisdom of signlessness as their essential nature.
Below, the three patiences are explained individually, elucidated in terms of the objects of the three types of suffering. One contemplates all suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

Knowing that all are fundamentally empty is called the patience of emptiness (*śūnyatā-kṣānti*). Contemplating that the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) in all places is fundamentally non-arising is called the patience of the practice of non-arising (*anutpāda-pratipatti-kṣānti*).

Contemplating the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) in all places, attaining its true characteristic, and knowing it to be the Dharma-body is called the patience of suchness-suffering (*tathatā-duḥkha-kṣānti*).
Without the power of these three patiences, none of the various gates of practice will be accomplished; therefore, [they are essential].
"Each practice of the measure is called 'patience' (kṣānti). This summarizes the preceding text. Below, the three types of patience and their contemplative wisdom are further elucidated:

by contemplating the realm of the suffering of disintegration with true insight, one realizes that internally there is no self that can receive [suffering], and externally there is no person who can inflict it.
In the interim, there is no use for weapons or staves; therefore, the mind of anger remains as unmoving as the principle of suchness (*tathatā*).

This is why it is called "patience in emptiness" (*śūnyatākṣānti*). By contemplating the realm of conditioned suffering (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) with precision, one realizes that there are no distinct truths such as suffering or its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), but only a single, true reality. Although there are no individual [distinctions],...
It is the truth. Furthermore, there is neither the signless nor non-signlessness. Although there is the single mark of reality, it is also without marks.

It is neither the mark of mind nor the mark of non-mind; it is neither the mark of the conditioned nor the mark of the unconditioned. This is called the patience regarding the practice of non-arising.
By observing with truth the realm of suffering, one thoroughly understands whether it is established, abiding, moving, or ceasing.
Whether it be self or person, bondage or liberation, all phenomena are, in their very essence, suchness (*tathatā*).
If all things are suchness, then even the characteristic of patience cannot be apprehended; this is called "patience regarding suffering as suchness" (*duḥkha-tathatā-kṣānti*).

That all phenomena are suchness is precisely what was referred to in the preceding passage as "attaining [the Dharma] in all places. These three types of suffering arise from the three kinds of sensation (*vedanā*). If they are correlated individually:

Regarding this: pleasant feeling is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); painful feeling is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
If discussed generally, all three feelings are the suffering of change, because they must inevitably undergo transformation and decay.

All three feelings are the suffering of conditioned formations, because their nature is that of flux and volitional construction. All three feelings are the suffering of suffering, because they are the unwholesome phenomena of birth and death. This may also be explained differently.
For those who dwell in cultivation, they practice immeasurable deeds by means of the power of the three kinds of patience.
△ Fourth, advancing the mind:

O Sons of the Buddha, if one practices at all times throughout the four modes of deportment, subduing the empty and the provisional to realize the dharma-nature, one ascends to the stage of non-arising.

Mounting the mountain, one perceives all that exists and does not exist as being both existent and non-existent. One enters into the blue, yellow, red, and white of heaven and earth, and even into the wisdom-nature of the Triple Gem, having full faith in them.
Advancing upon the path of emptiness, non-arising, and non-action, there is no [discriminating] wisdom; yet arising from emptiness, one enters the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise non-dual. With a mind of continuous emptiness, one thoroughly penetrates and advances through the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
This is signless diligence (*animitta-vīrya*), which is constant and uninterrupted, regardless of whether one is walking or sitting; therefore, it is called "practice at all times.

What kind of dharma is practiced? It refers to the constant cultivation and mastery of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), and the contemplation of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-vipaśyanā*).

By the power of these three contemplations, one is able to ascend the mountain of non-arising (*anutpāda*) and perceive all dharmas, whether existent or non-existent; even existence is thus *tathatā*.

Non-existence is also suchness (*tathatā*). Because it does not turn its back on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in its entirety, one has faith that all worldly phenomena, such as heaven and earth, and all supramundane phenomena, such as the Three Jewels, are entirely suchness. Thus, within these very mundane and supramundane phenomena, one cultivates and advances upon the Path;
this is in accord with the three gates of liberation: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

It is thus associated; furthermore, there is no wisdom of the three liberations to be attained. Even when one gives rise to the contemplation of true emptiness and enters the dharmas of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), these are non-dual with the dharma of emptiness.
It is solely by means of the continuous contemplation of true emptiness that one penetrates and advances in the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
This is called signless true diligence (*animitta-bhūta-vīrya*). This may also be specifically correlated with those abiding in the Stage of Noble Birth (*janma-kula-sthiti*).
Ascending the Mountain of Non-arising is precisely entering the lineage of the Tathāgata.
△ Fifth, the Settled Mind:
O Disciples of the Buddha, [this is] quiescent extinction, signlessness, signless immeasurable practice, and immeasurable mind-samādhi. Whether ordinary person or sage...

There is no person who does not enter into resonance with the essential nature of samādhi. Because all things are sustained by the power of meditative concentration, the views of self, person, agent, and experiencer—all such fetters—are the causes and conditions for obstruction.
The wind of distraction agitates the mind; it is through non-quiescence that [falsehoods] are extinguished. The eight inversions are empty and empty.
Through objectless, provisional stillness and wisdom, one contemplates all provisional gatherings; in every thought-moment, they are quiescent and extinguished. All three...
The realms, fruits, and the nature of offenses are all extinguished through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and from it, all that is wholesome arises.
"Quiescence and signlessness" (*śānta-nimitta*) defines the essence of concentration. Following "signlessness," it first clarifies that concentration can produce the wholesome;

following "all," it next clarifies that concentration can extinguish offenses; and with "objectless" (*anālambana*), it concludes by demonstrating the functional power of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*). First, it clarifies production.
"Virtuous one," he said, "although this samādhi is signless (*animitta*), it is able to encompass immeasurable practices, namely the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
All ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*) alike enter into correspondence with this samādhi.
Because of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it bestows holy bliss upon all; because of great compassion (*karuṇā*), it uproots all suffering of ordinary beings. Because of great...

Because of joy (*muditā*), one gives rise to celebration and delight toward all ordinary beings and noble ones alike. Because of great equanimity (*upekṣā*), the mind is non-dual toward all ordinary beings and noble ones alike.
Furthermore, these four immeasurable concentrations (*apramāṇa-samādhi*) are certainly cultivated in common by the noble ones of the three vehicles.

All ordinary beings have also previously realized this. At the time when the kalpa comes to an end and the calamities of fire, water, and wind are about to arise, all sentient beings naturally achieve this samādhi, as they are born into the realm of the fourth dhyāna. Next, to clarify the eradication of offenses:
it refers to all attachments to the notions of self and person, the nature of false views, and whatever constitutes the causes and conditions that obstruct the Path.

Scattered winds stir the mind; yet by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), all these do not require deliberate effort to seek stillness, for they are naturally and eternally extinguished.
Because they are extinguished, the four inversions of ordinary beings are empty; because they are extinguished without being stilled, the four inversions of the two vehicles are also empty.
Next, to summarize and demonstrate its efficacy: it is said that by employing this non-referential, provisional wisdom of stillness, one contemplates all provisional assemblies.

All phenomena are, in every moment of thought, quiescent and extinguished. Therefore, the fruits of suffering within the triple world, as well as the nature of their offenses, are all extinguished through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Once the nature of the offense is extinguished, it is the natural law that one gives rise to all virtues, such as compassion.
"Quiescent wisdom" refers to *dhyāna*; its Sanskrit name is *dhyāna*. "Without conditions or designations" means that all things are merely provisional designations.

They are called "all phenomena" (*dharmas*). In their essential nature, they are entirely empty; fundamentally, there is nothing that can serve as an object of cognition. Now, one realizes that these provisional phenomena are empty in their very nature.

Therefore, this is called "non-objectifying provisional quiescent wisdom. This concentrated mind may also be specifically correlated with the "abiding in the fulfillment of skillful means," which is the essential nature of *samādhi*.
