In this state, ordinary beings and sages are without exception in mutual correspondence, just as when a fetus has fully formed, its human characteristics are complete and lacking nothing.

△ Sixth, the Mind of Wisdom. O Disciples of the Buddha! The wisdom of emptiness is not without an object. Knowing the substance is what is called "mind. It discriminates all dharmas as provisional names and designates a master.

It is identical with the Way; it takes the fruit while practicing the cause; it enters the state of the sages and abandons that of the ordinary; it extinguishes offenses and gives rise to merit; and it brings to an end both bondage and liberation.

This is the functional nature of the essence. Because all views of permanence, bliss, self, and purity obscure the afflictions and the nature of wisdom is not luminous, one takes wisdom as the primary focus.
One cultivates the ineffable contemplative wisdom and enters the Middle Way of the Single Truth.

That ignorance which obstructs wisdom is neither a characteristic, nor something that comes, nor a condition, nor a transgression, nor the eight inversions; it is without arising or cessation. The radiant flame of the light of wisdom shines upon this, bringing joy.
"Empty expedient means" refers to the transformative supernormal powers, which constitute the function of wisdom (prajñā) based on the essential nature of gnosis.
"Empty wisdom" indicates the essence of the true wisdom of the ultimate emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā).

This wondrous wisdom is not the same as the mere non-objectification of the "emptiness of annihilation" (uccheda-śūnyatā) of the two vehicles; one should know that it is the very essence of numinous awareness. Furthermore...
This is called the True Mind. Externalists are deluded regarding this true essence, and thus they conceptually differentiate all phenomena, positing a provisional "master" as their lord.
Yet even the evil wisdom of these externalists is fundamentally identical to the path of awakening. Those of the Two Vehicles do not understand this essence;

therefore, they merely take the fruit while practicing the cause, entering the state of a sage by abandoning the state of an ordinary person, extinguishing sins and generating merit—all of which constitute fetters and attachments.
All of these have been completely understood and exhausted. Nevertheless, even this specialized wisdom of the two vehicles is a functional manifestation of this very essence.

It is only because the wisdom-nature of those non-Buddhists and followers of the two vehicles is not clear regarding all phenomena—such as omniscience, vision, permanence, bliss, self, purity, and the afflictions—that they either give rise to attachment or desire to abandon them. Therefore, now...

Taking wisdom as the foremost, one cultivates ineffable contemplative wisdom. This simultaneously shatters the two attachments and illuminates the two principles, entering the Middle Way of the Single Truth.

Once the Middle Way is revealed, one finally realizes that the ignorance which obstructs wisdom is fundamentally without characteristics, has no place of origin, possesses no causal conditions for birth, and carries no karmic burden; it is fundamentally not among the eight inversions.
Originally there is neither arising nor ceasing; therefore, the blazing flame of wisdom alone shines forth brilliantly.

According to the inclinations of beings, it is empty, harmonious, and unimpeded, giving rise to various skillful means. Through manifold transformations and supernatural powers, it guides and transforms all conscious beings.

All of these are brought about by the essential nature of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), for wisdom is its very function. This may also be correlated specifically with the "Abiding in the Right Mind" (*samyak-citta-vihāra*):

upon entering the Middle Way of the Single Truth (*ekasatya*), one’s appearance becomes like that of a Buddha; through delighting in skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), the characteristics of the mind likewise become identical [to those of a Buddha].
△ The Seventh: The Mind of Vows.
O Disciples of the Buddha, there are vows and vows; great seeking, universal seeking. Because one takes the fruit as the cause, the mind of vows is continuous.

This continuity of the mind of vows persists for a hundred kalpas, whereby one attains Buddhahood and extinguishes transgressions. Seeking and seeking with a sincere heart, non-arising, emptiness, and oneness—the vow is to contemplate and contemplate.

Entering meditative concentration, one illuminates the immeasurable bonds of views; by seeking the mind, one attains liberation. Through immeasurable sublime practices, one seeks the mind to achieve Bodhi.

Immeasurable merit takes this seeking as its foundation: with the initial arousal of the seeking mind, one cultivates the path in the interim, and because the practice fulfills the vow, the fruit of Buddhahood is realized.
One contemplates the Middle Way within the Single Truth, which is neither the aggregates, nor the elements, nor the view of extinction and birth.
It is seeing; it is not the wisdom of analytical understanding. It is the essential nature of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) and the source of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Regarding "aspiration upon aspiration": it follows the number of aspirations made, being repeatedly inexhaustible rather than ceasing after a single utterance. It is the great seeking.
It is solely for the sake of Bodhi; one does not turn toward the Two Vehicles, nor toward the three realms of existence (*trabhava*).
All who seek it have a mind without limit or measure, never abandoning a single dharma. Because one practices the cause by means of the fruit, the vow-mind is continuous;

first one realizes the principle that the Buddha, sentient beings, and the mind are non-differentiated in their threefold nature, and thus one practices the wondrous cause in accordance with the nature of the realized fruit. Therefore...

The great vows one has made shall continue in succession without interruption and never be subject to retreat or regret. Even for as long as a hundred kalpas, they will be just like the original practices cultivated by Śākyamuni;
thus, the path of enlightenment will surely be brought to ultimate completion, and the extinction of transgressions will surely be achieved without remainder.
People say that the mind of seeking through vows belongs to distraction and agitation, yet they do not realize that such seeking must reach the point of utmost sincerity.
This is because it is identical to non-arising emptiness. That is to say, when taking and rejecting reach their ultimate limit, they are not on a different track from non-taking and non-rejecting.
Therefore, when cultivating this vow, every contemplation enters right concentration, illuminating the Buddha-dharma.
Next, to further clarify the attainment of Buddhahood and the eradication of offenses: all immeasurable bonds of views are liberated precisely because of the seeking mind.
Immeasurable wondrous practices are all accomplished through the mind of seeking; immeasurable merits are all rooted in this mind of seeking.
Therefore, one first gives rise to the mind of seeking, then cultivates the path in the interim, fulfilling one's vows through practice.

It is simply by fulfilling one's practice that the vows are realized, and thus the fruit of Buddhahood is attained. If there is no mind of seeking, it is like carrying hemp while discarding gold; how could one then be liberated from the bonds of views?

If one’s vows are inferior, like a mere purple light, how could they accomplish the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*)? If one merely contemplates the three gates of liberation, how could one delight in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*)?
Next, I shall further clarify the contemplation that enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), namely, contemplating the Middle Way within the Single Truth. It is not...
The aggregates (skandhas) are not realms (dhātus), nor are they the views of one who has extinguished the view of arising; they are not the wisdom of liberation of the two vehicles.
One should know that this vow is the very essence of the Middle Way and the source of all practices. As for "the views of extinguishing and arising":
When there is cessation, there is no seeing; when there is arising, there is seeing. This may also be applied specifically to those who dwell in the stage of non-retrogression.
Because their vows are linked one after another, their body and mind increase and flourish day by day.
△ 8. Protecting the Mind.
O Disciples of the Buddha! One should protect the Three Jewels and protect the merit of all practices, so that the eight inversions and evil heterodox views of outsiders do not disturb right faith.

One must extinguish the fetters of self and the fetters of views, realize the two truths through the illumination of non-arising, and bring the contemplation of the mind before oneself. By means of this—

Protecting the root, one protects the signless; protecting emptiness, one protects the wishless and the signless. Through the continuity of mind and wisdom, one enters the path of non-arising and emptiness.
The path of wisdom is entirely luminous and radiant. With luminous radiance, one protects contemplation and enters into the emptiness of the provisional, which is a gradual illusory transformation.

The arising of this illusory transformation is like non-arising; it is a dharma-body that is non-existent. Its gathering and dispersal cannot be protected against; the observation of dharmas is likewise so.
This is precisely the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*). To protect the Three Jewels means not to be disturbed by the heterodox views and four inversions of the non-Buddhists.
To protect the merit of all practices means not to be disturbed by the partial emptiness and four inversions of the two vehicles.
Therefore, regarding the Buddha-way, one possesses perfect right faith, which can extinguish the dual attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

Through the wisdom of the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-vipaśyanā-prajñā*), one illuminates and penetrates the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—causing the mind of contemplation to be constantly present before one.

This wondrous protection of the mind is called the fundamental protection of signlessness (*animitta-mūla-rakṣā*). By means of this very protection of the fundamental signlessness, one protects emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The three gates of liberation—non-arising, signlessness, and wishlessness—proceed from the wisdom within this mind.

When these are linked together without interruption, one is able to realize and enter the path of non-arising emptiness, causing both the observing wisdom and the observed path of non-arising emptiness to become entirely radiant and luminous.
Furthermore, by means of this luminous path of wisdom, one protects and sustains the observing wisdom and enters into...

Regarding the two objects of emptiness and conventionality: within each and every illusory phenomenon, one thoroughly knows that all that arises through illusion is non-existent, meaning they are all identical to the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
This essence of non-existence neither accumulates nor disperses; whether accumulating or dispersing, it cannot be apprehended or protected. Since the object to be protected does not exist...
If [anything] were obtainable, then the contemplation of the Dharma that protects it would likewise be unobtainable.

Since both the protector and the protected are unobtainable, this is called the fundamental protection of signlessness (*animitta*). If even the slightest dharma were obtainable, one would be afflicted by the eight inversions (*aṣṭaviparyāsa*).
This may also be applied specifically to those dwelling in the stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūta*), because through such excellent protection, they are free from [inversion].
Free from all faults, fully endowed with spiritual marks.
△ Ninth, the Mind of Joy.
O disciples of the Buddha, when you see others obtain happiness, you should always give rise to joy; extend this to all things, using the provisional to illuminate the empty and the quiescent.

Yet one does not enter into the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). It is not that there is no profound, tranquil great bliss; there is no union with sensation, yet one transforms the phenomena of existence. One perceives them as provisional.

With the single contemplation of the equality of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the mind-moments proceed through extensive learning. All the meritorious virtues of the Buddhas' conduct consist of signless joy and wisdom;
from the arising of such a mind, one gives rise to mindfulness and serenely illuminates the joyful mind, taking all phenomena as its object.

This is precisely the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*). Because one skillfully understands the expedient means of the same essence, one not only cultivates merit oneself to benefit sentient beings, but also constantly gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) whenever one sees others attain worldly or supramundane happiness;
and by means of this merit of sympathetic joy, one is further able to universally gladden all beings.
To cut through all things: it is because that which is provisional is itself emptiness, and that which is illumination is itself stillness.

Thus, although one does not enter into conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there is nonetheless the great bliss of the quiescent *dharmatā*. Because one does not enter into the conditioned, there is no conjunction.
Because great bliss is not non-existent, there is sensation; because there is no union, phenomena are manifested to cause one to forget their marks.
Because there is sensation, they are seen as provisional, thereby allowing each other to benefit.
This is precisely the contemplation that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are fundamentally equal and of one essence within the dharma-nature; thus, these skillful means are accomplished.
This bodhisattva who cultivates skillful means practices with every thought upon extensive learning, causing contemplative wisdom to increase and become increasingly clear.

Even regarding the meritorious deeds and practices of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they employ the wisdom and skillful means of signless rejoicing (*anumodanā*) to gather these into the present within every moment of thought. Through the mindfulness of rejoicing in the Dharma, they constantly abide in this tranquility.
The mind that illuminates joy universally takes all phenomena throughout the entire dharma-realm as its object, causing them to serve as mutual adornments in an infinitely layered manner.
This is the joyful bliss within the dharma-realm being universally bestowed back upon the sentient beings of the dharma-realm; it is what is meant by "giving without waste.
It may also be correlated specifically with the stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarāja-putra-vihāra*), wherein skillful means are most subtle and refined.
Because it is wondrous.
△ Tenth, the Heart-Crown:
O Son of the Buddha, this is the person of supreme wisdom, who extinguishes the wheel of non-self, views of the body, doubt, and all anger, etc. As...

The summit and the connection are observed as one; the connection is like the summit. Within the *dharmadhātu*, cause and effect are a single path of suchness (*tathatā*), most supreme and superior like a summit.

Like the crown of a person’s head, it is not a view of selfhood (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), nor among the sixty-two views. Regarding the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there is no self (*ātman*) or master that moves, turns, bends, or stretches.

There is nothing that can be grasped or bound, whether in sensation (*vedanā*) or mental formations (*saṃskāra*). At that time, this person enters and encounters internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).

The Way: Mind-moment after mind-moment, sentient beings do not perceive conditions, nor do they perceive non-conditions. Abiding in the Samādhi of the Summit, they issue forth from the concentration of quiescent extinction and proceed toward the Way.
The nature of reality is that the self, persons, and the eight inversions arise from conditions; yet through the Dharma-gate of non-duality, one does not undergo the eight hardships.
Ultimately, the fruits of illusion are never received. There is only the single sentient being coming and going, sitting and standing, practicing to extinguish transgressions.
Eliminating the ten evils and giving rise to the ten virtues, one enters the Way through right personhood, right wisdom, and right practice.

When the Bodhisattva’s penetrating insight manifests before them, they no longer receive the fruits of the six realms of existence; they will certainly never retreat from the Buddha-nature and will enter the family of Buddhas in every lifetime, never departing from right faith.

This is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*). By means of discerning wisdom, one universally knows all phenomena and thoroughly masters the *dharmadhātu*, the suchness (*tathatā*), and the summit-dharma (*mūrdha-dharma*);

this is called supreme wisdom. This wisdom is capable of universally extinguishing all latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), whether dull or sharp—namely, the wheel of self, views, doubt, the body, and all forms of anger—and it enables the wisdom of the "summit-view" to remain continuous and uninterrupted.
Severance arises from the continuous connection of this contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), because one contemplates the "Dharma like the crown of the head" (*mūrdha-dharma*).
One thoroughly understands that within the *dharmadhātu*, whether cause or fruit, all are the single path of suchness (*tathatā*); there is no second suchness.

Therefore, this is called the "most supreme and superior Dharma like the crown of the head," just like the crown-mark of a person. Although it is metaphorically compared to a person's crown, in reality...
It is not the view of a non-self, nor can it be seen through the sixty-two views. It is not a phenomenon subject to the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates.
It is not the "self" or "master" imagined by non-Buddhists as that which moves, turns, bends, and stretches.

Furthermore, it does not itself receive any phenomena, nor is there any characteristic of activity to be found. Since it is the foremost right reception (*samyaksamādhi*), it is beyond the sphere of mental activity.
It is extinguished. Furthermore, how could it be grasped or bound? Regarding the term "non-view of self" (*asatkāyadṛṣṭi*): the upper character "non" (*a-*) is a word of negation or exclusion;

the lower character "non" (*-sat*) joins with the character "body" (*kāya*) to form the meaning. This means that ordinary people and non-Buddhists falsely conceive of what is not the body as being the body; therefore, it is called the "view of non-body.
Alternatively, one might suspect that the character "non" is redundant, yet this interpretation remains valid. At that time, such a person has already realized the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).
The Dharma extinguishes the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), up to the point where there is neither feeling nor volitional formations;
one then enters the samādhi of internal emptiness and personally encounters the Path, which is called the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).

At this time, although every moment of mind takes the liberation of sentient beings as its task, one perceives neither the characteristic of an object of conditions nor the characteristic of non-conditions. Abiding within this Samādhi of the Summit (mūrdhan-samādhi), from stillness...
They initiate sublime conduct through the meditative absorption of cessation and advance toward the Buddha-way.

All the views of substantiality, selfhood, personhood, and eternalism held by non-Buddhists, as well as the conditions for the arising of the eight inversions and so forth, all enter the gate of non-duality.

This is what is meant by "walking upon what is not the path" to attain mastery of the Buddha-way; thus, they do not undergo the retribution of wrong views or the eight difficult states, nor do they remain within the three realms.

All fruits of retribution produced by illusion are likewise ultimately not experienced. Since there is neither self nor person, and no one to receive the fruit, who is it that practices to achieve the Buddha-way?
There is only a collection of dharmas consisting of the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors, conventionally designated as "sentient beings.
They come and go, sit and stand; they are neither annihilated nor eternal, unfolding according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

The continuity of rebirth is transformed. One practices the extinction of offenses, eliminates evil and gives rise to goodness, enters the right path, and realizes the Dharma of right patience and right wisdom.
One initiates right practice; at that time, the Bodhisattva’s penetrating contemplative wisdom is constantly present before them.
Having no longer received the tainted fruits of the six realms of existence, they likewise do not regress from the Buddha-lineage.
They fall not into the stages of the two vehicles; in birth after birth they enter the family of the Buddhas and never again depart from right faith.
This may also be correlated specifically with the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka), because they abide in the samādhi of the summit.
△ Third, the summary reference.
This was explained extensively in the preceding "Chapter on the Ten Radiant Lights.
△ Second, clarifying the ten modes of nurturing. Part three: first, the general inquiry; second, the detailed explanation; third, the summary reference. Now, the first [the general inquiry]:
Vairocana Buddha said: "O thousand Buddhas, listen attentively. Regarding that which you previously asked about the ten nourishing minds (*daśa-poṣaṇa-citta*):

the four immeasurable concentrations (*catur-apramāṇa-samādhi*), the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni*), and wisdom are most capable of increasing the Buddha-way and nurturing sentient beings;
these are called the ten nourishing minds. Individually, each mind corresponds to a single practice; collectively, this mind is fully cultivated at every stage."

This mind is fulfilled even unto the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Now, for the sake of convenience in explaining the meaning, I shall provisionally base this interpretation on the entry from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) into the provisional (*prajñapti*).
Since the two truths are equal, the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) naturally manifests in its full perfection.

Furthermore, the Four Noble Truths are not devoid of contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*), and the Four Means of Attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*) are not devoid of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); yet, to categorize them now by assigning one to concentration and the other to wisdom is merely a conventional way of speaking.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the ten [minds]. First, the mind of loving-kindness (up to) the tenth, the mind of wisdom. Now, the first:

O Son of the Buddha, one should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness. Having generated the causes of happiness, one enters the Dharma through contemplation conjoined with joy within the wisdom of non-self.
Within the great dharmas of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is no arising, no abiding, and no cessation; they are like illusions and...
Transformation. Because suchness is non-dual, all spiritual practices constitute the Wheel of Dharma. This transformation pervades all beings and is able to engender right faith;
it does not follow the teachings of Māra and can also cause all sentient beings to attain the fruit of compassionate joy. It is neither real, nor is it the fruit of good or evil.
It is the samādhi that realizes the empty nature of reality.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has the meaning of bestowing happiness; therefore, one should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, which is able to produce the causes of happiness.
However, if it is not associated with the wisdom of non-self (*anātma-jñāna*), it merely belongs to emotional attachment.

Thus, one must enter into all phenomena through the contemplation associated with happiness within the wisdom of non-self—namely, by contemplating the great dharmas such as sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
All things are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way. Being without birth, abiding, or cessation is emptiness;
being like an illusion or a transformation is provisional existence; being suchness without duality is the Middle Way.

When all such practices are fulfilled in this manner, one accomplishes the Wheel of Dharma and brings transformation to all beings, enabling all sentient beings to give rise to right faith, never falling under the influence of Māra.
This teaching establishes the causes of bliss and enables all sentient beings to attain the fruit of ultimate compassionate joy.
This fruit of compassionate joy is not the verified cessation (*nirodha*) realized by the followers of the Two Vehicles, nor is it the retribution of worldly good or evil;
rather, it is the great Dharma-bliss of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which is the samādhi that realizes the essential nature of emptiness.
[The character] "er" (ear). This may also be applied individually to those who practice with joy; that it transforms and benefits all beings is the meaning of "accordance with the ten directions.
△ Second, the mind of compassion.
O disciples of the Buddha: with compassion that is empty, void, and signless, one practices the path by taking sentient beings as the object of compassion.

One personally extinguishes all suffering and gives rise to wisdom amidst the immeasurable sufferings of all sentient beings. Taking non-killing as the condition, taking the dharma of non-killing as the condition, and taking non-attachment to self as the condition, one constantly practices non-killing, non-stealing, and non-lust. Thus, one does not afflict any sentient being and brings forth bodhicitta.
As for the mind: within emptiness, one perceives all phenomena as they truly are. Within the conduct of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), one gives rise to the mind of the wisdom of the Path.

Toward the six types of kin and the six types of enemies—within these three categories of kin and enemies—one bestows the wisdom of supreme bliss. Amidst the conditions of supreme enmity, one attains the fruit of bliss in nine grades.
When emptiness manifests, one views oneself and all other sentient beings with equal, singular bliss, and gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Regarding "compassion that is empty, empty, and signless": one thoroughly understands that the essence of great compassion is fundamentally empty, empty, and signless.
Now, desiring to realize this essence, one practices the path of a bodhisattva by taking compassion as an object;

first, one extinguishes all causes of suffering within oneself, and subsequently, amidst the immeasurable sufferings of all sentient beings, one gives rise to the wisdom of rescue and deliverance. Even if [one were to] oneself...
As long as one’s own body has not yet escaped the wheel of suffering, how could one extensively deliver all beings? Regarding immeasurable suffering:
as for the causes, it consists of the suffering of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions), the suffering of *rajas* (dust-like delusions), and the suffering of *avidyā* (ignorance).

As for the results, it consists of the suffering of the evil realms, the suffering of *sāsrava* (outflows), the suffering of stagnation, and the suffering within delusion. "One who gives rise to wisdom" means giving rise to the wisdom of the *satya* (truth); [this] uproots...

One perceives the causes of suffering consisting of view and thought-affliction (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), thereby uprooting the two kinds of *paricchinna-vedanīya* (segmented) fruits of suffering—the outflows (*āsrava*) of the evil realms—and gives rise to the wisdom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

One uproots the causes of suffering consisting of *rajas* (dust-like afflictions), thereby uprooting the fruit of suffering that is quiescent and profound, and gives rise to the wisdom of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). One uproots the cause of suffering consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*).

It uproots the fruits of suffering resulting from the transformations within delusion. To state it briefly: this is the simultaneous, perfect cultivation of the three kinds of great compassion within a single thought-moment.
Because one cultivates the great compassion directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana-karuṇā*), one uproots the suffering of the evil realms as well as the suffering of stagnation and silence;
thus, the conventional truth samādhi is accomplished. This is called the non-harming [compassion] directed toward sentient beings. One contemplates that all sentient beings are oneself.

This refers to one's parents and so forth. Because one practices the great compassion conditioned by dharmas (*dharmālambana-mahākaruṇā*), one uproots the suffering of out-flowing, fragmented existence (*sāsrava-pratyaṅga-bheda-duḥkha*).
When the samādhi of ultimate truth is accomplished, this is called the "non-killing conditioned by dharmas. One contemplates that all earth and water were one's own former bodies.
All fire and wind are my original substance. Because one cultivates unconditional great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*), one uproots the suffering of transformation within delusion.

When the samādhi of the Middle Truth is accomplished, this is called "non-attachment to the conditions of self. One contemplates that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in the three aspects;
one does not take conditioned designations as objects, nor does one take substantial dharmas as objects, but takes only the Middle Way Buddha-nature as the object.

There is no object of focus, yet there is nothing that is not an object of focus. To explain according to the sequential stages: in the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao), upholding the precepts of essential nature constitutes the condition of non-killing.
In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), realizing that form is empty constitutes the condition of the dharma of non-killing.

In the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), practicing the Middle Way constitutes the condition of non-attachment to self. In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one cultivates the three types of compassion within a single thought-moment; therefore, it is able to be perfect.
They uproot immeasurable masses of suffering. Although their contemplation of compassion is profound, they universally take the precepts of ritual action (*śīla*) as their objective support.
If there were no objective support of ritual action, contemplation of principle would not arise. Therefore, they constantly practice non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexuality.
Toward all sentient beings, those who have aroused the bodhicitta, they do not afflict others with the acts of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct. Nor do others [afflict them].
Nor do they themselves afflict me; thus we do not afflict one another. This is the permanent uprooting of the cause of suffering.

Yet this perfect compassion does not merely uproot suffering, but immediately bestows happiness. This is because the Bodhisattva not only perceives emptiness, but also perceives the true nature of all phenomena within that emptiness.
Therefore, within the practices of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the seeds of the Path arise accordingly.
The mind of wisdom: toward each of the three categories—friends, enemies, and neutrals—it bestows the fruit of supreme bliss and wisdom.
Even regarding the category of the most extreme enemies, it causes those nine grades of beings to attain the fruit of happiness.
Practicing in this manner, until the essence of emptiness within emptiness and signlessness manifests before one, then oneself and all other sentient beings become equal.
It causes them to return to the single bliss [of nirvana], yet it gives rise once more to the great compassion of the Buddha-ground.
This may also be correlated specifically with the practitioner who benefits others, for such a one is well able to benefit all sentient beings.
△ Third, the Mind of Joy.

O Sons of the Buddha, when one experiences joy and the mind of non-arising, the nature, characteristics, path, and wisdom of the spiritual lineage are empty. This is the joy of emptiness; the mind does not cling to "mine.

Transcending the arising and ceasing of the three periods of time, there is no accumulation of cause and effect. All that exists enters into the practice of the contemplation of emptiness, which is perfected. Thus it is equal.
Rejoicing. All sentient beings arise in emptiness and enter the Way; they abandon evil associates and seek virtuous friends.
These virtuous friends show them the good path, causing all sentient beings to enter the household of the Buddha-Dharma and to constantly give rise to joy within that Dharma.

They enter the rank of the Buddhas, and furthermore, these sentient beings enter into right faith, abandon false views, and turn their backs on the suffering of the six realms; therefore, there is rejoicing.
"Joy" (*prīti*) means being refreshed and at ease; "gladness" (*muditā*) means being filled with delight. This is a general indication of the essential characteristics of the immeasurable samādhis.

From the phrase "not giving rise to" (*na utpādayati*) onwards, the four types of gladness are specifically distinguished; that is to say, this joy and gladness are not like those arising from worldly sensual desires.

Specifically, when one personally realizes the mind of non-arising, then all categories of nature and their essential characteristics are illuminated by the wisdom of the Path and are found to be entirely empty.
Thus, one gives rise to joy toward these empty phenomena. This is because, through one's own understanding of the principle of emptiness, one is no longer bound by rebirth;
having attained realization of the empty dharma, the mind no longer clings to "mine."

He seeks only his own liberation; yet, solely for the sake of transforming and delivering sentient beings, he manifests birth and extinction throughout the three periods of time without being dragged by karma.
Therefore, all causes and effects are entirely without accumulation.
Constantly, amidst all twenty-five realms of existence, he causes them to enter the practice of contemplation on emptiness wherever they may be, thereby attaining impartial joy. This...
He rejoices because he skillfully understands non-attachment and sports in the liberation of sentient beings.

He gives rise to the wisdom of true emptiness toward all sentient beings and enters the path of compassion. He causes each and every one to abandon evil associates and seek out virtuous friends, who in turn show them the excellent path.
Thus they mutually benefit one another, leading all sentient beings to enter the household of the Buddha-dharma; therefore, regarding the Dharma—
One constantly gives rise to joy within; this is because one rejoices in the cause of performing acts that celebrate others, as they lead to successive deliverance.
Furthermore, once [others] have attained the state of Buddhahood, one causes all these sentient beings to enter into right faith, abandoning the heterodox and turning away from suffering;
this is because one rejoices in the attainment of the fruit by delivering others and extensively transforming sentient beings. This may also be understood separately.
Regarding the practitioner who is free from anger and resentment, this constitutes awakening oneself and awakening others, because one attains the meaning of non-opposition.

As for the distinction between this and the mind of joy (*muditā*) within the [four] bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*), the former is the skillful means of sympathetic joy, whereas the latter is the immeasurable meditative concentration (*apramāṇa-samādhi*).
△ Fourth, the Mind of Equanimity.
O Disciples of the Buddha, you should constantly give rise to the mind of equanimity within the unconditioned, signless, and empty Dharma, which is like space.

Regarding the two states of good and evil, existence and non-existence, or sin and merit, one should illuminate them all equally as one. Free from the notions of "person" and "mine," one should [abide] by oneself...

He finds no inherent nature in other entities and practices great equanimity (*upekṣā*). Regarding his own body, flesh, hands, feet, sons, daughters, kingdom, and cities—as being like illusions, transformations, flowing water, or the flame of a lamp—he relinquishes them all, yet without a mind of arising, he constantly cultivates that equanimity.

Without discrimination and without attachment, with a mind that is equanimous, it is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*). Because it is free from all conceptualization, as indicated by the phrase "no creation," it is the "Great Equanimity.
Furthermore, because it is free from all attachments, as indicated by the phrase "and one's own self," it is called "Universal Equanimity.
Finally, the phrase "yet there is no arising" concludes by clarifying that one constantly gives rise to a mind of equanimity; this is precisely the "arising of the mind without abiding."
This is the meaning [of non-origination]. Non-origination is non-action. Within these three gates of liberation, one contemplates all phenomena as being equal to empty space.
Whether good or evil, existent or non-existent, sinful or meritorious, there is nothing that is not equally and uniformly illuminated.
One knows that their essential nature is fundamentally ungraspable; thus, regarding both the internal body and external objects, one realizes [their true nature].

Realize that all things are like illusions and transformations, lacking substantiality; they are like flowing flames, without abiding. Release them completely and let go, forever free from stinginess or attachment.

This may also be correlated specifically with the practice of inexhaustibility. To illuminate all with equal impartiality is what is meant by "the equality of the three periods of time" and "universal penetration throughout the ten directions."
△ Five Kinds of the Mind of Giving.
O Sons of the Buddha, one should be able to clothe all sentient beings with the mind of giving: giving by body, giving by speech, giving by mind, giving material wealth, and giving the Dharma.
One instructs and guides all sentient beings, offering their own internal and external bodies, kingdoms, cities, men and women, fields, and houses, all as [if they were not their own].
It is the nature of suchness, even to the point that there is no thought of wealth or property, neither recipient nor donor, whether internal or external;
there is no joining and no dispersing, and no mental activity in transformation. One penetrates principle and penetrates giving, so that all marks are present in practice.
This belongs to the category of giving (*dāna*) among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). Setting out upon the perfection of giving has "reaching the other shore" as its meaning;
within this context, the inclusion of giving takes "transforming sentient beings" as its primary aim. Therefore, it is said that it "encompasses all sentient beings."

Whatever physical, verbal, and mental actions a bodhisattva possesses, there are none that do not encompass sentient beings. As for the methods of such encompassment, they do not exceed the two types of giving:
material wealth and the Dharma. The three karmas serve as the giver, while material wealth and the Dharma serve as that which is given.

With both the giver and the gift presented together, these five modes of giving are used to guide and instruct sentient beings. Furthermore, one contemplates that the internal and external body and so forth are all identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

This is its characteristic. To the point where there is not even a single thought of discriminating between wealth and goods, nor between the recipient and the donor—one thus realizes that the three spheres are empty in essence.
One cultivates internal contemplation of principle while simultaneously practicing external giving. This contemplation of principle is without attachment, and this giving is without distraction.
Throughout the day one remains mindless, yet throughout the day one carries out transformative activity. Thus, one penetrates the principle within phenomena.
"Attainment" is the application of principle. By means of all these various characteristics, one manifests the practice of giving;

this is precisely what the *Buddhottama-sūtra* refers to as the various *dharmaparyāyas* that achieve freedom from error. Therefore, it may also be correlated specifically with the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.
△ Sixth, the Mind of Kind Speech.
If a Buddha’s disciple enters the Samādhi of Essential Loving Speech, regarding the meaning of the Dharma of the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha-satya), all true words accord with this single speech.
It harmonizes the minds of all sentient beings, being free from anger and contention—this is the nature of all dharmas.
The wisdom of emptiness is without objective conditions, yet it constantly gives rise to a heart of love. One acts in accordance with the Buddha’s intention and likewise accords with all others.
Using the speech of the noble Dharma, one teaches all sentient beings and always acts according to that mind, thereby initiating roots of goodness.
To clarify the nature of "loving speech," it is first stated that one enters the Samādhi of Loving Speech regarding the Essential Nature (*dharmatā*).

Since preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings is the most difficult of tasks, unless one has personally realized and entered the essential nature of the wondrous Dharma, one cannot skillfully provide teachings according to wisdom and according to sentiment through the four *pratisaraṇa* (causes and conditions). Only by entering this Samādhi of Essential Nature can one fully comprehend the One.
The nature of all phenomena is entirely ineffable; yet, because there are causes and conditions, it can also be expressed.

The teachings he expounds skillfully accord with the capacities of various beings, enabling sentient beings to feel love, joy, and delight; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Essential Nature and Loving Speech.
Once he has entered this samādhi, he may speak of the words and meanings of the Dharma of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya), or...
All various kinds of true speech, when ultimately considered, conform to and enter into the true discourse of the One Vehicle.
Regarding the meaning of the "primary discourse": it is speech that accords with one's own intention and speech that accords with wisdom.

All "true speech" refers to speech that accords with the intentions of others and speech that accords with their dispositions; though these are skillfully taught through various provisional means according to those dispositions, not even a hair’s breadth...
It is without deception. For example, it is like a householder who gives his children great ox-carts made of white oxen;
there is ultimately no fault of falsehood. Therefore, it is called "all speech that is true. Following wisdom, it firmly accords with the One Vehicle;

following worldly sentiment, it also uses skillful means to gradually lead them into the truth. Thus, it is said that "all accord with the one word. By means of these two modes of speech, he harmonizes the multitude.
He gives rise [to compassion]. Because he does not begrudge the true Dharma, he is without anger; because he constantly accords with the capacities of sentient beings, he is without contention.

This is due to the wisdom that all phenomena are empty; although there are no external conditions to draw him forth, he always gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings.
Therefore, whatever words he speaks, above, they accord with the Buddha’s intent and conform to the principle; below, they likewise accord with all [sentient beings].

To accord with others according to their capacities, always teaching all sentient beings with the Dharma-words of the sages, constantly acting in accordance with the mind, and never departing from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while initiating roots of goodness and not abandoning the skillful means of preaching the Dharma—this is called the Bodhisattva’s gathering through loving speech (*priyavāda-saṃgraha*).
Regarding the two types of speech, for oneself and for others, if one were to provide a general explanation: they function in accordance with wisdom.
The former accords with the principle of the Buddha; the latter, according to circumstances, accords with the capacities of sentient beings. To explain this fully:

these two phrases represent the Buddha’s two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate truth; thus, they both "accord upward" with the Buddha-mind. These two phrases universally reach both sharp and dull-witted sentient beings; thus, they both "accord downward" with others.
This may also be applied specifically to the practitioner who follows Subhūti, who, regarding the single dharma-nature, acts as...
There are two ways of explaining this: namely, that within sameness, a multitude of differences manifests. Although there are these two explanations, they both accord with a single statement;
that is, each distinct characteristic is seen as identical in its respective instance.
△ Seven: The Mind of Benefiting Others.

O Disciples of the Buddha, when practicing the mind of benefiting others, one should extensively cultivate the path of wisdom through the essence of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), gathering all dharma-gates of radiant illumination and collecting the seven riches of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
Because others thereby obtain benefit, one accepts body and life to enter into the act of benefiting them.
The Samādhi of Increasing Benefit manifests all bodies, all speech, and all minds, causing the great world-system to tremble.
In all that they do and undertake, others enter into the seeds of the Dharma, the seeds of emptiness, and the seeds of the Path, thereby obtaining benefit and joy.

They manifest forms within the six realms of existence; though there are immeasurable matters of suffering and affliction, these are not considered a burden, for they act solely to benefit and profit others.
This is precisely the inclusion through beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*). This method of inclusion employs expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) in its entirety;

yet, expedient wisdom takes true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) as its very essence. Therefore, by means of the nature of true wisdom, one extensively practices the path of expedient wisdom, gathering the radiance of all wisdom and amassing the wealth of all meritorious dharmas. With both merit and wisdom adorning one, one then causes—

Because those who preceded him have attained benefit, he himself, though long since separated from the conditions for birth, manifests for the sake of sentient beings by assuming a physical body and entering the Samādhi of Beneficial Action.
Thirdly, through the power of the flavors [of the Dharma], he manifests inconceivable transformations of the three wheels, shaking the great trichiliocosm.
Whether lifting his foot or taking a step, everything is nothing other than Buddha-work, causing all others to awaken to the gate of the Three Contemplations and attain [enlightenment].
It brings benefit in the present and attains ultimate bliss. Furthermore, it manifests forms within the six realms of existence to extensively respond to the various capacities of sentient beings.
Although there are immeasurable sufferings and afflictions within these six realms, they are not regarded as a source of distress;

rather, benefiting others is itself the very purpose. The seven riches are: first, faith; second, diligence; third, precepts; fourth, shame and remorse; fifth, learning; sixth, relinquishment; and seventh, concentration and wisdom. III.

Regarding the contemplations: the category of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) constitutes the Middle Contemplation; the category of emptiness (*śūnyatādhātu*) constitutes the Emptiness Contemplation; and the category of the path (*mārgadhātu*) constitutes the Provisional Contemplation.

This may also be applied individually to the practitioner who acts without attachment: manifesting body, speech, and mind, and shaking the world-systems—this is what is meant by "manifesting dust and manifesting realms" without mutual obstruction.
△ 8. Identical Mind. O Disciples of the Buddha:
Through the wisdom of the nature of the Path, one is identical with emptiness; within the dharma of non-arising, through the wisdom of non-self, one is identical with birth as being non-dual.

Emptiness and the source are identical in the objective realm. The suchness of all dharmas is eternally arising, eternally abiding, and eternally ceasing; worldly phenomena continue in succession, flowing on.
Transforming immeasurably, they are able to manifest immeasurable forms, bodies, colors, minds, and karmic activities, entering all six realms of existence.

In all matters they are identical; in emptiness they are identical with non-arising; in the self they are identical with non-substantiality. Thus, by dividing their bodies and dispersing their forms, they enter the Samādhi of Identical Dharma.

This is precisely the "sameness of purpose" (samānārthatā) among the four means of integration. While the previous "beneficial conduct" (arthacaryā) also manifested forms within the six realms of existence, it remained the leader for all beings.

Now, however, he moves among different species and practices what is not the Way, yet penetrates the Buddha-way; his skillful means (*upāya*) in transforming sentient beings are especially inconceivable.
This is truly because he has fully realized the wisdom of the lineage of the Way (*mārga-gotra*), which is identical to the Truth (*tathatā*).
Emptiness is what is called the ultimate truth within the conventional; thus, one realizes entry into the dharma of non-arising.
By means of the sublime wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness, one is non-dual with all sentient beings: when among devas, one is a deva; when among humans, one is human.
They did not know that they were being transformed by a bodhisattva. For having realized this state of ultimate emptiness and stillness where all phenomena share a single source—
the true suchness (*tathatā*) and real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas— they are thus able to manifest constant birth, constant abiding,
and constant extinction within the nature that is unborn, non-abiding, and unextinguished, following along with the continuity of worldly phenomena.
Transforming immeasurably, they are able to manifest immeasurable forms, bodies, colors, minds, and karmic activities, entering the six realms of existence.
They participate in all manner of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, becoming identical with them. Because they are ultimately empty, although they manifest birth, they are identical to the unborn;
because they have realized the unborn, although they manifest a self, they are identical to the non-existent. Thus, they divide their bodies and disperse their forms.
Working together with his colleagues, he guides them toward the Buddha Vehicle; thus, he enters the Samādhi of Identical Dharma.
This may also be understood as corresponding specifically to those who practice with reverence, for through various manifestations, he leads them all to return to the foremost pāramitā.
△ Ninth, the concentrated mind.
O Disciples of the Buddha, furthermore, from this concentrated mind, one contemplates with wisdom and realizes emptiness. Each thought-moment rests in stillness upon its object;

amidst the dharmas of "mine," within the realm of consciousness and the realm of form, one does not waver or shift. Because of emerging and submerging in both the inverse and the direct order, one constantly enters the hundred samādhis and the ten dhyānas.

Vasumitra, by means of the wisdom of a single thought-moment, perceives that all seeds of sentient beings—whether "self" or "person," whether internal or external—are devoid of both conjunction and dispersion;
they are neither accumulated nor produced through integration, and thus cannot be apprehended.

Furthermore, regarding "the mind emerging from meditative concentration": this refers to the accomplishment of the sublime and wondrous functions of the *vaiśāradya* (mastery) and *vyutkrāntaka* (leaping over) samādhis, having well-cultivated the samādhis of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
In the previous section on the "five stages of the path of application," the fifth stage of meditative concentration took quiescence and signlessness as its essence;

here, however, its functional capacity consists in emerging from and entering into [the states] in both reverse and direct order. This is because one enters through the realization of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*).
Because of the principle of emptiness, the mind is tranquil in every moment, yet it can constantly and universally take all objects of samādhi as its focus.
It is not moved or shifted by the realms of the *ātmīya-dharma*, consciousness, or form.

Within the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*), it exercises mastery at will, emerging and entering them in both forward and reverse order. Thus, it enters into a hundred samādhis and the ten factors of dhyāna, by means of a single thought-moment.
One should apply wisdom to see that all faculties, bodies, and the vessel-world, as well as active manifestations and seeds, arise through the false conjunction of causes and conditions;
yet they have no actual union. When causes and conditions separate, what is falsely called "extinction" does not disperse.
These are merely accumulated by the deluded mind and are termed "active manifestations"; they are produced by the deluded mind and are termed "seeds."
My son, you must realize that [the self] is ultimately unobtainable. For instance, the four dhyānas and eight samādhis can be practiced by both ordinary people and non-Buddhists;
however, because they have not yet realized the principle of emptiness, they are always governed by these meditative states rather than skillfully employing them.
Since they are governed by these meditative states, they cannot avoid being reborn according to the power of those states; thus, they are "possessed by me."

The consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*) is that which is moved and transformed by the form element (*rūpadhātu*). The consciousness element refers to the four formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*); because they possess only the four aggregates (*skandha*) and lack the aggregate of form, they are called the consciousness element.

Although the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*) can also be realized by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), [the consciousness element here refers to the state beyond them].

However, because they have not yet reached the wondrous emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they take the realization of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) as their final goal and can no longer manifest the various modes of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).

What is now called "appearing and disappearing in accordance with or contrary to [the order]" refers to emerging from meditative absorption as "appearing" and entering meditative absorption as "disappearing.

To emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) and enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), continuing down to emerging from the second dhyāna and entering the first dhyāna, is called "appearing and disappearing in reverse order. From... [text continues]

Emerging from the first dhyāna and entering the second dhyāna, continuing in this manner until emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and entering the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, is called "successive emergence and immersion" (*anuloma-pratiloma-samāpatti*).
If one emerges and immerses through the stages in both direct and reverse order, it is called the "Lion’s Bound" samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*).
If one emerges and immerses by skipping stages, it is called the "Leaping Over" samādhi (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*). This continues up to a hundred samādhis, all based on the nine successive stages.
Concentration is the foundation. Furthermore, the nine successive concentrations are collectively established based upon the ten factors of dhyāna (*daśa-dhyānāṅga*).

As for these ten factors of dhyāna, "factor" (*aṅga*) has the sense of a constituent part; that is to say, it refers to how meditative concentration is accomplished through various constituent parts consisting of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).

The first dhyāna possesses five factors: first, applied thought (*vitarka*); second, sustained thought (*vicāra*); third, joy (*prīti*); fourth, bliss (*sukha*); and fifth, one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*). The second dhyāna possesses four [factors].
The factors are: first, joy; second, bliss; third, one-pointedness of mind; fourth, internal purity. The third dhyāna has five factors: first, bliss; second, one-pointedness of mind;
third, equanimity; fourth, mindfulness; fifth, wisdom. The fourth dhyāna has four factors: first, one-pointedness of mind; second, equanimity; third, mindfulness; fourth, neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Now, discarding the duplicates and retaining the unique ones, they are collectively termed the ten factors. These may also be categorized individually.

Regarding wholesome dharmas, the practitioner, through the emergence and submergence of samādhi and the factors of dhyāna in both direct and reverse order, is able to fulfill the rules of conduct of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
△ Tenth, the Mind of Wisdom.
If, O disciples of the Buddha, you cultivate the mind of wisdom-vision, you shall observe that all fetters of false views, afflictions, and bonds lack any determinate essence or nature.

Because they accord with the patience of emptiness (*śūnyatā-kṣānti*), they are not the aggregates (*skandha*), not the elements (*dhātu*), not the sense-bases (*āyatana*), not sentient beings, not a single self (*ātman*), and not cause or effect.
It is not a dharma of the three periods of time. The nature of wisdom gives rise to light; the light is a single, brilliant flame. One perceives emptiness and non-reception.
This wisdom and skillful means nourish and develop the mind. This mind enters the path of the arising of emptiness within emptiness, giving rise to the mind of non-arising.
The "mind that perceives with wisdom" refers to the skillful wisdom of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). "To act" means to initiate.

In the sixth "mind of wisdom" within the preceding section on "Setting Out," the essence of the mind of wisdom regarding emptiness was clarified; here, the skillful means for initiating emptiness is clarified. These skillful means do not turn their backs on true emptiness.
Wrong views are the sharp afflictions (*kleśa*), while the bonds of suffering are the dull afflictions; fundamentally, they possess no fixed intrinsic nature.

When a Bodhisattva, within the stage of conformative patience (ānulomikī-kṣānti), has realized the principle of emptiness, they observe that both the sharp and dull latent propensities (anuśaya) are entirely identical with emptiness.

These are neither the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), or bases (āyatana), nor the phenomena of the three periods of time. From the essence of true wisdom, they give rise to the aspect of illuminating radiance, employing the flame of a single gnosis.
It thoroughly illuminates all phenomena, such that there is nothing not clearly understood. One perceives that their essence is fundamentally empty and tranquil, with no recipient thereof.
Furthermore, this wisdom-convenience (*prajñopāya*) is not only the foundation of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), but is also the foundation for the ten ways of nurturing the mind.

Through wisdom and skillful means, one nurtures and develops the mind; through the nurturing of the mind, one enters the path of the emptiness of arising and emptiness, whereby one is able to give rise to the Middle Way mind of non-arising and enter the ten adamantine stages. Regarding wisdom and skillful means:

wisdom is ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-prajñā*), while skillful means is provisional wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*). These two—provisional and ultimate wisdom—are not two distinct entities. This is the path of the emptiness of arising and emptiness.

This means that from emptiness one emerges into the provisional, yet the provisional does not obstruct emptiness. This may also be applied specifically to those who practice according to the ultimate truth:
namely, observing that every single phenomenon is pure, untainted, and the singular, true unconditioned.
△ Third: Joining the Fingers.
Above, in the "Chapter on the King of the Thousandfold Ocean-Eye," the One Hundred Dharmas of the Heart’s Gate of Illumination have already been explained.

Vairocana Buddha said: "Thousand Buddhas, listen attentively! You previously stated that the vajra-seeds consist of ten minds.
As for these vajra-seeds: by practicing Madhyamaka, they are able to serve as the seeds for the ten vajra-stages."
Furthermore, while all thirty minds are seeds, these ten minds alone are doubly firm and solid; therefore, they are named "Vajra.

Specifically, each mind is applied individually to its respective stage. Generally, however, one cultivates these minds in every stage up to the ultimate realization of *miao-jue* (wonderful enlightenment).
Now, for the sake of convenience in exposition, I shall provide an explanation based on the progressive Middle Way (*madhyamaka*). Moreover—

Furthermore, it bears a strong resemblance to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*): first, faith; second, mindfulness; and the sixth, non-retrogression—the names and meanings of which are identical.

Profound mind and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) correspond to the meaning of diligence (*vīrya*); penetration corresponds to the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*); and directness corresponds to the meaning of concentration (*samādhi*).

The Great Vehicle is not different from the protective mind; signlessness is equivalent to dedication; and the wisdom-mind, together with the precepts, constitutes the indestructible vow—this is how the meanings are taken.

The differences are slight and not very far-reaching; they arise fundamentally because the capacities and circumstances outside the [specific] realm differ. Whether through direct reception or indirect borrowing, these lead to divergent approaches.

For those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), who cultivate contemplation in accordance with their inherent nature, all things are universally gathered into the single thought-moment of the mind, without any contradiction or hindrance.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the ten [stages], from the first, the mind of faith, to the tenth, the indestructible mind. Now, for the first:
O Disciples of the Buddha, as for "faith," faith is the foremost of all practices and the root of all virtues. One does not give rise to the heterodox views of external paths;
though one may be attached to various views and names, one will certainly not undergo the karma created by those fetters. One enters into the unconditioned dharma of emptiness.
The three marks do not exist; non-existence does not exist. There is no arising of arising, no abiding of abiding, and no cessation of cessation.

There is no knowledge of the emptiness of all dharmas regarding either conventional truth or the ultimate truth. All distinctions are extinguished in emptiness. Form is empty of subtle mind; mind is empty of subtle mind.
Because mind and mind are empty, faith and faith are quiescent. There is no essence, nor is there any union. Furthermore, there is no persistent master, self, person, or individual.
The provisional designation of "self" is applied to the three realms; since the self has no attainable characteristics of accumulation, it is called the "faith of non-attainment.
Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness.
By the power of faith, one does not give rise to the heterodox views of external paths, nor to any of the various deluded views, names, or attachments of the mundane world.
That which can bind the fruits of retribution in the three realms of existence and can create all manner of wholesome and unwholesome karma need not necessarily undergo [rebirth].
Upon entering into the true emptiness of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing are, in their very substance, entirely non-existent;

furthermore, there is not even the characteristic of "no-characteristic" to be attained. That which is called "arising" is itself non-arising, and that which is non-arising is itself arising. There is abiding without abiding, and abiding is itself non-abiding.
Abiding, there is extinction without extinction; extinction is itself non-extinction. It is not merely that all phenomena are absent, but even the emptiness of all phenomena is absent.

This is solely through the wondrous wisdom of the provisional and the real, which illuminates and realizes both the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), thereby completely extinguishing the subtle mental conceptions regarding the "emptiness" imagined by ordinary people and outsiders as distinct from form, as well as the subtle mental conceptions regarding the realm of form and the realm of space. II.
Riding upon the subtle and refined mental wisdom of the emptiness of mind, because each and every moment of mind is empty, one then gives rise to true faith in the Middle Way.
One believes in the principle of the quiescent cessation of the Middle Way, understanding that all phenomena do not arise from themselves and therefore lack intrinsic nature;
they do not arise from both [self and other] and therefore lack conjunction; they do not arise without cause and therefore lack dependence. Dependence is...

This is spontaneous; it is not produced by another. Therefore, there is no master, no self, and no person. It merely employs the provisional designation of "self" within the three realms, yet this self truly lacks any characteristic of being acquired or accumulated. Hence, it is called the "conviction of non-existence.

This may also be specifically correlated with the dedication "protecting sentient beings while remaining free from the mark of sentient beings," as one enters into the unconditioned dharma of emptiness.

"Centered" means the sense of being purely immaculate and essentially true. "Not giving rise to false views and not undergoing the accumulation of karma and afflictions" means the sense of distancing oneself from all lingering calamities.

"Using the provisional 'self' of the triple world, yet realizing that no self can be found and that the marks of accumulation do not arise" means that one should deliver sentient beings while extinguishing the very mark of delivering them.
Because each thought-moment is empty, faith and faith are quiescent; this is the turning of the unconditioned mind toward Nirvana.
The Meaning of Panlu (Pāramitā).
△ Second, the Mind of Recollection.
If a Buddha-son practices the six recollections—ranging from constant awareness to constant giving—he realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): emptiness and non-attachment.

There is no liberation. The marks of arising, abiding, and ceasing do not move, nor do they arrive or depart. Yet, regarding the single unified mark of the recipient of all karmas, one dedicates [merit] to enter the wisdom of the Dharma-realm.
Wisdom and wisdom ride upon one another; vehicle and vehicle are quiescent. Each flame is impermanent; each radiance is non-existent.

Birth after birth does not arise; one transforms through the path of emptiness. The former changes as the latter turns; transformation follows transformation, and transformation leads to further transformation. Transformation...

Transforming and transforming; simultaneously abiding together; each flame having a single characteristic; arising and ceasing at one time; already transformed, not yet transformed, and in the process of transforming;
transformation also attains oneness, and sensation is likewise so.

The "one who forms the thought" refers to the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) that is capable of recollecting. The "six recollections" refer to the truths (*satya*) that are the objects of recollection.

That which is capable of recollecting is nothing other than the one mind and three contemplations; that which is recollected is nothing other than the one realm and three truths. Regarding the phrase "constantly aware," this first explains the object of recollection.
Regarding the phrase "turning toward," this next explains the subject of recollection. "Constantly aware" means that there is no Buddha outside the mind; the Buddha is [the mind itself].
"Mind. As for "and so forth," this is a concise reference to the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, and the devas. There is no phenomenon apart from the mind;

phenomena are themselves the mind, which is called the "eternal Dharma. There is no Sangha apart from the mind; the Sangha is the harmony of awakened dharmas, which is called the "eternal Sangha. [This is] the wondrous precept of non-action.

The ultimate characteristic of form is called the "eternal precept" (*nitya-śīla*). The heaven of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-deva*)—the inherent virtue of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—is called the "eternal heaven" (*nitya-deva*).

The three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) being quiescent in essence, the ultimate great giving is called "eternal giving" (*nitya-dāna*). Although there are six names, they are in reality but the single ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

This generally clarifies the realm where the three truths are perfectly interfused. The character "emptiness" (*śūnya*) is specifically named the "truth of reality" (*tattva-satya*); it is non-attachment.

There is no further explanation. To separately clarify the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing are motionless in the present; they do not reach the past or the future.
To separately clarify the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*): since it is the object of contemplation, the three truths and the one truth are inconceivable.
As they are but a single unified characteristic, one should know that this applies equally to the various karmas of the six recollections and to those who partake in and utilize this Dharma.
This is the single, unified mark of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). For one who dedicates [merit] to entering the wisdom of the dharma-realm:
when recollecting the Buddha, the Buddha is the dharma-realm, and all dharmas tend toward the Buddha; even when recollecting giving, giving is the dharma-realm, and all dharmas tend toward giving.
This generally clarifies the mindfulness in which the three contemplations are perfectly integrated. "Wisdom and wisdom mounting each other," and so forth.

The separate elucidation of the wondrous contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is as follows: the "flame" is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*); "impermanence" is the meaning of the vehicle (*yāna*); and the "light" is a metaphor for the vehicle.

"Non-existence of non-existence" is the meaning of quiescence (*nirvāṇa*). Regarding "the arising of arising does not arise," etc., this is the separate elucidation of the wondrous contemplation of the conventional (*upādāya-prajñapti*).

This means that although it is the "arising of arising" which does not arise, it nevertheless undergoes transformation within the path of emptiness—namely, the transformation of the former and the transition to the latter. Transformation...

Transformation leads to transformation; transformation leads to further transformations, like elephants [following one another] in infinite succession. This is inconceivable. "Transformation" (*bian*) refers to the wisdom that is capable of recollecting;
"transformation" (*hua*) refers to the objects being recollected. Because the wisdom capable of recollection arises due to objects such as the Buddha-dharma, it is called "transformation.
Because objects such as the Buddha-dharma are further produced due to the wisdom of recollection, it is likewise called [transformation].
Regarding "transformation," it refers to those who are simultaneous and co-resident; this specifically clarifies the subtle contemplation of the Middle Way.

That is to say, although there is transformation and change, they remain simultaneous and co-resident, just as the flame of a lamp wick is a single characteristic where each flicker arises and ceases at the same time.
This means that while the past has already changed, the future has not yet changed, and the present is changing—there is nothing that does not exist simultaneously and co-residently.
Furthermore, regarding what is called "simultaneity," consider the three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing. On the surface, these are said to belong to the three time periods;

however, when the characteristic of arising arises, the characteristic of ceasing ceases. When the characteristic of abiding arises, the characteristic of arising ceases. And when the characteristic of ceasing arises...

The characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) is cessation. Because the characteristic of abiding ceases, abiding is also called cessation. Because the characteristic of cessation arises, cessation is also called arising.
Because the characteristic of arising ceases, arising is also called cessation. Because the characteristic of abiding arises, abiding is also called arising.

Furthermore, at the very moment of arising, arising is also called abiding; at the very moment of ceasing, cessation is also called abiding. Thus, within a single characteristic, all [characteristics] are fully present.
The three meanings each possess three names; therefore, they are simultaneous. As for what is called "co-dwelling," in meaning it lacks an intrinsic nature, and in name it lacks a substantial entity.
Arising does not arise from itself, nor does it arise from another, nor does it arise from both, nor does it arise without a cause.
Abiding does not abide by itself, nor does it abide through another, nor does it abide in common with another; it does not abide without cause.
Cessation does not cease by itself, nor does it cease through another, nor does it cease in common with another; it does not cease without cause.

When one investigates these four natures, seeking the distinct characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, they are found to be utterly unobtainable. There is only the single state of non-arising, non-abiding, and non-ceasing.

Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such, they abide together. Each flame has a single characteristic, which serves as a metaphor for abiding together; arising and ceasing occur simultaneously, which likewise serves as a metaphor for being at one time.

Since the wisdom that can maintain this mindfulness consists of three contemplations within a single contemplation—an inconceivable state where there is only a single characteristic and a single time—then the transformed realm that is the object of mindfulness also attains a single characteristic and a single time, whereby one partakes in the enjoyment of this Dharma.
This is likewise of one characteristic and occurs at one time. This may also be distinguished in contrast to the "indestructible dedication":
if it is not the three truths within a single object, nor the three contemplations within a single mind, these are all destructible dharmas.

To speak of the conventional apart from the true, to speak of the true apart from the conventional, or to speak of the middle apart from both the true and the conventional—none of these constitute the ultimate Dharma-realm.
The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Now, being entirely free from all these [conceptual] separations, it is called "indestructible.
△ Third, the mind of dedication.

O disciples of the Buddha, as for the "profound mind" (*gambhīracitta*), it is the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Through the wisdom of the emptiness of real dharmas, it illuminates the existence of the true reality (*satyadharma*). Regarding karma—

The continuity of the Path is the Middle Way within causes and conditions; this is called the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The provisional designations of all phenomena—such as self, person, and master—are called the Worldly Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Within these two truths, one enters deeply into emptiness where there is no coming or going; like a magical illusion, one experiences the fruits [of karma] yet remains without a recipient.
Therefore, through this profound and deep mind, one attains liberation.
The title is called "Dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*), and the text is named "Profound Mind" (*gambhīracitta*). This is because it turns away from the two extremes and directs itself toward the Middle Way;
its principle is ultimately profound and subtle. This "profound mind" is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

That is to say, within the wisdom of the emptiness of true reality, one simultaneously illuminates both the provisional and the real of the two truths, all of which converge into the single reality. Here, "existence" (*yu*) refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and "reality" (*shi*) refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

What is called the True Truth? It is precisely the principle within the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), which is the continuity of the paths of karma (*karmapatha*).

Karma arises from delusion (*kleśa*) and inevitably brings about bitter fruit (*duḥkhaphala*). By mentioning one, both are encompassed, forming the Great Dependent Origination (*mahā-pratītyasamutpāda*).
The principle therein is what is known as the fundamentally pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana, which is able to give rise to all conditions, yet is not left behind by those conditions.
Although these are what has been left behind, they do not exist outside of conditions. What is meant by "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*)?
