It refers to the various dharmas designated by provisional names, such as "self," "person," and "master. Originally, there are no real dharmas; they exist only through worldly conventional designations.

Ordinary people and non-Buddhists fail to understand this, and thus give rise to the two attachments. Regarding these two truths: in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the emotional aspect is absent while the principle exists; in the conventional truth, the principle...
Because insentient things possess [existence], they are likewise termed the "truth of existence" (*satya*).

To enter deeply into the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) such that there is no coming or going means that within the true and eternal nature, one seeks coming and going, delusion and awakening, or birth and death, and finds absolutely nothing to be obtained.
Although illusory transformations receive fruits, there is no receiver; what returns is the harmony of causes and conditions, which exists as a false appearance.
Birth is the separation from causes and conditions; that which is falsely called "extinction" is actually born in its own place and extinguished in accordance with that very place.
This may also be applied specifically to the dedication of all Buddhas: fundamental enlightenment is profoundly still, and this awakening is equal to the awakening of the Buddhas.
Therefore, it is called the profound liberation of the deep mind.
△ Fourth, the Mind of Penetration.

O Sons of the Buddha, as for those who penetrate and illuminate: they endure and accord with the true nature of all things. In each and every nature, there is neither bondage nor liberation; they are unimpeded.

Dharma-penetration, meaning-penetration, expression-penetration, and the penetration of teaching and transformation; the causes and effects of the three periods of time; the faculties and practices of sentient beings—all are suchness, neither conjoined nor dispersed.
They have no reality, yet they function through non-functioning; they have no name, yet they function through every kind of functioning. All is empty, even emptiness itself is empty.
To illuminate and penetrate this emptiness is called "thoroughly penetrating the emptiness of all dharmas. Emptiness and emptiness are suchness; their characteristics cannot be apprehended.
When the essence of purity is brilliantly manifested, it is called "penetrating illumination.

Because this bodhisattva’s realized dharma of patience accords with the true nature of all things, they know that within the nature of those natures there is fundamentally neither bondage nor liberation. Consequently, they are able to give rise to the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*):

namely, the unimpeded eloquence of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), by which one can know the various characteristics of dharmas; and the unimpeded eloquence of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), by which one can know...
Regarding the meanings and purports to be expressed, their words reach the mark; they are able to discern the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.

Their skill in teaching and transforming beings reaches its full extent, enabling them to produce various forms of adornment and eloquent discourse. Because their mental wheel (*citta-cakra*) has attained thorough penetration, their verbal wheel (*vāk-cakra*) is unimpeded.

This is because they have already realized that the causes and effects of the three periods of time, as well as the faculties, natures, karmic actions, and behaviors of all sentient beings, are all entirely identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Neither combined nor separate, fundamentally there are no real dharmas; thus, one can employ the non-existent as a function, thereby making an exposition that accords with wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, fundamentally there are no names; thus, one can employ function as a function, thereby making an exposition that accords with sentiment (*ruci*).
In this way, whether reality or name, all are empty; the wisdom that realizes emptiness is also empty. To illuminate and penetrate this stage...
The principle of the emptiness of a single meaning is called the thorough penetration of the emptiness of all dharmas.

The wisdom of that "emptiness of emptiness" and the principle of suchness—both their characteristics are ungraspable. This may also be specifically correlated with the dedication that reaches everywhere (*sarvatragatā-pariṇāmanā*);
this penetrating illumination is precisely the manifestation of true essence, which is the meaning of the stage being like the Buddha-stage.
△ Five: The Upright Mind.

O Disciples of the Buddha, as for "upright": it means to directly illuminate and grasp the conditions so that the divine self (*ātman*) enters the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). The divine self of ignorance is empty;

within emptiness, even emptiness itself is empty. This mind of the principle of the emptiness of emptiness remains whether in existence or non-existence, yet does not destroy the seeds of the Path within the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The Way is one contemplation, by which one teaches and transforms all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, turning all sentient beings toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
It is emptiness itself, the direct nature, and the direct practice. For those born within the three realms of emptiness, they encounter fetters and bonds yet do not undergo suffering.

Right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness) is called the "direct mind. Since *tathatā* pervades all phenomena and is omnipresent, one employs this direct mind to illuminate and realize that the *ātman* which grasps at conditions enters the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Ignorance refers precisely to this grasping at conditions.
The *ātman* that grasps at conditions is fundamentally empty; even emptiness is itself empty. This constitutes the "double negation" (*ubhayapratipakṣa*), and this emptiness—
The mind of the principle of emptiness abides in both existence and non-existence without destroying the seeds of the Middle Way; this is what is meant by "shining forth both.
By means of this single contemplation of the untainted Middle Way, one teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them all to enter the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
In Sanskrit, this is *sarvajñajñāna*, which is translated here as "the wisdom of all-knowledge. It is called the wisdom of all-knowledge because it is attained within a single moment of mind;

it is the ultimate realization of the fruit. Because one realizes that ignorance and the divine self (*puruṣa*) are fundamentally empty, one attests to the principle of the single reality of the Middle Way.
Thus, internally upholding a direct nature and externally practicing a direct conduct, the internal and external are of one suchness.

Thus, within the triple world—which is like a flower in the sky, a magical illusion, or a dream—though all sentient beings are bound by fetters and may at will sport, appear, or disappear therein, they do not undergo its inversions.
This can also be correlated specifically with the dedication of merit toward the inexhaustible treasury of virtues:
teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they all attain *sarvajñā* (omniscience). This is precisely what is meant by the "Tathāgata of the World."
They interpenetrate one another, attaining freedom from all obstructions.
△ Sixth, the Mind of Non-retrogression:
O Sons of the Buddha, as for the mind of non-retrogression, one does not enter the stage of any ordinary person, nor does one give rise to new growths of [defilements].

Seeing this, one likewise does not give rise to a semblance of a self or person that serves as a cause for accumulation. Entering the karma of the three realms, one practices emptiness without dwelling in or regressing from it.
Because one is liberated through the practice of the unified Middle Way, one does not regress. Since the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is non-dual, one does not even conceive of regression.
The wisdom of contemplation arising from emptiness is suchness; continuing in this vehicle upon vehicle, the mind enters the non-dual and remains eternally so.
Emptiness gives rise to the mind. A single path and a single purity constitute the stage of non-retrogression;

a single path and a single illumination constitute the three stages of non-retrogression. These are accomplished through the wisdom of the three non-retrogressions. The first phrase provides a general heading; "not entering" follows below.
The section beginning with "Specifically explaining the three stages of non-retrogression" (*kōshō*) separately clarifies the wisdom of the three non-retrogressions.

The section beginning with "Constantly empty" (*jōkū*) concludes that the three wisdoms are cultivated within a single mind; it is the realization of these three stages within a single mind. Thus, one does not enter the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
This is the fruit of non-retrogression in this stage. Not giving rise to new, nurtured views such as those of a self or a person is the cause of non-retrogression in this stage.
"New" refers to when a practitioner, having already subdued their fundamental afflictions (*kleśas*), enters *dhyāna*;
yet, if within that *dhyāna* they do not observe skillfully and instead give rise to the habitual tendencies of craving and views, it is called "new. Now, one skillfully cultivates non-retrogression.
Because of this, past delusions are extinguished and new delusions do not arise; the two habitual tendencies of views and craving are both completely stilled.
Although one manifests entry into the karma of the triple world, one constantly practices the principle of emptiness; thus, one attains the stage of non-retrogression.
What is called "non-abiding retrogression" is precisely the stage of non-retrogression. Although this stage of non-retrogression appears to be shared with the two vehicles, [it is distinct].
However, how could those of the Two Vehicles ever enter the karma of the triple world? Thus we know that the stage of the Perfect [Teaching] is preeminent. This emptiness is not merely empty;

it suffices simply to clarify this one kind of non-retrogression, which already transcends the realm of the provisional and the small vehicles, let alone fully clarifying the three kinds of non-retrogression.
Next, we clarify the liberation realized therein: it proceeds by unifying with the primary Middle Way. It does not...

Because they share the same liberation as those of the two vehicles, they do not regress from their practice. Next, they clearly understand that the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of birth and death is the original limit of nirvāṇa;
the original limit of afflictions (*kleśa*) is the original limit of awakening (*bodhi*). There are no two distinct limits.

Moment by moment, they are constantly in accord with the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and thus they do not conceive of regression. This constitutes the three non-regressions; its underlying principle is profoundly deep.

This is truly because it is realized through the three wisdoms. The arising of emptiness within contemplative wisdom is suchness; this is the wisdom of non-retrogression in stage (*avasthā-avaivartika-jñāna*).

Continuously riding upon the Mahāyāna is the wisdom of non-retrogression in practice (*caryā-avaivartika-jñāna*). The mind entering the fundamental limit of non-duality is the wisdom of non-retrogression in mindfulness (*smṛti-avaivartika-jñāna*).
Cultivating these three wisdoms within a single moment of mind is called the "mind that constantly gives rise to emptiness. This is...
This is the meaning of the arising of the mind from non-abiding. Skillfully accords with the essence of the mind and is called "the One Way.

It is unstained by the two extremes and is called "the One Purity. This constitutes the non-retrogressive "One Way" and "One Illumination," which is the ultimate realization of the identity of principle and wisdom (*jñāna*).
This may also be correlated separately with the dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality; that is, regarding sameness...

Within the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), each gives rise to the causes for purity and takes up the path to *nirvāṇa*; thus, one is able to perfectly realize the principle of the three non-regressions (*tri-avaivartika*).

However, if these three non-regressions are categorized according to their respective stages: in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-dharma*), the non-regression of position (*sthānāvaivartika*) occurs at the seventh abode (*vihāra*).

Non-retrogression in practice occurs at the stage of the ten dedications; non-retrogression in mindfulness occurs at the Stage of Joy. In the Perfect Teaching, non-retrogression in position occurs at the first stage of faith;
non-retrogression in practice occurs at the tenth stage of mind; and non-retrogression in mindfulness occurs at the Abiding in the Arising of the Mind.
These are now explained together in order to correctly reveal the meaning of the roots of goodness that accord with equality.
△ 7. The Mahāyāna Mind.

O Sons of the Buddha, as for those who possess only the Mahāyāna mind: because they understand and understand that all is one emptiness, all practices of the mind are called the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
One mounts the vehicle of empty wisdom—the vehicle of wisdom, the vehicle of practice, and the vehicle of the mind of wisdom. This mind serves as a vessel for carrying and employing;
it carries and employs [the path] by ferrying all sentient beings across the river of the three realms, the river of the bonds of afflictions, and the river of birth and cessation.

The practitioner sits upon this vehicle and employs its capacity to carry and employ the vehicle of wisdom, thereby entering the ocean of the Buddhas. Therefore, as long as all sentient beings have not yet attained the employment of the wisdom of emptiness, they are not so named.
Regarding the Mahāyāna, it is merely called a "vehicle" because it enables one to cross the ocean of suffering;
there is only the single Buddha-vehicle, neither two nor three. Having spontaneously realized the path to Buddhahood, one transforms all others so that they too may attain Buddhahood;
therefore, it is called the "exclusive Mahāyāna mind. This refers to the ultimate understanding, whether it be the understanding of the two vehicles or the understanding of the bodhisattvas.

All return to the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). To penetrate this ultimate emptiness of the final truth is why all practices and minds are termed the "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*);
that is, they ride upon the single emptiness of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Furthermore, this mind of the Great Vehicle alone is called the "Vehicle of Wisdom" and also the "Vehicle of Practice," because one rides upon this knowledge of all modes.
This mind is capable of carrying all sentient beings and capable of leading them toward the ocean of Buddhahood;
therefore, it is named the Vehicle of Wisdom and the Vehicle of Practice. What is meant by "capable of carrying"?

It means to bear the burden of sentient beings, causing them to cross the river of the fruits of suffering within the triple world, the river of the fetters of afflictions and karma, and the river of the arising and ceasing of ignorance. And this...
The practitioner does not dwell on either of the two shores, nor does he abide in the middle of the stream; he constantly sits upon this vehicle and proceeds to deliver others across.

For this reason, it is called the "vehicle of practice. What is meant by "employment"? It means that all sentient beings being carried [by this vehicle] are made to employ the vehicle of wisdom, so that they may all enter the ocean of the Buddhas, and not allow even a single person to fall into the stage of the two vehicles. For this reason...

This is called the Vehicle of Wisdom. Therefore, if among all sentient beings there is even one person who has not yet attained the functional application of this wisdom of emptiness, it cannot be called the Mahāyāna; it is merely called a "vehicle," serving only to cross over the ocean of suffering.
This, in turn, reveals that the mind of the Mahāyāna alone is necessarily able to contemplate all sentient beings equally, delivering them all through the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
That the wisdom of emptiness is freely employed is precisely the Middle Way responding to its fundamental source.
This is precisely the meaning of "the mind arising from non-abiding. If one does not enable sentient beings to attain this path together, it cannot be called the Mahāyāna.
Not only do the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas lack this great mind, but even the Buddhas of the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) teachings ultimately end in the cessation of ashes and extinction;
thus, they also cannot be said to possess the unique Mahāyāna mind. This may also be applied specifically to other cases.
It is the dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings.
△ Eighth, the markless mind:
O Disciples of the Buddha, as for the markless mind, it is liberation from deluded thoughts; it illuminates the Prajñāpāramitā as non-dual and one.

All conditioned karma and the dharmas of the three periods of time are, in their suchness, the single truth. Yet one practices within the emptiness of non-arising; thus, one knows for oneself that one shall attain Buddhahood.
All Buddhas are my teachers, and all worthy ones and sages are my fellow students, for all are identical in the emptiness of non-arising.
This is called the signless mind.
There is no characteristic of birth and death; no characteristic of nirvāṇa; no characteristic of affliction; no characteristic of bodhi;
no characteristic of the differentiation of the ten realms; and no characteristic of the equality of the ten realms. This is called the signless mind.
Therefore, whether it be delusive conceptualization or liberation, when illuminated by the prajñāpāramitā, they are both non-dual. All fetters and karmas—[the third...]

All worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*) are, in their very essence, suchness (*tathatā*), the single truth (*ekam satyam*). "Bondage" (*bandhana*) refers to afflictions and delusions; these delusions are themselves *prajñā*.
"Karma" (*karman*) refers to wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable karma with outflows (*sāsrava*); this karma is itself liberation (*vimukti*).

Regarding the phenomena of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—the bitter fruits of suffering within the triple world (*tridhātu*) are themselves the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the secret treasury of the three virtues, the sole reality-principle, and the wondrous suchness.
Wisdom is called the wisdom of the emptiness of non-arising. Practicing within this wisdom, one clearly knows for oneself that one will become a Buddha;
the Buddhas are my teachers, and the noble sages are my fellow students, because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas together cultivate and realize this emptiness of non-arising.
This may also be applied specifically to the dedication toward the characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*); it is the thought of liberation as non-dual. What...
This refers to all phenomena as suchness, the single truth, which is to say: being free from all marks and practicing the emptiness of non-arising;
that is to say, there is no attachment to either "being" or "leaving."
△ Ninth, the Mind of Wisdom.
O Sons of the Buddha: As for the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*), within the immeasurable *dharmadhātu*, there is no accumulation and no taking up of birth.
Though afflictions arise in every birth, they do not bind. It is the path traversed by all worthies and the dharma contemplated by all sages among all gateways to the teachings.
It is also thus with existence. All the Buddha’s teachings on the skillful means of conversion, I have gathered entirely within my mind.

As for all the treatises of the non-Buddhists, the illusory workings of those fixed in false determination, and what is spoken by Māras and what is spoken by Buddhas—all these are analyzed and categorized according to the two truths.
It is neither one nor two; it is not comprised of the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases. It is the radiance of wisdom. This radiance illuminates the nature and enters into all phenomena.

Although the essence of this wisdom that initiates progress toward the middle way is known as "mind" (*citta*), because its entry into the meaning of emptiness is predominant, it is designated here as "wisdom of emptiness."
It nurtures middle-way wisdom (*madhyamā-prajñā*). Although it also gives rise to the mind of non-arising (*anutpāda-citta*), its emphasis lies on the provisional meaning;

therefore, it is called "the mind that acts through wisdom-vision" (*prajñā-darśana-citta*). Now, this [passage] correctly reveals the wisdom that accords with the Middle Way; therefore, it is called "suchness-wisdom" (*tathatā-prajñā*).

This wisdom does not fall into ordinary sentiment, nor does it cling to the conceptual understanding of the sages. What is meant by "not falling into ordinary sentiment"? It refers to the realization of the immeasurable.
The Dharma-realm has no one who accumulates [karma], nor does it have anyone who undergoes rebirth.
Although there appear to be afflictions that arise incessantly, in reality, they do not bind. What is meant by "not clinging to noble understanding"? It refers to all dharma-gates.
That which is practiced by the wise and observed by the noble—so too are all phenomena likewise unbound and unattached.
Since one is forever without attachment to both the mundane and the noble dharmas, one is able to skillfully employ all such dharmas;
thus, all the expedient means of the Buddhas' teachings are gathered within the mind, even including external treatises and heterodox concentrations. All of these...

This is the section on the discernment of the two truths (*satya*). That is to say, the Buddha-dharma is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while Māra and non-Buddhists are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, the distinction between Māra and the Buddha is the conventional truth, whereas the oneness of Māra and the Buddha is the ultimate truth.

Because the ultimate does not contradict the conventional, they are not one; because the conventional does not contradict the ultimate, they are not two. Once this principle is realized, even the five aggregates (*skandha*) are not aggregates. [The ten...]
The eight elements (*dhātu*) are also not elements; the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are also not bases. They are pure from the very beginning, being solely the radiance of true wisdom.
This radiance illuminates the nature and universally enters into all phenomena; this is what is called truly attaining that which is as-it-is (*tathatā*), unimpeded throughout the ten directions.
Therefore, it may also be specifically correlated with the dedication of merit toward liberation without bondage.

△ Ten Unbreakable Minds. O Disciples of the Buddha, as for those with unbreakable minds: they enter the wisdom of the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*); they draw near to the state of liberation; they attain the true gateway to the Way; they clarify the bodhicitta;
through the patience of subduing (*kṣānti*), they accord with emptiness; the eight māras cannot break them; the various sages touch their heads, and all Buddhas exhort and inspire them to enter.
The Samādhi of Touching the Crown of the Head emits bodily radiance; this light illuminates the lands of the ten directions.

Entering the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, one appears and disappears with sovereign ease, shaking the great trichiliocosm. This is non-dual and indistinguishable from the mind of the ground of equality, yet it is not the path of the Middle Way.
By the power of samādhi, within the light he beholds Buddhas in immeasurable lands appearing and preaching the Dharma for him.

At that time, he immediately attains the *mūrdhan-samādhi* (Crown Samādhi) and realizes the *dhāraṇī* gate of the stage of the equality of space. His noble practices (*ārya-caryā*) become fulfilled; mind after mind acts within emptiness.
Because the Middle Way of non-characteristic (*animitta*) is illuminated within the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness, all marks (*nimitta*) are extinguished, and he attains the *vajra-samādhi*.
This is the Dharma-gate. It is the entrance into all gates of practice; it is the entrance into the ground of the equality of space.
The ten adamantine minds all take "indestructibility" as their meaning. This one stands at the very end, uniquely receiving the name "indestructible.
This mind is precisely the wisdom capable of entering the noble grounds; it has already approached the stage of liberation and attained the middle way.
It is the true gate of the Way. Entering the wisdom of the noble stages is the virtue of *prajñā*. Approaching the stage of liberation is the virtue of *vimukti*.
Attaining the true gate of the Way is the virtue of *dharmakāya*. Entering the wisdom of the noble stages clarifies the *bodhi* of ultimate reality-wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Approaching the stage of liberation clarifies the *bodhi* of skillful means (*upāya*). Attaining the true gate of the Way clarifies the true nature (*tathatā*).

Bodhi. Furthermore, entering the wisdom of the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*) clarifies the mind of wisdom regarding the causal factor; being close to the stage of liberation clarifies the virtuous mind regarding the contributory cause;
and attaining the correct gateway to the Path clarifies the mind of principle regarding the direct cause. Therefore, it is called the "Clarifying Bodhicitta.

This constitutes the ultimate stage of the preparatory forbearance (*kṣānti*) prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), which accords with the principle of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). First...

First is the emptiness of meaning (*artha-śūnyatā*). Because one does not abide in saṃsāra, one cannot be destroyed by the four māras within the realm—namely, the aggregate-māra (*skandha-māra*), the affliction-māra (*kleśa-māra*), the death-māra (*mṛtyu-māra*), and the celestial-māra (*devaputra-māra*).
Because one does not abide in nirvāṇa, one cannot be destroyed by the four māras outside the realm—namely, suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity.
All the sages, both partial and complete, simultaneously touch the crown of one’s head; all the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise [bestow their blessing].

He exhorted him, whereupon [the latter] entered the *mōdō* (crown-of-the-head) samādhi. He emitted light that shone everywhere and was able to enter the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*vīrya*), appearing and disappearing with sovereign ease.
He could shake the great trichiliocosm, remaining as solemn and indistinguishable from those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) as any of them;

yet he was still not called one of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*). This was because he was still at the level of "patience through suppression" (*kṣānti-vinaya*) and still belonged to the stage of "semblance" (*pratirūpaka*) contemplation, rather than being established in the true [path].
This is because one truly knows the Way through the Middle Way Contemplation (*madhyamaka*).

However, by the power of the *mou-ding* (crowning the head) samādhi, one sees the Buddha and hears the Dharma within the light, and immediately attains entry into the *zhengding* (crowning the head) samādhi.

Among the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), this is the most honored and supreme, comparable to what the Tripitaka teachings call the "Stage of the World's First Peak" (*laukikāgradharma*). Having entered this stage, one immediately realizes the equality of empty space without interval.
The stages and gates of the earth encompass all phenomena and sustain all meanings. One realizes that all phenomena are the self-nature of the mind;
their inherent merits manifest spontaneously, and the wondrous practice of non-action is fulfilled in this very moment.
Yet, the reason a Bodhisattva is able to abandon the mundane and enter the sacred is precisely due to the Dharma-gates of the thirty mental states (*citta*), wherein every thought-moment is...

One practices the principle of emptiness. By means of this wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness, because the Middle Way illuminates the signless, all phenomena (*nimitta*) are entirely quiescent and extinguished.
Thus, one is able to attain this gate of the Vajra-samādhi, enter all gates of practice, and enter the stage of the equality of empty space.
This may also be correlated specifically with the infinite turnings of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As previously stated, when the nature-virtues are perfectly fulfilled and the dimensions of the dharma-realm cease, this is the meaning of true indestructibility.
△ Third, the summary reference:
as explained in detail in the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the ten stages (bhūmi) has two parts: first, a general inquiry; second, a detailed exposition. Now, the first:
Vairocana Buddha said, "O thousand Buddhas, listen attentively! Regarding what you previously asked about the 'stages,' what is their meaning?"
Above, it bears the Buddha-dharma; below, it bears sentient beings. It is that toward which merit and wisdom converge, and from which compassion and skillful means arise;

therefore, it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*). Specifically, the ground of equalizing wisdom is the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), up to the entry into the Buddha-realm, which is the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
In its totality, these ten grounds range from the Ground of Joy to the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud. This is the Ground.
The stages (bhūmi) all fully possess the meaning of equality; they possess the meaning of excellent wisdom; they possess the meaning of radiance; they possess the meaning of *jvālā* (flame);
they possess the meaning of the illumination of wisdom; they possess the meaning of the light of flowers; they possess the meaning of fulfillment; they possess the meaning of the Buddha’s roar;

they possess the meaning of the adornment of flowers; and they possess the meaning of the Buddha-realm. Furthermore, principle (*li*) is itself equality, up to and including ultimate equality. Principle is itself the Buddha.

From the realm of the elements up to the ultimate Buddha-realm, the intermediate stages should be understood by analogy. Now, for the sake of convenience, this shall be explained briefly in terms of the partially realized Dharma-body.

As for the relationship between one stage and all stages, or all stages and one stage—wherein the sequential progression and the perfect interpenetration mutually illuminate one another without obstruction—those who enter these stages shall know it for themselves.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the ten stages. First, the Stage of the Nature of Equal Wisdom (up to) the tenth, the Stage of Entering the Buddha-realm. Now, the first:
O Sons of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva enters the stage of the essential nature of equal wisdom, they are transformed by the true Dharma;

the radiant flowers of all practices are fully perfected. They employ the fruition-vehicle of the four heavens, transforming beings without fixed direction through rational transformation and supernatural powers, as well as the ten powers.

The ten titles, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), dwelling in the Buddha’s pure land, immeasurable great vows, eloquence, fearlessness, all treatises, and all practices—I have entered them all.

Born into the family of the Buddhas and seated upon the stage of the Buddhas’ nature, I shall ultimately never again undergo the causes and effects of ordinary beings or any hindrances. With great joy and bliss, I enter from one buddha-field into immeasurable others.
The Buddha-land. From one kalpa, they enter immeasurable kalpas; they take that which is inexpressible and make it expressible. They reflect back to perceive all dharmas;
they perceive all dharmas both in their inverse and their natural order. They constantly enter the two truths while remaining within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
With a single wisdom, they know the sequence of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), manifesting each and every matter to sentient beings, while always abiding in the Middle Way within the mind of the mind.
With a single wisdom, one knows the various qualities of all Buddha-lands and the teachings expounded by the Buddhas, yet the body and mind remain unchanged.
With a single wisdom, one knows the twelve links of dependent origination and the natures of the ten non-virtuous actions, yet remains constantly established in the good paths.

With the wisdom of omniscience, one perceives the two aspects of existence and non-existence. With a single wisdom, one knows the entry into the branches of the ten dhyānas and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, yet manifests them.
All physical bodies within the six realms are known by a single wisdom that discerns every form and every part throughout the ten directions.

One clearly understands the arising of entry into the retribution of form, yet mind after mind remains unbound. Light upon light illuminates all; therefore, there is the patient acceptance of non-arising and the wisdom of emptiness.
It is constantly present before me. From the first bhūmi and the second bhūmi, up to the realm of the Buddhas, all the dharma-gates within that interval are practiced simultaneously.
Therefore, I have briefly set forth this ocean-treasury of practices and vows of the stage of equality, which is like a single drop from the sea or a mere hair-tip of its contents.

Regarding the designation "the stage of the equality of essence" mentioned in the previous title, this establishes a position based on principle and also reveals that cultivation arises entirely from the nature.

Now, this name "entering the stage of the essence of equalizing wisdom" subsumes the positions back into the essence and also reveals that all cultivation resides within the nature. This stage is born from true reality itself.

Because of the transformation through the Dharma, all the flowers and lights of the various practices are entirely fulfilled. The "flowers" symbolize liberation, which is the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*);

the "lights" symbolize *prajñā*, which is the practice of wisdom (*jñāna-caryā*). Although both of these two practices are present within the thirty moments of mind, [they are here specifically distinguished].

However, while the previous understanding and practice were merely semblances, this is now the true transformation through the Dharma. That is to say, it is the direct Dharmakāya, not [a mere] Dharmakāya;

for the Dharmakāya must necessarily possess two virtues (guṇas) to be called "fulfillment according to its nature" (xing manzu). Having realized the three virtues and the three bodies (trikāya), [one attains this fulfillment].
One is immediately able to manifest [forms] at will and attain the fruit of Buddhahood in the fourth dhyāna heaven.

By means of the function of this Great Wisdom of Equality, one spontaneously teaches and transforms beings without fixed direction or limit. All such supernormal powers and transformations do not depend on deliberate mental effort;

they arise solely from the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). This is called "supernormal power through the transformation of principle" (*li-hua shentong*), which is what is meant by the term "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).

"Transformation and further transformation" refers to the supernatural power of manifestation (*nirmāṇa*). Regarding the "four heavens," it may refer to the fourth heaven of the desire realm, the Tuṣita Palace—as in the case of the thousands of billions of Śākyamunis and others—or it may refer to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven of the fourth dhyāna—as in the case of the thousand Śākyamunis and others.
Because these bodhisattvas of the first stage have already attained the Middle Way in accordance with their original vows, they are all able to manifest [these forms] up to...
The ten powers, the ten titles, and the eighteen unique qualities are all fully perfected at once.

One dwells securely in the land of true recompense free from obstacles, and likewise partially realizes the land of eternal quiescent light. In short, regarding all the merits of the Buddha-ground, such as great vows and eloquence, I have entered them all;
having abandoned the nature of an ordinary being and entered the nature of a Tathāgata, there is great bliss and joy. Therefore, it is also...
This is called the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Knowing that the Buddha-lands are equal and devoid of intrinsic nature, the one is the infinite;
thus, one can pervade the ten directions horizontally. Knowing that time and kalpas are likewise equal and devoid of intrinsic nature, the infinite is the one;
thus, one can exhaust the three periods of time vertically. Having thoroughly realized the ineffable *dharmatā*, one skillfully [employs] the four *siddhāntas* through various causes and conditions.
Through skillful means, he teaches for the sake of sentient beings without turning his back on the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
To know that all phenomena are the very nature and virtue of the Middle Way is called "reflective insight" (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*); to know that all phenomena are empty is called "contrary vision";

and to know that all phenomena are merely provisional designations is called "conformable vision. Prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), one practices the Middle Way with an upward gaze, still considering it to transcend the two extremes; now, one knows the Middle...
Because the Way pervades all phenomena, it constantly enters the two truths; yet it resides precisely within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Thus, one realizes that phenomena and principle are identical, and for this reason, the events of the ten stages are manifested to sentient beings while the mind remains in the Middle Way at every moment.
One realizes that differentiation is itself non-differentiation; therefore, although the Buddha-lands and the teachings therein appear in diverse forms, the body and mind remain unchanging.

One deeply penetrates that inherent evil is itself inherent goodness. Thus, one knows that although there are the ten evil paths of causes and conditions, they are eternally abiding in the path of goodness.

Illuminating simultaneously the two aspects of existence and non-existence is called "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñā*); therefore, it is not a partial emptiness. Although one practices the supramundane path, [one remains within the mundane].
Yet they do not abide in nirvana; therefore, they manifest bodies of all forms throughout the six realms.
They are skillfully able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena, yet remain unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Thus, although they understand the place of origin, the place of entry, and the place of receiving retribution for every form and every limb, their minds are unbound at every moment, and their radiance illuminates all things. This is realization.

In the stage of non-retrogression through mindfulness, one enters the path of effortlessness; thus, the emptiness-wisdom of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena is constantly present before one.
Within a single stage, one penetrates the dharma-gates of all stages, and is therefore able to practice them simultaneously.
This is because, although the paths of teaching differ, the path of realization is equally perfected; hence, the ocean-treasury of merit cannot be fully described in words.
This concludes the [eighth stage].
△ Second, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
If, O Sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva’s stage of the essence and nature of excellent intelligence is pure and clearly penetrates all roots of goodness.
What are called compassion (*maitrī*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are the foundation of all merit.

Entering from contemplation into the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga-jñāna*) within the wisdom of great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā-prajñā*), one perceives that among all sentient beings there is none who is not the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). All possess a conscious mind;

consciousness arises within the conditions of all the afflictions of the three evil realms, such as blades and weapons, and this is termed the Truth of Suffering. As for the characteristics of the three types of suffering, they are like the body itself.
Initial cognition arises from two conditions—the weapon and the physical aggregate (rūpa-skandha)—and thus serves as the condition for the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkha).

Subsequently, mental cognition takes the object of that bodily cognition as its own object; by apprehending phenomena such as the weapon and the bodily wound or swelling, it constitutes the condition for the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkha).
Because it is heavy, it is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Next, there are the two mental states of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).

Because they take as their object the physical aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*)—which is like a festering wound—and give rise to the perception of suffering, they are called the conditions for the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). Thus, because these three perceptions arise in succession within the three mental states, they constitute the suffering of suffering.
All sentient beings who possess a mind perceive these three sufferings and thereby give rise to immeasurable causes and conditions for affliction; therefore, I...

Within this state, he enters the Samādhi of Entering the Path of Transformation and manifests all physical forms. Amidst the six realms of existence, through ten kinds of eloquence, he expounds various Dharma-gates:
namely, that consciousness of suffering arises from the conditions of suffering; that weapons and implements serve as its conditions; that the consciousness of suffering acts upon the body;

that it causes sores and swellings to erupt and溃烂 (fester); and that within internal and external contacts, whether conditions are complete or incomplete, consciousness arises when two conditions are present—consciousness acting as consciousness.

Feeling, contact, and consciousness are termed the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkhānupaśyanā*). Because they function as two conditions, the mind and its mental factors take form as their object; the mind’s contact brings about affliction.

When feeling experiences the poison of distress, this is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). When the mind takes consciousness as its object, initially abiding in the sense faculties and perceiving conditions, this is termed the perception of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*).

When the mind acts upon the mind and receives feeling, and contact and consciousness perceive that touch before the poison of distress has been experienced, this is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). It is like the arising of a perception through oppression.
Like sparks struck from stone, within the body and mind, moments arise and perish in succession. The body disperses, decays, and undergoes transformation;

consciousness enters into decaying conditions, and those conditions gather and disperse. The mind suffers and is distressed; as it perceives subsequent objects, it becomes defiled by attachment, and moment after moment, it does not let go. This is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

Regarding all truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the three realms, one further contemplates the accumulation of ignorance: the immeasurable mind creates all karma, and its characteristics [manifest].

The continuous succession of accumulated causes is called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Right view, liberation, emptiness of emptiness, wisdom, the path, and the mind-moments are termed the Path of Wisdom;
this is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). The exhaustion of karmic retribution and the exhaustion of its causes constitute the pure, singular illumination of the essence of wondrous wisdom.

This is the single truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). When the category of wisdom is fully perfected, it is called the "faculty" (*indriya*); all wisdom-natures arise from emptiness and enter into contemplation.
This is the first root of goodness. Second is contemplation: relinquishing all attachment and practicing universal equanimity and emptiness;
observing without a focal point that the limit of emptiness of all phenomena is of a single characteristic.

I contemplate all the earth and soil of the ten directions as the very soil used by my former bodies; the waters of the four great oceans are my former water; and all the fires of the kalpas are my former...
The fire that was used by my physical body and all the wind-circles were the breaths used by my former self. Now that I have entered this earth-element, my Dharma-body is fulfilled;
I cast off my former body and shall ultimately never again receive a defiled, segmented body composed of the four great elements.
This is the fulfillment of the Chapter on Renunciation. Thirdly, one contemplates all sentient beings to be transformed, as well as human beings.

The joy of the heavens; the joy of the ten stages; the joy of being free from the fear of the ten non-virtues; the joy of attaining the *Sukhāvatī* (Wondrous Flower) Samādhi; and even the joy of the Buddhas.
One who contemplates in this way is fully endowed with the category of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). At that time, the Bodhisattva dwells within this stage, free from delusion and free from greed.
Free from anger, one enters the wisdom of the single truth of equality, which is the root of all practices.
One traverses all Buddha-worlds and manifests immeasurable transformation-dharmakāyas, as described in the "Chapter on the Celestial Flowers of All Sentient Beings."

This section on the "Son" is divided into three parts. First, from "Bodhi... onwards, the fundamental roots of virtue are generally indicated. Second, from "From contemplation... onwards, the three types of contemplation are explained.

Third, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva... onwards, the manifestation of virtuous function is concluded and revealed. Regarding the first part, the term "Good Wisdom" (Sādhumatī) is used as follows:

This stage is also called "Free from Defilement. Defilement is that which is abandoned; wisdom is that which abandons it. Furthermore, defilement is that which is to be remedied; goodness is the remedy.
By means of wholesome wisdom, one is freed from defilement and impurity; because defilement is abandoned, the roots of goodness become pure.
Because wisdom is clear, one's former roots of goodness become bright and penetrating. When it says "all," this refers to the ten wholesome dharmas;

these are the foundation of the five vehicles, as explained in detail in the second bhūmi of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Furthermore, these ten wholesome deeds do not transcend the five categories of contemplation, such as compassion and so forth.
Next, regarding the explanation of the three categories of contemplation: they serve as remedies for the three poisons of delusion, greed, and hatred.
This is fundamental. Since the three poisons are the source of the ten non-virtuous actions, they must be treated with the three grades of sublime contemplation.

When the category of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is fully realized, compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) are inherently contained within it. These are further divided into three; first, the category of wisdom (*prajñā*) is explained.
Next, the Chapter on Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is explained; following that, the Chapter on Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is explained. Within the first [chapter], there are three parts:

the phrase "From contemplation, entering the wisdom of great emptiness through the skillful means of the path of knowledge" serves as the general heading; "Seeing all sentient beings... and so forth serves as the detailed explanation;

and "The Chapter on Wisdom is complete... and so forth serves as the concluding summary. Within the heading, it is generally clarified that by the power of contemplative practice, one enters the essence of the wisdom of great emptiness and gives rise to...

The functional application of the wisdom of the path of skillful means consists in fully contemplating the Four Truths of the three realms. Next, the four [truths] are explained in detail: first, contemplating the truth of suffering;

second, contemplating the truth of origination; third, contemplating the truth of the path; and fourth, contemplating the truth of cessation. Regarding the first, the contemplation of the truth of suffering:
it refers to the fact that all sentient beings possess a conscious mind, and they [experience it] within the three evil realms and...

From various weapons and implements, up to all conditions of suffering for humans and devas, the consciousness that arises experiencing such suffering is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
This Truth of Suffering possesses three characteristics; these three characteristics of suffering exist throughout the entire triple world (*tridhātu*).
Now, to provide an illustration based on matters easily perceived before one’s eyes, it is said:
Regarding "as it is": for instance, when the body has not yet contacted an object, there is an original nature of cognitive awareness;
this is the fifth consciousness, the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*). From the two conditions of the weapon or staff and the aggregate of bodily form (*rūpaskandha*), cognitive awareness arises.

Before it has received the poison of affliction, it serves as the condition for the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*); subsequently, the awareness on the mental ground is the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Taking this body as the object of perception, one encounters weapons and staves, as well as phenomena such as physical sores and swellings, thereby fully experiencing affliction and poison;
thus, one perceives the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) as its condition. Because the distress is heavy, it is called the suffering of suffering.

Next, from the perception of the suffering of sensation (*vedanā-duḥkhatā*) and the perception of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), these two mental states take as their objects the previously mentioned physical form-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) that has been broken and wounded, and further arise therein.

The sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) is termed the condition for the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*). The sensation of suffering arises simultaneously with what is induced by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The sensation of conditioned suffering (*saṃskāraduḥkha*) is that which is induced by the five bodily consciousnesses (*kāyavijñāna*).

Therefore, because the three sensations—the subsequent bodily sensation, the sensation of the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), and the sensation of formations (*saṃskāra*)—successively give rise to the three minds of the suffering of formations, the suffering of suffering, and the suffering of change, [they are so designated].

Collectively, these are termed the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Within the context of the three types of sensation (*vedanā*), this explains the three sufferings by way of the sensation of suffering alone.

Furthermore, within the sensation of suffering, it is designated as the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) at the time of its arising, and as the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) at the time of its abiding.

The moment of cessation is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). In reality, however, these three types of suffering pervade all three times, as well as all three feelings, and even all three realms.
When all sentient beings encounter these states of the three sufferings, they fail to comprehend their causes and do not understand their conditions;
thus, they become increasingly deluded and give rise to immeasurable further causes and conditions for suffering. This is indeed so.
Filled with compassion and pity, he intentionally enters the Samādhi of the Path of Transformation through the Wheel of Mind. Through the Wheel of Body, he universally manifests all physical forms;
through the Wheel of Speech, he expounds various Dharma gates with ten inexhaustible eloquences. What Dharma does he teach?

He teaches that for all sentient beings, suffering-consciousness is the root, which arises from the conditions of suffering. When they encounter the conditions of weapons and staves, they experience the touch of suffering.
The body, which is the object of the activity of consciousness, becomes inflamed and溃烂 (festers and breaks open).

Although there may be internal contact within the mind or external contact through the five sense organs—whether these are sometimes complete or incomplete—as long as the two conditions of the faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) are present, a discriminating consciousness arises.
Since this is originally produced by consciousness and consciousness itself experiences it, this very consciousness that perceives the touch is called suffering (*duḥkha*).

Consciousness (vijñāna) arises from the two conditions of the sense-faculties and their objects. When the mind and its mental states take form as their object, the mental factor of contact (sparśa) associated with that mind encounters a painful or harmful object.
At the time one experiences such afflictive poison, it constitutes the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā).

The consciousness that cogitates within that mind, first situated at the gateway of the faculties, perceives the objective condition; this is termed the "perception of suffering" (duḥkha-vedanā). It fundamentally originates from the activity of the mind.

The mind then experiences it for itself; that is, through contact and consciousness, one perceives the object of touch before yet experiencing the poison of affliction—this is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

Due to the pressure of objective conditions, there further arise discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), arising and ceasing moment by moment like sparks struck from stone, without pausing even slightly.
Since the body is already subject to disintegration and transformation, that consciousness enters into conditions of decay.

Within this, as these conditions arise, suffer, and disperse, one experiences mental distress and affliction; yet the mind remains attached to subsequent conditions, never relinquishing them from thought to thought.
This is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). This is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of all three realms.
Second, regarding the contemplation of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself the Truth of Origination. That is to say, by means of immeasurable...

The ignorant and defiled mind performs all tainted (sāsrava) karma of wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable (āniñjya) types, serving as the cause for the continuous succession of the six realms of existence.
This very cause of accumulation is truly the cause of suffering; there is no other cause. This is called the Truth of Accumulation (samudaya-satya).
"Succession" means that there is no interruption between preceding and succeeding moments, referring to the period from beginningless time until the present.
"Constantly revolving like a wheel" means that they are interconnected; one is all. This refers to the causes and effects of the six realms of existence, which mutually entangle one another.

Regarding the "threefold contemplation of the Truth of the Path": by means of right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), one destroys the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, all karmas are liberated and the retributive fruits become empty and void.
There remains only the path of wisdom, manifesting moment after moment before the mind. This is called the "Truth of the Path as the Path of Wisdom. This is the Truth of the Path.

Although there are many [qualities], wisdom is foremost. "The path of the mind of wisdom" (*zhidao xinxin*) refers to the mind that knows the path of wisdom. Regarding the fourfold contemplation of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*):
it exhausts the retributive fruits of all existence (*bhava*) and exhausts the causes for the arising of all existence;

it is solely the wondrous wisdom of the essence-nature of pure, singular illumination, which is named the Single Truth of Quiescent Extinction (*śānta-ekasatya*). As for the phrase "wondrous wisdom of the essence-nature":
It is the immovable wisdom (acala-jñāna) that is inherently complete. Purity is the virtue of liberation (vimukti-guṇa). This single illumination is the virtue of wisdom (prajñā-guṇa).
Its essential nature is the virtue of the Dharma-body (dharma-kāya-guṇa). Regarding "wondrous wisdom" (miao zhi): it is the wisdom that accords with suchness (tathatā).
One speaks of "wisdom" rather than "suchness" because there is no wisdom outside of suchness, and no suchness outside of wisdom. The three concluding summaries refer to suchness.
Contemplating the Four Noble Truths in this manner brings the aggregate of wisdom to fulfillment; this is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

Within the nature of all wisdom, one gives rise to the essence of emptiness and enters into the function of contemplation; this is termed the first root of goodness. Next, the aggregate of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is explained:

by relinquishing the four great elements and realizing the Dharma-body, one is said to fulfill the aggregate of equanimity. Finally, the aggregate of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is explained: it accords with the faculties of sentient beings.

Regarding the nature [of compassion]: it bestows happiness in succession, yet it must ultimately take the bliss of the Buddha as its essential goal; only then is it called the "perfection of the category of loving-kindness.

As for the statement "fearing the ten unwholesome acts": foolish people, being deluded and insane, do not fear evil karma. A bodhisattva at the initial stage deeply fears the ten unwholesome acts, though they have not yet been able to distance themselves from them completely.
From the second bhūmi onward, by means of the wondrous precepts of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), one accords with the undefiled nature.
Being forever free from transgressions, one attains fearlessness and thus achieves great bliss. Regarding the "Samādhi of the Exquisite Flower":

the ten paths of wholesome action in their highest degree constitute the foremost and most exquisite adornment. As for the manifestation of its virtuous functions through the three fetters (*saṃyojana*):

because the category of wisdom (*prajñā*) is perfected, there is no delusion; because the category of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is perfected, there is no greed; and because the category of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is perfected, there is no [hatred].
Absence of hatred; absence of delusion is the virtue of *prajñā*; absence of greed is the virtue of the *dharmakāya*; and absence of hatred is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).
These three virtues are the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*). The three truths are the single truth of equality. The single truth of equality is the one mind with its three wisdoms.
Furthermore, absence of delusion is entry into all practices of emptiness; absence of greed is entry into the one [truth].
All practices of the Middle Way are comprised herein. Non-anger is the entry into all practices involving existence. These three practices are the foundation of the ten thousand practices.
By means of this wisdom-practice, one adorns the two kinds of adornment and is thus able to travel everywhere through the Buddha-realms and manifest transformation bodies everywhere.
Each and every transformation body is both the recompense-body and the dharma-body; the three bodies are one essence, inconceivable, like all sentient beings.
This is explained in the "Chapter on Celestial Flowers," which summarizes the concise and points toward the extensive.
△ Third, the Ground of Radiance:
O Sons of the Buddha, in the Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Essential Nature of Radiance, one knows the three [realms] through the wisdom that understands by means of samādhi.
All the gates of the Buddha’s teachings in the world consist of the twelve divisions of the Dharma:

*sūtra* (discourses), *geya* (versified repetitions), *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies), *gāthā* (verses), *udāna* (inspired utterances), *nidāna* (causal narratives), *avadāna* (parables), *itivṛttaka* (accounts of past events), *jātaka* (birth stories), *vaipulya* (extensive treatises), *adbhutadharma* (marvelous accounts), and *upadeśa* (instructions).

These are the essence, nature, names, and all distinct meanings of the Dharma; within these names, phrases, and sentences, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are explained in their various parts.
Birth: first entering consciousness into the womb; the growth of the four great elements and the development of form and mind is called the six abodes (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Within the sense faculties, the arising of actual cognition, prior to the differentiation of suffering and pleasure, is called contact-consciousness (*sparśa-vijñāna*). Furthermore, the cognition of suffering and pleasure is called the three feelings (*trivedanā*). This involves continuous cognition and attachment.

Suffering is inexhaustible. Through desire, the view of self, and attachment to precepts and rituals, there exist good and evil. The beginning of consciousness is called birth; the end of consciousness is called death.
These ten categories are the causes, conditions, fruits, and results of present suffering. One who contemplates these modes of activity has long since been detached from them;

therefore, they possess no intrinsic nature. Entering into the light, supernormal powers, dhāraṇīs, and eloquence, every thought and mental activity is empty, and thus throughout the ten directions...

Within the Buddha-field, he manifests the transformation of kalpas and the transformation of turning the wheel of Dharma. For hundreds and thousands of kalpas within these lands, he cultivates spiritual powers, pays homage before the Buddhas, and receives their teachings.
He further manifests bodies within the six realms of existence, preaching immeasurable categories of Dharma with a single voice;
yet sentient beings each hear, according to their own respective capacities, the Dharma they desire—namely, suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.

The sounds of the Truths vary according to different lands, and the physical and mental bodies are transformed differently. Within this Ground of Sublime Flower Radiance, I shall briefly open up a space no larger than a hair-tip.
This is as explained in the *Dharmapada* regarding the gate of contemplating the Dharma, and in the *Thousand Samādhis Chapter*.

Regarding the wisdom that understands through samādhi: the wisdom arising from samādhi is called "the emergence of light" (*prabhākara*), as it is said that when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, clarity arises.
It consists of *nāma* (name), *pada* (phrase), and *vyañjana* (syllable); these are also termed *nāma-pada-vyañjana*. Here, *vyañjana* refers to the phoneme (*akṣara*).

A *nāma* expresses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); a *pada* expresses a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). A *vyañjana* is the syllable, serving as the basis for names and phrases. These are the twelve factors (*dvādaśa-dharma*).

Regarding the categories [of the Dharma]: first, the *geya* (repeated verses), which is the *geyā*; second, the *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies), which is the *vyākaraṇa*; third, the *sūtra* (straightforward discourse), which is the *sūtra*;
fourth, the *gāthā* (verses), which is the *udāna* (isolated verse) and is also called *gāthā*; fifth, the *anudharmapada* (unrequested teachings), which is the *svayambhū-bhāṣita* (self-spoken);
sixth, the *vinaya* (discipline/precepts), also called *nidāna* (causal origins), because the precepts are established only upon the occurrence of an occasion for transgression.
Seven: Avadāna (Parables). Eight: Buddhavastu (The Buddha-realm), also called Jātaka (Birth Stories). Nine: Itivṛttaka (Past Events), also called Vṛttaka (Former Deeds). Ten:
Vaipulya (Vast/Correct Teaching), also called Fangguang (Extensive). Eleven: Adbhutadharma (Marvelous Events). Twelve: Upadeśa (Discourses), which refers to treatises (*śāstra*).

Regarding the statement that "the essence of these dharmas is named 'all distinct meanings'": "essence" (*tattva*) refers to the substance itself, namely the written words and the physical scrolls. Furthermore, [it refers to]...
On the other hand, all six sense objects may serve as its substance, as clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). "Nature" (*xing*) refers to the fundamental principle that serves as the basis;
this refers to the three seals of the Hīnayāna: the seal of impermanence and the seal of non-self regarding saṃsāra, and the seal of cessation regarding nirvāṇa.
The Mahāyāna seal of the single true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇamudrā*) is so named because there is no duality between the limits of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
These names are both general and specific; "all meanings" refers to the essence, function, teaching, characteristics, and so forth.

Although immeasurable Dharma-gates are expounded within these names, phrases, and sentences, they do not transcend the ten categories of cause and effect. That is to say, although the dharmas of conditioned birth and existence...
Each stage has its distinct characteristics, yet all without exception possess the ten links. First, entering the womb as consciousness is the link of *vijñāna*.

The growth of the four great elements is called the six stages, which constitute the two links of *nāmarūpa* and *ṣaḍāyatana*. When there is actual awareness but not yet the discrimination between suffering and pleasure, it is called contact-consciousness;
this is the link of *sparśa*. The three types of sensation are the link of *vedanā*. When one continuously perceives and clings to these sensations without end, this is *tṛṣṇā*.
The *upādāna* (clinging) branch arises from a mind of craving and desire, giving rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

The resulting good or evil existence is the *bhava* (becoming) branch. The initial arising of consciousness in a future existence is the *jāti* (birth) branch. The final cessation of that consciousness is death, which is the *jarāmaraṇa* (aging and death) branch.
Excluding the two branches of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), which constitute the past causes, these constitute the ten categories of the present.

These are the fruits of the causal conditions of suffering. Furthermore, these ten categories of shifting and conditioned phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another, nor do they arise from both, nor do they arise without cause; their very substance is emptiness, and their entire form is the conventional.
The whole is itself the Middle. Whether Buddhas appear or do not appear, its nature and characteristics are eternally abiding.
It is not created by devas, humans, asuras, Brahmā, Māra, or non-Buddhists; nor is it created by arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or all Buddhas.

It is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and it is also called the Dharma-position (*dharmasthiti*), the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the Dharma-abiding (*dharmasthiti*), and the profoundly deep Middle Way.

The ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is observed as the Middle Way; thus, one can forever transcend the conditions for birth. Consequently, one realizes that all ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
One thereby enters into the light, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), dhāraṇī, and eloquence (*pratibhāna*). What is meant by "light and supernormal powers"?
It means that although the activities of the mind are empty, one manifests kalpas and transformations within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.

Transformation. This refers to the cultivation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) throughout hundreds and thousands of kalpas. Regarding "transformation through kalpas," it means mastery over the extension or contraction of time.
Regarding "transformative transformation," it means that purity and impurity follow the mind. What is meant by "dhāraṇī and eloquence"? It refers to pervading the realms of the ten directions.

Throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he consulted upon the words of the Dharma above and issued edicts to all sentient beings below. His preaching of the Dharma was not uniform, for his body and mind transformed beings differently.
This section, "The Wondrous Flower," concludes the brief summary and points toward the extensive exposition.
△ Fourth, the Stage of Radiance (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).

O Sons of the Buddha, within the stage of the essential nature of a Bodhisattva, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is radiance and conventional reality (saṃvṛti-satya) is non-interruption and non-permanence;

they arise, abide, and cease simultaneously. Within a single world, a single time, and a single existence, various seeds manifest as various appearances because of the conditions among causes and effects.
The Way is neither one nor two; it is neither good nor evil; it is neither ordinary nor Buddha.

Therefore, the Buddha-realm and the ordinary realm—each and every one of these is termed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The wisdom of the Path contemplates that there is neither one nor two.

This is the section on the Profound Path and Concentration (*samādhi*), which explains the causes of concentration for the initial awakening of the Buddha’s mental activity: faith-awakening, contemplation-awakening, stillness-awakening, superior-awakening, mindfulness-awakening, and wisdom-awakening. One contemplates...

The perception of awakening, the perception of tranquility, the perception of bliss, and the perception of equanimity constitute the path of skillful means for each stage; these are the fruits of entering meditative concentration moment by moment.

When such a person dwells within concentration, they see the dharmas as empty with brilliant clarity. If a thought arises, concentration enters the state of arising-mind, and concentration gives rise to attachment and compliance.

The Way is born through transformation by means of the Dharma; it is called the patience of the joy of the Dharma, the patience of abiding, the patience of realization, and the patience of quiescent extinction.

Therefore, within the Samādhi of Entering the Radiant Flowers, all Buddhas manifest immeasurable Buddhas who stroke the crown of the head with their hands and preach the Dharma with a single voice, giving rise to hundreds of thousands of inspirations without emerging from meditative absorption.
They abide in concentration, savoring the bliss of concentration, becoming attached to concentration, and craving concentration for the duration of one kalpa or a thousand kalpas.

Abiding in meditative concentration, he sees the Buddha seated upon a lotus flower preaching a hundred dharma-gates. This person makes offerings and listens to the Dharma while remaining in concentration for one kalpa.

At that time, the light of all Buddhas touches his head, giving rise to the categories of concentration (*samādhi-pakṣa*). This is because of the emergence of signs, the advancement of signs, and the movement toward signs.
Without perishing, without regressing, without falling, and without abiding, the supreme joy and patience of the Dharma of the *mūrdhan-samādhi* are forever exhausted without remainder.
One then enters into all Buddha-lands and cultivates immeasurable categories of merit; every practice is luminous.
Entering into skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one teaches and transforms all sentient beings, enabling them to perceive the Buddha-nature as eternal, blissful, self, and pure.

This person dwells within this stage, practicing the Dharma-gate of transformation; gradually becoming profound and subtle, they attain the wisdom of contemplating flowers in the sky and enter the Middle Way of essential nature.
All categories of Dharma-gates become fully perfected, like a diamond, and they ascend to the stages of the Sun and Moon.
The meaning of this has already been clarified.

As for "the ultimate is the blaze and the conventional," the ultimate is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the blaze is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Because the conventional is the ultimate, there is no discontinuity;

because its nature is non-discontinuous. Because the ultimate is the conventional, there is no permanence; because its characteristics are impermanent. Furthermore, because the ultimate is the conventional...
It is not discontinuous, because it is empty of discontinuity. It is not eternal, because the conventional is itself the ultimate and its nature is quiescent emptiness.
This means that all phenomena arise, abide, and perish simultaneously; they exist within the same world, at the same time, and within the same infinitesimal moment of a conscious mind.
Therefore, they are not eternal. Nevertheless, the seeds are distinct from one another, being different from the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

Because they are each distinct, yet precisely uninterrupted—such is the Middle Way of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). One should know that it is not one, because it illuminates both poles;
nor is it two, because both are simultaneously extinguished. Even down to good and evil, or ordinary beings and sages, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, the Buddha-realm and the realm of ordinary beings are each established as mere conventional designations (*prajñapti*); collectively, they are termed the "world" (*loka*).
Truth. This contemplation of the path of wisdom realizes that there is neither one nor two; it is the category of the profound and wondrous Middle Way Samādhi.
It is what the Buddhas of the past practiced within their minds, the causal samādhi for initial awakening. There are ten categories in total;
these ten categories are the path of skillful means for the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). As each thought-moment enters the fruit of samādhi, it is so named.
These serve as the causes for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). However, among the ten factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), these are derived from the seven factors of awakening:

faith, wisdom, investigation, and examination are collectively subsumed under the factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); volition, mindfulness, and attention are collectively subsumed under the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*);

tranquility is the factor of concentration (*samādhi*); exertion is the factor of vigor (*vīrya*); and pliancy—also called the factor of relinquishment (*praśrabdhi*)—is the factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
The perception of pleasure is the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*); the perception of equanimity is the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-aṅga*).
Once this person abides within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they perceive all phenomena with brilliant clarity and practice in emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

If they are well able to arouse mindfulness (*smṛti*) within that concentration, they will then definitively enter the sphere of the non-abiding mind. However, one who has first attained this concentration will inevitably give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
It is compliance. Within these dharmas of the Middle Way, he manifests through transformation;

this is called the patience of the joy of the true Dharma (*dharmasukha-kṣānti*), also called the patience of abiding, also called the patience of realization, and also called the patience of ultimate quiescence.

If one were to sit forever in compliance with the realm of craving, one would lose it for all eternity. Therefore, when the Buddhas see that this Bodhisattva has correctly entered into the radiant light...

When entering the Flower Samādhi (*puṣpa-samādhi*), one inevitably beholds immeasurable Buddhas who stroke one’s head with their hands and preach the Dharma with a single voice, inspiring one through hundreds of thousands of skillful means.
This Flower Samādhi is what is called "the blazing vision of dharmas proceeding toward emptiness.
Because this bodhisattva has given rise to attachment and compliance, they do not yet emerge from samādhi; they remain within it, savoring it, and clinging to it.
They are also attached and even covetous; they may remain in meditative concentration for one kalpa or a thousand kalpas.

Nevertheless, due to the power of their original vows and roots of goodness, although they remain in concentration for a long time, they do not ultimately enter parinirvāṇa. They are still able to see the Buddhas and hear hundreds of Dharma-gates.
This person, while within that very concentration, makes offerings and listens to the Dharma, and further remains in concentration for another kalpa. Therefore...
The Buddhas again stroked his head within the light, causing him to give rise to the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*).

He came to clearly discern the signs of emergence, the signs of progress, the signs of departure, and the signs of direction. Because he knew the sign of emergence, he did not sink; because he knew the sign of progress, he did not regress; because he knew the sign of departure, he did not fall;
and because he knew the sign of direction, he did not remain stationary. Thus, he attained the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of delight in the dharma of the Summit Samādhi (*mūrdha-samādhi*).

Exhausted forever without remainder, they do not fall from the summit as bodhisattvas; they immediately enter all buddha-lands, and even the dharma-gates for practicing transformation gradually become profound and subtle.
Through the wisdom that contemplates flowers in the sky, they enter together into the Middle Way of essential nature.
All dharma-gates are fully perfected, like a vajra, without any deficiency. Emptiness is the ultimate truth.
The "Flowers" represent conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The *Sūrya-candramas-prabhāsa-dharmapada* summarizes the essentials to point toward the vast.
