△ Fifth, the Stage of Wisdom Illumination (Prajñā-avabhāsa-bhūmi).

O Sons of the Buddha, regarding the Bodhisattva’s dharma of the essential nature of wisdom illumination, there are ten kinds of categories for the arising of power that give rise to all meritorious practices.
By means of a single wisdom-expedient, one knows the distinct workings of the two karmas of good and evil. This is the category of the Power of Abiding (sthāna-bala).
The Chapter on the Power of Wisdom regarding Good and Evil Deeds; the Chapter on the Power of Desire regarding all cravings and the fruits of birth within the six realms of existence;

the Chapter on the Power of Nature regarding the distinct differences in the natures of the six realms; and the Chapter on the Power of Roots regarding the individual differences among all wholesome and unwholesome faculties.
The Chapter on the Faculties and Powers. Erroneous determination, correct determination, and indeterminate determination—these are called the Chapter on the Power of Concentration.

All causes are karma; the vehicle is the cause, and the vehicle is the fruit. Reaching the place of the fruit by means of the causal path—this is the Chapter on the Power of the Path. The five eyes know all phenomena.

Because of seeing all births, there is the Chapter on the Power of the Divine Eye (*divyacakṣus-bala*). In the Chapter on the Power of Past Lives (*pūrvanivāsa-bala*), one knows each and every event of a hundred kalpas.
In the Chapter on the Power of Liberation (*vimukti-bala*), afflictions are extinguished in all births and ignorance is extinguished in all sensations;

this is the wisdom of the Chapter on the Ten Powers (*daśabala*) that knows the causes and effects of one's own cultivation, as well as the distinctions between the causes and effects of all sentient beings, while [remaining detached in] body and mind.
They employ their mouths perversely: they regard a pure land as an evil land, and an evil land as a land of sublime bliss.
They can transform the good into evil and the evil into good; they turn form into non-form and non-form into form; they take a man to be a woman.
They regard women as men; they regard the six realms of existence as not being the six realms, and that which is not the six realms as the six realms;
even earth, water, fire, and wind are regarded as not being earth, water, fire, and wind.

At that time, by the power of great skillful means, such a person perceives within all sentient beings that which is inconceivable—the manner in which their feet are lifted and set down, something that those of lower stages cannot know or perceive.

This person’s great wisdom gradually advances; the light of their wisdom increases bit by bit, becoming immeasurable and immeasurable, as unspeakably unspeakable Dharma-gates manifest and proceed before them.
Regarding "Wisdom-illumination": it is the wondrous wisdom of the ten powers (*daśabala*), which illuminates all phenomena such that they are fully and thoroughly understood.
In both mundane and supramundane paths, there is none equal to it; it is also called "Difficult to Conquer" (*durjayā*).

These ten powers are produced through the thorough cultivation of practice, and are therefore termed the "Category of Arising. They are capable of universally giving rise to all meritorious deeds. What are these ten?
First, by means of the skillful method of single wisdom, one thoroughly understands the distinct operations of the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome.

That is to say: it is possible that performing wholesome deeds results in a wholesome retribution; it is impossible that performing wholesome deeds results in an unwholesome retribution. It is possible that performing unwholesome deeds results in an unwholesome retribution;
it is impossible that performing unwholesome deeds results in a wholesome retribution. This is called the Chapter on the Power of the Possible (*sthāna-bala*).

Second, to thoroughly and universally know the karmic causes, conditions, and retributive fruits of all wholesome and unwholesome deeds performed by all sentient beings—this is called the category of the power of knowledge regarding karma (*karma-jñāna-bala*).

Third, to [know] all the desires and aspirations of all sentient beings, namely their preferences for rebirth in the various realms of existence (*ṣaḍ-gati*) and the resulting fruits thereof—this is called the category of the power of knowledge regarding inclinations and dispositions (*adhimukti-jñāna-bala*). Fourth, to know the seeds of the six realms of existence...

The differentiation of natures is called the Faculty of Nature (*dhātu-bala*). Fifth is knowing the various roots of goodness and evil throughout the six realms of existence—each being distinct as superior, middling, or inferior—which is called the Faculty of Roots (*indriya-bala*). Sixth is knowing whether sentient beings are of wrong determination, right determination, or undetermined;
this is called the Faculty of Concentration (*samādhi-bala*). Seventh is knowing all causes and effects, both mundane and supramundane...

The Dharma is the vehicle; the vehicle is the cause, and the vehicle is the fruit. It is like a person for whom the human vehicle is the cause and yet the human vehicle is also the fruit, up to and including the Buddha-vehicle, which is the cause and yet the Buddha-vehicle is also the fruit. That one attains the state of fruition is precisely due to riding upon this causal path;
this is called the Chapter on the Power of the Path. Eighth, by means of the five eyes, one knows all dharmas and sees them.
The category called the "Power of the Divine Eye" (*divyacakṣurbala*) is so named because it discerns the differences in the births of all sentient beings.
Ninth is the category called the "Power of Past Lives" (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*), which refers to knowing every single event throughout a hundred kalpas.

Regarding the term "a hundred kalpas," this refers to what is called the "mind-ground" (*cittabhūmi*) cultivated over a hundred kalpas; in reality, it does not stop at merely a hundred kalpas. Tenth is [the power] regarding all that is summoned...
The afflictions of分段生死 (paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa) are extinguished; all ignorance regarding 變易生死 (pariṇāma-jarā-maraṇa) is also extinguished.
This is called the Chapter on the Power of Liberation, which is the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-bala).

This is the wisdom of the Chapter on the Ten Powers, which is able to know the causes and effects of one's own cultivation, as well as to discern the causes and effects of all sentient beings. Furthermore, it enables the body, mind, and speech to...
Each is used separately. Because one thoroughly realizes the equality of purity and impurity, one should subdue [the mind] by regarding a pure land as an evil land;
one should embrace [it] by regarding an evil land as a wondrous land of bliss.
Knowing that the nature of good and evil is empty, when issuing a warning, one turns good into evil; when issuing an exhortation, one turns evil into good. [Knowing] form...
Emptiness is non-dual. Therefore, for those attached to existence, he causes them to see form as non-form; for those attached to emptiness, he causes them to see non-form as form.

Knowing that male and female have no real characteristic, he manifests as a man to deliver those who should be delivered by a woman's body, and manifests as a woman to deliver those who should be delivered by a man's body, and so on according to the circumstances.

The mind manifests transformations, as in the case of the celestial maidens in Vimalakīrti’s room and others. Because they know that ordinary beings and sages are equal, they should attain liberation through the understanding of the sage;
thus, they regard the six realms as not being six realms. They should attain liberation through the perspective of ordinary beings;
thus, they regard what are not the six realms as being the six realms. Knowing that the four great elements have no intrinsic nature and are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, therefore, up to...

Earth, water, fire, and wind are not earth, water, fire, and wind. At that time, by the power of great skillful means, this person contemplates that the realm of all sentient beings is itself the Buddha-realm. Whichever single dharma they take up, they perceive it as inconceivable.
Whether lifting or lowering their feet, those on the ground do not know; this extends even to the ineffable and inexpressible Dharma-gates.
This is now the stage of Manifesting Before One's Eyes. For this reason, it is also called "Difficult to Conquer" (Duranjaya) and also called "Wisdom Illumination.
6. The Flower-Light Stage (*Puṣpārāga-bhūmi*):
If a disciple of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva, abides in the Flower-Light Stage which is their essential nature, they are able, within all worlds, to [manifest] the ten...

The Chapter on Supernatural Powers and Clear Wisdom: To manifest various transformations to all sentient beings, one employs the clear wisdom of the divine eye to perceive all forms within the lands of the three periods of time, as numerous as motes of dust, and discerns how each part constitutes the bodies of sentient beings in the six realms.
One discerns each individual atom of the body’s subtle form as it constitutes the great form.

With the wisdom of the divine ear, one knows the sounds of suffering and joy of sentient beings in the six realms throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—sounds that are neither non-sounds nor non-noises, but the sounds of all phenomena.
By means of the wisdom of the celestial body, one knows all forms—whether material or immaterial, and whether they possess the form of male or female.
In a single thought-moment, one manifests bodies as numerous as atoms throughout the lands and kalpas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, both large and small.

By means of the celestial knowledge of others' minds, one knows the mental activities of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time and within the six realms of existence across the ten directions.

The mind and mental factors attend to matters such as suffering, pleasure, good, and evil. By means of celestial knowledge (*divya-jñāna*), one knows the past lives, sufferings, pleasures, and lifespans of all sentient beings within the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time; one knows each individual’s continuity of life for a hundred kalpas.

By means of celestial knowledge of liberation (*divya-vimukti-jñāna*), one knows the liberation of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, and how they have severed and eliminated all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Whether many or few, from the first stage up to the tenth stage, all cessations are completely extinguished.

By means of the celestial concentration-mind-wisdom, one knows the minds of sentient beings within the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether they are concentrated, unconcentrated, or neither concentrated nor unconcentrated—as well as the methods for arising concentration and the samādhis that involve objective apprehension, such as the hundred samādhis. By means of celestial awakening-wisdom, one knows all sentient beings.
They know those who have already attained Buddhahood and those who have not yet attained it, even down to every single thought-moment of the minds of beings in the six realms of existence.
By means of the wisdom of celestial recollection, they know the teachings spoken within the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

By means of the wisdom of celestial vows, they know the lifespans and the duration of the lives of all sentient beings throughout hundreds, thousands, and great kalpas. By means of the wisdom of celestial aspirations, they know the ten stages of the noble ones and sages of all sentient beings.

Within each and every practice-vow among the thirty minds, whether seeking suffering or pleasure, or seeking all things—whether dharma or non-dharma—one is fully endowed with ten vows and hundreds of thousands of great vow-chapters.
This person, abiding within the stages (*bhūmi*), manifests immeasurable distinct functions of body, mind, and speech through the ten supernormal powers and clarities (*abhijñā*).
To describe the merits of these stages would be inexhaustible even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; yet it is so.

Regarding the "Śākyamuni," this briefly opens the Chapter on the Clarity of Supernatural Powers (*abhijñā-prakāśa-varga*), as explained in the Chapter on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-varga*).
Because the Chapter on the Tenfold Knowledge of Supernatural Powers (*daśābhijñā-jñāna-varga*) gives rise to various functions, it is named "Flower Light" (*Puṣpa-prabhā*).

Because unconditioned *tathatā* is pure by nature and luminously manifest, it is named "Manifestation" (*Pratyakṣa*). Due to the manifestation of true nature, one subsequently achieves the ten supernatural powers; thus, it is called "Exquisite Flower Light."
"Brilliance" refers to self-adornment. "Neither non-sound nor non-voice" points to the sounds of insentient things.

"The sound of all dharmas" points to the voice of transcendence. "Extinction upon extinction, all exhausted" means that at every stage, the severing of delusions is ultimately and completely finished.
"Neither fixed nor unfixed" refers to not arising from the samādhi of cessation while manifesting various dignified demeanors. Therein lies something...
Regarding the "Samādhi of Gathering": it means that each samādhi possesses various functions.
As for "the minds of people in the six realms," this refers to the Buddha-mind being inherent within the human mind. Regarding "seeking suffering or pleasure, or the Dharma or non-Dharma":
ordinary beings seek suffering, while sages seek pleasure; ordinary beings seek what is non-Dharmic, while sages seek the Dharma. Furthermore, they vow to be born in the turbid [world].
Seeking existence in this world is seeking suffering; wishing to be born in a pure land is seeking happiness; wishing to manifest in the good realms is seeking the Dharma;
wishing to manifest in the evil destinies is not the Dharma. These ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are also merely the six supernormal powers expanded out.

The wisdom of the celestial body still belongs to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); with the eye one perceives the various distinctions of forms, while with the body one knows that the nature of forms is without differentiation.

They are distinct. The knowledge of the heavenly beings (*deva-jñāna*) and the wisdom of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) both belong to the supernormal power of recollecting past existences (*pūrvenivāsābhijñā*).

The knowledge of the heavenly beings knows the differences in the past lives of sentient beings; the wisdom of recollecting past lives knows the differences in the increase and decrease of the number of eons (*kalpa*). The wisdom of heavenly liberation (*deva-vimukti-jñāna*) is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).

The wisdom of heavenly concentration (*deva-samādhi-jñāna*), the wisdom of heavenly awakening (*deva-bodhi-jñāna*), and the wisdom of heavenly vows (*deva-praṇidhāna-jñāna*) all belong to the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*). All are as follows:
