△ Seventh, the Stage of Fulfillment.
O Sons of the Buddha, when Bodhisattvas reach the stage of the fulfilled essential nature and enter into these dharmas, there are eighteen types of noble beings.

The Chapter on Wisdom: That which is not shared with those in the lower stages consists of the body being free from outflows and faults, speech being free from verbal transgressions, mindfulness being free from lapses, and being detached from the eight worldly dharmas.
Maintaining equanimity toward all phenomena and constantly abiding in samādhi—these constitute the six qualities fully perfected upon entering the stages.

Furthermore, from this wisdom arises the wisdom of the six bases (*ṣaḍpāda-jñāna*). Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) within the three realms are ultimately not received, there is the fulfillment of desire.
Because all merits and all dharma-gates sought are fulfilled, there is the fulfillment of vigor (*vīrya*).
Because all matters of dharmas, all matters of kalpas, and all matters of sentient beings are known simultaneously with a single mind, there is the fulfillment of mindfulness (*smṛti*). This...
The characteristic of the two truths consists of all phenomena pertaining to the sentient beings of the six realms; thus, there is the fulfillment of wisdom (*prajñā-saṃbhāra*).

Because one knows the ten stages of development (*daśa-pratipatti*) up to all Buddhas being free from fetters (*anusaṃdhi*) and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), there is the fulfillment of liberation (*vimukti-saṃbhāra*).

By seeing all sentient beings and knowing that others, oneself, and one's disciples are without outflows (*anāsrava*) and free from the habitual tendencies of afflictions, one possesses the fulfillment of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) through wisdom that knows the bodies of others.
This person enters into the six kinds of perfected, clear wisdom and thereby gives rise to the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*).
Following the mental activities of sentient beings throughout the six realms, they eloquently expound immeasurable categories of Dharma-doors (*dharmaparyāya*) for the sake of all sentient beings.

Following the mental activities of all sentient beings, they constantly enter samādhi, whereby the great earth of the ten directions trembles and flowers manifest in the void; thus, they are able to cause sentient beings—
Regarding mental activity: through the perfection of great illumination, one perceives the appearance of Buddhas throughout all past kalpas; this also demonstrates the minds of all sentient beings.
Through non-attached wisdom, one perceives the mental activities of all Buddhas and all sentient beings within all lands of the ten directions in the present.
Through the wisdom of the path of supernatural powers, one perceives [the future]... one [kalpa].
Throughout all kalpas, as all Buddhas appear in the world, all sentient beings receive the Way and hear the Dharma from these Buddhas;

thus they abide within these eighteen noble stages. With every thought-moment in samādhi, they contemplate the forms of the three realms, as numerous as motes of dust, as having been their own bodies in the past.
All sentient beings have been their parents, and now they enter this stage wherein all merits are unified.
I have already entered all the divine radiances, all the dharmas practiced by all Buddhas, and even all the categories of dharma-gates within the eighth and ninth stages.
Therefore, throughout all Buddha-lands, I manifest as a Buddha, attain enlightenment, turn the wheel of Dharma, and demonstrate entry into parinirvāṇa,
transforming others throughout all lands of the past, future, and present in other directions.

It is fully endowed with the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) that extend to the limit of true suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, it is called "fulfillment" and is also named the "Far-Reaching Stage" (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).
As for the eight dharmas: gain and loss, suffering and pleasure, praise and blame, and fame and insignificance—these are also called the "eight winds.
Regarding equanimity toward all phenomena, it is also termed "equanimity through knowing nothing. This must be analyzed by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), namely:
Not knowing and not relinquishing; knowing and yet not relinquishing; not knowing and relinquishing; and knowing and then relinquishing.
Ordinary persons do not understand the fundamental cause of all phenomena and thus cling to them through false conceptualization; this is "not knowing and not relinquishing.

Although Bodhisattvas of Understanding and Practice know the true nature of all phenomena, because the seeds of delusion have not been severed, they are unable to be completely and eternally free from them.
This is "knowing and not abandoning. The wisdom of non-differentiation of the two vehicles does not know the various essential natures of all phenomena;
it can only ensure that there is forever no attachment. This is "not knowing and abandoning. Only the Buddha thoroughly exhausts the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Like a round mirror reflecting objects, [the mind] appears clearly before one, forever free from attachment; this is "having abandoned through complete knowledge.

"Constantly abiding in samādhi" means that among the four modes of deportment, there is never a state of non-concentrated mind. "The desire to be fully endowed" is also called the non-diminution of aspiration;
with all habitual tendencies exhausted, one constantly desires to deliver sentient beings. "The fulfillment of the mind of exertion" is also called...
Vigor is undiminished, spontaneously delivering sentient beings. When the mind of mindfulness is fulfilled, mindfulness is undiminished;
when wisdom is fulfilled, insight is undiminished. In transforming and enlightening sentient beings, one never departs from the two truths—ultimate and conventional.

Based upon these two truths, one provides teachings according to wisdom and according to sentiment. Fully possessing all categories of dharmas, one transforms and enlightens those in the six realms of existence.

The "feet of liberation" (vimukti-pāda) are the non-diminution of liberation. The "feet of the six superknowledges" (ṣaḍ-abhijñā-pāda), through which wisdom knows the bodies of others, are the non-diminution of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana).
This means that regarding all liberations, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are clear and distinct, and his discernment is unimpeded.
Thus, he gives rise to the body of wisdom (jñāna-kāya) and so forth; all his bodily actions follow the movement of wisdom, as do his eloquent verbal explanations and the like.
All these verbal actions follow the movement of wisdom; they accord with the mental activities of sentient beings and so forth.
All these mental actions follow the movement of wisdom, which is able to cause the mental activities of sentient beings to proceed [in this way]—this means to transform them.
By means of the perfection of the Great Illumination (*mahāvidyā*) and so forth, this wisdom knows the past without obstruction. By means of unattached wisdom and so forth...
This wisdom knows the present world without obstruction through the supernormal powers, the knowledge of the path, and so forth.
This wisdom knows the future world without obstruction. The past is called "Great Illumination" because it is free from darkness and forgetfulness.
The present is called "Non-attachment" because it illuminates universally like a mirror. The future is called "Supernormal Power" because it is inconceivable. In reality, however, it is...
The three periods of time are all brilliantly illuminated; all are without attachment; all are the spiritual power of the Way.
From this point on, he repeatedly manifests the eight phases of enlightenment, transforming the ten directions and the three periods of time, pervading everywhere without exception.
This is called fulfillment, and it is also called the Far-Reaching [Bhūmi]. Is this not indeed fitting?
△ Eighth, the Stage of the Buddha’s Roar.
If, O Sons of the Buddha, one is on the Bodhisattva stage of the Essential Nature of the Buddha’s Roar, they enter the Samādhi of Entering the Rank of the Dharma King.

Their wisdom is like that of a Buddha because of the Buddha’s Roar Samādhi; thus, the ten grades of the Great Illumination Gate of Emptiness are constantly present before them. This is the Flower-Light Sound.

Entering the samādhi of the mind: as for the wisdom of emptiness, it refers to the gate of internal emptiness-wisdom, the gate of external emptiness-wisdom, the gate of conditioned emptiness-wisdom, the gate of unconditioned emptiness-wisdom, the gate of essential nature emptiness-wisdom, the gate of beginningless emptiness-wisdom, the gate of ultimate truth emptiness-wisdom, the gate of emptiness-of-emptiness wisdom, the gate of emptiness-of-emptiness-and-again-emptiness wisdom, and the gate of emptiness-of-emptiness-of-emptiness-and-again-emptiness wisdom. As...
These are the ten gates of emptiness. Each of the lower stages is unaware of them.

Through the inconceivable, ineffable supernatural powers, paths, and wisdom of the Stage of Equal Emptiness, one uses the wisdom of a single thought-moment to discern the distinctions and differences among all phenomena, yet enters into immeasurable Buddha-lands.
Before each Buddha, one receives and accepts the Dharma, turning the wheel of the Dharma to deliver all sentient beings.
Bestowing the medicine of the Dharma upon all sentient beings, one becomes a great Dharma teacher and a great guide.
Having destroyed the four Māras and perfected the Dharma-body, one transforms and leads others into the Buddha-realm, becoming numbered among the Buddhas.

Within the ranks of the ninth and tenth stages, one nurtures the Dharma-body through hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates, hundreds of thousands of samādhi gates, and hundreds of thousands of golden... [gates].

The Gate of Firmness. The hundred-thousand gates of spiritual powers (*abhijñā*). The hundred-thousand gates of liberation (*vimokṣa*). Thus, within these hundred-thousand gates of the equality of space, one possesses great mastery.
In a single thought-moment and at a single time, one traverses [all realms]. One speaks of eons as non-eons; one speaks of non-eons as eons.

One speaks of what is not the Path as the Path; one speaks of the Path as not the Path. One speaks of those who are not the sentient beings of the six destinies as the sentient beings of the six destinies; [one speaks of] the sentient beings of the six destinies...
Birth is said to be neither the sentient beings of the six realms, nor the Buddha as taught by the Buddha, nor the non-Buddha as taught by the Buddha;

yet one enters and emerges from the Samādhi of the Essential Nature of all Buddhas. Therein, one performs retro-reflection, forward-reflection, reverse-reflection, anterior-reflection, posterior-reflection, causal-reflection, resultant-reflection, reflection on emptiness, reflection on existence, and reflection on the ultimate truth of the Middle Way.
This wisdom is realized only in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*); it is not [attained] by those in lower stages.
It is not attained; it is unmoving; it does not arrive; it does not go out; it does not enter; it is neither born nor extinguished.

This is the Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Grounds, which is immeasurable, immeasurable, unspeakable, and unspeakable. Now, I shall briefly reveal but a single hair-tip’s worth of the matters within these grounds.
This has already been clarified in the Chapter on Arhats.

Because it is the single mind of true suchness, it is called "immovable. Being of the same essence as the Buddha, when emerging from supreme meditative concentration, it is further called the "Buddha’s Roar.
Because it realizes the true patience of non-arising within the dharma-nature of equality, it is named the "Samādhi of Entering the Rank of the Dharma King."
"Flower-Light Sound" refers to the sound of the sevenfold exhortations of all Buddhas, as fully elucidated in the eighth stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Although he originally arose from meditative concentration through these seven exhortations, the reason it is called "entering the mind-samādhi" is that, having received the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas, he has now realized the wondrous function of the one mind;
thus, his every movement—whether entering or emerging—is nothing other than samādhi. Regarding "emptiness-wisdom": wisdom is...

The essence of the Great Illumination (*mahāprajñā*) is realized through true wisdom by attesting to the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*); therefore, it is called the "Gate of Emptiness of Great Illumination. Regarding internal emptiness:

one contemplates that the pure characteristics of internal form (*rūpa*) are unattainable. Regarding external emptiness: one contemplates that the pure characteristics of external form are unattainable. Regarding the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*):

within the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) are unattainable. This is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

Regarding "the conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*): it is in contrast to the conditioned that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is spoken of; since the conditioned is empty, the unconditioned is likewise unapprehendable. Regarding "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*):

both the conditioned and the unconditioned lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding "emptiness of the beginningless" (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*): worldly sentient beings have no characteristic of a beginning.
Regarding "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*): among all phenomena, that which is supreme and foremost is called *nirvāṇa*.
And yet it is also signless. Regarding "the emptiness of emptiness": although the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is empty, the principle that can effect this emptiness still remains.

Now, even that which can effect emptiness is itself empty. Regarding "the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness": although the principle of emptiness is empty, the wisdom that realizes the principle of emptiness still remains.
Now, the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness is also empty. When the emptiness of emptiness is further emptied, both principle and wisdom are empty;
yet the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness still remains. Now, when that emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness is also emptied, one becomes a member of the Buddhas.
Having already realized the Dharmakāya and entered the rank of Buddhahood, those in the ninth and tenth stages do nothing more than allow their Dharmakāya to grow spontaneously.

*Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "Total Retention" (*saṃgraha-dhāraṇa*). It summarizes all phenomena and retains all meanings. Based on this, one is able to give rise to unimpeded eloquence (*asaṅga-pratibhāna*).
Regarding "retro-reflection": internal reflection refers to the illumination of body and mind; forward reflection refers to observing the gate of transmigration (*pravṛtti-mukha*);
reverse reflection refers to observing the gate of cessation (*nivṛtti-mukha*). Prior reflection refers to observing the past; subsequent reflection refers to observing the future.

"Coming" refers to the illumination of the causes of all phenomena. "Fruition-illumination" refers to the illumination of the fruits of all phenomena. "Emptiness-illumination" refers to the illumination of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"Existence-illumination" refers to the illumination of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "Illumination of the meaning of the supreme Middle Way" refers to the illumination of the middle truth.

"Immovable" means that攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective conceptual clinging) has forever ceased. "Non-arriving" means that the paths of speech and thought are cut off. "Non-emerging" [is the state of non-arising].

There is no time when it does not illuminate. "Not entering" means that its illumination does not consist in entering meditative absorption. "Not arising" means that the nature of illumination is without arising.
"Not ceasing" means that the nature of illumination is without cessation. Regarding the "Chapter on Arhats," this briefly summarizes the preceding and points toward what follows in detail.

At this stage, one forever abandons the name of the *ālayavijñāna*; it is also called the stage of the Arhat (*arhan*). However, there are differences in meaning and category between those within the realm (*dhātu*) and those beyond the realm.
If you wish to know this in detail, you must consult the *Comprehensive Commentary on the Rituals of the Four Teachings* (*Sijiaoyi Jizhu*).
△ Ninth, the Ground of the Avataṃsaka:

"O Disciples of the Buddha! This is the ground of the essential nature of the Buddha-Flower Adornment (*Buddhāvatamsaka*) for Bodhisattvas. By means of the majestic deportment of the Buddha and the three [modes of conduct] of the Tathāgata..."

He dwells in the Samādhi of the Sovereign King of Profound Clarity. Without fixed time for entering or emerging from it, he simultaneously attains Buddhahood, turns the wheel of Dharma, and even enters parinirvāṇa throughout the ten directions, across three thousandfold world systems, ten billion suns and moons, and ten billion sets of four continents.
Within a single mind, he simultaneously manifests all Buddha-activities—every physical form and eighty minor marks—to all sentient beings.

Excellent. Possessing the thirty-two marks, sovereign bliss, and a radiance equal to space, adorned with the signs and excellences of immeasurable great compassion, you are beyond all phenomena—neither gods, nor humans, nor any of the six realms.

Yet you constantly traverse the six realms, manifesting infinite bodies, infinite mouths, and infinite minds, preaching infinite Dharma-gates, and being able to transform the realm of Māra into the realm of the Buddha.
The Buddha-realm enters the realm of Māra; furthermore, all views are transformed to enter the Buddha-view. The Buddha-body enters all views;
the Buddha-nature enters the nature of sentient beings, and the nature of sentient beings enters the Buddha-nature. Its ground is light; light illumines light, and wisdom illumines wisdom.

Brilliant flame, brilliant flame! Fearless one, immeasurable one, possessor of the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities, liberated one, nirvāṇa, unconditioned, the single path of purity—regarding all sentient beings as one's parents and brothers, one preaches the Dharma for them.
Throughout all kalpas, they attain the fruits of the Way. Furthermore, they manifest in all lands for the sake of all sentient beings, regarding one another as fathers and mothers;
even toward celestial Māras and followers of external paths, they regard them as fathers and mothers.
Abiding in this stage, from the limit of birth and death up to the adamantine limit, they manifest such deeds within a single thought-moment and are able to enter into transformation.
The immeasurable realms of sentient beings are likewise immeasurable; to speak briefly, they are like a single drop from the ocean.
Adorned by the adornments of the Buddha, it is named the "Buddha-Flower Adornment" (*Buddhāvatamsaka*).

Because it brings forth the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and is skillful at preaching the Dharma, it is also called the Stage of Good Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*). Regarding the "King of Sovereign Samādhi": this refers to the King of Sovereignty Samādhi.
It is the king among all samādhis. It emerges and enters simultaneously; it enters and emerges simultaneously.
Even such things as entering meditative concentration in the east and arising in the west are therefore called "entering and emerging at no fixed time.

As for the simultaneous manifestation of all Buddha-activities within a single mind, this means that one does not merely manifest the eight phases of enlightenment in succession, but furthermore— [The text continues with: ...the marks [of a Buddha].

Within these marks, each mutually possesses all eight marks; that is to say, some see him dwelling in the womb, some see his initial birth, some see his renunciation, and so on, up to some seeing his final nirvana. Regarding "the radiance of that ground," this refers to the essence of its light.
"Light illuminating light" and "wisdom illuminating wisdom" clarify its inexhaustibility within inexhaustibility. "Radiant flames illuminating radiant flames" [clarifies its unceasing brilliance].

This reveals their mutual penetration and fusion. That such matters manifest within a single thought-moment means that from beginning to end, one does not depart from the samādhi of the limit of a single kṣaṇa.

That one enters the realms of immeasurable sentient beings means universally manifesting as both ordinary beings and sages throughout all worlds. All other points may be understood according to the text.
△ Entering the Stage of the Buddha-realm.
O Sons of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva enters the essential nature of the Buddha-realm, their Great Wisdom is empty, empty again, and empty yet again;
it is the wisdom of equality like the nature of space. It is fully endowed with the ten qualities of the Tathāgata-nature.

Emptiness is of one single characteristic; its essential nature is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The spirit is void and the substance is one; phenomena are identical with the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
He accords with the Four Truths and the Two Truths, exhausting the limits of the wheel of birth and death. His Dharma-sustenance and Dharma-body are non-dual; thus, he is named Arhat.
Pervading all things within all worlds, he knows everything through right wisdom and the noble wisdom of liberation.
Because he possesses the faculties of all sentient beings regarding the existence or non-existence of phenomena, he is the Samyaksaṃbuddha (the Perfectly Awakened One).
Because his cultivation of clear knowledge is perfected at the time of attaining Buddhahood, he is the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct).

Because the Buddha-dharma of the three times is well-gone, and because the Buddha’s dharma is identical to the dharma of previous Buddhas—being excellent in departing and excellent in arriving—he is called the Sugata (Well-Gone). This person practices these supreme virtues and enters into the world.
He teaches and transforms sentient beings so that they may be liberated from all fetters and bonds; therefore, he is called the "Liberator of the World.

This person, standing above all dharmas, enters the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha; his deportment is like that of a Buddha, and as one who dwells in the sphere of action of a Great Being, he acts as the Liberator of the World.
He tames and harmonizes all sentient beings and is thus named a "Great Man" (Puruṣa). Among gods and humans, he teaches and transforms them all.
Because sentient beings inquire of and receive his words of Dharma, he is the Teacher of Gods and Humans. His wondrous source is non-dual;
the Buddha-nature is profound awakening, eternally and fully perfected. Because all sentient beings prostrate and revere him, he is the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Because all people of the world inquire of, receive, and follow his teachings, this is the Buddha-ground. This ground is the place entered by all sages.
Therefore, it is called the Ground of the Buddha-realm. At that time, seated upon a precious lotus flower, all who were granted the prediction of enlightenment rejoiced.
The Dharma-body hand stroked their crowns, and the bodhisattvas who shared the same vision and the same practice praised them with one voice, without duality.
Furthermore, all Buddhas and all bodhisattvas from hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds gathered like clouds and requested him to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
The Wheel of Dharma that is ineffable; the Dharma-gate of transformation and guidance through the Treasury of Space; the chapter on the ineffably wondrous Dharma-gates of these stages;
the wondrous gates of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) and samādhi; and the gates of dhāraṇī—these are not known by the mind-consciousness of ordinary beings in lower stages.
Only the immeasurable body, speech, and mind of Buddha after Buddha can exhaust their source, just as [the light of] the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
In this chapter, it is taught that the ten fearlessnesses (*daśa-vaiśāradya*) are identical to the Buddha-way.
Having received the office of a Buddha and being included within the number of Buddhas, it is called the Stage of Entering the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu-bhūmi*).

Because the wondrous cloud of the compassion-shade covers the ocean of *nirvāṇa*, it is also called the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). Within the first eight stages, the tenth gate of emptiness is named...

The gate of wisdom is the emptiness of emptiness, and yet again the emptiness of that emptiness. Now, by further emptying this great wisdom as well, one realizes the wisdom of equality with the nature of space-like suchness;
thus, the merits of the ten titles are all fully perfected. Regarding "emptiness being identical to the mark of sameness":
the wisdom of true emptiness and the principle of the real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are non-dual; their essential nature is precisely this.
Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Its spirit is empty and penetrating; its substance is one reality. These three phrases clarify the meaning of "thusness" (*tathatā*).
All phenomena (*dharmas*) whatsoever are without exception identical to the *dharmatā*. This phrase clarifies the meaning of "coming" (*āgata*).

One should accord with the fourfold Four Noble Truths and the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional, exhausting the limits of the wheel of the two kinds of birth-and-death, and nourishing them through the Dharma.
Wisdom is non-dual with the principle of the Dharmakāya; thus, it eternally experiences the bliss of the foremost offering of Dharma and is therefore called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
"Right Wisdom" refers to the Fundamental Wisdom (mūla-jñāna), while "Noble Wisdom of Liberation" refers to the Discriminative Wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna).
The "Root" (mūla) is the meaning of ultimate correctness. "Joyful differentiation" is the meaning of pervasiveness. Regarding "brightly bright" (ming-ming):

the upper "bright" character refers to initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*), while the lower "bright" character refers to original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*). Because initial enlightenment merges with original enlightenment, it is called "brightly bright. "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to the power and function that accords with the nature.

"Practice" (*caryā*) refers to the merits inherent in the nature. One initiates cultivation from the nature and manifests the nature through cultivation; therefore, it is called "cultivation and practice" (*bhāvanā-caryā*).

That which was partially realized on the first stage is now brought to ultimate completion; therefore, it is called "perfected" (*pāda*). Regarding the phrase "the Buddha-dharma of the Sugata throughout the three times":

*sugata* has the meaning of "having entered. As for "the Dharma and the Buddha being the same as those of former Buddhas," this means that although his manifestations and transformations are boundless, their ritual protocols and formal standards are entirely identical to those of former Buddhas, and his *dharmakāya* is non-dual. Alternatively, "going" (*gata*) refers to manifesting entry into *nirvāṇa*.
Sometimes he manifests birth in the human world as an advent; there is nothing that does not accord with principle and accord with capacity.

Therefore, it is good and yet good. Question: Principle has no coming or going; coming and going follow according to capacity. One can only accord with capacity—how can one say it accords with principle? Answer:
Principle has no coming or going, nor is there any non-coming and non-going. Simply causing one to accord with capacity is itself to accord with principle. Furthermore, he manifests...
Coming accords with the capacity; thus it accords with the occasion (*ki*). Coming has no mark of coming; going has no mark of going; thus it accords with the principle (*ri*).

If a Bodhisattva of the Tripitaka Teaching can only come to deliver sentient beings but cannot go to reach Nirvana, then even if they accord with the capacity, they ultimately do not accord with the principle.
If those of the Two Vehicles can only go to reach Nirvana but cannot come [to deliver beings], [they likewise do not fully accord with the principle].

To deliver sentient beings: even if one accords with the principle, one ultimately does not accord with the capacity [of the audience]. To speak in absolute terms, since it does not accord with the principle, it also does not accord with the capacity;
for it cannot reach those whose capacities lie beyond its sphere. Since it does not accord with the capacity, it also does not accord with the principle;
for it has not yet attained non-abiding nirvana, but merely realizes partial emptiness, failing to exhaust the nature of reality. Furthermore, as for the provisional...

O Great Being, although you are universally able to manifest both going and coming, when emerging from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) one must give rise to the empty (*śūnya*), and when entering the empty one must abandon the conventional;

thus, this cannot yet be called "skillful within skillfulness. Now, without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), you manifest all dignified demeanors (*īryāpatha*).
Within these four demeanors, your mind is constantly in samādhi, like the bright moon in the sky: when the water is clear, its reflection appears, yet it does not come.
When water is turbid, the reflection vanishes, yet it does not depart; thus, one speaks of both coming and going as being entirely wholesome.
The sphere of activity of the Mahāsattva is the liberation of the world; it should be called that of the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*), for the text contains an error.

That "the wondrous essence is non-dual" means that initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) perfectly merges with original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) such that there is no duality. That which is "eternally and constantly great fulfillment" refers to—
It is ultimately fulfilled; all people of the world consult it, receive it, and follow its teachings.
Therefore, as for what is called the "Buddha-ground," when viewed from the perspective of the lower stages, this stage is also called "Buddha. It is the place entered by all holy beings.
Thus it is called the Stage of the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu-bhūmi*). This stage is the proximate cause for attaining Buddhahood and is also termed the "Bodhisattva.
At that time, sitting upon the precious lotus flower and so forth, one first ascends this stage and formally receives the office of a Buddha.

Furthermore, there are hundreds of thousands of billions and so forth; this refers to matters subsequent to having received the office of a Buddha. This ground contains that which is ineffable and so forth;
this concludes by manifesting the meritorious deeds. As in the "Chapter on the Light-Sound Heaven" (Ābhāsvara-deva-varga), it concludes briefly while pointing toward the extensive.
△ Third, the entrustment for wide propagation, in two parts: first, the entrustment by Vairocana; second, the propagation by Śākyamuni. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the formal conclusion and indication of the entrustment; second, the entrustment through the emission of light. This is the first.

At that time, Vairocana Buddha, for the sake of this great assembly, briefly opened up a portion of the Ground of the Mind (*cittabhūmi*), as small as a hair-tip, from among the inexpressible Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers.

This has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, will be taught by the Buddhas of the future, and is being taught now by the Buddhas of the present. Bodhisattvas of the three periods have studied it, will study it, and are studying it now. I have [already taught it] a hundred...
Having practiced this mind-ground for kalpas, I am named Vairocana. You, all Buddhas, shall turn what I have taught to open the path of the mind-ground for all sentient beings.
The source-ground of the mind is that which all sentient beings share in common; however, it has long been obstructed and blocked by the veil of ignorance.
Now, by turning this Dharma-gate, one causes it to open and unfold; therefore, it is called "opening the path of the mind-ground."
△ Second, the Emission of Light and Entrustment.
At that time, from the Lion Throne of radiant celestial light within the Lotus-Womb World, Vairocana Buddha emitted a light.
This light addressed the Buddhas upon the thousand petals, saying: "Take this 'Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground' and depart. Furthermore, transmit it..."
To the billions of Śākyamunis and all sentient beings, I shall now sequentially expound this chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Grounds of the Mind Above.
You should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and practice it with single-minded devotion.
Having already performed the formal conclusion and entrustment, the subsequent emission of light to announce it universally is precisely to manifest the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
Whether in terms of the fundamental or the derivative, whether cause or fruit, there is nothing that does not take wisdom as its precursor.

Thus, at the beginning, Śākyamuni emits light to initiate the teaching, signifying that the nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) is luminous and capable of perfuming initial enlightenment (*ādi-avabodha*). Next, the Bodhisattvas emit [light].
The gathering of light symbolizes the wisdom and virtue of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-jñāna*), which is able to seek out fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Now, Śākyamuni emits light and transmits the entrustment, symbolizing that the cause arises from the fruit, thereby excellently manifesting the fundamental principle.

Subsequently, Śākyamuni again emits light and recites the precepts, symbolizing that the fruit is realized within the cause, thereby skillfully cultivating the traces of practice. As these lights mutually reflect one another, one comes to fully understand the relationship between the initial and the fundamental.
Non-dual: cultivation and nature share a common source.
△ Second, Śākyamuni’s Broad Dissemination has three parts: first, receiving the Dharma and taking leave; second, returning to his original realm;
third, benefiting sentient beings in accordance with the imperial decree. Now, the first part.
At that time, the Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotuses—the hundreds of thousands of myriads of Śākyamunis—arose from their majestic lion thrones within the world-system of the Lotus Treasury.
Each withdrew respectfully and emitted inconceivable light from every part of their bodies.
From this light, immeasurable Buddhas were manifested, who simultaneously offered immeasurable flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white to Vairocana Buddha. They received and upheld [this teaching].
The "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" has been concluded above.
Regarding the emission of inconceivable light from the entire body: the manifested light (*jiki*) and the fundamental light (*honkō*) are no different;
both are the subtle, wondrous illumination of wisdom within the secret treasury of the three virtues. As for the light transforming into immeasurable Buddhas: this wisdom is all...
She is the Mother of the Buddhas; it is from her that all Buddhas are born. Regarding the "offerings of immeasurable flowers": flowers symbolize the wondrous cause.
This wondrous cause arises from the virtue of the fruit, and in turn, it is used to adorn that very virtue of the fruit.
△ Second, returning to their original realms:

each of them vanished from this Lotus-Womb World (Padmagarbha-lokadhātu). Having vanished, they entered the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature Emptiness (Tixing-xūkōng-huaguāng-samādhi) and returned to their original source-world, beneath the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa. From the Essential Nature Emptiness...
One emerges from the Flower-Light Samādhi (*Puṣpa-prabhāsa-samādhi*).
Regarding the name of this samādhi, "Flower-Light of the Void-like Essential Nature" (*Ākāśa-svabhāva-puṣpa-prabhāsa*):

it means that when one thoroughly realizes the essential nature which is fundamentally like space, then the flower-light manifests spontaneously and naturally. This essential nature is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*); the flower symbolizes liberation.

"Deliverance" (*mukti*) represents the virtue of *prajñā*. "Returning to the source-world of Jambudvīpa, beneath the Bodhi tree" refers, according to the opening text of the lower fascicle, to returning first to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara in the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven;
there he first preached the *Sūtra on Māra’s Conversion*, and only then descended to the human realm to manifest his renunciation.
He proceeded to the Bodhi tree; now, having gone directly to the foot of the Bodhi tree, he emerges from samādhi and correctly manifests the eight phases of attaining enlightenment.

From beginning to end, he never departs from this samādhi. Furthermore, since his previous arrival at the Flower Treasury World (Huazang) was termed a "return," his current arrival in the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa) is likewise called a "return to the world of the original source. The former represents the principle.

Regarding the "root of phenomena": here, phenomena are presented as the root of principle; thus, both may be termed "returning" (*huan*), signifying the "original source. What is meant by principle being the root of phenomena?

It means that the fundamental reality is solely the single, true principle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Yet, sentient beings differ in the depth of their delusion and the ease or difficulty of their awakening.
Therefore, the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), and the Tripitaka Teaching (*zangjiao*) were further established to reveal and instruct them. Furthermore...

Originally, there was only the single practice, which is the practice of the Tathāgata. However, because the faculties of sentient beings vary between sharp and dull, and their cultivation varies between skillful and clumsy, five practices, ten thousand practices, and so forth were further established to encompass them all. Furthermore, originally there was only the true, eternal Dharmakāya.
Yet sentient beings have long remained in saṃsāra, unable to see for themselves; therefore, [the Buddha] further manifests superior and inferior response-bodies and so forth to awaken them.
Furthermore, while the fundamental realm is solely the pure land of the Dharma-realm light, sentient beings have turned their backs upon it for a long time.

Since there would be no way to enter [enlightenment], he further manifests lands such as the Land of True Reward, the Land of Expedient Means, and the Land of Shared Dwelling to gather and sustain sentient beings.
This is called "principle being the foundation of phenomena. What is meant by "phenomena being the foundation of principle"?

It means that these very dharmas produced through causes and conditions—these dharmas are themselves emptiness, they are themselves the provisional, and they are themselves the Middle Way. In total, nothing can be separated from this realm of true causes and conditions. And yet...

Let us set aside further discussion of principle (li). Furthermore, regarding these very practices of giving, precept-keeping, and so forth—whether one realizes that their three spheres (trimaṇḍala) are empty of intrinsic nature, or knows that their adornment is inexhaustible, or understands that their essence is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu)—in no case may one abandon the practical cultivation of these six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) to engage in lofty talk of theoretical contemplation.
Moreover, this very body of sixteen feet in height, which is the eternal body, is called the fundamental object (ālambana).
Those of sharp faculties within the realm perceive him seated upon a celestial robe throne, turning the Dharma wheel of the Four Truths of Non-arising.
Those of dull faculties outside the realm perceive his marks and signs as infinite, pervasively seated throughout the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Those of sharp faculties outside the realm perceive each and every physical form as, in its very essence, nothing other than the true Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...
The Sūtra says: "The subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body possesses the thirty-two marks. Where else are there four Buddhas who preach four teachings for four types of people?

Furthermore, within this very same land of common residence (*sahā-loka*), those who have severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are immediately able to see the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*) horizontally;
those who have shattered ignorance (*avidyā*) are immediately able to see the Land of True Retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*) horizontally; and those whose ignorance is exhausted...
One may be able to see the *sukhāvatī* (Peaceful Light) horizontally; as a land of skillful means (*upāya*), it may still be said to exist separately outside the realm.
However, regarding the *sambhogakāya* (True Reward) *sukhāvatī*, there is nothing that is separated from this land. This is what is meant by "phenomena being the basis of principle."

△ Third, complying with the imperial decree to benefit sentient beings, which has two parts: first, clarifying the Buddhas of a single world-realm; second, applying this by way of analogy to the Buddhas of all other realms. Now, the first part.
Having emerged [from the ocean], he then sat upon the Vajra-Thousand-Rays King Throne and in the Hall of Sublime Light, where he expounded the ten world-oceans. Furthermore...

Rising from his seat, he went to the palace of Śakra and expounded the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*). Rising again from his seat, he went among the Yāma devas and expounded the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*).
Rising again from his seat, he went to the fourth heaven (*Tuṣita*) and expounded the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Rising again from his seat, he went to the Nirmāṇarati devas and expounded the Ten Meditative Concentrations (*daśa-dhyāna*). Rising again from his seat, he went to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas and expounded the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*). Then he went to the first dhyāna.
Within the second dhyāna, he taught the Ten Vajras; then, reaching the third dhyāna, he taught the Ten Vows;

and finally, reaching the fourth dhyāna, in the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, he taught the Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground as expounded by Rocana Buddha in the Lotus-Womb Treasury World, which is his own source.
"Method" (fang) means "correct. Because one dwells securely in the True Dharma, it is called "sitting in the method" (fangzuo).
Regarding the "Vajra Thousand-Light King Seat," the title in the lower fascicle reads "Flower-Light King Seat"; the character "thousand" (qian) is an error for the character "flower" (hua).

Vajra symbolizes the virtue of the Dharmakāya; flower symbolizes liberation; and light symbolizes prajñā. Thus, it is entirely constituted by the True Dharma of the secret treasury of the three virtues.

As for that seat: the Hall of Sublime Light is the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-maṇḍapa*). Among the seven locations and nine assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka*, it is frequently stated that [the Buddha] does not rise from his original place;
here, however, it says he "again rises from his seat. These differences arise because the capacities of the audience vary, resulting in different perspectives.
This is briefly explained as analyzed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). The Palace of Śakra is the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, located at the summit of Mount Sumeru.

This is called the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa). It consists of eight celestial ministers in each of the four directions, together with the Lord of Gods in the center, making thirty-three.

The Yama Heaven is also called the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; this is translated as "Time-portion" (Śivagaṇa), because it distinguishes day and night not by the light of the sun and moon, but by the opening and closing of lotus flowers. The fourth heaven is Tuṣita Heaven.
This is called "Contentment. Those born in this heaven are content with all five sensory desires;

therefore, it contains an inner court where those in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) reside. Furthermore, having reached the fourth dhyāna, he then expounded this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
Originally, this was initiated by emitting light from within the fourth dhyāna and proceeding to the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) to receive this Dharma;
therefore, it is now still taught within the fourth dhyāna. Furthermore, in the palace of Śakra and other such places, this Mind-Ground Dharma is taught in various parts.

Within the palaces of the four dhyānas, this Dharma of the Mind-Ground is explained collectively; its separate explanation manifests the sequential arrangement (prabhu), while its collective explanation manifests the perfect fusion (yuanrong).
Furthermore, it reveals that although the stages of this Dharma of the Mind-Ground are differentiated, they all ultimately converge toward the supreme fruit.
△ Second, the analogy concludes by applying it to the remaining Buddha-fields:
"The other thousands of myriads of kotis of Śākyamunis are likewise; they are non-dual and without distinction, as explained in the 'Chapter on the Worthy Kalpa' (Bhadrakalpika-parivarta)."
The Combined Commentary on the "Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Heart" Chapter from the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Second;
The Combined Commentary on the "Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Heart" Chapter from the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Third (Beginning of the Lower Volume).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Commentary by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Zhixu of Ancient Wu;
Revised by the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Daofang of Wēn’lǐng. Part Three:

The Exposition of the Śākyamuni’s Proclamation of the Bodhisattva Precepts. I. Preface: Narrating the Profound Causes for the Proclamation of the Precepts. II. Illustration: Distinguishing the Gravity and Lightness of Offenses.

The Characteristics of the Precepts. Third, exhorting the great assembly to practice them. This section has two parts: first, a recapitulation of the manifestation of traces and the transmission of the Dharma;
second, the formal explanation of the exhortation under the tree. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, the prose; second, the verse.
This section consists of two parts: first, the formal description of the Trace Buddha’s propagation of the Dharma; second, the clarification of how he gathers sentient beings through the precepts.
Now, for the first part:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emerged from the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury World in the east and entered [the assembly].
Having preached the *Sūtra on the Conversion of Māra* within the palace of the Heavenly King, I descended to be born in Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
My mother’s name was Māyā and my father’s surname was Śuddhodana; my name is Siddhārtha. At the age of seven I left the household life, and at thirty I attained the Way.

He is titled Śākyamuni Buddha. At the site of the terrace of tranquil extinction (*śānta-mārga-maṇḍala*), seated upon the Vajra-flower-light-king throne, and extending even unto the palace of the celestial king Maheśvara, he taught sequentially throughout these ten successive abodes.
At that time, the Buddha observed the net-bannered standards of the Great Brahmā Kings and, on that account, spoke of immeasurable worlds as being like the mesh of a net.
Each and every world is distinct and different, their varieties being immeasurable; the gateways of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so.

I have now come to this world eight thousand times. For the sake of this Sahā world, I have sat upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King Throne, and even in the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, to briefly open the heart for all the great assemblies therein.
The section on the Dharma-gate of the Grounds is concluded.
Regarding "from the initial manifestation of the Lotus-womb World," this refers to the beginning of the preceding volume:
from the emission of light that thoroughly illuminates the fourth dhyāna heaven, up to the event of being received and returned. [The Buddha] enters the palace of the Heavenly King from the east.
This means that having already received and upheld the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi*), he entered the Samādhi of the Nature of Empty Space and Flower-Light (*ākāśapuṣpaprakāśa*).
Within this samādhi, he returned to this land, specifically to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara.

Since this land lies to the east of the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpakaraṇḍa*), it is said that he "came from the east. As for the *Sūtra on the Demon Receiving Transformation*, it is distinct [from the others].

For those of sharp faculties in the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna), it is shown that he has already finished subduing Māra in the fourth dhyāna heaven before descending again to be born [in this world], as clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning);
this differs from what is seen in the Tripiṭaka, which holds that he only subdued Māra upon reaching the foot of the tree. Kāpilavastu is also called Kapilavastu; in its full form, it is Kapilavastu.
It is translated as the site upon which the yellow color depends. In ancient times, there was a rishi with yellow hair who relied on this place to practice the Way.
The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) calls it Kapilavastu; this is translated as "Red Marsh. It is also named Bodhisiṃha or Siṃha;
this is translated as "Abode of the Able One" (Śākyamuni). Māyā—its full name is Mahāmāyā.
Yes. This is translated as "Great Art" (Mahāmāyā) or "Great Illusion. It means that by means of the dharma-gate of the illusion of great vow-wisdom, she serves as the mother of the Tathāgata.
She is called Śuddhodana; alternatively, she is called Śuddhodana, Śuddhodana, or *Śuddha*. In the Sanskrit language, she is called Śuddhodana.
Some call him Śuddhodana. Siddhārtha is fully rendered as Sarvasiddha;
this translates as "Utterly Auspicious," because at the time of the Prince's birth, all auspicious omens were fully present. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* translates it as "Accomplished Benefit.
The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: *Sarvārthasiddha*, which in the language of Tang means "All Meanings Accomplished. Formerly he was called Siddhārtha.
"Da" (達) is a corruption or abbreviation. "Seven years of leaving home" (*chūjiā qīsuì*) means that he left home at the age of seven.

This refers to the time when, having first left home, he first studied the *ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi* (the concentration of the sphere of nothingness) and attained realization before long; yet he knew it was not the ultimate goal.

Next, he studied the *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi* (the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception) and again attained realization before long; he knew that this, too, was not the ultimate goal. Thereafter, he again traveled through various countries. In all cases...
After one year, he further practiced austerities for six years; at the age of thirty, he attained perfect enlightenment.
All that occurred prior to this was within the Samādhi of the Empty Nature of Flower-Light.
Having manifested the attainment of Buddhahood, it is said that he emerged from samādhi and sat upon the Vajra-Flower-Light King Throne and in the Hall of Sublime Light to expound the Ten [Dharmas].

The ocean of worlds. Next, he again traveled extensively through the realms of Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin, as well as the first, second, and third dhyānas, and the palace of Maheśvara—ten locations in total. There he expounded ten kinds of Dharma gates.

Having completed his preaching of the Dharma, he further provided parables to enable those to be reached by the teaching to understand both the capacities of the recipients and the teachings that could reach them.
All are like the Brahma-net; none transcend the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground. The site of tranquil extinction is itself the site of Bodhi.
Bodhi is wisdom, and tranquil extinction is principle. By sitting in this place, one employs the wisdom of Bodhi.
Because one realizes the principle of quiescent extinction, it is called the Bodhimanda (the Place of Enlightenment) and also the Mandala of Quiescent Extinction.
The statement that [the Buddha] has come to this world eight thousand times specifically indicates the matter of attaining perfect enlightenment;

it does not refer to other transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), as has already been clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). The phrase "briefly opening the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground" concludes the preceding discussion.
△ Second, clarifying the gathering of sentient beings through the precepts. Furthermore,
from the Palace of the Heavenly King down to the Bodhi tree beneath the Jambūdvīpa tree, for the sake of all sentient beings upon this earth—
those ordinary people shrouded in the darkness of ignorance— I have explained the initial aspiration within the mind-ground of my original self, Vairocana Buddha.
The one precept that is constantly recited within the mind is the Radiant Vajra Jewel Precept.
It is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all Bodhisattvas, and the seed of Buddha-nature. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
all consciousness, form, and mind—whether emotional or mental—all enter into the Buddha-nature precept, for there is always a cause at every moment. At every moment...
It shall abide eternally as the Dharma-body. Thus do these ten *pratimokṣa* emerge in the world;

they are the Dharma-precepts, which all sentient beings of the three periods of time wear upon their crowns and uphold. Now, for the sake of this great assembly, I shall again proclaim the Chapter on the Inexhaustible Treasury of Precepts.
This is the precept of all sentient beings, pure by its original source and intrinsic nature.
When the ten assemblies have concluded, regarding the subsequent explanation of the Chapter on Precepts:

although these subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates—such as the stages of abiding, practice, transference, and the grounds—are inherently complete within the nature of every person, because they have been mired in delusion for a long time, they currently sit upon the ground of ignorance and darkness.
How can one gain entry? Although even deluded and ignorant ordinary beings possess their own skillful means for entering, I fear only that they do not resolve their minds [to seek enlightenment].
Consider, for instance, Vairocana Buddha: he was originally an ignorant and deluded ordinary being as well;
however, as soon as he first resolved his mind, he received the precepts, and after receiving the precepts, he constantly recited and practiced them. It is for this reason that he achieved success.
The Dharma-gate of Realizing the Mind-Ground: from now until the attainment of Buddhahood, this single precept shall serve as the most supreme cause and condition.
This precept has been transmitted successively by all Buddhas of antiquity; it was not newly established.
It is the foremost, most sublime, and wondrous precept that dispels all darkness and is thus called "Luminosity," and which crushes all afflictions—this is the metaphor.

If it is like a diamond (*vajra*), it is called a "jewel" because it extensively possesses all the wealth of meritorious qualities (*guṇa-dharma*). Furthermore, because it illuminates all phenomena, it is called "light.
This refers to the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint). Because its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called "diamond. This refers to the *pratimokṣa-śīla* (the morality of discipline).

Because it benefits and utilizes sentient beings, it is called a "jewel. This refers to the *upapatti-śīla* (the morality of benefiting others). Thus, it is not merely Śākyamuni alone [who possesses these].
By means of this, one attains Buddhahood. Generally speaking, there are no Buddhas who do not take these precepts as their source.
Likewise, there are no Bodhisattvas who do not take these precepts as their source.

For if one is separated from these precepts, then the Dharma-gates of the thirty minds and the ten stages will all fail to be accomplished; even all the merits of the stage of Buddhahood will likewise not be attained.
It is because of accomplishment. Regarding the "seed of Buddha-nature," this precept takes the *dharmatā* (true cause) Buddha-nature as its seed.
As stated in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, because one knows that the *dharmatā* is free from defilement, one practices the *śīla-pāramitā* in accordance with it;

thus, the *pratyaya* (conditional) and *nirmāṇa* (evolving) Buddha-natures are also involved. Furthermore, taking these precepts as the seed, as stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, [it is] the One...
All sentient beings, although they possess the Buddha-nature, must first maintain the precepts before they can perceive it.
By perceiving the Buddha-nature, they then achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Since all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature and this Buddha-nature pervades all phenomena, whether it be thought, consciousness, form, or mind—whatever is mundane...
These emotions and this mind—there is nothing that does not enter into the Buddha-nature precepts.
These precepts are truly and eternally the true cause; these precepts are truly and eternally the wondrous fruit of the Dharmakāya.
Thus, these ten *pratimokṣa* emerge in the world to universally benefit all sentient capacities. Therefore, these dharma-precepts are [the source] of all things throughout the three periods of time.
All sentient beings should receive and uphold this upon the crown of their heads. "Contemplation" (*manas*) refers specifically to the seventh [consciousness];
"discrimination" (*vijñāna*) refers specifically to the first six; "arising through accumulation" (*citta*) refers specifically to the eighth.

"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the five sense organs and the four great elements. "Sentient being" (*sattva*) excludes that which is insentient; "possessing mind" (*sacittaka*) excludes that which is without mind. This is intended to exclude [the latter].
Wood and stone have no mind and are incapable of receiving the precepts; however, all that possesses a mind has Buddha-nature.

Those who possess Buddha-nature immediately enter into the precepts of Buddha-nature. These wondrous precepts arise entirely in dependence upon the fundamental essence of the principle of Buddha-nature.
It further reveals and adorns the Buddha-nature; therefore, it is called the "Buddha-nature precept. The term *dangdang* means precisely and certainly.
Since it arises from the entirety of the nature (*xing*), it is truly the eternal true cause.
Since it reveals and adorns the Buddha-nature through this, it is truly the eternally abiding wondrous fruit of the Dharma-body. This is what is meant by the "Ten Non-" [precepts].
The exhaustion of precepts: it is the root of all precepts. Because it ensures that the practitioner reaches the shore of liberation, it is named *prātimokṣa*.

This precept is itself an inexhaustible treasury; because it takes the fundamentally pure nature of the source as its supporting substance, it constitutes the wondrous substance of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) precepts. Thus, it gives rise to this non-action precept.

The essence [of the precepts] further comprises three points: first, the formal presentation of the unmanifest (avijñapti) discipline; second, the concurrent clarification of the two types of restraint—those of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and the Path (mārga);
and third, the further elucidation of the threefold aggregate of precepts (tri-skandha-śīla). Regarding the first, the formal presentation of the unmanifest discipline, Master Tiantai said:
"As for the essence of the precepts, it is simply non-arising; when it arises, it is the nature of unmanifest form. Master Pan’s commentary states:

This means that as for the essence of this precept: if it does not arise, that is one thing; once it arises, it is the entirety of its nature (*dharmatā*). Thus, nature and cultivation are mutually accomplished.
There must necessarily be non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*). Regarding "informative matter," the nature [of the precept] must rely on informative matter as its manifest expression.

Once the non-informative has been produced, it spontaneously ceases evil and spontaneously performs good without requiring further effort; therefore, it is called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*). This...
The Bodhisattva’s unconditioned discipline (*anabhisaṃskāra-śīla*) should be elucidated through seven points of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*):
first, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is primordial purity; second, its cause (*hetu*) is the superior wholesome mind;
third, its conditions (*pratyaya*) are the three kinds of sublime objects; fourth, its essence (*bhāva*) is the threefold ritual of formal motion and announcement (*jñapti-karman*); fifth...
First, its characteristic is manifested through untainted, sublime form. Second, its goal is the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood.
Third, its fruition is the most wondrous Dharma-body. Regarding "having purity as its nature":
this refers to the true mark of all phenomena—neither arising nor ceasing, neither eternal nor annihilated—and such is that upon which this precept relies.
This is the essence of its principle. Second, regarding the superior causal mind:
this refers to the arousal of the bodhicitta, donning the armor of the Four Great Vows, seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below, with the aspiration for the ultimate fruit.

Furthermore, it requires the initial mind of the Distinct and Complete Teachings to evoke this precept; the minds of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings cannot give rise to this unsurpassed precept. Third, superiority...

Regarding "taking the objective field as a condition," the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) states: "Receiving [the precepts] in the presence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is called the superior grade of precept.
Receiving them before a Bodhisattva Dharma Master is called the middle grade of precept. Where there is no teacher for a thousand li, one vows and receives them before a sūtra or an image;
this is called the inferior grade of precept. Regarding the vow to receive the precepts oneself, there are further distinctions, as this very sūtra states:
One must obtain a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*). Whether it be the *Yingluo jing* or the *Dichi jing*, all emphasize the importance of generating the bodhicitta;

some prioritize internal causes while others emphasize external conditions, each having its own justification. One must personally examine and weigh these matters. Regarding the fourth method—attaining [the precepts] through the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*)—Master Pan stated:
"At the time of the first formal motion (*jñapti*), the wondrous and wholesome dharma of the precepts from the worlds of the ten directions enters through the mind."

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the section on mindfulness of the precepts (*śīla-anusmṛti*), states: "Although it has no form or color, it can be guarded and maintained;

If one receives it through a personal vow, it is likewise obtained at the moment of the three announcements (*tri-śrāvaṇa*), or at the time of seeing auspicious signs.

Furthermore, regarding the five aspects of untainted form (*anāsravarūpa*): immediately upon completing the reception of the precepts, one attains the aspect of non-killing with respect to sentient beings within the dharma-realm;

One attains the non-disruption of form (*rūpa*). Although these dharmas, such as non-killing and non-stealing, have no visible form or characteristics, they are manifested by way of form.
That is to say, they are not the form of the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana-rūpa*), but rather the form of the sense-base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).

Furthermore, since killing, stealing, and so forth are outflowing (*sāsrava*) dharmas, their opposites—non-killing and so forth—are outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharmas; therefore, they are called "outflow-free form-dharmas" (*anāsrava-rūpa-dharma*). For this reason:

Before receiving the precepts, although one does not necessarily commit acts such as killing or stealing in every moment of thought, the worlds of the ten directions are none other than the field for my killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying;

Therefore, within a single thought-moment, one accomplishes untainted, subtle, and wondrous wholesome form, each instance pervading the entire dharma-realm.

The precepts have no separate substance; therefore it is said: "If a person receives the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas, because they share the same substance of the precepts as the Buddhas of the three periods of time. All possess the precepts of meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*) and the precepts of the Path (*mārga-saṃvara*). That which refers to the natural cessation of all evils through the power of meditative concentration is called the precepts of meditative concentration.
That which refers to the natural and permanent departure from all evils through the power of the Path is called the precepts of the Path.

Regarding these two types of restraint—those of concentration and the Path—if one has previously received the restraint of the precepts (*saṃvara-śīla*), it is merely through concentration and the Path [that the unmanifest restraint arises].

It becomes increasingly bright and pure, and there is no longer any distinct entity. If one has not previously received the vows of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), they will immediately give rise to such restraint through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or the Path (*mārga*).

Furthermore, that which is concomitant with concentration is also called the "dhyāna-precept" (*dhyāna-śīla*); that which is concomitant with the Path is also called the "untainted precept" (*anāsrava-śīla*).

It takes non-action as its essence. Although the *vinaya* fully enumerates all aspects of the grave and light offenses, it mentions only the ten *pārājika* rules because the forty-eight minor offenses are all the outflows and attendants of these ten grave precepts.

The Dharma can accomplish the *saṃbhogakāya*; by gathering sentient beings, it can accomplish the *nirmāṇakāya*. Furthermore, through the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), one accomplishes the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*);

through the morality of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*), one accomplishes the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*); and through the morality of gathering sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyā-śīla*), one accomplishes the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*).

The mind of the Hīnayāna aspires only for its own liberation; seeing suffering and abandoning its origin, it possesses only the morality of restraint and does not yearn for the stage of Buddhahood. Thus it is said.

The words of the sūtra’s compiler: The initial verse describes the beginning of the bestowal by Vairocana:
I, now Vairocana, Am seated upon the lotus pedestal; Upon the thousand petals surrounding me, There further appear a thousand Śākyamunis.
Within each petal are ten billion lands, And in each land is one Śākyamuni.
Each sitting beneath a Bodhi tree, they simultaneously attain the Way of Buddhahood.
Thus, from the original body of Vairocana, there arise a thousand billion Śākyamunis;
each receives a multitude of beings as numerous as motes of dust, who all come together to my presence to hear me recite the Buddha’s precepts, whereby the Gate of Ambrosia immediately opens.

Ambrosia (*amṛta*) is the medicine of immortality; it is a metaphor for the one who upholds the precepts, who is able to attain the eternal bliss, selfhood, and purity of *nirvāṇa*, forever free from old age and death.
A gate is that which enables passage; the teaching enables one to penetrate the principle. By the power of the teaching and the precepts, one is enabled to reach the city of Great *Nirvāṇa*.
△ Second, the verse on Śākyamuni’s transmission of the entrustment:

Just as with the pearls of a necklace, so too do the multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as motes of dust, thereby achieve perfect enlightenment.
This is what Rocana recites; I likewise recite it. You, newly initiated bodhisattvas, should receive and uphold these precepts upon your heads.

To be rich in jewels is the meaning of gathering wholesome dharmas (śubha-saṃgraha). Just as the sun and moon adorn the heavens and all gaze up toward them in reverence, and as necklaces upon the body are loved and respected by all who behold them, so too is the meaning of gathering sentient beings (sattva-saṃgraha).

Having thus exhorted others to receive and uphold [the teaching], one should further exhort them to transmit it to others, so that the lamps may continue from one to another and the transformations [of the Dharma] may be inexhaustible.

These five also belong to the fourth dhyāna and are the abodes of noble ones who have attained the three fruits. Although these eighteen heavens are [inhabited by] ordinary beings...
The sages are not the same; they have all abandoned desire and defilement and attained pure meditative concentration (dhyāna), and are therefore called Brahmā-devas.

As for the sons of the six heavens of desire, these specifically refer to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*): first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; third, the Yāma Heaven; fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven;
fifth, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and sixth, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. Although these six heavens of desire still possess males...
The five desires of women are naturally provided as their karmic retribution; they need not be sought through effort. Therefore, they are all called "devas" (heavenly beings).
Regarding the kings of the sixteen great nations, these are the most numerous among the various kingdoms of the Western Regions;
taking those that are particularly large, there are sixteen nations: first, Śākya; second, Magadha; third, Kāśī; fourth, Kośala; fifth, Vṛji; sixth, Malla; seventh...
1. Ceti; 2. Aṭavi; 3. Vatsa; 4. Bhaṭṭa; 5. Kuru; 6. Kośala; 7. Cedi; 8. Vatsa; 9. Nīla; 10. Pañcāla; 11. Aśmaka; 12. Vatsa; 13. Sura; 14.
Gandhāra; 15. Kamboja; 16. Aparāntaka. "With palms joined" refers to the solemnity and respect of the bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
"With a focused mind" refers to the single-minded devotion of the mental action (*manaskarman*). "Listen" refers to the [verbal action].
The karma is stilled. Listen attentively with focused ears.
△ Second, Śākyamuni’s own discourse has three parts: first, citing his own recitation to exhort others; second, clarifying the causes and conditions for emitting light.
Third, the exhortation for the great assembly to practice and study. First:
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying, "I now recite the Dharma-precepts of all Buddhas every half-month.

You who have all resolved your minds upon bodhisattvahood, including those in the ten stages of setting forth (*niryāṇa*), the ten stages of nurturing (*puṣṭi*), the ten adamantine stages (*vajra*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*)," and so forth.
The Bodhisattva also recites it.
Regarding "every half-month": the day of the full moon is the fifteenth of the white fortnight, and the day of the new moon is the fifteenth of the black fortnight.

The white represents the gradual fulfillment of the virtues of wisdom, while the black represents the gradual exhaustion of the virtues of abandonment; therefore, on these days, one recites this precept.
The Dharma is called *poṣadha*. It is correctly transliterated as *bōsuītó* (poṣadha). *Poṣa* has the meaning of "nurturing" (*dīrgha-poṣa*), and *dha* has the meaning of "purifying.
This refers to nurturing wholesome dharmas and purifying away unwholesome ones. Even the Buddha himself recited it; how much more so others?
Since the Buddha himself recited it, we know that the claim that the practice was abolished upon reaching Buddhahood does not accord with the ultimate principle.
△ Second, explaining the causes and conditions for the emission of light.
For this reason, the light of the precepts issues from the mouth. Because there is a condition and it is not without cause, there is light. This light is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black;
it is neither form nor mind; it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is not a phenomenon of cause and effect. It is the fundamental source of all Buddhas. Practice.
This is the root of the Bodhisattva path; it is the root of all the sons of the Buddha in the great assembly.
The first phrase directly explains the conditions for the emission of light. This light represents the essence of non-active (anabhisaṃskāra) precepts.
This non-active precept takes the inherent virtues (prakṛti-guṇa) entirely as its fundamental cause; therefore, it is not without cause. Since it arises entirely from the nature, [it is so].
Thus, it is in its entirety the very nature itself. Therefore, it is neither blue nor yellow, and so forth, up to being neither cause nor effect.
It is not colors such as blue or yellow; it is not the discriminating consciousness-mind; and it does not fall into the false emotions or false objects of ordinary, ignorant beings.
It is neither existent nor non-existent; it does not fall into the fruit of the false views of annihilationism or eternalism. It is not a phenomenon of cause and effect;
it does not fall into the fruit of provisional, small-scale cultivation or realization. Not falling into any such fruits, it is the wondrous fruit of the Dharmakāya.

Since it is the wondrous fruition of the Dharma-body, it is also the true cause for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the great assembly of Buddha-sons, take this as their fundamental source.
△ Third, the exhortation for the great assembly to practice and study:
"Therefore, O sons of the Buddhas in the great assembly, you should receive and uphold it; you should read and recite it; you should learn it well. Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively!"
If one receives the Buddha’s precepts, this applies to kings, princes, ministers and officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, the eighteen Brahmā heavens,
the sons of the gods of the six heavens of desire, commoners, eunuchs, male and female libertines, slaves, and the eight classes of spirits and deities.
Vajra deities, animals, and even emanated persons—provided they understand the words of the Dharma Master—all may receive the precepts;
they are all called those of the foremost purity.
To experience [an object] is called "feeling" (*vedanā*); to grasp it firmly is called "retention" (*dhāraṇā*). To recite its words orally is "reading and recitation" (*svādhyāya*);

to personally practice its meaning is "proper study" (*śikṣā*). *Paṇḍaka*: here translated as "not male. There are five types in total: namely, the innate (*jāti*), the castrated (*kṛta*), the transformed (*pakṣa*), the envious (*īrṣyā*), and the half-impotent (*pārśva*).
There are two interpretations regarding the eight classes [of beings]. One version states: first, devas; second, nāgas;
third, yakṣas; fourth, gandharvas; fifth, asuras; sixth, garuḍas; seventh, kiṃnaras; and eighth, mahoragas.
Another version states that each of the Four Heavenly Kings leads two classes: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King of the East, leads the gandharvas and the piśācas.
The Heavenly King Virūḍhaka of the South leads the kumbhāṇḍas and the pūtanas.
The Heavenly King Virūpākṣa of the West leads the nāgas and the pūrṇas. The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa of the North leads the yakṣas and the rākṣasas.
The Vajra Deities—also called the Vajradharas and the Vajrapāṇis—hold the vajra.
The *mudgara* (pestle) is that which attends upon all Buddhas. "Transformed persons" refers to devas, nāgas, and others who manifest in human form.
They understand the Dharma Master’s speech; those who do not understand the speech are excluded. If they do not understand, they cannot generate the bodhicitta as a supreme cause;
therefore, they must be excluded. Yet, their specific types are not distinguished, for they all equally possess the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
If one understands [the precepts], then upon receiving them, one fully attains the precepts; those who do not understand, even if they receive them, do not obtain them.
Prior to receiving the precepts, there may be distinctions between purity and impurity; however, once this precept is received, all become supreme vessels for the Dharma.
Therefore, all are called the foremost purity.
△ Next, the enumeration of the grave and light precepts has two parts: first, the ten grave precepts; second, the forty-eight light precepts. Within the first part, there are three sections:
first, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation; third, the summary conclusion. Now, the first section.
The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddhas, saying: "There are ten grave *prātimokṣa* precepts.
If one has received the Bodhisattva precepts and does not recite these precepts, they are not a Bodhisattva; they are not the seed of a Buddha. I have likewise recited them;

all Bodhisattvas of the past have studied them, all Bodhisattvas of the future shall study them, and all Bodhisattvas of the present are studying them. Thus he briefly explained the Bodhisattva *prātimokṣa*.
One should study the characteristics of the *prātimokṣa* and respectfully uphold it.
That which is called the ten grave precepts of the *prātimokṣa*: if one violates them, one is forever cast out from the ocean of the Buddha; if one maintains them, one secures liberation.
Having received them, one must recite them; by reciting them, one comes to know what is upheld and what is violated, and one knows what is light and what is grave.
Know that one must skillfully protect and uphold [the precepts]. If one does not recite them, they will gradually fall into oblivion;

in the present life, one loses the rank of a bodhisattva, and in the future, one loses the seed for attaining Buddhahood. Thus, it is very clear that one must not fail to recite them. Regarding their characteristics:

although the precepts have no physical form, they are manifested through their observance or violation. In detail, there are the ten grave and forty-eight light offenses; in brief, they are as follows:
