"Nirvāṇa" (*mie*) refers to that which is expressed (*so-quan*). The two characters "Sūtra" (*jing*) and "Vinaya" (*lü*) refer to that which expresses (*neng-quan*). That is to say, the Sūtra expresses the Dharma (*fa*), while the Vinaya expresses the *vinaya*.
However, since *vinaya* is correctly translated as "discipline" (*lü*), and "Sūtra" is also glossed as "Dharma" and "eternal" (*chang*), the phrasing appears redundant.
The principles must be clearly understood. These refer to the two categories of Sūtra and Vinaya, which are common to the world.
However, worldly sūtras do not necessarily expound the True Dharma (saddharma), and worldly vinayas do not necessarily expound the Vinaya (discipline).
Only within the Buddha’s sūtras and the Buddha’s vinayas is that which clarifies the five kinds of practices corresponding to detachment designated as "Dharma" and also as "Vinaya. Furthermore...
This is called the instruction of the Buddha. That is to say: it is renunciation, not worldly dharma; it is transcendence, not craving for existence; it is desirelessness, not having desires;
it is freedom from fetters, not having fetters; it is non-approaching toward birth and death, not approaching them.
Furthermore, that which is associated with the fivefold practice of deliverance is called the Vinaya, and is also called the Dharma. It is also...
This is called the Buddha’s instruction and admonition. That is to say: it causes one to have few desires rather than many desires; it causes one to be content rather than insatiable;
it causes one to be easy to protect rather than difficult to protect; it causes one to be easy to sustain rather than difficult to sustain;

it causes one to possess wisdom rather than ignorance. For this reason, it is called the *Dharmavinaya Sūtra-vinaya*. This *Dharmavinaya* is to be equally honored by both the Great and Small Vehicles, and is common to all seven classes of followers.
This practice is not restricted solely to Śrāvakas.

This constitutes an obstructive karma (*vāraṇīya-karman*). A transgression is established through four conditions: first, the actual teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya; second, the perception that one is teaching the Dharma and Vinaya;

third, the absence of a desire to go [to listen], whether due to anger, pride, or other such defilements—which constitutes a defiled (*kliṣṭa*) offense—or due to indolence, which constitutes a non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*) offense; fourth, the failure to...
Go to listen. Every day one incurs an offense. In the *Sūtra on Good Birth*, it is prescribed that one must go within forty *li*;
this case should be treated likewise. There is no offense if: one does not understand; if one is ill; if one lacks strength; if the speaker explains erroneously;

if one protects the mind of the speaker; if one has heard it repeatedly; if one has already received and upheld it; if one already knows the meaning; if one is of great learning; or if one has [already] heard it.
If one maintains [the precepts]; if one practices according to the teachings; if one cultivates meditative concentration and does not wish to abandon it even for a moment;
or if one has dull faculties and finds it difficult to realize, difficult to receive, and difficult to maintain—none of these constitute an offense if they do not go.
The seven assemblies are the same; the differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are as previously explained.

Regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited, the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma while mixing it with the doctrines of non-Buddhists, a virtuous bhikṣu who diligently seeks the Way should leave his seat. If he does not leave, he is not a virtuous bhikṣu. It also says: "Furthermore..."
One is not called a follower of the Buddha’s teachings.

Regarding the karmic fruit: the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* states that when a bodhisattva listens to the Dharma from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), there are five points concerning the person who preaches the Dharma that one should not dwell upon while listening with a pure mind and single-minded attention. First, one should not dwell upon their broken precepts.
That is to say, one does not think: "This person has violated their vows; I should not listen to or receive the sūtras and Dharma from them.
Second, one does not think of their inferior nature, meaning one does not think: "I will not listen to or receive the sūtras and Dharma from this person of inferior nature."
Third, not dwelling on ugliness: this means not thinking, "I will not listen to or receive the Dharma from this ugly person.
Fourth, not dwelling on the corruption of flavor: this means not thinking, "I will not listen to or receive the Dharma from that person of improper speech";
rather, one relies upon the meaning and does not rely upon the flavor. Fifth, not dwelling on the corruption of... [text truncated]
"Beautiful speech" means not thinking: "I will not listen to or receive the Dharma from that person who speaks coarse words.

When a bodhisattva does not harbor such recollections regarding these five points, they are diligently upholding the True Dharma and do not give rise to thoughts of aversion toward the teacher of the Dharma.
It should be known that if a bodhisattva of inferior faculties gives rise to thoughts of another's faults, they will regress and take no pleasure in listening to the Dharma.
This bodhisattva cannot save himself; his wisdom has declined and diminished. The commentary explains: "The decline and diminution of wisdom is the fault of not listening.

If one can listen with a sincere heart, then even a novice monk who playfully tosses [a seed] would be capable of realizing the four fruits of arhatship—how much more so when the True Dharma is actually being preached?"
Regarding "understanding": not observing the mind through the phenomena is precisely not going to listen to the Dharma.
Regarding "repentance": in terms of phenomena, one does not go; in terms of the ritual procedure, one does not go; in terms of principle, one does not go—this is non-arising.

Regarding practice and realization: as for the movement toward phenomena (*dharma*), one should follow the examples of Sadāprarudita and Sudhana; as for the movement toward principle (*tattva*), it is like contemplating emptiness within a stone chamber.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva achieves mastery over supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), they can travel everywhere throughout the ten directions to hear the Dharma.
Having achieved the dharma of non-retrogression in mindfulness, they are able to never be separated from the Dharma in every thought-moment.
Regarding those of evil nature: one should not, by means of the Dharma, further listen to the Dharma.
Eighth, the mind turns its back on the Mahāyāna precepts.

If a disciple of the Buddha, with a mind that turns its back on the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya of the eternal abiding, says they were not spoken by the Buddha, yet instead accepts and upholds the teachings of the two vehicles (Hīnayāna).
Those who hold the evil views of śrāvakas and non-Buddhists, as well as all prohibitions, false views, sūtras, and vinayas—this constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).

"To turn one's heart away" clarifies that this refers to more than mere verbal expression. To say "it was not spoken by the Buddha" refers to the conceptualization and deliberation of mental discursive thought.
"To uphold" means to intend to receive and maintain [such views].

This [precept] prohibits both the nature of the offense (*svabhāva-karma*) and its commission (*prayoga-karma*). Those who calculate [the offense] according to the Two Vehicles consider it merely the commission;

those who calculate it according to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) consider it both the nature and the commission. Because these are wrong views, they directly restrain hesitation and indecision. This is the preliminary means for the two lower grades of wrong view.
Since their calculation has not yet been finalized, it is temporarily categorized as light. If the calculation were finalized, one would lose the Bodhisattva precepts.
Thus it is. This applies equally to the seven classes of disciples;

however, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not fully coincide on this point. Since the Hīnayāna is one's fundamental training, it does not constitute an offense. Even according to the external calculation, one incurs an offense of mental censure (*tatsvabhāvika-āpatti*). It is manifested...

If one intends to go [to them], at every step one must perform a ritual confession (*pratideśanā*) for the transgression. If one hears the teachings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), but they do not enter one's mind, one may repent and return;
it is still permitted to confess and purify the fault so that one may dwell together with the community.

However, if even a single word enters the mind and one practices their dharma—even to the extent of plucking out a single hair—one loses the bhikṣu precepts and incurs a grave impediment (*durgati*). In this present life, such a person is no longer permitted to be counted among the ranks of the Saṃgha.
Only that which obstructs is not permitted.

Regarding "retribution": if one calculates based on the external, it constitutes false views and leads to falling into the three miserable realms; if one calculates based on the small, it obstructs great bodhi.
Regarding "understanding": with the exception of the perfect principle of the One Vehicle, all others are termed false and small.
Regarding repentance: it is contrary to phenomena in its practice and contrary to principle in its ritual procedure; one must cultivate with single-mindedness and the realization of non-arising.

Regarding cultivation and realization: those at the stage of non-retrogression never again calculate external things; those at the stage of non-retrogression in conduct never again calculate the Lesser Vehicle.
Those who have attained non-retrogression in their mindfulness never turn their backs on the Principle.
Regarding those of evil nature: by employing external and minor means, they engage with those of external and minor capacities, manifesting in accordance with their calculations.
○ Ninth: The Precept Against Neglecting the Sick.
If a Buddha’s disciple sees anyone who is ill, they should always provide for them with offerings no different from those given to the Buddha himself.

Among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit consisting of nursing the sick is the foremost. Whether it be one's parents, teachers, monks, or disciples who are ill, lacking in sensory faculties, or afflicted by a hundred kinds of maladies, one must provide for them all so that they may recover. Yet, if a Bodhisattva, out of a heart of anger or resentment, fails to do so...
Look! Even if one sees someone who is ill within a monastery, a city, a wilderness, a mountain forest, or on a road, and fails to provide relief, one commits a minor offense.
As for the eight fields of merit: first, the Buddha; second, holy persons; third, the preceptor (upādhyāya); fourth, the teacher (ācārya); fifth, the Sangha; sixth...

The father is the first; the seven mothers are the second; and the eight types of sick persons are the third. Of these, the seven are fields of respect (*gurutva-kṣetra*); because the sick are both objects of compassion and respect, they are designated as the foremost.

This constitutes a prohibitive offense (*pratiṣedha-karman*), which is established through four conditions: first, there is a sick person; second, one perceives them as being sick; third, one lacks the intention to care for them.

If one acts out of anger or resentment, it is a defiled offense; if out of laziness, it is a non-defiled offense. Regarding the four cases where one should look but does not look, the offense is determined according to the specific circumstances.
There is no offense if one is personally ill, lacks the physical strength, or instructs someone else who is capable and compliant to act on behalf of the sick person.
If one knows that the person has their own attendants; or if they have the strength to manage [their own affairs];
or if the illness recurs frequently; or if it is a chronic illness; or if they are cultivating superior practices and do not wish to abandon them even for a moment;

or if they are dull-witted and find it difficult to awaken, difficult to receive, difficult to maintain, and unable to abide within the conditions [of practice]; or if one has previously attended to others' illnesses and observed that their suffering was likewise [intense]. Furthermore—

It is said: If one sees sentient beings facing difficulties regarding their relatives or their wealth, and out of a heart of resentment fails to provide relief or resolve their distress, this constitutes an afflicted offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*).
If it is due to indolence or laziness, it is a non-afflicted offense (*akliṣṭāpatti*). This precept should also be understood as encompassing both cases.
The seven classes of disciples all commit offenses together;

however, the rules for major and minor transgressions are not entirely shared. In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), only those who live together—such as teachers and friends, or monks and nuns who share a room—must look after one another;
beyond this, no further regulations are prescribed. For the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas), whose great vows encompass all beings, they must look after everyone.

The rules regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited are as explained in the section on non-offenses. Furthermore, one should know the regulations for nursing the sick. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"There are five qualities by which one is able to nurse a patient: first, knowing what the patient may eat and what they may not eat, and being able to provide what they may eat;
second, not loathing or despising the patient’s excrement, urine, vomit, or saliva; third, possessing a heart of compassion; [fourth, not acting] for the sake of..."
1. [One] can provide clothing and food. 2. [One] can manage the medicinal decoctions and medicines. 3. [One] can attend to the patient’s needs until recovery or even death. 4.
[One] can provide instructions for the sick person to bring them joy. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One should not appoint an ignorant person as a nurse.
If there is an unavoidable circumstance requiring one to go outside, one should instruct a person who is unskilled in nursing."

One must not allow the patient to be harmed through improper means. One should prevent them from falling into water or fire, consuming poisons, wielding knives or axes, falling from cliffs or ditches, climbing high trees, or eating forbidden foods; all such acts should be restrained. The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states:
"If a patient is poor and lacks the funds for medicine, the preceptor, spiritual friends, and others should provide it for them, or seek it from donors."
Alternatively, one may sell items belonging to the Saṃgha, items belonging to a stūpa, or ornaments such as banners and canopies at their appraised value to provide for the cost of medicine.
If the illness is later cured, the items should be repaid. However, if one lacks the means, there is no offense in not returning them.

As the son of the Great Master, one is the heir to the father’s wealth; therefore, if a bhikṣu who is tending to the sick provides for the patient, he should perform all duties except for those that constitute natural transgressions (prakṛti-sāvadya).
As for the retribution: one fails to receive the benefit of being cared for, loses both the fields of compassion and respect, and suffers from illness while having no one to look after them.
Conversely, one who is able to care for others fulfills the foremost field of merit.
Regarding "understanding": sentient beings possess the maladies of views, afflictions, the sands of ignorance, and so forth.
To fail to treat them with the medicinal teachings of the Fourfold Dharma is called "not tending to the illness."
Regarding repentance: it does not depend on phenomena; it does not depend on ritual procedures; it is non-arising.
Having personally attained thorough mastery over the four kinds of non-arising, one is then able to heal others with the medicine of the Dharma.

Regarding cultivation and realization: compassion conditioned by sentient beings can perceive the disease of the body; compassion conditioned by phenomena can perceive the diseases of views and thoughts;
and unconditioned compassion can perceive the disease of ignorance.

Regarding those whose nature is evil: they are constantly associated with a mind of indifference, which is termed "neglecting to attend to the sick. Furthermore, they manifest the conduct of being ill.
○ Tenth is the precept against possessing implements for killing.
If a Buddha’s disciple, they must not keep any weapons for combat, such as swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, or axes, nor any evil nets, snares, or instruments for killing living beings;
none of these may be kept. Furthermore, a Bodhisattva would not even retaliate against those who kill their own parents, much less kill any other sentient being.
One must not keep instruments for killing sentient beings; if one should intentionally keep them...
This constitutes a minor transgression.
"Mao" refers to a long spear; "juan" refers to a snare used to tether the feet of birds and beasts. Even toward those who murder one's parents, one should not seek retribution.
To cite the heavy as an illustration for the light:

these are the two types of karma, natural (*prakṛti*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepa*). Regarding the preliminary means (*upakrama*) of killing, one first incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*); at the moment the creature is actually harmed, one further incurs the full sin of killing (*vadhāpatti*).

The seven classes of followers commit this offense equally. Regarding weapons for combat: while those for kings and princes were previously permitted, all other instruments of killing are prohibited for both monastics and laypeople alike, regardless of seniority or rank.

Regarding the rules of permission and prohibition: one may exhort others to refrain from killing. If [an animal] has been purchased or captured, it is even better to hide its implements, keep it, and then destroy it;
the karmic retribution for this is as explained in the section on the precept against killing.
"Understanding" refers to the contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*) of the three preceding teachings; these are all instruments for slaying [deluded] principles.
"Repentance" involves maintaining material requisites; the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) involves maintaining the requisites of principle. One must maintain a single-minded state of non-arising.

Regarding those who cultivate and realize [the path]: from the first fruit (srotāpanna) upward, they eternally abandon the vessel of phenomena (the objective world); they dwell perfectly in the eternal abandonment of the vessel of principle (the subjective mind).
As for "inherent evil" (xing'e), it is precisely the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) *śamatha-vipaśyanā* that serves as the ultimate instrument of slaughter.
These ten precepts should be studied and reverently upheld. They are explained in detail in the sixth chapter below;
this serves as a summary of the first section of ten precepts, pointing forward to the extensive text.
○ The Eleventh Precept on National Missions:

If a disciple of the Buddha, out of a malicious mind for the sake of profit and gain, acts as a messenger for a state mission—conveying orders for military arrays and assemblies, or for raising armies to strike one another and slaughter immeasurable sentient beings—a Bodhisattva must not even enter the army to come and go; how much less so [to engage in such actions]?
Thus, one becomes a traitor to the state. If one acts intentionally in this way, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
This refers to the evil mind regarding gain and offerings; it clarifies that such conduct is not a cause for reconciliation or the settling of disputes.

One is not even permitted to enter or frequent military camps, as they are noisy and chaotic places, unsuitable for the conduct of a son of the Buddha. This is an illustration of a light case used to exemplify a grave one.
Regarding "enemies of the state," Mencius said: "Those whom the present age calls good ministers are what the ancients called enemies of the people.
To despise righteousness and incite military conflict inevitably harms the people. Since the people are the foundation of the state, harming the people is precisely harming the state.

These are the two types of karma—natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*prajñapti-sāvadya*). They are specifically prohibited because they serve as the causes and conditions for harming others for the sake of gain.

The sūtras are compiled according to the specific facts and the specific words [of the offenses]: if the cause and condition is one of anger, it falls under the precept against killing; if the cause and condition is one of greed and seizing precious objects, it falls under the precept against stealing.
The seven classes of followers commit the same offenses, as both major and minor precepts are equally binding.
Regarding permissions and prohibitions: examples include Hiyong using his flying staff to halt an army, and Tancheng using his divination bell to quell calamities.
As for the retribution: causing discord and losing the joy of companionship constitutes the superior-grade retribution for divisive speech and harsh speech;
killing and taking profit constitutes the superior-grade retribution for killing and stealing.
The one who understands [sees that] the realm of ignorance is impassable. The army of afflictions incurs transgression through coming and going.
For the one who repents: the phenomenal aspect functions as the agent, while the principle aspect functions as the agent of non-arising.

Regarding those who practice and realize: from the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) upward, they are not driven by phenomena; through the four teachings, they partially realize [the truth] and are not driven by principle.
As for those with "inherently evil" nature (*prakṛti-pāpa*): some may be driven by phenomena, such as Fotudeng and others;

others may be driven by principle, whereby they skillfully employ expedients to shatter the realm of ignorance and tactically destroy the army of afflictions. Furthermore, they enter and exit within the realm of ignorance... [afflictions].
He disturbs the army’s movements in order to deliver sentient beings.
○ Twelfth, the Precept Against Selling:

If a Buddha’s disciple intentionally buys and sells free people, male or female slaves, or the six classes of domestic animals; or trades in coffins, planks, and wood used for containing the dead; [he commits an offense].

Even these implements one should not make oneself, much less teach others to make. If one intentionally makes them oneself or teaches others to make them, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
To sell free persons, male or female slaves, brings about the suffering of separation from one's kin; to sell domestic animals... [brings about... the suffering of separation from one's herd.
It serves as a condition for killing. To trade in coffin planks and timber is necessarily to profit from the deaths of others;
whether one teaches others to make them, makes them oneself, or causes others to make them, one incurs guilt in all such cases.

This also involves both the nature of the offense and the two types of karma: seeking profit and harming living beings, which contravene a compassionate mind. Each such act incurs a formal offense (*pāyattika*).

If one steals and sells living beings, or sells livestock intending for them to be killed, or uses incantations to cause a person's death in order to sell their coffin, these constitute separate offenses of theft and killing.
The seven classes of followers do not all share the same rules. For laypeople, keeping plow-oxen and the like does not constitute an offense;

however, according to the *Śrāddhakarman-sūtra*, one must first perform the ritual of "pure giving" (*śuddha-dāna*) before receiving the precepts. Otherwise, one incurs the offense of losing the resolve for enlightenment (*saṃkalpa-vilopa*).
Both the great and the small are equally prohibited.
Regarding permissions and prohibitions: purchasing livestock to release them, providing coffins for the poor, and so forth.
As for the retributive fruits: family members will be scattered, one will suffer from many illnesses, and life will be short.
As for "understanding," to grasp at the fruit while practicing the cause is called "peddling. To regard partial truth as *nirvāṇa* is called a "tool for death.

Furthermore, failing to realize the principle that all is inherently complete, yet separately scheming to accumulate merit and virtue or seeking a separate Middle Way—all such acts are termed "peddling."
Regarding repentance (*pratideśanā*): there is the repentance of phenomena (*dharma*), the repentance of ritual procedures (*vidhi*), and the repentance of principle (*li*).

One must practice with single-mindedness and non-arising. Regarding cultivation and realization: those from the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) upward have no repentance of phenomena; those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*) have no repentance of principle.

Regarding those of evil nature: having separated them from the retinue of ignorance and severed the twelve causes of birth, one takes all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm and enshrines them in a seamless coffin—namely, by bringing them all to extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.
○ Thirteenth: Slandering the Precepts.

If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, slanders without cause other virtuous people, good people, Dharma masters, teachers, monks, kings, or nobles, saying they have committed the seven reversals or the ten grave offenses—then among one's parents, brothers, and six types of relatives, one ought to give rise to filial piety.

To respond with even greater hostility and harm toward those who treat one with a compliant mind or a mind of compassion, and thereby fall into an undesirable state, constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
"Evil mind" refers to a mind of anger and vexation that desires to cause another to sink into ruin. "Without cause" means there was no seeing or hearing [of such an offense].

Regarding the doubt concerning the three roots [of unwholesome action]: as for parents, brothers, and the six types of kinsmen, the Mahāsattva regards all people as being like his own parents, brothers, and six types of kinsmen.

This concerns both natural (*prakṛti*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepa*) offenses. There are six permutations regarding the commission of an offense through six conditions: first, there is no offense; second, there is the perception that there is no offense. These constitute the six cases.
1. The four types of offenses. 2. The two types of non-offenses. 3. The mind of slander and defamation; this is precisely the primary factor for the offense. 4.

The content of what is said, such as the seven grave offenses (*ānantarya*) or the ten heavy precepts (*daśa-guru-dharma*). 5. The person toward whom it is directed: if one slanders a fellow practitioner (*saddharmika*) before another fellow practitioner, or slanders a layperson before another layperson, it is considered light.
However, if one slanders a fellow practitioner before a layperson, it falls under the category of a heavy offense. 6. The person [before whom the slander is made].

Understanding this: the offense is determined according to the words spoken and the person addressed. If one speaks the truth, there is no transgression; however, if one speaks with an evil intent, one also commits a light secondary offense (*āpatti*).
This applies equally to all seven groups of followers. It is common to both the Mahayana and Hinayana; it is a prohibitive rule (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) and is not exempted.
The retribution is as described in the section on the evil of false speech.
The understanding is also as explained in the section on the heavy precepts.
Regarding repentance: for slander of phenomena, there is the ritual method; for slander of principle, there is non-arising.

Regarding those who practice and realize [the truth]: those in the first fruit (srotāpanna) do not engage in unreal slander; those in the third fruit (anāgāmin) do not speak of reality with an evil mind; and those of perfect realization (yuanren) do not engage in slander based on principle.
As for "inherently evil" (xing'e), this refers to the expedient teaching of the dharma-gate of inherent evil, which states that the Buddha is ultimate great greed and so forth.
○ The Fourteenth Precept on Prohibiting Arson:
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, sets a great fire to burn mountains, forests, or wilderness; or sets fire from the fourth month through the ninth month;
or burns the houses, dwellings, cities, monasteries, fields, and timber of others, as well as those belonging to spirits, deities, or officials.
Regarding objects: one must not intentionally burn any living things. If one burns them intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
As for "with an evil mind," this refers to acting according to one's own whims and desires without knowing how to exercise caution.

The period from the fourth to the ninth month is stated here based on a general consideration of cold countries; however, in countries with less cold, one must especially examine what is appropriate for the time.
Regarding "burning another's house or dwelling," this refers to cases where fire is accidentally set due to a lack of care and happens to spread to it.

If one burns something for the purpose of harming another, it falls under the category of offenses flowing from the precept against stealing. Regarding the prohibition against burning any living things:

setting fire to them is not intended merely to burn the objects themselves; rather, because there is inevitably the potential for injury to living beings, the rule specifically restricts [the practice] during the four months [of the rainy season].

This continues until the ninth month, during which time one must guard against the conditions that lead to killing. If one burns [something] for the purpose of killing, it is subsumed under the precept against killing.
The present formulation—"if one intentionally burns"—clarifies that this refers to an act committed without due care rather than an accidental error.

This is a prohibitive action (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). An offense is established through four conditions: first, it is not the proper time; second, there is the perception that it is not the proper time; third, there is a lack of carefulness of mind;
and fourth, one actually sets fire to it.
This applies equally to the seven classes of followers and is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited: for laypeople, engaging in activities such as farming is permitted; for those who have left the household life, it is prohibited. By choosing the proper time and being careful not to cause harm through burning, there is no offense.
Regarding the retribution: if one is not careful, there is the karma of unintentional killing.

Regarding the understanding: one lets loose the fire of views and thoughts, which burns the wisdom of the ultimate truth; one lets loose the fire of ignorance, which burns the wisdom of the Middle Way.

Regarding repentance: the burning of phenomena refers to the practice of ritual methods; the burning of views and thoughts refers to the four kinds of non-arising (*anutpāda*); and the burning of ignorance requires the successive application of the one mind and two kinds of non-arising.
Regarding cultivation and realization: the fruit of the first stage burns away the afflictions of phenomena; the fruit of the fourth stage burns away the afflictions of views and thoughts;

and the Buddha burns away the afflictions of ignorance. Regarding inherent evil: it emits the fire of the three wisdoms to completely incinerate the dwellings of the three delusions within the Dharma-realm.
○ The Fifteenth Precept on Deviant Teachings:

If a disciple of the Buddha—whether toward fellow disciples, non-Buddhist practitioners, evil persons, the six types of close relatives, or all spiritual friends—should fail to teach each of them to receive and uphold the Mahayana sutras and vinaya, and fail to teach them to understand their meanings and principles, thereby causing them to give rise to the bodhicitta, this constitutes a transgression. (10)
The mind of setting forth, the ten minds of nurturing, and the ten adamantine minds— within these thirty minds, one must understand the sequential application of their dharmas.
If a Bodhisattva, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, recklessly teaches the sūtras, vinayas,
or heterodox treatises of the two vehicles, śrāvakas, or those with false views, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).

"Buddha's disciples" refers exclusively to the internal assembly. "Heterodox practitioners and evil persons" refers exclusively to the external assembly. "Six types of relatives" encompasses both the internal and external assemblies.
"All virtuous friends" refers to those with whom one associates and interacts, who have long been familiar and well-disposed toward one another.

Regarding those "who should be taught the principles so that they may resolve to attain Bodhicitta": it is by understanding these principles that one first becomes capable of generating the aspiration for enlightenment. It is not otherwise.
This is the same as practicing blindly and training recklessly. Furthermore, to understand the meaning without generating the resolve for awakening (*bodhicitta*) increases wild wisdom;
to generate the resolve without understanding the meaning increases ignorance. Therefore, one must instruct them so that they may come to know true understanding and true cultivation.
Those with malicious intent generally desire to lead others into partiality and heterodoxy; those with a hateful mind specifically afflict such persons, failing to employ the correct [method].

Regarding the teachings: "Horizontal" refers to cases where the practitioner's root-nature is distorted such that it does not accord with their capacity; this clarifies that the teaching was not a case of "prescribing medicine according to the illness.

When the teaching addresses external paths (*tīrthika*), there are both obstructive and prohibitive karmas. When the teaching addresses the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*), there is only prohibitive karma.
An evil mind or a mind of anger constitutes a defiled transgression; ignorance regarding the faculty of wisdom does not constitute a defiled transgression.
The seven assemblies are the same;

however, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not entirely coincide. Regarding what they share: both agree that one must not instruct non-Buddhists. Regarding their differences: in the Hīnayāna, since one’s original training was in the Lesser Vehicle, such [instruction] does not constitute an offense.

Regarding "opening and prohibiting": this refers to teaching according to the dispositions of others to suit their specific capacities, even to the point of appearing identical to non-Buddhists and the like.
Regarding "fruition": through the teachings of external schools, one receives the retribution of false views; through the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, one obstructs great bodhi;
and through the teachings of the Mahāyāna, both self and others are benefited.
As for "those who understand": with the exception of the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle, all others are termed heterodox and inferior. Therefore it is said:
"From this point onward, we have all been called people of heterodox views."
Regarding repentance: if the ritual action is heterodox or Hinayana, and the ritual procedure is heterodox or Hinayana, one must realize the non-arising of the single mind.
Having awakened to the dharma of the non-arising of the single mind, one may then provisionally employ expedient means for the sake of others, revealing the provisional to manifest the real.
Thus, entering the heterodox through the orthodox and leading the heterodox back to the orthodox—there is nothing that cannot be done.

Regarding "cultivation and realization": in the first fruit (srotāpanna), there are no heterodox teachings; in emerging from the provisional, there are no Hinayana teachings. For those of the Perfect [Vehicle], there are no heterodox or Hinayana teachings within their principle.
As for "inherently evil" (prakṛti-pāpa), one universally employs all heterodox and Hinayana dharma-gates to gather all types of capacities, and furthermore, this is ultimately heterodox.
Small. That is, the ultimate One Vehicle.
○ Chapter Sixteen: Precepts for Correcting Perverted Explanations.

If you, O Disciple of the Buddha, should with a sincere heart first study the Mahāyāna Vinaya and Sūtras on dignified conduct (*vīrya*), extensively opening up and understanding their meanings and essences, and then—

Furthermore, if there are newly initiated bodhisattvas who come from a hundred or a thousand *li* away to seek the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, you should, in accordance with the Dharma, explain to them all forms of ascetic practice, such as burning the body, the arms, or the fingers.

If one does not burn the body, arms, or fingers as an offering to the Buddhas, one is not a renunciant bodhisattva; this extends even to [offering to] starving tigers, wolves, lions, and all hungry ghosts.

One should offer one’s own body, flesh, hands, and feet as an offering. Thereafter, one should explain the True Dharma to each person in successive order, causing their minds to open and their intentions to be understood.

If, however, for the sake of gain and offerings, a Bodhisattva answers what should not be answered, explains the words of the Sūtras and Vinaya in a distorted manner, lacks proper sequence, or slanders the Triple Gem, they commit a minor offense.
The "benevolent heart" refers to the aspiration to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below. The "prior study" is the foundation for benefiting both oneself and others.
"Dignified deportment" is the model for guiding and transforming others. The "Sūtras and Vinaya" are the gateways for spiritual progress and cultivation.

To "extensively open up the meanings and flavors" means to reach the vast while exhausting the subtle and minute; it is clear that this is not merely shallow or superficial. [To] "burn the body" [is to practice asceticism].
Offering one’s arms and fingers to all Buddhas represents the ultimate pinnacle of seeking the Buddha-way upward through shared sorrow and longing with sentient beings.

Sacrificing one’s own body, flesh, hands, and feet to hungry ghosts, tigers, wolves, and the like represents the ultimate pinnacle of transforming sentient beings downward through shared compassionate power with the Tathāgata. First, he expounded this Dharma-conforming asceticism for their sake.
Having made his mind firm and his vows steadfast, he then expounds the True Dharma to him one by one in proper sequence;
that is, he speaks in accordance with the questions asked, speaking without inversion and without error, thereby enabling his mind to open and his understanding to be resolved.
This is truly the duty of those who have previously studied as Bodhisattvas. To fail to answer when one should answer is to be non-comprehensive;

to explain erroneously is to lack proper sequence; and to slander the Triple Gem is to deviate from the True Dharma. Furthermore, explaining erroneously is itself termed slander—namely, preaching the Dharma in a way that does not accord with the capacities of the listeners, such that what is spoken lacks authoritative validity (*pramāṇa*).

This is a prohibitive action (*pratiṣedha-karman*). Not having studied first is one fault; teaching incorrectly is another fault. If it is for the sake of profit, it is an afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) offense;
if it is due to a lack of knowledge or skill, it is a non-afflicted offense.

This applies equally to the seven assemblies and is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Even when those of the Hīnayāna instruct others based on the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, they must not obscure the underlying principles.

Regarding what is permitted or prohibited: one may refrain from speaking out because of knowing the student's capacity; or, in order to sever wrong livelihoods, one may censure asceticism to shatter ignorance.

Regarding the practice of grasping at principles and actions as being karmic retribution: if it is for the sake of profit, it is subsumed under wrong livelihood; if it is a distorted explanation, it is a derivative of slandering the Dharma.
As for understanding through intellectual comprehension, if one does not know the causes and conditions of the four *siddhāntas*, all such instances are termed distorted explanations.
Regarding repentance: the practice of the ritual is inverted, and the principle is inverted. Regarding non-arising and cultivation-realization:

the fruit of the first stage is the unconditioned benefit-mind; emerging into the provisional world, one possesses the wisdom of the faculty of knowing-all. Through perfect contemplation, one clearly understands the four *siddhāntas*.

Regarding the nature of evil: all phenomena are inverted; all phenomena are correct. One enters the characteristics of inversion through the characteristics of correctness; one enters the characteristics of correctness through the characteristics of inversion.
○ Seventeenth: The Precept Against Begging by Relying on Power.
If a disciple of the Buddha, for the sake of food, drink, wealth, offerings, or reputation, associates with kings, princes, ministers, and officials,
relying on their power and influence to beg, beat, or drag others, and thereby takes money and goods by improper means— seeking all manner of profit—
this is called "evil seeking" and "excessive seeking. To teach others to seek in this way, being utterly devoid of compassion and lacking a heart of filial obedience, is likewise so.
"Minor offenses" refers to defiled transgressions.
"For oneself" clarifies that it is not for the sake of the Triple Gem and so forth, but rather for food, drink, and even reputation; this clarifies that it is not for the sake of the Path.
"Evil seeking" means it is not virtuous because it involves coercion. "Excessive seeking" means it is not moderate because of lack of contentment. Thus he taught.
Another [type of offense] is when one instructs another to seek something for oneself, such as dispatching a messenger to write a letter and so forth;

this constitutes both a formal act (*vijñapti*) and an informal act (*avijñapti*), and is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the precept against stealing. Whether seeking profit from one's own capital or using letters of recommendation to exert pressure, these all fall under this precept.
If, however, there is an unjust usurpation, that belongs specifically to the precept against stealing. Furthermore, the root text of the precept...
The Sūtra states: "To have many desires and lack contentment, and to be greedily attached to wealth and goods—this is a defiled offense, and it is also subsumed under this precept.
It is an offense common to all seven classes of followers; it is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna."

Regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited: for the sake of the Triple Gem, for the sake of the sick, and for the sake of seeking in accordance with the Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings, there is no offense.
Regarding the karmic fruit: if one begs, it obstructs the Path and causes distress to others; if one does not beg, one maintains a pure livelihood, benefiting both oneself and others.

Regarding "understanding": the followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) horizontally grasp the True [Dharmadhātu]; Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings horizontally grasp the Conventional;

those of the Distinct Teaching horizontally grasp the Middle. Regarding "repentance": there is grasping through phenomena, which is the ritual method; and grasping through principle, which is the single mind of non-arising.

Regarding cultivation and realization: in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one abandons the grasping for phenomena; through perfect contemplation, one subdues the grasping for principles; and in the perfect dwelling (*anāgāmin*), one abandons the grasping for principles.

Regarding the inherent evil (*xing'e*): it horizontally pervades the nine realms to press upon and seize the roots of goodness within the Buddha-realm; it horizontally pervades the twenty-five states of existence to press upon and seize the nature of the true, eternal self.
○ The Eighteenth Precept: Against Acting as a Preceptor Without Understanding.
If a disciple of the Buddha, they should study the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Those who recite the precepts should uphold the Bodhisattva precepts six times every day.
To understand its meaning and principle— that which is the nature of Buddha-nature— yet for a Bodhisattva to fail to understand even a single phrase or verse,
as well as the causes and conditions of the precepts, while falsely claiming to understand them, is to deceive oneself and also to deceive others.
To act as a teacher for others and bestow the precepts while failing to understand each and every point and remaining ignorant of all dharmas constitutes an offense of light defilement.

Since the Great Being takes the transmission of the Dharma and the salvation of sentient beings as his primary duty, he should study the twelve divisions of the scriptures as the foundation for saving beings.
Furthermore, since the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra is the very root of the Great Being, he should recite and uphold it six times every day until he has mastered it thoroughly.
However, he must not merely recite the text; he must also necessarily understand its underlying principles and meanings.
The nature of Buddha-nature refers to first awakening to the fact that one’s original source and fundamental nature are pure.

This serves as the essential substance upon which the unconditioned precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*) rely; furthermore, by relying on these unconditioned precepts, they in turn become the seeds for attaining Buddhahood.

Thus, it should be known that self-nature purity is the direct cause of Buddha-nature (*dharmatā-hetu*), while the Bodhisattva precepts are the conditional and developmental causes (*pratyaya* and *nirvṛtti-hetu*). These are entirely one in nature.
By initiating the two types of cultivation, one fully integrates these two cultivations to achieve a single nature; therefore, it is called the "nature of Buddha-nature.

This is equivalent to what is meant by the "original source of all Buddhas" or the "seed of Buddha-nature. Regarding the phrase "not understanding even a single sentence," etc., this cites a minor case to illustrate a major one.
For those of ordinary people with shallow wisdom, who could possibly attain complete penetration in every dharma? One simply knows what one knows and does not know what one does not know.

It is no fault not to know. However, if one does not understand even a single sentence or a single verse, or even a small portion of the causal conditions of the precepts, yet refuses to acknowledge one's ignorance and instead falsely claims to understand, this constitutes an internal betrayal of one’s own mind and self-deception, as well as an external error that deceives others.
How much more so when one does not understand each and every precept? All...
If one knows nothing at all of the Buddha-dharma, then one will not even have leisure to seek learning from a teacher for oneself;
how then could one act as a teacher for others to bestow the precepts?

This constitutes an obstructive karma (*āvaraṇa-karman*). Not studying after having received the precepts is one fault; the vain desire to act as a teacher is another fault. Following [these faults]...
The offense is established by the act itself.

Regarding the "seven assemblies," the old tradition states that the offenses apply to *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs*, while for the remaining five assemblies there was no practice of acting as a teacher, as it had not yet been prescribed.
However, according to the *Susheng jing* (Upāsakaśīla-sūtra), a lay bodhisattva may also accept lay disciples. It appears that...
The regulations are likewise the same. However, although a layperson may take on disciples, there is no matter of bestowing the precepts;

therefore, it is said that there is no offense. Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna prohibit this. The *Yìshù* states: "In the Mahāyāna, one who acts as a teacher must necessarily be an ordained bodhisattva who is fully endowed with five virtues:

first, observance of the precepts; second, twenty years of seniority (*lǎ*) [in the saṃgha]; third, mastery of the Vinaya-piṭaka; fourth, proficiency in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and fifth, wisdom."
The profound mysteries are preserved in the Tibetan [tradition]. That which was transmitted by Master Kumārajīva and transcribed by Master Tanyong has been passed down to the present day;

this is the authentic teaching. Next, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "One must possess precepts and virtue that are strict and luminous, be well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, and be capable of inspiring a heart of reverence in others before one may receive [the precepts] from them.
Otherwise, one incurs an offense. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says: "If five factors are not accomplished..."
One must not confer the full precepts (upasampadā) upon others. One must not act as a preceptor (niśrayācārya) for others.
One must not maintain śrāmaṇeras. [Furthermore, one who lacks] first, morality; second, concentration; third, wisdom; fourth, liberation;

and fifth, the knowledge and vision of liberation—and who is moreover unable to teach others to firmly abide in these five—furthermore accomplishes five unrighteous qualities and must not confer the full precepts upon others. With...
Relying [on such a person] as a preceptor and keeping a śrāmaṇera [is improper for one who]: first, lacks faith; second, lacks shame; third, lacks dread of blame;

fourth, is indolent; fifth, is forgetful. Furthermore, another five: one who violates the higher training in ethics, violates the higher view, violates the higher discipline of deportment, has little learning, and lacks wisdom.
Furthermore, another five: one who does not attend to the sick, does not properly maintain the dwelling place, cannot dispel doubts, and does not provide instruction.

Having abandoned wrong views; being less than ten years [of standing]; another five: not knowing what constitutes an offense or what does not constitute an offense, whether it be light or heavy; being less than ten years [of standing]; another five:

not knowing how to instruct disciples in higher decorum (*adhiśīla*), higher pure conduct (*adhicitta*), and higher discipline (*adhiprajñā*), nor in the formal procedures of motion (*jñapti*) and formal act (*karmavācanā*); another five: not knowing the higher training in morality, the higher training in mind, and the higher training in wisdom.

If one does not know how to perform the *jñapti* (motion) or the *karma* (formal act), yet understands each of these in reverse order, one may confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*), provide dependence (*niśraya*), and maintain a novice (*śrāmaṇera*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If ten qualities are accomplished, one is permitted to ordain others for renunciation and the reception of the full precepts:
first, upholding the precepts; second, great learning in the Abhidharma; third, great learning in the Vinaya; fourth..."
1. Training in the precepts; 2. training in concentration; 3. training in wisdom; 4. being able to expel offenses oneself; 5. being able to cause others to expel offenses;

6. being able to tend to the sick oneself; 7. being able to cause others to tend to the sick; 8. when a disciple encounters difficulty, being able to escort them out of danger oneself; 9. being able to cause others to escort them out of danger; 10. having completed ten years [of seniority].
These are called the ten matters by which one is permitted to ordain others, allowing them to leave the household life and receive full ordination. At the very least...

If one has completed ten years [of seniority] and knows the two divisions of the Vinaya, it is also permissible. The same applies to those who receive dependence (*niśraya*). The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

"Only after fulfilling ten years of summer retreats does one abide in the position of a teacher (*ācārya*); furthermore, one must accomplish five dharmas: first, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what is non-offensive;
third, knowing what is light; fourth, knowing what is heavy; and fifth, being extensively capable regarding the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*."

He was capable of providing explanations. Regarding the various rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), he knew when they were first established and when they were subsequently relaxed; when encountering difficult circumstances, he skillfully understood the points of obstruction and passage.

He constantly recited the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra and was able to resolve the doubts of others. Possessing ethical discipline, right view, and extensive learning, he benefited both himself and others. His deportment and performance of rituals were exemplary.
Being free from transgressions and possessing such virtues, one is called an *upādhyāya* (preceptor), for it is through his intimacy that he can teach the Dharma of renunciation.

Even if one has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), if they do not discern the gravity or lightness of the various training rules (*śikṣāpada*), they must still rely upon and dwell under the guidance of a person of superior virtue, even if they have sixty years of seniority.
If the teacher is junior in seniority, with the sole exception of the prostration at his feet, all other [duties]...
All such individuals are termed "old or young bhikṣus. They are not permitted to grant others the going forth (*pravrajyā*) or the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Zhi Xu said: "To transmit the Dharma and save sentient beings is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness and virtue.
This precept does not prohibit one from acting as a teacher; it merely holds one accountable for lacking understanding. Alas, in this degenerate age, there are many forms of perversion."

Some claim to ferry sentient beings across [to liberation] and falsely act as teachers; lacking understanding, they pretend to possess it, maintaining a haughty demeanor while their sense of self is ablaze.
Others are too indolent to study the Vinaya and thus fail to become teachers; still others pride themselves on their own religious doctrines.

They hold the Vinaya school in contempt and erect the banner of arrogance; thus they revile and disparage the study of the precepts. Out of greed to gather disciples, they still bestow monastic names upon them.
No act is more egregious than this in its blindness of heart and brazenness of face. Furthermore, some erroneously claim that the Mahāyāna is characterized by universal integration.
There is no need for the *Vinaya* of the Śrāvakas. How could one know that the "Small" does not encompass the "Great," whereas the "Great" must necessarily encompass the "Small"?

It is like a river that does not contain the ocean, yet the ocean must necessarily contain the river. If one does not study both the Great and the Small together, how can one be called a Bodhisattva Bhikṣu?
Therefore, I now briefly cite the virtues of the Śrāvaka masters to supplement the noble regulations of the Mahāsattvas; may those who observe this not weary of its prolixity.

Regarding the principles of permission and prohibition: bestowing the lifelong five precepts upon laypeople (*avadātavasana*) and bestowing the eight precepts on the six fast days (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa-dina*) are both entirely without fault.
However, one must also understand the underlying meaning and purpose of the five and eight precepts.
Furthermore, as for the method of bestowing the eight precepts, if no bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī is available, then a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī may also bestow them.
Regarding this Dharma of the Five Precepts: even if the five groups of the ordained community do not exist, the two groups of the laity may still receive them.

As for the karmic retribution, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "If one occupies a high seat without having personally realized the Dharma, and teaches others while remaining ignorant oneself, that person shall fall into hell."
Regarding "understanding": those who have not yet truly seen the Truths are collectively termed "lacking understanding.

Regarding "repentance" (*pratikramana*): for those lacking the understanding derived from the gates of the teachings, one must perform the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) and train well; for those lacking the understanding of entry into reality, one must realize the non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Regarding those who practice and realize: those at the stage of semblance through contemplative practice possess a correct understanding based on the teachings; those at the stage of partial realization possess true understanding that enters into principle.
As for "inherent evil," all phenomena are fundamentally inexplicable; when one forgets emotions and severs conceptual understanding, this constitutes the dharma-realm.
The Master.
○ The Nineteenth Precept on Divisive Speech:
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, sees a precept-keeping bhikṣu holding an incense burner and practicing the bodhisattva path, [and yet slanders him].
To instigate strife between two parties, to slander and deceive the worthy, and to commit every kind of evil—this constitutes a minor offense of defilement. Regarding the "evil-minded":
this refers to one who harbors anger toward another and seeks to incite quarrels, or who, out of envy for that person's virtue and goodness, intends to cause them harm and distress.
Holding a fragrant incense burner is merely one instance cited to illustrate virtuous conduct. "Instigating strife between two parties" means to act as an intermediary.
To instigate others to create grounds for dispute—though one speaks the truth here, it still constitutes an offense; how much more so when it involves slander or deception?
This [offense] comprises both natural (*prakṛti*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepa*) karma. It is established as an offense through six conditions: first, a sentient being;

second, the perception of that being as such (which should be analyzed through the six permutations of observing or not observing the precepts); third, [the intent to cause] slight aggravation; fourth, [the intent to cause] slight mitigation; and fifth, divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
1. The mind itself is the primary agent. 2. The four points of censure, whether true or false. 3. The person addressed;

if one addresses someone who lacks precepts, it falls under the grave precepts. If one addresses a fellow practitioner who is not a close friend, it falls under the thirteenth offense of slandering the precepts.
Now, focusing specifically on the intent of the quarrel, one must address that person's intimate associates.

Therefore, both [speaking what is] real and [what is] unreal constitute an offense. If one intends to address a certain person but mistakenly addresses another, one incurs an offense of preliminary effort (*prayoga*).
When the six types of persons understand the meaning, an offense is incurred for every word spoken.
Common to the seven assemblies and shared by both the Great and Small Vehicles,

regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who have been taken under the influence of evil companions and,
out of affection, do not abandon them, the bodhisattva, having seen this, gives rise to a heart of compassion and generates...

With an intention for their benefit and happiness, one speaks divisive words to the best of one's strength and ability in order to separate them from evil friends and cause them to abandon their mutual intimacy, so that they will not suffer meaningless and disadvantageous consequences for a long night. Thus, with a mind of altruism—
To speak divisive words that cause others to be estranged from those they love constitutes no transgression and generates much merit;
its karmic fruit is as explained in the sixth heavy precept.

Regarding "understanding": to speak of existence and non-existence constitutes divisive speech; to speak of the ultimate and the conventional constitutes divisive speech; to speak of the extremes and the middle constitutes divisive speech. Regarding "repentance":

divisive speech regarding phenomena must be addressed through ritual action (*vidhi*); divisive speech regarding existence and non-existence involves the fourfold non-arising; [this applies to] the ultimate and the conventional.

Regarding divisive speech: the latter two types of non-arising refer to divisive speech regarding both extremes and the middle. As for those who practice and realize through the single mind of non-arising:
one who has attained the first fruit has no divisive speech regarding phenomena; a person of perfect realization has no divisive speech regarding principles.

Regarding the nature of evil: engaging in divisive speech according to one's emotions or intellect constitutes two-tongued talk; even speaking what is entirely true or entirely false is likewise two-tongued talk.
○ The twentieth precept: not failing to provide rescue and protection.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of a heart of compassion, practices the act of releasing living beings:
all men have been my fathers, and all women have been my mothers; there is no birth through which I have not received life from them.
Therefore, the sentient beings of the six realms are all my parents. To kill and eat them is to kill my own parents, and it is also to kill my own former bodies. First.
All earth and water are my former bodies; all fire and wind are my original substance. Therefore, one should constantly practice releasing living beings.
This is the eternally abiding Dharma that is received life after life. One should teach others to release living beings. If one sees people of the world killing animals, [one should intervene].

One should skillfully provide rescue and protection, liberating them from their suffering and distress. One should constantly teach and expound the Bodhisattva precepts to save and deliver sentient beings.
On the anniversary of the death of one's parents or siblings, one should invite a Dharma Master to lecture on the sutras and vinaya of the Bodhisattva precepts.
This merit shall assist the deceased, enabling them to behold the Buddhas and be reborn among humans or in the heavens. Should one fail to do so, one incurs a minor offense.

Because of a compassionate heart, one should cultivate the three kinds of compassion in their entirety: first, compassion with sentient beings as its object, which is to contemplate that all beings in the six realms have been one's own parents;
second, compassion with phenomena as its object, which is to contemplate that earth, water, fire, and wind constitute one's own body; third...
Regarding "unconditioned compassion" (*anālambana-maitrī*): it is the realization, within the very process of successive births, of the Dharma that is unborn, undying, and eternally abiding.
To teach others to release living beings, one uses these three forms of compassion to instruct them. By providing protection, one relieves their present suffering;
by teaching and preaching, one uproots the causes of future suffering, ensuring they do not undergo it.

"Future suffering" refers to the rescue from that [suffering]. "Deliverance" refers to the bestowing of happiness. As for those who attain the vision of the Buddhas and are born among humans or devas:
having seen the Buddhas and heard the Dharma, they constantly cultivate the path within the realms of humans and devas, forever leaving behind the difficult conditions of animal existence;
only then can it be called ultimate deliverance and rescue.

This constitutes a prohibitive offense (*pratiṣedha-karman*). An offense is established through four conditions: first, there is a suffering sentient being; second, the perception that they are a suffering sentient being;

third, the absence of a compassionate mind. If one wishes to rescue them but lacks the power to do so, it is not an offense provided that one sincerely recites the names of the Buddhas or preaches the Dharma for them, thereby creating the causal conditions for saving their life-force.
Fourth, if one sits by and watches without rescuing, an offense is incurred according to the specific circumstances.
This is an offense. Not saving one's own physical life is one fault; not saving one's life of wisdom is another fault.

These offenses are common to all seven assemblies, though they are not entirely shared between the Great and Small Vehicles. In the Small Vehicle, there is an offense for failing to save one's kinsmen; in other cases, it is not prescribed as an offense. For the Mahāsattva, however...
Vast compassion rescues all beings; it is only those who obstruct [the Dharma] that are not permitted to be saved.

Regarding the karmic retribution: if one does not rescue them, one loses the dharma-benefits of the three types of compassion; if one rescues them, one accomplishes the dharma-gates of the three types of compassion.

The "one who understands" perceives that the external ordinary person slays the Truth of Ultimate Reality (paramārtha-satya), the Two Vehicles slay the Truth of Conventional Reality (saṃvṛti-satya), and those of the provisional teachings slay the Truth of the Middle Way (madhyama-satya), yet they do not release or save them.
Regarding "repentance": failing to save through phenomena requires ritual action; failing to save through principle requires the realization of non-arising.
Regarding the practitioner who attains realization: through the samādhi of a compassionate mind, they constantly provide both practical and principled salvation for those of evil nature.
As for those of evil nature, there are times when one does not save them through practical means, such as killing; as an ancient said of a piglet: "While it had only two legs, it did not struggle;
now that it has four legs, where can it struggle? Or, there are times when one does not save them through principled means, killing them until the end of the summer retreat.
Not only do they fail to save others from their own actions, but they even assist them in doing so.
Thus, regarding these ten precepts, one should train oneself and uphold them with a reverent heart. Each precept is explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Extinction of Sin."
This concludes the second section on the ten precepts; it also serves as a forward reference to the detailed exposition.

○ The Twenty-first Precept: Against Retaliating with Anger or Blows.

If a disciple of the Buddha, they must not respond to anger with anger, nor respond to blows with blows. Even if one’s parents, brothers, or six kinds of relatives are killed, one must not seek retribution.
Even if a sovereign is killed by another, one must likewise not seek retribution. To kill living beings [is a violation].

Regarding retribution born of karma: it is contrary to the way of filial piety not even to keep slaves, yet to beat, strike, or insult them, thereby daily giving rise to the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, results in immeasurable verbal offenses.
How much more so for the intentional commission of the seven grave transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*).
If an ordained Bodhisattva lacks a heart of compassion and seeks revenge—even against their own six relations—intentionally inflicting harm upon them, they commit a minor offense (*mṛdu-āpatti*).

Those who do not follow the way of filial piety and are killed by others must have karmic causes from past lives. To seek immediate gratification in revenge only serves to further increase the bonds of enmity for future lives;
this is certainly not the way to love those who have died. As for not keeping slaves—even this minor matter is prohibited, let alone more serious offenses.
However, those who have left the household life may not keep them at all, whereas those living at home may keep them, provided they do so without violating the principles of righteousness.
It is merely a matter of beating and scolding. Regarding the seven heinous crimes (*saptānantarya-karmāṇi*), as Mencius said: "If one kills another's father, that person will also kill one's father;
if one kills another's elder brother, that person will also kill one's elder brother. There is only a single interval between killing another and committing suicide.
Now, if I were to take revenge for my father, the other would in turn form an enmity toward my father and plant the causes for future harm to my father.
Therefore, taking revenge may indeed be termed one of the seven heinous offenses.

The concluding statement, "the renunciant bodhisattva," is intended to clarify that a lay bodhisattva may still employ secular law to respond to enmity with straightforwardness, whereas for a renunciant, this is absolutely impermissible.

This constitutes both a natural transgression (*svabhāva-avadya*) and a proscribed transgression (*prajñapti-avadya*), for it both violates loving-kindness and patience and binds one to future enmity.

A crime is established through five conditions: first, there must be an enemy; second, there must be the perception of them as an enemy, which has six permutations. The first two permutations are minor:

namely, perceiving an enemy as an enemy, or being in doubt about an enemy, yet proceeding to retaliate with anger. The next two permutations are somewhat more serious: namely, perceiving a non-enemy as an enemy, or being in doubt about a non-enemy [yet proceeding to retaliate].
The second phrase is even more serious. That is, when one who is not an enemy acts with the perception that they are not an enemy, yet strikes out of malice;
this is subsumed under the ninth grave precept. Third, there is the intention to retaliate; fourth, the performance of the act of retaliatory anger;

fifth, the victim’s acceptance—meaning they receive the beating or abuse. This constitutes a light offense. However, if life is harmed, it is classified under the first precept against killing. It resides [in that category].

A bodhisattva repays enmity with straightforwardness. Entrusting matters to judicial officials to be adjudicated according to the law without partiality, whether one strikes or kills, it constitutes no offense.
However, this does not apply to those who seek private revenge or who bribe and entreat government officials.
Excessive punishment—each instance of physical humiliation constitutes a light offense, while taking a life constitutes a grave offense. Furthermore, the *Śīlasūtra* states:
"If a bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of resentment toward another and maintains it without relinquishing it, this is a defiled offense.
This precept may also concurrently govern such cases. Moreover, a bodhisattva should not retaliate against an enemy, but should repay kindness; thus, the *Śīlasūtra* [states]:...
It is said: To receive the kindness of another and, with a mind of resentment, fail to repay them with an equivalent or greater benefit constitutes a defiled offense.
If one fails due to laziness or indolence, it is a non-defiled offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if one has applied skillful means but lacks the power;
if one employs skillful means to subdue the other; or if one wishes to repay the kindness but the other person does not accept it.
The seven classes of followers commit the same offenses; both the major and minor precepts are equally prohibited, and there are no exceptions for prohibitions.

As for the retribution: if one retaliates, then mutual enmity and harm will continue without end; if one does not retaliate, then resentment is resolved and fetters are released, such that there is forever no further hostility.

The one who understands perceives the afflictions of views, thoughts, and the sands of ignorance as enemies; to destroy them by means of the contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way is the retribution for anger.
If one thoroughly realizes that afflictions are identical to bodhi, then there will be no retribution for anger; this is also called "repaying enmity with straightforwardness."
Regarding repentance: there is retribution through phenomena and retribution through ritual procedures. Regarding the realization of the principle of non-arising with a single mind:
at the first fruit (srotāpanna), there is no retribution through phenomena; at the stage of perfect abiding (the fruit of arhatship), there is no retribution through the principle.
Regarding the nature of evil: it destroys the enemies of affliction and slays the thieves of ignorance.
The twenty-second precept: Not requesting the Dharma out of arrogance.
If a disciple of the Buddha, having first left the household life, has not yet attained any understanding, yet relies on their own cleverness and intelligence, or relies on...
They are of noble birth, advanced in years, or perhaps rely on their prestigious lineage, high social standing, great learning, great merit, or great wealth and abundance of the seven treasures.
Because of such arrogance, they do not consult or receive the sūtras and vinaya from learned Dharma masters.

These Dharma masters may be of humble lineage, young in age, from lowly families, poor, of inferior status, or lacking in physical faculties; yet they truly possess virtue and mastery of all the sūtras.
This is fully explained in the Vinaya. However, a newly initiated Bodhisattva must not examine the lineage of a Dharma Master;
if they fail to come to consult and receive from such a master the *paramārtha-satya* (the ultimate truth), they commit a minor offense (*āpatti*).
Regarding those who have newly left the household life: it is clear that their defilements are not yet deep and they have not yet attained any understanding;
thus, they lack the correct realization within the Buddha-dharma. Since their defilements are not yet deep and they have not yet opened to correct realization, they should especially avoid arrogance.
Yet, precisely because their defilements are not yet deep and they have not yet opened to correct realization, they often easily give rise to arrogance, relying on themselves.
There are seven such matters in total: first, relying on mundane general knowledge; second, relying on high status; third, relying on advanced age; fourth, relying on noble lineage;
fifth, relying on great erudition; sixth, relying on great merit; and seventh, relying on wealth and property. As for such a Dharma teacher:
To be of low birth is not to be of great lineage; to be young in years is not to be of long standing; to be from a humble family is not to be from a high-ranking house;
to be poor is not to be wealthy; to be of low station is not to hold office; and to have incomplete faculties is not to possess intelligence and great understanding.
Yet, if one truly possesses virtue, this constitutes genuine cultivation. To fully understand the Sūtras and Vinaya constitutes right understanding. This is understanding.
When both [virtues] are practiced together in beauty, how can one further discuss lineage? If one does not come now to seek instruction, what is the nature of that fault?

This concerns the two types of karma: natural obstruction and prohibitive obstruction. Pride is like a high mountain; the water of the Dharma cannot abide there, and thus one loses the benefit of the transmission and transformation [of others].

This deviates from the method of study. Four conditions constitute an offense: first, the Dharma teacher; second, the six permutations regarding the perception of the Dharma teacher—two heavy offenses, two light offenses, and two non-offenses;
third, an arrogant mind, which is precisely the primary factor of the offense, differing from the sixth [condition] mentioned previously, the affliction of anger;
fourth, failure to consult and receive instruction. One incurs an offense for failing to consult when one ought to have consulted. Furthermore, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:

It is said: To speak lightly of the Dharma teacher, failing to give rise to respect, ridiculing and disparaging them, and clinging merely to the literal words while not relying on the true meaning—this is a defiled offense, and it is also governed by this precept.

The seven classes of followers are the same in this regard; however, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not entirely coincide. In the Hīnayāna, if one is arrogant and fails to invite those who should be invited, one commits an offense;
in other cases, one must simply refrain from arrogance and invite everyone without exception. In the Mahāyāna, seeking the Dharma is the primary task; therefore, one should invite all without fail.
One should never be arrogant; only that which obstructs [the Dharma] is prohibited, not that which opens it.
Regarding the karmic fruit: arrogance causes one to lose the seed of the True Dharma, leading to stubborn folly and inferiority, whereas honoring the Dharma leads to wisdom.
Illumination and the growth of bodhi.
Regarding "one who understands": within all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss.

Yet, by not skillfully employing contemplation, one arbitrarily grasps at some things and rejects others among them; regarding that which is rejected, one is unable to contemplate those phenomena as they truly are.
Regarding "nature": it refers to arrogance that does not seek instruction.
Regarding "repentance": there is arrogance regarding phenomena (*dharma*), and arrogance regarding principle (*li*). Regarding "single-mindedness and non-arising" and "cultivation and realization":
in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), there is no arrogance regarding phenomena; in the stage of perfect abiding (*yuanzhu*), there is no arrogance regarding principle.
Regarding those of an evil nature: throughout the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am supreme.

I see none among the various devas and humans of the world who are worthy of receiving the Tathāgata’s welcome or prostrations; were I to rise to greet them, it would cause their heads to shatter into seven pieces instantly.
○ Twenty-third: Preaching the Precepts with Arrogance and Bias.
If, O Sons of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one wishes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts with a sincere heart, one may take the vow before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva.
One must perform repentance before the Buddha for seven days; once a favorable sign is seen, [one may proceed].
