One obtains the precepts. If one does not obtain an auspicious sign (*lakṣaṇa*), one should continue for two weeks, three weeks, seven weeks, or even up to one year, until an auspicious sign is obtained.

Once an auspicious sign has been obtained, one may then receive the precepts before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva. If one does not obtain an auspicious sign, although one receives the precepts before an image of the Buddha, it is not called "obtaining the precepts.
If one first receives the Bodhisattva precepts from a Dharma Master, one receives them before that Dharma Master.

At that time, it is not necessary to see auspicious signs. Why is this? Because these Dharma masters have transmitted the precepts to one another through a continuous lineage; thus, there is no need for auspicious signs.
Consequently, when receiving the precepts before a Dharma master, one immediately attains them. Because a mind of profound reverence has arisen, one thereby attains the precepts.
If there is no qualified master capable of conferring the precepts within a thousand li, one may take the vow of self-administration before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva.
Upon receiving the precepts, one must seek auspicious signs. If a Dharma Master, relying on his own mastery of the sutras and vinaya,

studies the Mahayana precepts, and acts as a virtuous friend to kings, crown princes, and high officials, yet when newly initiated Bodhisattvas come to inquire about the meaning of the sutras or the vinaya,
he responds with a frivolous mind, a malicious mind, or a conceited mind, failing to answer each question well, he commits a secondary offense.
Regarding the statement that "teachers transmit it to one another without requiring auspicious signs":

because it has been passed down through successive generations, it is the direct lineage of the Tathāgata and is also the eternally abiding Dharmakāya. Thus, the Vinaya Piṭaka states: "A person who upholds the Vinaya is one who succeeds to the Buddha’s position.
To give rise to a profound sense of respect means to regard one's teacher as a Buddha; one need not seek auspicious signs.
This is called "attaining the precepts. It clarifies that receiving the precepts through self-vow is so difficult that one attains them only when a profound sense of reverence arises.
It also clarifies that receiving the precepts from a teacher is likewise not easy. Once they have been received, one must inquire of those who are more advanced;
how could those advanced ones possibly neglect such inquiries or fail to answer them well? One with a frivolous mind neglects the person who has come to them; one with an evil mind...
"Those who are stingy, envious, and arrogant" refers to those who rely on their own merit and wisdom.

This constitutes both a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and a proscribed transgression (*prajñapti-sāvadya*), as it violates the path of guidance and instruction. A sin is established through four conditions: first, a person seeking the Dharma;
second, the perception that they are seeking the Dharma; third, a mind of pride and arrogance; and fourth, the act of speaking with perverse explanations. For every such utterance, a sin is incurred.
The seven classes of followers equally commit this offense, as all are permitted to preach the Dharma.
This applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, for even in the Hīnayāna, biased preaching is not permitted;
thus, it is strictly prohibited and never allowed.
Regarding the retribution: stinginess with the Dharma leads to ignorance; arrogance leads to baseness and inferiority.
By being neither stingy nor arrogant, one adorns oneself with merit and wisdom.
Those who understand [this] yet possess cultivation and realization all name it arrogance; those who do not know the causes and conditions of the four *siddhāntas* all name it perverse teaching.
Regarding repentance:
ritual arrogance is perversion, and ritualistic practice is perversion; the principle of the non-arising of the single mind is [the truth].

Regarding those who cultivate and realize: those at the first stage [of the path] sever the perversions of pride regarding phenomena; those established in the perfection [of the path] sever the perversions of pride regarding principle.
Regarding the inherent evil: "I am the Dharma King, sovereign over all dharmas," thus giving rise to various perverse explanations according to one's intellect or emotions.
Twenty-fourth: Not Practicing the Buddha’s Precepts.

O Disciples of the Buddha, if there are Buddhist sūtras, vinaya, and Mahāyāna teachings, possessing right view, right nature, and the true Dharma-body, yet one cannot diligently study and practice them, but instead abandons the seven treasures to study the false views of the two vehicles, external paths, and secular classics—such as the Abhidharma...
To record all miscellaneous treatises that sever the Buddha-nature and serve as causes and conditions for obstructing the Path—this is not the practice of one who follows the Bodhisattva path.
If one intentionally commits such an act, they incur a minor offense (light defilement).
The "Sūtras, Vinaya, and Mahāyāna Dharma" refers generally to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. "Right View" is the understanding of the myriad practices.
"Right Nature" is the nature of the right cause. "Right Dharmakāya" is the nature of the right fruit. "Wrong Views" refers generally to the various dharmas mentioned below:
the two vehicles falling into biased emptiness, non-Buddhists clinging to their erroneous calculations, and secular classics.
To speak only of worldly affairs: the *Abhidharma* refers to the treatises of the Two Vehicles; the *Saṃyukta-śāstra* refers to the treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);
and all written records refer to secular classics and worldly discourses. Those who sever the Buddha-nature cause the sprouts of Bodhi to wither away for those of the Two Vehicles.

Non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) gouge out the seed of perfect enlightenment. Regarding the causes and conditions that obstruct the Path: internal delusions are the cause of right understanding, while external distractions are the condition for right cultivation.

To practice exclusively the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) constitutes only the obstruction of karma (*pratikṣepa-karman*), not a defiled transgression (*kliṣṭāpatti*). To practice exclusively the non-Buddhist paths involves both natural and obstructed [transgressions].
This is an afflicted offense. There is no offense if one is exceptionally intelligent and able to receive and learn [the teachings] quickly; or if one has studied for a long time and does not forget;
or if one understands the meaning through reflection; or if one possesses complete analytical observation regarding the Buddha’s Dharma and attains unshakable wisdom.
If, on a daily basis, one constantly devotes two parts of one's study to the Buddhist scriptures and one part to non-Buddhist texts;
furthermore, if a Bodhisattva bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī does not study the Vinaya of the Śrāvakas, they also commit a minor defilement.
Therefore, the *Śīla-sūtra* states: "If a Bodhisattva, regarding the Tathāgata’s Prātimokṣa, [neglects] the prohibitions established within the Vinaya..."

For the sake of protecting sentient beings, they cause those without faith to have faith and increase the faith of those who already have it. They train in the same manner as the śrāvakas. Why is this?
Because even the śrāvakas, who seek their own liberation, do not fail to protect others; how much more so must the Bodhisattvas, whose liberation is that of the ultimate truth (paramārtha)?
Furthermore, regarding those prohibitive offenses (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya) that involve limited benefit, limited activity, and limited skillful means, the Bodhisattva does not train in these precepts.
These are: first, begging for robes from one who is not a relative; second, accepting what is offered at will; third, accepting many alms bowls;
fourth, personally begging for thread and having it woven; fifth, [accepting] bedding and sitting mats; sixth, gold and silver. Only...
Regarding these six precepts, for śrāvakas they are prohibited when performed for one's own sake, whereas for bodhisattvas they are permitted when performed for the sake of others.

It should be understood that as for the remaining two hundred and forty-four precepts, one must study and observe them equally. If one neither studies nor maintains them, then having already violated the bhikṣu precepts, one also violates the bodhisattva precepts;
the gravity of such an offense is one degree greater than that of a śrāvaka. For this reason, the bodhi-...

Because a *śrāvaka* bhikṣu is not the same as a bodhisattva śrāmaṇera and so forth, even a bodhisattva śrāmaṇera must likewise study the ten precepts along with the rules of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), for he is not a bodhisattva upāsaka.

If he does not study or uphold them, he incurs one additional offense compared to a *śrāvaka* śrāmaṇera. This is because when the seven classes of followers receive these bodhisattva precepts, [they are all required to do so].

He then raised the five precepts, the ten precepts, the six major and six minor precepts, the two hundred and fifty precepts, and so forth, declaring that all these are transformed into the inexhaustible essence of the precepts;

they are all that which a Bodhisattva ought to study. Therefore, the scriptural text states only that one commits an offense by studying the Abhidharma of the Two Vehicles, but does not say that one commits an offense by studying the Vinaya, because the Vinaya...
This is the universal path for both the great and the small vehicles, as it does not originally belong exclusively to the Two Vehicles alone.
The seven classes of followers are equally subject to the regulations, each having their own priorities. First, one should study this sutra and the two sections of the Vinaya.
For nuns, they should first study this sutra and the full set of precepts (*upasampadā*). For *śikṣamāṇās*, they should first study this sutra and the two sets of six rules. For *śrāmaṇeras*...
Men and women should first study this sutra and the dignified conduct of the ten precepts; while at home, they should first study this sutra and the upāsaka precepts.
Only when there is remaining strength may one be permitted to study them all extensively.

Regarding those points where the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not fully agree: they are identical in that both regard their respective fundamental laws as urgent, and likewise identical in that neither may practice external teachings.
As for their differences: in the Mahāyāna, failing to study the *vinaya* constitutes an offense; in the Hīnayāna, failing to study this sūtra does not constitute an offense.
Regarding "opening and prohibiting": this refers to manifesting as if one were the same as those of heterodox or Hinayana paths in order to attract and guide them.
Regarding "fruition and retribution": if one practices exclusively the Hinayana, it obstructs bodhi; if one practices external paths, one falls into attachment and views.
Understood. Repentance, cultivation, and realization are the same as the eighth precept.
Regarding those of inherently evil nature: the ultimate state of heterodox and Hinayana practitioners is itself the Great [Vehicle].
○ Twenty-fifth: The Precept Against Improper Knowledge of the Assembly.

If a disciple of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, serves as a master of the Dharma, a master of the practice of the Dharma, a master of the monastic quarters, a master of instruction, a master of seated meditation, or a master of communal affairs, they should give rise to a heart of compassion.

They should skillfully reconcile quarrels and disputes and skillfully guard the property of the Triple Gem, never using it without restraint as if it were their own. Yet, on the contrary, they may incite the assembly to chaos and strife, using the property of the Triple Gem according to their own whims.

As for "objects," one commits a minor offense (*āpatti*). The "Master of Dharma-preaching" is the current *dharmabhāṇaka*. The "Master of Dharma-practice" is the one who presides over the monastic regulations; he may also be a *vinayadhara* (Vinaya Master).

The "Master of the Monastery" is the one who oversees matters such as the quarters for the *varṣā* retreat; he is the current *kāyastha* (Director of Affairs). The "Master of Edification" is the one who exhorts others to practice.

The Director of Meritorious Works (*puṇyakarmika*) is the presiding master of seated meditation (*zuo-chan-zhu*), who oversees the practice of dhyāna, such as the head seat (*shouzuo*) of the Sangha hall.

The Director of Traveling Guests (*xinglai-zhu*) is one who manages the affairs of newly arrived guests; he is now called the Guest Master (*zhibin*). The Compassionate One (*cixin*) reconciles disputes and guards communal property.
It is able to bestow happiness upon all people.

This is a prohibitive action (*pratiṣedha-karman*). It is unwholesome to extinguish disputes; one incurs a transgression according to the specific matter. It is unwholesome to misappropriate property; one incurs a transgression according to its use.
If the Three Jewels are used interchangeably, it falls under the precept against stealing. If one initiates a dispute, one separately incurs a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs commit the full offense. As for the other five assemblies, they do not commit an offense because they are unaware of the monastic affairs; however, if they hold office, they also commit an offense.
This regulation applies equally to both the senior and junior members; it is strictly prohibited with no exceptions.

Regarding the karmic retribution: if one is unskillful in extinguishing disputes, one incurs the offense of attempting to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; if one is unskillful in guarding property, one invites the retribution of poverty and suffering.
If one is skillful in harmonizing and skillful in guarding, one will lead the great assembly, free from all obstacles.
The practitioner of contemplative understanding cannot harmonize phenomena and principle, nor do they know how to properly maintain the Dharma-wealth.
The practitioner of repentance does not skillfully understand ritual procedures, nor do they skillfully understand the contemplation of non-arising.
Regarding those who practice and realize: one who has attained liberation through the absence of doubt can mediate disputes over material affairs and can guard material wealth;
one who has perfected the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) can mediate disputes over principles and can guard and manage wealth.
As for those of evil nature: they raise the weapons of *prajñā* to wage war against all dharmas; this is called "disturbing the assembly and engaging in strife.
To give the great white ox-carts equally to all their sons is to use the property of the Triple Gem at will.
The twenty-sixth precept on receiving offerings alone:

If a disciple of the Buddha is already residing in a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*), and subsequently sees visiting Bodhisattvas or Bhikṣus entering a monastic dwelling, a private residence, a city, the palace of a king, or even a place of summer retreat (*varṣā*) or a great assembly; [if they see them there...]

The resident monks shall welcome them upon arrival and see them off when they depart, providing food and drink, as well as rooms, bedding, rope beds, and wooden beds, granting them all necessary items.

If there are no goods available, they should sell their own bodies, or even the bodies of their sons and daughters, or cut flesh from their own bodies to sell, so as to provide whatever is required and give it all to them.
If there are donors who invite the assembly of monks, and there are guest monks present...
Regarding the distribution of offerings and sustenance: the master of the monastery should appoint visiting monks in turn to accept invitations.
If the resident monks alone accept invitations while failing to appoint visiting monks, the master of the monastery incurs immeasurable sin. He is no different from a beast;
he is not a śramaṇa, nor is he of the Śākya clan. This constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
"Bodhisattvas" refers to the assembly of Mahāsattvas; "bhikṣus" refers to the assembly of śrāvakas; both should have their share of offerings and sustenance.

Regarding "the king's residence," this refers to the dwellings established by the king for the sake of housing the saṃgha. As for the phrase "one should sell one's own body and so forth," this is an illustration of the heavy case to imply the light:
if even selling one's body or cutting one's flesh should be done to provide for them, how much more so when [these things] are originally all one's rightful share?
Is this for the sake of gain and offerings?

This fully possesses both the nature [of the offense] and the obstruction of the two karmas. When the Sangha is invited according to the order of seniority, all those within the boundary should have a share of the offerings;
yet now, by not appointing visiting monks, one violates the donor’s intention and, out of greed for profit, receives it alone. This is...

This is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the precept against stealing. A transgression is established through four conditions: first, there is a guest, meaning one who is entitled to a share of the offerings has arrived within the boundary;
second, there is the perception of them as a guest, which comprises six permutations—two grave, two light, and two non-offenses;

third, the intention to receive it alone, which constitutes the actual ownership; and fourth, the completion of the assignment. According to the *Yi-shu* (Commentary on the Meaning), if one knows the order of seniority...
If one has reached that person but the appointment is not finalized, one merely incurs a minor offense (*laghu-āpatti*).
This is because at the time of the appointment, there may still be others arriving from outside the boundary who have not yet secured their specific share.

If, after the appointment is complete, one separately gives [the food] to another person, and that other person—knowing they should not have received the invitation—accepts the alms-food from the donor’s house and five *kārsāpaṇas* enter their hand, it constitutes a transgression.
Those who fail to do so shall likewise incur a grave offense; there is no difference from [the case of] animals.

Furthermore, if a guest arrives and one does not share the goods of the Saṃgha with them, nor rise to welcome them, this precept also concurrently governs such conduct; one commits the same minor transgression.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs commit the full offense. As for the other five assemblies, if they are unaware of the monastic affairs, they do not commit an offense.

However, there may be times when they receive the distribution of food; if it is distributed with partiality—whether being excessively generous or stingy, or being given in some cases and withheld in others—they all commit a minor transgression (*laghu-āpatti*).
The *Śubhavyūha-sūtra* states: "When food is served within the Saṃgha, if one shows partiality toward their teacher by selecting the finest portions and giving them in excess, this is [an offense]."
An upāsaka incurs the offense of transgression of intention (*āpatti-śaṅkita*).
This is proscribed by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; it is strictly forbidden and no exceptions are granted.
The karmic retribution for this is explained in detail in the *Cibei daochang chanfa* (The Ritual of Repentance at the Altar of Compassion).
Regarding "the one who understands": if one does not universally transform all beings through the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is called "receiving offerings and sustenance alone.

Regarding "the one who repents": there are two ways of receiving offerings and sustenance alone. If one has merely committed a light offense of preparatory action (*upakrama*), one must perform a ritual repentance (*dharmakarma-pratikramaṇa*).

If one has already taken five *kārsāpaṇas* into one's hand, a grave offense is established and the Bodhisattva precepts are lost; in this case, one must perform a repentance by taking signs (*nimitta-pratikramaṇa*). This is "receiving [offerings] alone."
Regarding the reception of nourishment: one must perform the repentance of non-arising with single-mindedness.

As for those who cultivate and realize: those at the first fruit do not exclusively receive the benefit of affairs; those at the stage of perfect dwelling do not exclusively receive the benefit of principle.
Regarding the nature of evil: throughout the ten directions, this is one's own self. How could there be a second person to receive offerings together with oneself?
Twenty-seventh: The Precept Against Accepting Separate Invitations.
If a disciple of the Buddha, he must not under any circumstances accept special invitations for offerings and take them for himself. Such offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions;
to accept a special invitation is to take the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself. Furthermore, among the eight fields of merit...
If one takes the property of the Buddhas, the sages, individual teachers, parents, or the sick for one’s own personal use, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

This includes taking the property of the Sangha of the ten directions and incorporating it into one’s own possession; for when a donor cultivates merit, the Dharma dictates that it should be universal.

It is universally equal; all beneficial gifts fundamentally pertain to the monastic community of the ten directions. Because you receive them individually, you cause that community of the ten directions to be deprived of offerings.

This carries the remote implication of usurping what belongs to the ten directions. Furthermore, among the eight fields of merit, each possesses the principle of being entitled to receive offerings in the order of the monastic assembly.
For instance, if the Buddha sometimes manifests as a monk, the rest may be understood accordingly.
This is an act of prohibition. It causes the donor to lose their impartiality of mind and deprives the Sangha of the ten directions of their regular offerings; therefore, it is proscribed.
A transgression is established through three conditions: first, it must be a private invitation. If one person from the monastic roster accepts along with others, there is no offense.
Second, the six phrases regarding the thought of a specific invitation: two cases are grave, two are light, and two are non-offenses.

Furthermore, there is no offense if one invites [the monk] to receive precepts or preach the Dharma, or if one knows that the person is not for oneself and thus does not cultivate merit. Third, the conclusion of the offense upon its acceptance.
The five groups of monastics commit this offense equally; for laypeople, there is no matter of receiving offerings. The *Śraddhākaravarman-sūtra* states:
"If an upāsaka accepts bedding, seats, or couches belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, he incurs an offense of negligence. This [offense] should also be governed by this precept.

The regulations differ according to the scale [of the vehicle]. In the Hinayana, eating apart from the community (gaṇabhojana) is prohibited; however, if among four people there is one who belongs to the monastic succession (saṃghaparyāya), there is no offense.
In this case, eating apart from the community by accepting a separate invitation is not prohibited.
Regarding the rules of permission and prohibition, the *Śīla-sūtra* states:

If a donor invites [a bodhisattva] to their own home, to a monastery, or to another’s house, and offers clothing, food, or various requisites, if the bodhisattva refuses to accept or does not go because of anger or pride, it is a defiled offense.
It is not an offense if one is ill, lacks physical strength, is insane, or is too far away.
If the location is dangerous; if the road is fearful and difficult; if he knows that by not accepting [the invitation], the other will be disciplined; if he has previously accepted an invitation;
if he wishes to practice wholesome dharmas without even a moment’s interruption; if he desires to hear unprecedented teachings, their beneficial meaning, and definitive treatises;
if he knows that the requester acts out of deceit or malice; or if he wishes to protect many people from resentment.

Because of the mind. If one observes the monastic regulations (*saṃgha-karman*), the explanation says: this refers to receiving offerings while leading the assembly, not receiving them individually. It further states:

if a donor offers gold, silver, pearls, *maṇi* gems, lapis lazuli, and various other precious objects to a Bodhisattva, and the Bodhisattva, out of anger or pride, refuses to accept them, this constitutes a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*), because it involves abandoning sentient beings. [If done out of] indolence...
Laziness and indolence constitute a non-defiled offense. There is no offense if one knows that after receiving [the gift], greed and attachment will inevitably arise;
or if one knows the donor will feel regret; or if one knows the donor will become confused; or if one knows the donor is impoverished and distressed;
or if one knows it is property belonging to the Three Jewels or stolen property; or if one knows that after receiving it, much suffering will ensue, namely: being killed, bound, exiled, or punished.
"Seizing wealth" and "reproaching. The commentary explains: This refers to receiving [wealth] for the sake of the community, not for one's own enjoyment.
As for "retribution," since it involves the meaning of seizing from the ten directions over a long period, it is also a derivative of the precept against stealing (*adattādāna*).

Regarding the contemplative understanding: receiving the invitation to enter emptiness distinguishes it from the conventional truth; receiving the invitation to emerge into the provisional distinguishes it from the ultimate truth;
and receiving the invitation to abide in the Middle alone distinguishes it from the two truths.

Regarding repentance: one accepts formal invitations for specific rites and performs the ritual procedures; one accepts invitations for specific offerings with a single-minded focus on non-arising. Regarding cultivation and realization:

this corresponds to the initial stage of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha) and the first level of faith in the Perfect Teaching (Bodhisattva). One does not accept formal invitations for specific rites; this corresponds to the initial stage of the Separate Teaching and the first dwelling (bhūmi) in the Perfect Teaching.
One does not accept invitations for specific offerings.

Regarding those of an evil nature: the wondrous offerings of the Dharma-realm are received by each person for themselves, moment by moment. It is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves.
Who can share this with them? The twenty-eighth precept: The Precept Against Inviting Monks Separately.
If, O sons of the Buddha, there are monastic bodhisattvas, lay bodhisattvas, or any donors who, when inviting the Sangha as a field of merit to seek the fulfillment of their vows,
should enter the monastery and inquire of the administrative officers (karmadāna), saying, "I now wish to invite the Sangha to seek the fulfillment of my vows," and the administrative officers reply,
"Those who invite according to the prescribed order obtain the Sangha of worthy and holy ones from the ten directions; whereas those worldly people who invite only five [monks]..."
A hundred arhat bodhisattva saṃghas are not equal to a single ordinary person (pṛthagjana) in the regular order of the saṃgha. To invite the saṃgha separately is the dharma of external paths;

none of the Seven Buddhas had a practice of separate invitation, nor does it accord with the way of filial piety. If one intentionally invites the saṃgha separately, one commits a minor offense (āpatti).
Regarding the phrase "by requesting in succession, one immediately obtains the assembly of worthy sages of the ten directions":
because ordinary beings and sages are difficult to discern, one should not give rise to arbitrary discrimination. As for the seven Buddhas: first, Vipaśyin Buddha, also called Vīra;
this translates as "Victorious Vision. Second, Śikhin Buddha, also called Śikhi; this translates as "Fire. Third, Viśvabhū Buddha, also called...
He is called Viśvabhū; alternatively, he is called Śibi or Śyāma. This translates as "pervasive sovereignty over all.
These three World-Honored Ones all appeared in the past during the Adorned Eon (Bhadrakalpa). Fourth is Krakucchanda Buddha; alternatively, he is called Kḷuśin.
This translates as "that which is to be severed. Fifth is Kanakamuni Buddha; this translates as "Gold."

Śākyamuni Buddha, also called Śākyamunī; this is translated as "Silent Sage of the Śākya Clan" (Nengren Jimo) or "Capable Confucian" (Nengru). These four Tathāgatas: 1. Vipaśyin Buddha, also translated as "Golden Immortal. 2. Śikhin Buddha, also translated as "Drinking Light" (Yinguang). 3. Viśvabhū Buddha, also translated as "Universal Manifestation" (Puguang). 4.

Krakucchanda Buddha, also translated as "Tranquil" (Ji) or "Golden Immortal. 5. Kanakamuni Buddha, also translated as "Drinking Light" (Yinguang). 6. Kāśyapa Buddha, also translated as "Drinking Light" (Yinguang). 7. Śākyamuni Buddha, also called Śākyamunī; this is translated as "Silent Sage of the Śākya Clan" (Nengren Jimo) or "Capable Confucian" (Nengru). These are the four Tathāgatas.

All appeared in the world during the Bhadrakalpa. Throughout various passages in the sutras, the seven Buddhas are frequently cited as proof of this principle, because they all appeared in this very land and were active within the most recent hundred minor kalpas; thus, those in the Heaven of Long Life have all seen them.
Those who do not accord with the way of filial piety fail to follow the Buddha’s instructions and treat the Sangha with contempt.

This constitutes a prohibited action (*pratiṣiddha-karman*), for it discriminates between fields of merit and non-fields, and because such a mind is narrow and inferior, failing to accord with the dharma-gate of equality.

According to the Vinaya of the Śrāvakas, if one person has been invited from within the monastic succession (*saṃgha-paṅkti*) and another is requested by specifically naming them, there is no offense;
this case may be similar. It would be even better, however, if the invitation were made to the monastic succession as a whole without distinction.
This applies equally to the seven classes of followers and is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited: for instance, when seeking a teacher or choosing friends, one must carefully exercise discernment; however, this is not required when one wishes to preach the Dharma or bestow the precepts.
In converting and guiding the multitude, one should invite those whose talent and virtue are both preeminent.

To invite separately those who have committed offenses or are subject to karmic retribution would violate the Dharma-gate of equality and signlessness, and result in the loss of vast and perfect merit.
Conversely, if one does not invite them separately, it is like a single drop cast into the ocean, instantly becoming one with the essence of the sea.

The "understander" knows the subtlety of relative opposition (*pratipakṣa*), but does not know the subtlety of absolute transcendence (*atyantānupama*). They disparage the teachings of the *Hīnayāna* (Śrāvaka), *Pratyekabuddha*, and the Distinct Teaching (*Bhedavyākaraṇa*), while exclusively esteeming the Perfect Teaching (*Pūrṇavyākaraṇa*); this is the meaning of the "distinct invitation."

Regarding repentance: the ritual procedure involves the separate invitation of the objective (the object of worship), while the principle involves the separate invitation of the noumenon (the ultimate reality). One must employ a single mind to harmonize these with the fourfold non-arising. Regarding cultivation and realization:
at the stage of the first fruit (srotāpanna), there is no separate invitation of the objective; in the stage of perfect faith, there is no separate invitation of the noumenon.
Regarding those of evil nature: among the ten realms of existence, they specifically cause each to obtain the benefit of the Buddha-realm.
○ Twenty-ninth, the precept against wrong livelihood:

If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, for the sake of profit and sustenance, sells the sexual favors of men or women, prepares food with their own hands, or [engages in other such acts]...
Grinding [grains] for oneself, performing divinations to determine the sex of a child, interpreting dreams for good or bad fortune, determining whether a child will be male or female,
practicing incantations, crafts, and methods for training hawks, or compounding hundreds or thousands of kinds of poisonous drugs— including snake venom, poisons derived from living gold and silver,
and *gū* (insect-poison)— if one does so without any heart of compassion or filial piety, and intentionally commits such acts, one incurs a minor offense of defilement.

"Those with evil minds" clarifies that these are not the intentions of one who perceives the opportune moment to benefit sentient beings. For the sake of gain and sustenance, seven matters are enumerated:
first, trading in women; second, preparing food; third, divination of physiognomy and interpretation of dreams; fourth, incantations and sorcery; fifth, craftsmanship; sixth, training hawks.

Regarding the seven types of poisonous substances: these constitute both natural (*prakṛti*) and prohibitive (*pratikṣepa*) offenses. However, among them, only the two activities of selling and [administering] color-poisons (poisonous dyes) also constitute natural sins (*prakṛti-āpatti*);

the remainder are merely prohibitive sins (*pratikṣepa-āpatti*). Furthermore, the contemporary practice of raising hawks for the purpose of hunting is likewise a natural sin, or it may be classified as a sin of harming (*vihiṃsā*).
This precept subsumes the prohibition against harming sentient beings. When poisonous substances are being compounded, a minor offense (duṣkṛta) is incurred;

however, at the moment of harming a living being, one incurs the full offense of killing (*prāṇātipāta*) accordingly. The same applies to training hawks. Furthermore, the four wrong means of livelihood, the five wrong means of livelihood, and the eight impurities of monastics are all concurrently regulated by this precept.

Regarding the four wrong means of livelihood: the first is "looking upward for food," which refers to observing the stars and calculating the movements of celestial bodies to predict auspicious times.
1. Seeking food by means of falsehood and the like; 2. Seeking food by lowering one’s mouth, such as cultivating fields and gardens; 3.

Seeking food by looking toward the four quarters, such as seeking audiences with those in power and forming alliances with the influential; 4. Seeking food by looking toward the four intermediate directions, such as practicing medicine, divination, various arts, and diverse means of livelihood;
5. The five types of wrong livelihood: first, manifesting extraordinary signs; second, speaking of one’s own merits; third, divining and interpreting omens of good fortune.
The eight types of impurity are: first, preaching the Dharma for the sake of those who are wicked; second, speaking loudly and manifesting an air of authority to inspire awe and reverence in others;

third, preaching in order to obtain offerings so as to stir the hearts of people; fourth, fields and houses; fifth, gardens and groves; sixth, planting and cultivating seeds; seventh, hoarding grain and silk;
eighth, maintaining male and female servants; ninth, raising and tethering birds and beasts; tenth, money, jewels, and precious objects; eleventh, [the aforementioned items].
Regarding woolen rugs, blankets, cauldrons, and large pots, as well as eight types of elephant-ornamented couches and other heavy valuables:

members of the five monastic orders commit a full offense by possessing them. Lay followers (upāsakas) are exempt from these three items—selling silk, training falcons, and dealing in poisons—but for all other matters, if they maintain themselves in accordance with the Dharma, they do not commit an offense.
Furthermore, the *Śrāddhāvidhi-sūtra* states: "If an upāsaka requires to work in the fields..."
If one does not seek out pure water or dry land for planting, one incurs an offense of negligence (*duṣkṛta*). This may also be subsumed under this precept.

"Pure water" refers to water free of living organisms. "Dry land plants" refers to grains such as rice and wheat that grow on land; these do not require water and thus would not cause injury to insects.
Both the great and the small [precepts] are equally prohibited.

Regarding what is permitted and what is forbidden: if a renunciant occasionally employs divination, incantations, or technical arts to adapt to the capacities of beings and lead them into the Buddha-way—provided it is not out of a desire for profit—it likewise constitutes no offense. Incantations are for the purpose of curing illness and rescuing those in distress.
Therefore, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles possess this as well. Regarding "fruition" (*vipāka*), the *Jingxun* (Admonitions for the Monastic Community) states:

"In the present age, those who lecture and study devote themselves solely to profit and fame; they do not feel shame in committing the five perversities and frequently accumulate the eight impurities.
They merely follow worldly customs and do not contemplate the words of the Sages. From the time they descend from the ordination platform, many years pass..."
Regarding the summer retreat and the pure precepts (*śīla*), if one has not yet once touched them with one's person, how can one know that what one relies upon daily is nothing but defiled things?
That which is accumulated in trunks and bags is entirely wealth acquired through transgression. To be arrogant toward the Dharma and deceive one’s own mind is to bring calamity upon oneself.

Those who study the Vinaya know this yet deliberately commit such acts; as for those of other schools, it goes without saying. Who realizes that retribution follows the mind and is thereby formed? How could it...
Faith is the fruit that arises from causes and conditions. We see before our eyes that while the *kāṣāya* may be separated from the body now, in the future one will be bound by iron leaves.
If one becomes a human, one will be born into poverty, with garments soiled and filthy; if one becomes an animal, one will fall into impurity, with fur and feathers foul and rank.
How much more so for the two vehicles, Great and Small, which universally clarify the pure Dharma—if one harbors deep faith, how could one hesitate to practice it?
Those who understand [only this] do not know that nature is inherently complete; yet they grasp at effects and cultivate causes, accumulating merit and virtue—this is called "peddling.
Failing to reach the path of non-action and cessation is called "cooking food. Failing to realize the direct manifestation of one's own mind is called "divining signs.
Not knowing how to reveal the ultimate by opening the provisional is called "incantation. Failing to reach the path of effortless spontaneity is called...
To be skillful in craft and to seize or snatch at things is called "taming hawks. To be biased toward either the ultimate truth or the conventional truth is a dharma-gate called "poisonous medicine.
As for repentance, its practice is erroneous and its principle is erroneous; [the correct way] is the single mind of non-arising.
Regarding cultivation and realization: Is there no objective basis for the first fruit? Is there no principle for perfect abiding?
Regarding the inherent evil of nature: as in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, where accepting food from those who have fallen into the three [lower realms] is considered ultimate wrong livelihood;
and again, such as the analogy of placing poison in milk.
The thirtieth principle: The Precept on Refraining from Associating with Laypeople.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, slanders the Triple Gem himself, feigns intimacy and attachment, and speaks of emptiness with his mouth;
To engage in worldly affairs, manage the business of laypeople, act as a go-between for men and women to facilitate sexual union, create various forms of bondage and attachment,
and on the six fasting days or during the three months of the long fast, to commit acts of killing or robbery, thereby breaking the fast and violating the precepts—
this constitutes a minor offense of defilement.

Regarding the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*): these are the six days each month, namely the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth; if the month is short, they are the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth.
On these six days—the eighth, the twenty-third, and [the others]—the messengers of the Four Great Kings (*catur-mahārāja*) patrol the world to examine and investigate good and evil.
14. On the twenty-ninth day, the princes of the Four Heavenly Kings patrol the world. 15.
On the thirtieth day, the Four Heavenly Kings themselves travel through the world. If they see many who cultivate goodness, the devas rejoice and protect the realm.
If they see few who cultivate goodness, the devas become sorrowful and unhappy, and calamities will abound in the realm.
Therefore, the Buddha ordained that laymen and laywomen— whether they have merely taken the Three Refuges, received the Five Precepts, or received the Bodhisattva Precepts—
should, upon encountering these six days, all observe and uphold the Eightfold Precepts of the Uposatha for one full day and night.
Abstaining from eating at improper times is correctly termed *upavāsa* (fasting). This is further supported by the eight precepts, such as non-killing and so forth;

thus, it is called the "Eightfold Restraint Fast" (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*). By means of these eight precepts and the fast, one shuts off sensual desires and establishes the correct cause for transcendence.
As for the eight precepts: first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual misconduct—whether with those who are improper or proper.

1. To abstain entirely from taking life; 2. To abstain entirely from taking what is not given; 3. To abstain entirely from sexual misconduct; 4. To abstain entirely from false speech; 5. To abstain entirely from drinking intoxicants; 6.

To abstain entirely from wearing perfumes, floral garlands, or anointing the body with scents; 7. To abstain entirely from singing, dancing, music, and theatrical performances, and from going to witness them; 8. To abstain entirely from sitting or lying on high, wide, or large beds.
Regarding the three months of the "Long Fasting" (Cāndra): Vaiśravaṇa Deva-king divides his governance over the four continents.

In the first, fifth, and ninth months, he presides over this Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa). Therefore, the Buddha established that laymen and laywomen should observe the fasting precepts (*upavāsa*) as described above for the entirety of these months.
This precept was formerly called "not honoring auspicious times. The *Yìshù* states: "The three fasts [occur] in the sixth..."
The days of fasting (*upoṣadha*) are all days upon which spirits and deities gain power. On these days, one should cultivate merit and virtue more than on other days;

yet now, during such auspicious times, people are negligent and even commit transgressions. According to each specific offense, the corresponding penalty shall be assigned from the relevant section of the precepts.
At such a time and on such a day, one ought not to remain ignorant. Furthermore, this applies as an additional injunction for all seven classes of followers; everyone should respect these times. (2)

It is said that the prohibition applies only to laypeople. On the sixth day of the third month, it was originally intended for laypeople; those who have left the household life should observe the fast for the duration of their lives, regardless of specific seasons.
(Text) Now, observing the force of the scriptural passage, it appears rather that the transgression is being attributed to the side of the monastics.
Therefore, the section is reclassified as a principle for managing laypeople (*baiyi*). The general meaning is that the dharma for monastics should involve the induction and instruction [of others].

Laypeople are led toward liberation and are encouraged to observe the fasts and precepts; yet you, on the contrary, preach that emptiness exists within conditioned phenomena and manage their affairs for them.

Even during the six fast days, the three fast days, and other auspicious times, you are unable to lead them to cultivate merit and perform wholesome deeds, but instead cause them to commit acts such as killing and stealing.
Is this not to slander the Triple Gem with one's own person?
This is a prohibitive action (*pratiṣedha-karman*). One incurs guilt solely through the principle of managing laypeople's affairs.

What are called killing, stealing, breaking the fast, and violating the precepts are matters pertaining to worldly people; they are not things for which one instructs those who have left the household life to perform.

Nevertheless, since there are interactions involving men and women and the like, one cannot avoid creating distant conditions for acts such as killing and stealing; therefore, [the text] attributes [the fault] to...

This is the limit; it merely demonstrates that [such acts] are not appropriate. If one were to actually teach others to kill or steal, they would simultaneously incur the karma of nature (svabhāva-karma), which falls under the precepts against killing and stealing.
The five groups of monastics commit a full offense at all times if they manage the affairs of laypeople.

As for the two groups of householders who have already received the Bodhisattva precepts, it is also an offense if they do not respect auspicious times. The *Susheng jing* (Sūtra on the Good Life) states:
"If an upāsaka cannot observe the eight precepts on six days within a month and make offerings to the Triple Gem, he incurs [an offense]."
This constitutes an offense of negligence. For other occasions, such as marriage and so forth according to worldly custom, no prohibition is established.
If one commits killing, robbery, or violates the precepts by breaking the fast, each act shall be judged and classified separately according to its specific nature.
Both the major and minor precepts prohibit this;
it is strictly forbidden without exception.
Regarding the karmic retribution: managing affairs for laypeople also constitutes wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*), as previously explained. Furthermore, one does not respect auspicious times.

If husbands are sorrowful and anxious, they can summon calamities and anomalies; if they respect and cherish the proper seasons, the various devas will rejoice, protect the state, and bestow auspiciousness.

As for the "observer who understands," one who contemplates the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) separately from the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is called a "layman who manages affairs"; such a person does not know others.

Life exists within the space of a single breath; this is called "not honoring the precious time. Furthermore, though one may not know the ten generations of past and future, one does not depart from the present moment.
In even a single, minute thought-instant, there is horizontal pervasiveness and vertical exhaustion; this is called "not honoring the precious time."
Regarding repentance: there are transgressions of fact, transgressions through ritual procedure, and transgressions of principle. Regarding one-pointed mind and non-arising:
at the first fruit (srotāpanna), there are no transgressions of fact; at the stage of perfect abiding (the Buddha-stage), there are no transgressions of principle.

Regarding the "inherent evil" (xing-è): flowing along with the nine realms is called "managing affairs as a layperson" (jīng-lǐ bái-yī); severing the continuity of the three periods of time is called "not respecting favorable times.
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart; they are explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Formulation of Precepts" (Zhìjiè pǐn).
This concludes the third section on the ten precepts.
○ The thirty-first: the precept against failing to provide ransom.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the midst of this evil age, if you see non-Buddhists or any wicked people..."
If there are bandits who sell images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or their parents; who sell the Sūtras and Vinaya; who trade in Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs;

or who even sell those Bodhisattvas and practitioners of the Way who have resolved upon Bodhicitta—making them servants for officials or slaves to all people—when a Bodhisattva sees such matters, they should give rise to a heart of compassion and provide protection through skillful means.

If one takes objects from places where they are being used for teaching and transformation— such as images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment],
or any of the sūtras or vinayas— and does not redeem them, one commits a minor offense.

In an evil age, it is precisely when a Great Being arouses kindness and exercises compassion that they must employ skillful means to rescue and protect others to the utmost of their mental and physical strength;
they must not remain indifferent or look on with passive resignation.

This is a prohibitive action (*pratiṣedha-karman*). An offense is established through four conditions: first, the object to be redeemed, namely sacred images, sūtras, vinaya texts, monks, and so forth;

second, the six permutations of the perception regarding the object to be redeemed—two cases of gravity, two cases of lightness, and two cases of non-offense; third, the absence of an intention to redeem.
If one lacks the power [to prevent it], there is no offense. Fourth, if one causes another to be humiliated, one incurs an offense according to the specific circumstances.
Even if one lacks the power, if one remains indifferent and does not care, one also commits an offense.

The seven classes of followers share this [precept] equally; however, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not fully coincide on this point. In the Hīnayāna, one incurs an offense if one does not ransom one's parents, whereas no such prohibition is seen regarding others.
For a Bodhisattva, the responsibility is to extensively protect and defend; thus, all should be ransomed.
Only prohibitions are not permitted; however, there is no offense if it concerns the circulation of scriptures in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding the karmic retribution: if one does not save others, one fails in the two benefits; if one saves them, one fulfills the two adornments.

One who understands [this] but does not know that nature is inherently complete is said to be "selling the Triple Gem. To use skillful means (*upāya*) to reveal and instruct others so that they may know that nature is inherently complete is called "redeeming" it.
As for repentance (*pratikramaṇa*): ritual acts do not save; performing the rites does not save in principle. One must attain single-mindedness in non-arising.

Regarding those who practice and realize: those at the first stage of faith in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), the first dwelling (*zhù*) in the Separate Teaching (*bie*), and Bodhisattvas on the ground of seeing (*jiàn-dì*) in the Shared Teaching (*tōng*)—as well as Bodhisattvas of the *āgama* who practice through the perfections (*pāramitā*)—are all able to provide rescue through the full exercise of practical deeds.
Those at the first dwelling in the Perfect Teaching and the first ground in the Separate Teaching are both able to provide rescue through the full exercise of rational principles.
Regarding the "inherent evil" (xing-è): it refers precisely to the desire to forcibly sell the Three Jewels of the Dharma-realm to those within the Dharma-realm.
[This concludes] the thirty-second precept: the Prohibition Against Harming Sentient Beings.
If a Buddha’s disciple sells swords, staves, bows, or arrows; keeps light scales or small measures; uses official authority or influence to seize the property of others;
binds others with harmful intent; destroys successful works; or raises cats, raccoons, pigs, and dogs—if they intentionally raise such creatures, they commit a secondary offense (light defilement).
Swords, staves, bows, and arrows are instruments of harm; light scales and small measures are instruments of deception, as are short cubits.
Furthermore, taking goods in by means of heavy scales, large measures, and long cubits is subject to the same prohibition.

However, this is merely a light offense because it concerns temporary use; if one were to shift or substitute items by means of deception so that the previous owner does not notice, it would fall under the category of theft (*steya*).
As for those who act through official authority or influence, they practice violent seizure, wounding compassion with their power and might.
The offenses are light. To take what is not one's own is likewise subsumed under theft. "Binding" refers to injuring their limbs.
"Destroying successful work" refers to ruining their completed projects. Cats and dogs can harm rodents; pigs ultimately meet with slaughter.
All the aforementioned acts are things that those possessing a compassionate heart ought not to do.
This fulfills both the nature and the prohibition of the offense; the transgression is determined according to the specific act.
All seven classes of followers commit this offense equally. The *Susheng jing* (Sūtra on the Origin of Goodness) states:

"If a lay follower (*upāsaka*), for the sake of his own livelihood, engages in trade and sells goods using measures and scales, once the price has been stated, he must not retract it or shift from a lower price to a higher one by manipulating the measures and scales."
When measuring objects, one should use them as they are laid out in front. If they are not level, one should tell the person to make them level. If one does not do so, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The commentary states: "If this is so even for those living at home, how much more so for those who have left the home life?"
Both the great and the small [vehicles] prohibit [killing and stealing]; they are merely barred and never permitted.
The retribution for these acts is the outflow of killing, stealing, and so forth.

Regarding the understanding [of these truths]: ordinary beings and outsiders damage the ultimate; those of the Two Vehicles damage the conventional; those of the *Zang* and *Tong* [teachings] damage the Middle; and those of the *Bie* [teaching] damage the two truths.
Regarding repentance: the phenomenal aspect is damaged; the ritual procedure damages the principle; and non-arising [damages] cultivation and realization. Regarding the fruits:

the first fruit does not damage the phenomenal, nor does it damage the truth; emerging into the provisional does not damage the conventional; the stage of the Separate Teaching’s direction does not damage the Middle;
and the stages of the Separate Teaching’s grounds and the Perfect Teaching’s abidings do not damage the two truths.
Regarding "inherently evil": it damages the nine realms and establishes the Buddha-realm; yet even the Buddha-realm is not established [as a fixed entity], thus it completely damages all ten realms.
○ The thirty-third is the precept of deluded thought and observation regarding perverse karma.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, watches men and women fighting, or armies, generals, and bandits fighting,
they must not listen to the sounds of conchs, drums, horns, lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, or *konghou* lutes,
nor to the sounds of singing, shouting, or female musicians. They must not play *chupu*, go, *parase* (chess), *tanqi*, *liubo*, ball games, or stone-throwing games.
Playing pitch-pot (tōu-hú), playing games such as *qiāndào*, *bā dào*, *xíngchéng*, *zhuǎjìng*, divining with *shī* stalks, using willow branches, or using a begging bowl or a skull for divination;
one must not engage in these as a messenger for thieves or bandits. One must not do any of these things. If one intentionally does so, one commits a minor offense (*qīnggòu-zuì*).

Regarding those with "evil minds": this clarifies that they do not perceive the opportune moment to benefit sentient beings; rather, it refers simply to their perverse thoughts and perverse perceptions.
Five matters are listed together: first, quarreling; second, entertainment; third, the *bèi* (a conch shell); fourth, the seven-stringed *qín*; fifth, the twenty-five-stringed *sè*;
sixth, the *zhēng* (a zither), which has a bamboo body and thirteen strings; and seventh, the *kōnghóu* (a lute), which has a bamboo body and twenty-four strings. Three.
Miscellaneous games include *chupú* (a gambling game), which is the same as the money-betting games of today; *pārasīka-krīḍā* (Persian chess), which is the same as the elephant chess of today;

*tánqí* (a board game), which was a cosmetic box game for palace ladies during the Han dynasty; *liùbó* (six-sided dice), which is the same as the *shuānglù* of today; *pàijù* (ball-pounding), which is the same as the kicking of the ball (*tíqú*) of today;

and *zhìshí tóuhú* (stone-throwing at the pitch-pot), where stones were used in antiquity but arrows are used today. As for the "pulling the path" and "eight paths moving through the city," these refer to the vertical and horizontal [movements].
Each consists of eight paths. It is played with chessmen; it is a game of the Western Regions. Fourth, divination:

the "claw-mirror" is the method of the *maṇḍala*; the *śi* grass is the method of the *Yī* hexagrams; the willow branch is the deity of the *zhāngliǔ*; the alms bowl is the method of the "stirring-water bowl";
and the skull is the method of "ear-report. Fifth, messengers: these five all belong to the category of heterodox practices.

The acts of robbing and dispatching messengers are both of the nature of prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*); all others are merely prohibitive offenses, with their gravity determined according to the specific circumstances.
Furthermore, the *Śīla-sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva is indolent and lazy, addicted to the pleasure of sleep, or if they eat at improper times or without moderation..."
This is a defiled offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill; if one lacks strength; if one is exhausted from traveling a long distance;

if, for the sake of severing that [affliction], one has initiated the application of desire and adopted counteractive measures; or if the naturally sharp afflictions arise again and again despite such efforts.
This precept may also encompass these cases:

those in the five monastic groups commit the offense in its entirety, whereas laypeople who make offerings to the Triple Gem are permitted to employ music and dance. Monastics, however, may not perform these themselves;

they are permitted to have laypeople do so. Furthermore, the game of *touhu* (pitch-pot) originated in the *Liji* (Book of Rites), and the use of *shī* stalks and tortoise shells originated in the [divination] traditions.
According to the *Yi* and the scriptures, even those living at home should not commit transgressions;
the precepts apply equally to both the great and the small.

Regarding what is permitted or prohibited: there may be occasions where one perceives a karmic opportunity to benefit sentient beings and so forth. Furthermore, for monastics who wish to resolve their doubts, there are [the teachings] themselves.
One may rely upon and employ the method of selecting signs from the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, the method of casting the three wheels from the *Sūtra of Divination and Observation*,
and the hundred bamboo slips of the Brahma Deity from the *Great Consecration Sūtra*.

Regarding the karmic retribution: if one engages in [discursive] contemplation, it obstructs and abandons the Right Path, causing one to lose the benefits of both worlds; if one does not engage in such contemplation, one is free from agitation and regret, and concentration and wisdom arise easily.
As for contemplative understanding: with the exception of the inconceivable and wondrous contemplation, all others are termed "false awakening."
Regarding repentance: is it a matter of ritual action, or is it a matter of principle? Regarding cultivation and realization through single-mindedness and non-arising:
is it that there is no matter in the three fruits, or is it that there is no principle in the distinct stages and perfect abidings?
Regarding "inherently evil": one observes through the three natures and universally awakens to the true reality within all perverse karmas.
○ Thirty-fourth: the precept of temporarily departing from the bodhicitta.

O Sons of the Buddha, you who protect and uphold the prohibitive precepts: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, at the six periods of day and night, you shall read and recite these precepts as if they were a vajra.
You shall be like one carrying a life-preserving float intending to cross the great ocean, or like the bhikṣu bound by grass.

You shall constantly give rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna, knowing for yourself that you are a Buddha-to-be, while all Buddhas are Buddhas already perfected. You shall resolve upon Bodhicitta...

Maintain mindfulness; let it not depart from the mind at every thought. If one gives rise to even a single thought of the Two Vehicles or of non-Buddhist paths, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
"Vajra" means that which can destroy all things, yet cannot be destroyed by anything. "Life-preserving bag" refers to that which crosses the sea.
[The story of] the "Grass-Tied Bhikṣu" is found in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Regarding the bhikṣu bound with grass:
once, during the Buddha’s lifetime, there was a bhikṣu who was robbed of his robes and belongings by bandits on the road.

Fearing that the monastic community would come to search for him and might even take his life, one of the bandits—who understood the Dharma of the bhikṣus—said to the others, "There is no need to kill him; simply bind him with living grass."
Regarding his hands and feet: that precept prohibits harming grasses or trees; he himself did not even move them. The bandits followed their words and bound him.
The bhikṣu maintained his precepts; he would rather die than waver. Once the bandits had gone far away, a traveler later came by and finally untied his bonds.
Now, it should be understood that when a Great Being protects this Bodhicitta precept, they ought likewise to protect it as a śrāvaka does.
Regarding the *vinaya* (precepts): it is better to die than to violate them.

To give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles constitutes only a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offense); every thought-moment is not a defiled violation. To give rise to the mind of non-Buddhists constitutes both *prakṛti-sāvadya* (natural offenses) and *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*; every thought-moment is a defiled violation.
The seven groups [of disciples] are the same;

however, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are not entirely shared. They are alike in that they must not give rise to the mind of an outsider (tīrthika). The two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are their original training.
Regarding permissions and prohibitions: if one provisionally enters the two vehicles or the ways of outsiders for the sake of transforming them, it is permitted.
Regarding retribution: a single thought of the mind of the two vehicles also obstructs bodhi; a single thought of the mind of an outsider also obstructs transcendence of the world.
Only by maintaining the thought of bodhicitta in every moment can one attain the three kinds of non-retrogression.
Regarding "understanding": with the exception of the One Vehicle, all others are heterodox or Hinayana, as previously stated.

Regarding "repentance": it is also as previously stated. Regarding "cultivation and realization": in the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), it corresponds to the first stage of faith; in the Separate Teaching (Bie), it corresponds to the first dwelling (bhūmi); in the Common Teaching (Tong), it corresponds to the stage of seeing (darśana-bhūmi); and in the Treasury Teaching (Zang), it corresponds to the first fruit (srotāpanna). From this point on, one never again gives rise to external [views].

The Bodhi-mind. In the stage of non-retrogression in practice, one never again gives rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles. In the distinct stages and the perfect dwelling, one never again gives rise to the narrow, inferior mind of deviation within the principle.
Regarding those with inherent evil, every thought-moment they observe the realms of externalists and the Two Vehicles as being precisely the inconceivable realm; thus they achieve perfection.
The ultimate of the non-Buddhists; the ultimate of the Two Vehicles. ○ Thirty-fifth: The Precept Against Not Making Vows.

If a disciple of the Buddha, one should constantly make all manner of vows: to be filial toward parents and respectful toward teachers and the Sangha; to vow to obtain a good teacher, and to [practice] together with...

One should study with virtuous friends who constantly teach me the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas— the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the ten bhūmis—
so that I may attain understanding and practice according to the Dharma, firmly upholding the Buddha’s precepts even at the cost of my own body and life,
never letting them depart from my mind for a single thought-moment. If all Bodhisattvas do not make this vow, they commit a minor offense.
"Vow" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to the longing for a superior state based upon a virtuous object of the mind.
That which "should always be generated" means that it is not merely a single generation; rather, it should be generated repeatedly so that the bodhicitta continues without interruption.
"All vows" collectively refers to the ten vows: first, the vow to be filial toward one's parents, teachers, and the *saṃgha*; second, the vow to obtain a good teacher; third...
1. May I obtain fellow students and virtuous friends. 2. May you teach me the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya. 3.
May I understand the stages of progress (*pratipatti*). 4. May I understand the stages of nourishment (*puṣṭi*). 5. May I understand the Vajra stage. 6. May I understand the stages (*bhūmi*). 7.

May I practice according to the Dharma. 8. May I firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts. For the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, the precepts are its foundation; without upholding the Buddha’s [precepts],...
Regarding the precepts: by what means does one advance? Therefore, one forms a vow to uphold the precepts.

This constitutes the prevention of unwholesome karma. If there is no great vow, it is difficult to achieve the great fruit. Whether one should have generated [the vow] but did not, or whether one fails to generate it at the appropriate time, one incurs a transgression accordingly.
The seven classes of followers are the same in this regard;

the distinction lies between the Great and Small Vehicles. In the Small Vehicle, if one does not aspire to swiftly emerge from birth and death, but instead hopes for the continued succession of future existences as humans or devas, they likewise commit an offense requiring mental reproach.
Only prohibition applies; there is no allowance.

Regarding the karmic fruit: if it does not arise, one loses the definitive, supreme benefit; if it arises in a continuous succession, one can attain Buddhahood and extinguish transgressions, as explained in the *Prasthānacitta* (The Mind of Aspiration).
Regarding "understanding": although one has not yet attained non-retrogression in practice, there may still be times of interruption.
Regarding "repenting": repeatedly making vows to ensure that the bodhicitta does not cease is what is meant by "repentance."
Regarding those who practice and realize: they are persons of non-retrogression who adorn themselves by never departing from their great vows.

Regarding those of inherently evil nature: they do not seek by clinging to the Buddha, they do not seek by clinging to the Dharma, and they do not seek by clinging to the Sangha; they should not seek the Dharma-realm apart from the Dharma-realm itself.
○ Thirty-sixth: The Precept Against Failing to Make a Vow.
O Disciples of the Buddha, having made these ten great vows, you shall uphold the prohibitions of the Buddhas and make this vow:
"I would rather cast this body into a blazing, fierce fire, into a great pit, or onto a mountain of blades, than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time."
He engages in impure conduct with all women and further makes this vow:
"I would rather have my body encircled on all sides by a thousand layers of glowing iron nets than ever accept any clothing from a faithful donor with this body of broken precepts.
He further makes this vow: "I would rather swallow glowing iron balls and a great torrent of fierce fire with this mouth..."
For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he shall never, with this mouth of broken precepts, consume the food of a hundred flavors offered by faithful donors.

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather let this body lie upon a great torrent, amidst fierce flames, or upon a ground of iron nets and heat, than ever receive a hundred kinds of couches and seats from faithful donors with this body of broken precepts. Furthermore...

He made this vow: "I would rather have this body endure three hundred spears piercing it for one kalpa or two kalpas, than ever again, with this body of broken precepts, accept the medicines of a hundred flavors offered by faithful donors. He further made this vow:

"I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than, with this body of broken precepts, accept the thousands of kinds of dwellings, houses, gardens, groves, fields, and lands offered out of faith by donors. Furthermore, he made this vow:"
"I would rather have this body smashed with an iron hammer from head to foot until it is reduced to fine dust;
I will never, with this body of broken precepts, accept the respectful prostrations of faithful donors. Furthermore, he makes this vow:
'I would rather have my two eyes gouged out by hundreds of thousands of hot iron blades and spears; I will never, with this mind of broken precepts, look upon others.'"

Regarding sensual desire, he further made this vow: "I would rather have my sense organ of hearing pierced by a hundred thousand iron awls for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, listen to pleasant sounds. He further made this vow:
"I would rather have my nose cut off by a hundred thousand sharp blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily smell various fragrances. Furthermore...
He makes this vow: "I would rather have my tongue cut off by hundreds of thousands of blades than, with a mind of broken precepts, ever consume the hundred-flavored pure food of others.

He further makes this vow: "I would rather have my body split apart by a sharp axe than, with a mind of broken precepts, ever crave pleasant tactile sensations. He further makes this vow: "May all sentient beings..."
All shall attain Buddhahood. If a Bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense.
A "vow" (śīla) is a firm resolve of the heart, a courageous self-exhortation to ensure non-retrogression, with the aspiration serving as a guide for the way ahead.

I vow to drive away those that follow. Furthermore, I vow to take the advancement of virtue and the cultivation of goodness as my power and application, and to take the prevention of wrongdoing and the eradication of evil as my function and efficacy.
The "Ten Great Vows" refers to the ten vows within the preceding section on precepts.
This composition of vows consists of thirteen sections, collectively forming five categories. The first section constitutes the vow against desire and defilement, as found in the Vinaya.
It is said: "A fierce fire or a mountain of blades may only injure this single lifetime's body and life;

however, a woman’s lustful defilement causes one to fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering, while simultaneously injuring the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom. Therefore, it is better to throw oneself into blades and fire than to engage in unchaste conduct.
Now, even for men and women living as householders—which is considered the proper way of life in the world—they still maintain such solemn vows; how much more so for those of the Yellow [Robe]?"

A man who enters the inner quarters violates principle and disrupts the constant order; why then need one say more? As for those who claim that the sin of female desire is heavy while the sin of male desire is light, this is truly a perverse view.
The *Mahābuddhatoṣaṇī-sūtra* (Great Buddha-Crown Sūtra) states: "In the past, evil māra-masters and their māra-disciples transmitted lustful practices to one another;
they are truly the seeds of hell. Furthermore, a sūtra says: "At the beginning of the kalpa, there were no men or women."
The two sexual organs arise because food eliminates impurities; it is due to these two organs that mutual lust and attachment develop, thereby initiating the beginning of birth from a womb.
Yet, in the beginning, male sexual misconduct was unheard of. It was only when the lifespan decreased to five hundred years that illicit sexual conduct first arose.
Once this misconduct began, evils became extreme, and [the lifespan] suddenly decreased by another half to two hundred and fifty years.
"One hundred years. From this perspective, it is clear that the transgression of male lust is more grave than female lust.
Therefore, within the Vinaya and the Āgamas, when a wild fire was raging, the Buddha preached these various vows for the sake of the bhikṣus.

Those whose faculties were mature immediately severed their defilements; those whose faculties were not yet mature feared the offense and relinquished the precepts. The Buddha did not forbid them from doing so.

Truly, I do not wish for them to destroy the Dharma-gate. Even in the case of a noble one who has attained the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*), although the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) have already been severed, if sexual habits manifest and they return to lay life to marry a wife, they ultimately do not break their precepts;
this is because they have formally renounced the precepts according to the Dharma, and in the future they may still leave the household life.
However, if the root is once broken, then they will never again be among the factors of the Path. Moreover, how could one bear to [treat] such as sages and worthies in such a manner?
Within the banner-sign, it says: "How base and defiled this is! This vow is fully undertaken by a bodhisattva who has left the household life.
A bodhisattva remaining at home, however, undertakes it only regarding the objects of sexual misconduct; sexual intercourse with one's own wife is not something to be abandoned.
Therefore, bodhisattvas who have left the household life today must examine themselves most carefully; even if this habit was originally slight, or even if it is grave, [one must remain vigilant].
If you can skillfully discipline yourself, you may then dwell peacefully among the ranks of the Sangha.
However, if your afflictions and habitual tendencies are strong and you cannot restrain yourself, it would be better to renounce the precepts. Be careful not to break them;

for by renouncing the precepts and returning to lay life, although you lose the status of a bhikṣu or śrāmaṇera in the present, you still remain a bodhisattva upāsaka, and in the future, you may yet become a śramaṇa once again.
O Bhikṣu, if one once breaks the essence of the precepts, then the Bodhisattva precepts, the Bhikṣu precepts, the Śrāmaṇera precepts, and the Upāsaka precepts are all completely broken.
Even the Eightfold Precepts (Aṣṭāṅga-śīla) for one day and one night can no longer be received.
Although the Bodhisattva precept dharma contains a provision for re-receiving them through the manifestation of signs, yet...
To perceive the sign and the object as one—how difficult this is to discuss! Reflect upon it, reflect upon it; be cautious, be cautious.

The subsequent five sections constitute the vow of making offerings. A faithful donor is fundamentally one who provides for those who walk the Way; yet to accept offerings while violating the precepts [is a grave error].
The retribution for suffering will surely be severe. This is a vow not to break the precepts, not a vow not to accept offerings.

Some say that faithful offerings are difficult to digest and thus wish to pursue their own livelihood; yet they fail to consider that drinking water and treading upon the earth are themselves the King’s offerings.
Since this does nothing to rescue one from the sin of breaking the precepts, it further incurs the fault of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
How truly lamentable! The subsequent section concerns the vow of reverence. This, too, is a vow not to break the precepts; it is not a vow to accept prostrations.

There are those who, claiming their virtuous conduct has greatly declined, bow their bodies in return for salutations, even to the point of worshipping celestial deities and showing respect to laypeople.
Since this neither remedies the sin of breaking the precepts nor preserves the integrity of the monastic life, it is utterly ruinous.
Family rituals are likewise foolish and delusive. The next five sections constitute the vows of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

These involve the five faculties in relation to the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), all of which take the mind of breaking the precepts as primary; that is, the faculty of mind (*manas*) acts as the sovereign.

Regarding the phrase "eating the hundred flavors of pure food," this was previously stated in reference to receiving offerings from others while violating the precepts; here, it refers to the greed of a depraved mind.
Regarding the attachment to flavors: one should know that craving for flavors is precisely what is called a mind that violates the precepts.
The final section concerns the vow to save sentient beings;

this is a prohibitive action (*vāraṇa-karman*) intended to prevent the mind from regressing. When encountering sensory objects, one must not give rise to [defiled thoughts]; failing to do so constitutes an offense according to the specific circumstance.

The five groups of monastics fully undertake [these vows]. Laypeople do not have the duty of receiving offerings; they merely possess the vow to deliver sentient beings through the six sense faculties.
