Regarding those shared by both the Mahayana and Hinayana, they are identical to the aforementioned four vows. Both the Vinaya and the Āgamas explain these extensively.

As for the difference: the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) does not enjoin the vow to deliver sentient beings across the five realms; it merely prohibits [the opposite] without providing an opening [for such a vow].
Regarding the karmic fruit: if one does not generate this resolve, one loses the benefit of being fixed in non-retrogression; by generating it accordingly, one attains it with firm stability.
Regarding the benefit of progress:

for one who understands [the teachings], there is no regression from the stage of realization (*avasthā*); for the first four vows, there may be intervals. For one who has not yet realized [the practice], there is no regression from the stage of practice (*caryā*);
for the fifth vow, there may be intervals.
Regarding repentance: to repeatedly make vows so that one's correct aspirations do not regress is what is called repentance. Regarding cultivation and realization:

for those who have attained non-retrogression in terms of spiritual stage (*bhūmi*), the first four vows are purified; for those who have attained non-retrogression in terms of practice (*caryā*), the fifth vow is purified.
Regarding those of an inherently evil nature: since they do not move from the *dharmadhātu*, what vow could they possibly make? Furthermore, they vow to delight in the defiled dharma as their wife;
they vow to don the robe of patience; they vow to consume the food of *dhyāna* and the joy of the Dharma; they vow to recline upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena;

they vow to take the medicine of the four teachings; they vow to roam the garden of liberation; they vow to receive the prostrations of self-nature; they vow to contemplate the wondrous forms of the *dharmadhātu*; they vow to listen...
With the sublime sound of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, I vow to inhale the wondrous fragrance of the Dharmakāya; I vow to partake of the exquisite flavor of the Dharma-food;
I vow to receive the touch of the sovereign bliss of human mastery; and I vow to cause all sentient beings to attain the gate of liberation that reaches the limit of non-extinction.
○ The Thirty-Seventh Precept: Traveling Despite Perilous Conditions.
If a disciple of the Buddha, one should always practice *dhūta* austerities during the two seasons; practice seated meditation in winter and summer; observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*);

and constantly use a willow branch for tooth-cleaning, cleansing powder, the three robes, a water flask, an alms bowl, a sitting mat, a mendicant’s staff, an incense burner and censer, a water-strainer, a hand towel, and a razor.
A son, a fire-stirring tool, tweezers, a corded bed, the Sūtras, the Vinaya, an image of the Buddha, and images of Bodhisattvas—

these eighteen kinds of items are always carried on one's person by a bodhisattva when practicing the dhūta austerities or when traveling abroad, even if journeying for hundreds or thousands of *li*. As for the dhūta practitioner,
from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month...
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month, during these two periods, these eighteen kinds of items shall always accompany his person like the two wings of a bird.

On the days of the *poṣadha*, the novice Bodhisattva shall regularly observe the *poṣadha* every half-month, reciting the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts. When reciting the precepts, he should do so before images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Recite. Whether it is for one person’s *poṣadha*, that one person recites; or whether there are two, three, up to a hundred thousand people, likewise only one person recites.
The reciter sits on a high seat, while those who listen sit on lower seats. Each should don the nine-strip, seven-strip, or five-strip *kāṣāya*.
When observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one should likewise act according to the Dharma in every respect. When practicing the *dhūta* austerities, do not enter [the assembly].

Regarding difficult places: whether it be a wicked realm, a wicked king, terrain that is uneven, dense vegetation, lions, tigers, wolves, the perils of water, fire, or wind, or even bandits, venomous snakes on the road—none of these difficult places may be entered.
Whether practicing *dhūta* austerities or observing the summer retreat (*vassa*), one must not enter any such perilous locations.
If one enters [the village] intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).

Regarding the constant practice of *dhūta* during the two seasons: it is appropriate to travel to transform sentient beings during the temperate periods of spring and autumn, as this will not cause harm or obstruction.

*dhūta* (sometimes transcribed as *dutuo*). This is translated as "shaking off" (*ke-sǒu*). There are twelve practices, all of which are superior modes of conduct for distancing oneself from worldly attachments and are praised by the Noble Ones.
First, dwelling in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*); second, always practicing alms-gathering; third, begging for food in regular order;
fourth, observing the practice of eating only one meal a day; fifth, moderation in the quantity of food; sixth, not drinking fruit juice, honey, or other liquids after midday.

7. Wearing robes made of discarded rags (*pāṃśukūla*); 8. Possessing only the three robes (*tricīvara*); 9. Dwelling among burial mounds; 10. Staying beneath trees; 11. Sitting in the open air; 12. Sitting only and not lying down.
Regarding those who practice meditation throughout winter and summer: during extreme cold or extreme heat, one should always remain in quiet sitting.
For those who observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*), traveling during the summer months is particularly obstructive to the Path; therefore, it is necessary to enter the formal retreat (*kaṭhina*). 9.
[This refers to] the ten [precepts]. Tooth-sticks are for cleansing the mouth; soap-nuts are for purifying the body. Regarding the three robes:
first is the *saṃghāṭī*, called the upper robe; second is the *uttarāsaṅga*, called the middle robe; third is the *antarvāsaka*, called the lower robe. There are three kinds of water-jars:
first, the pure jar (*śaucakumbha*), which stores water for drinking; second, the jar for general use (*prayogakumbha*), which stores water for washing...
The hand. Third, touching the water jar to wash the places for defecation and urination. Regarding the bowl (*pātra*): it is fully called *pātrā*; this translates as "appropriate vessel" (*yingqi*).
This means that its substance, color, and capacity must all be appropriate to the Dharma. As for the substance, it may be made of either clay or iron;
one must not use gold, silver, copper, wood, the seven precious gems, or the like. The color is produced by fumigating with sesame oil. As for the capacity, it follows the size of its belly.
The capacity is divided into large, medium, and small; the largest does not exceed three *sheng*, and the smallest does not fall short of one and a half *sheng*.
As for the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), its Sanskrit name means "cloth for sitting upon"; it is used to protect the body, the robes, and the bedding.
The mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) stands as the banner of the worthy and the holy. The incense burner cultivates the offering of purity. The water filter (*parisrāvaṇa*) serves as...

These are the implements for saving sentient beings. A hand towel is required for removing dirt. A knife shall not exceed three finger-widths in length nor one finger-width in width, so as to be convenient for use.
A fire-stirring rod is for preventing hot food from burning the mouth and also for dispelling darkness.
Tweezers are for pulling out nose hair. A corded bed is for resting in various places; all these are items among the "one hundred and one necessities."
The Sūtras accord with the single mind; the Vinaya regulates the three karmas. The image of the Buddha marks the ultimate fruit of the mind;

the form of the Bodhisattva entrusts one’s will to the true cause. Since both are essential to daily life, they may also manifest the Dharma through concrete things; thus, they are likened to the two wings of a bird.
Those who do not understand the meaning of the Dharma, but instead busily concern themselves only with the eighteen articles, [are like those who possess only one wing].

This is certainly not the grand standard of a Mahāsattva. If one were to indulge in lofty discourse on names and principles while neglecting the phenomena of concrete reality, I fear this would also not be the Buddha’s original intent.
It is essential that both principle and phenomenon be fully integrated; only then will both wings remain unimpaired.

Regarding the *poṣadha*, it is mentioned only for those who are new learners; as for Bodhisattvas who have studied for a long time, it goes without saying. [They] don the nine-strip, seven-strip, and five-strip robes.
Regarding the *kāṣāya*: the nine-strip robe is the *saṃghāṭī*; the seven-strip robe is the *uttarāsaṅga*;
and the five-strip robe is the *antarvāsaka*. These refer specifically to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
As for the *śikṣamāṇās*, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, they are permitted to use only the single-strip robe (*mañcīvara*), which is called the "seamless *kāṣāya*. For the two types of lay followers...
The assembly: When reciting the precepts or entering the maṇḍala, one may also use a seamless robe (anantaka), but at other times it is not permitted.
However, the *Sujāta-sūtra* states: "If an upāsaka does not keep a saṃghāṭī robe, an alms bowl, and a mendicant’s staff, he incurs an offense of negligence (*duṣkṛta*).
This is a specific injunction requiring them to be kept in reserve; it is not an injunction for their daily use. Furthermore, regarding the saṃghāṭī and so forth...
This refers to the garment of plain strips, further distinguished by three types of dharma-designations, namely the seamless triple robe (*tricīvara*).

These differ from the nine-strip, seven-strip, and five-strip robes of the *bhikṣu*. Each item must be in accordance with the Dharma; that is, one must possess the eighteen requisites in accordance with the Dharma, as well as recite the precepts in accordance with the Dharma, and so forth.

This constitutes a prohibitory action (*pratiṣedha-karman*). It primarily prohibits traveling while facing dangers, while concurrently prohibiting the failure to prepare the eighteen requisite items and the failure to recite the precepts according to the Dharma.
Traveling while facing dangers risks premature death; when one is in peril, the consequences for the mind are grave.

Although a Mahāsattva should indeed be willing to sacrifice his body for the sake of the Dharma, how could he fail to exercise caution and thereby invite harm? This is comparable to the Confucian scholars who, despite having...

Regarding the principle of sacrificing one's life to fulfill righteousness, it is also said that "one who knows their destiny does not stand beneath a crumbling wall. There are three conditions that constitute an offense:

first, a difficult location, referring to such things as a wicked realm; second, the six permutations regarding the perception of a difficult location—two being grave, two being light, and two being non-offenses;
third, the actual wandering. After setting out, with every step one incurs a minor defiling offense (*pāyattika*), or [if] previously...
In a place of reproach, if a difficulty suddenly arises while one is properly traveling, this is also not an offense.

Regarding the eighteen kinds of requisites that ought to be prepared, if they are not prepared, the fault is determined according to the specific matter. During the fortnightly recitation of the precepts, if they are not recited, or if they are recited but not in accordance with the Dharma, the fault is likewise determined according to the specific matter.

The seven classes of followers commit this offense equally. The *Susheng jing* (Sūtra of Good Birth) states: "If an upāsaka travels alone through dangerous places without a companion, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
According to this, even if there is a necessary reason, going with many companions together does not constitute an offense.
It further states: "If an upāsaka violates the laws of the state, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. This should also be understood as being subsumed under this precept.
Regarding those points where the Mahāsattvas and Śrāvakas do not fully agree: they may not travel together during times of difficulty. As for their differences:

the Mahāsattvas are enjoined to carry eighteen articles, whereas the Śrāvakas are enjoined to carry only six articles with them—namely, the three robes, the sitting mat, the alms bowl, and the water filter;
the rest are not prescribed for them. Furthermore, while a Mahāsattva performs the *poṣadha* alone, reciting it by himself, a Śrāvaka must have [another present].
When there are four or more people, one person is selected to sit on a high seat and recite [the *poṣadha*]. If there are three or two people, they perform the *poṣadha* facing one another.
If there is only one person, they perform the *poṣadha* through mental recollection (*cittamanasikāra-poṣadha*). These details are exactly as described in the Vinaya;

those who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*) should not know them beforehand, and thus they are not explained in detail here. However, in the various monasteries of the Western Regions, the large and small dwellings are separate. Zhèn...
In the morning within the *sīmā* (monastic boundary), members of the community—both senior and junior—reside together; thus, the ritual procedures for the *poṣadha* must also be briefly explained.

Now, six points will be set forth together: first, a general enumeration of the nine assemblies; second, a specific discussion of the sequence of the precepts; third, clarifying the person who recites the precepts;

fourth, clarifying the dharma to be recited; fifth, clarifying the boundary used; and sixth, clarifying the detailed and abbreviated rituals. First, regarding the general enumeration of the nine assemblies:
Regarding the general ritual procedure for the fortnightly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), men and women should each perform it separately.
For men, the bhikṣus are the presiding authorities, while śrāmaṇeras and upāsakas may listen as permitted.
For women, the bhikṣuṇīs are the presiding authorities, while śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇerīs, and upāsikās may listen as permitted. Thus, there are distinct boundaries for the monks and nuns. Not...

There may be instances of intermingling. If other circumstances happen to arise—such as when bhikṣuṇīs come to request instruction and admonition, or upāsikās come to offer worship—and one happens to be reciting the Bodhisattva Precepts, since they have already received them, they may also listen accordingly.
Thus, once all the bhikṣus have finished sitting, next come the bhikṣuṇīs; once the bhikṣuṇīs have finished, next come the śrāmaṇeras.
Next are the śikṣamāṇās; next, the śrāmaṇeras; next, the śrāmaṇerīs; next, the ordained upāsakas and upāsikās; and finally, the lay upāsakas and upāsikās.
Those who have left the household life are called "near-dwellers" (upavāsaka), while those who remain in the household are called "lay followers" (upāsaka).
These nine ranks of the community must not be disordered under any circumstances. Furthermore, there must be a distinction between men and women. Not...
This gives rise to derision and suspicion. Second, regarding the specific discussion of the order of the precepts:
within each of the nine assemblies, one should sit according to the sequence of the ordination received. However, in the Western Regions, those of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna reside separately;
thus, those of the Mahāyāna sit according to the order of the Bodhisattva precepts, while those of the Hīnayāna sit according to the order of the Bhikṣu precepts. Now, as for the Mahā...
When living in a mixed community of both small and great [vehicles], one should recite the Bodhisattva precepts according to the sequence of the Mahāyāna precepts;

however, when reciting the Bhikṣu precepts, one must still follow the order of seniority based on *saṃgha-ratna* (monastic age). One must not allow the great to displace the small. Therefore, the *Shiqian* states:

"When a Bodhisattva is among a community of the Small Vehicle, he sits according to the sequence of the Small Vehicle precepts; when among a community of the Great Vehicle, he then follows the Great Vehicle [sequence]."

Next, regarding the seating order: if a person first receives the bhikṣu precepts and later receives the bodhisattva precepts, they shall use their bhikṣu ordination seniority as their bodhisattva ordination seniority.

This is because at the time of receiving the bodhisattva precepts, all the bhikṣu precepts are transformed into the inexhaustible essence of the precepts (*ananta-śīla-sarīra*). If, however, a person first receives the bodhisattva precepts and later...
Regarding those who receive the bhikṣu precepts: within the Mahāyāna, they follow the sequence of the bodhisattva precepts; within the Hīnayāna, they still follow the sequence of the bhikṣu precepts.

One must not take the ordination year (*varṣa*) of the bodhisattva precepts as the ordination year for the bhikṣu precepts, because the bodhisattva precepts do not pertain to the count of the Saṅgha-ratna (the Jewel of the Sangha) in its institutional maintenance.
Thus, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "If one first [receives] the Hīnayāna..."
If one is of the Great [Vehicle], then one opens up the Small Summer Retreat to form the Great Summer Retreat.

If one first receives the Great [Vow] and later receives the *vinaya* (disciplinary code), then when in the Small [Vehicle] one relies on the Small, and when in the Great [Vehicle] one relies on the Great. It is the same for the community of *bhikṣuṇīs*.
As for *śrāmaṇeras*, *śrāmaṇerīs*, and others, in the Small Vehicle one considers only the year of birth, whereas in the Great Vehicle one must consider the sequence of the Bodhisattva precepts.

The same applies to those who observe the one-day precepts and the lay followers. Regarding the recitation of the precepts by one possessing the three types of knowledge (*trividyā*), if all nine assemblies are present, a Bodhisattva Bhikṣu must necessarily occupy a high seat to recite them while the others listen in silence.
If there is no Bhikṣu and only the eight assemblies are present, a single Bodhisattva Bhikṣuṇī must necessarily recite them. If there is no [Bhikṣuṇī]...
O Bhikṣuṇī, among the seven classes of followers below, it is essential that one Bodhisattva Śikṣamāṇā recite this.
If there is no Śikṣamāṇā at all, it is essential that one Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera recite it.
If there is no Śrāmaṇera either, it is essential that one Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇerī recite it. If there is no [Śrāmaṇerī]...

Māṇava. It must be recited by a male *upāsaka* who dwells near the Bodhisattva. If there is no male *upāsaka* dwelling nearby, then it shall be recited by a female *upāsikā* dwelling near the Bodhisattva.
If there is no female *upāsikā* dwelling nearby, then it shall be recited by a male *śrāvaka* dwelling near the Bodhisattva.
If there is no male *śrāvaka* dwelling nearby, then a single female *śrāvikā* dwelling near the Bodhisattva shall ascend a high seat and recite it. As for the other Bodhisattvas...
The female lay follower (*upāsikā*) should sit in a lower position and listen in silence. Question: Suppose there is a bhikṣu who cannot recite [the precepts], while a bhikṣuṇī can;
or even if there is a male lay follower (*upāsaka*) who cannot recite them, while a female lay follower can—what should be done in such cases?
Answer: The Sūtra says: "If one has received the bodhisattva precepts but does not recite these precepts, one is not a bodhisattva, nor..."
As for the seeds of the Buddha, how could one who has received the precepts fail to recite them? Question: What is the case for a person who has newly received the precepts? Answer:
Since one who has newly received the precepts is not yet able to recite them, they must not remain apart from their teachers and friends. Question:
Suppose there is a circumstance that prevents one from being near their teachers and friends; what then? Answer: In ordinary times, it is permitted to follow one another in succession.
When the junior assembly has mastered the training rules (*śaikṣa-dharma*), they must ascend the seat before the senior assembly when it is time to recite the precepts. Question:

When one is normally training under a junior assembly through successive stages, may that person still be addressed as a "teacher" (*ācārya*)? Answer: A bhikṣu who has received the precepts earlier may address a bhikṣu who received them later as an *ācārya*.
Furthermore, he may perform all duties toward him with the etiquette due to a teacher, with the sole exception of prostrating at his feet.
Training under a śrāmaṇera is also like this. If one trains under a group of three nuns, one must take further precautions to ensure that no cause for criticism or suspicion arises.
If one trains under an upavāsastha or an upāsaka, one must not address them as "Teacher.

This is just as when, in the time of the Buddha, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada constantly bestowed the Dharma upon newly ordained bhikṣus, yet he would instead pay homage at the feet of those bhikṣus. Thus it is.
This is an example of that. Question: It is said that a bhikṣu must not prostrate before a layperson (avadātavasana).
Why, then, in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, does a newly ordained bhikṣu prostrate at the feet of a layman (gṛhapati)? Answer: This was a manifestation by an ancient Buddha.

Desiring to stimulate and inspire the Great Teaching, he temporarily displayed such censure and rebuke; furthermore, he entered samādhi to cause [the bhikṣu] to recognize his past lives, whereby he suddenly regained his original mind.
Therefore, one must break with conventional etiquette and prostrate at his feet; this cannot be cited as a standard rule.

Furthermore, during the Liang dynasty of the Xiao clan, there was the Great Master Fu (Fotuo Dashi), who was a manifestation of Maitreya himself; this is not something that other ordinary beings or sages may use as a pretext.
Now, one should simply take Anāthapiṇḍada as the model. Thus, for a layperson to preach the Dharma is truly without [fault].

This transgression is not a sign of the decline of the Buddha-dharma. However, if one were to address a layperson as "Teacher," it would constitute a great violation of the Dharma and would truly be a sign of decay.

Regarding the Dharma recited by the masters of Siming: since in the Western Regions the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna followers reside separately, those of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) recite only the Bhikṣu precepts, whereas those of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) recite both the Bhikṣu and Bodhisattva precepts together; first, they recite the Bhikṣu [precepts].
When the precepts are being conferred, Bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, Bodhisattva upāsakas, and others are not permitted to listen.

However, when the Bodhisattva precepts are subsequently recited, all seven assemblies should follow and listen. Now, as the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna practitioners dwell together, one should make threefold distinctions:
first, if this community consists solely of those of the Hīnayāna, they should rely on their own Vinaya laws, and there is no need for further discussion. Second...
If it is solely for the Mahāyāna, there may be bhikṣus, śrāmaṇeras, or upāsakas living together.
If there are four or more bhikṣus, they first perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and complete the recitation of the bhikṣu precepts.

Next, they summon the śrāmaṇeras and upāsakas to listen together as the Bodhisattva precepts are recited. If there are only three or two bhikṣus, they first recite them three times facing one another.
When the *poṣadha* ceremony is concluded, next summon the *śrāmaṇeras* and lay attendants (*karmadāna*) to listen together as you recite the Bodhisattva precepts.
If there is only one bhikṣu present, first perform the *poṣadha* through mental recitation; thereafter, summon the *śrāmaṇeras* and lay attendants to listen to the Bodhisattva precepts.
If there are no bhikṣus, but only śrāmaṇeras and upāsakas living together, one should simply recite the Bodhisattva precepts oneself;

this is also consistent with the usual custom in the Western Regions (India). Third, if bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as upāsakas, live together, one should first have the śrāmaṇeras and others depart, and then perform the *poṣadha* ceremony in harmony solely with the Hīnayāna bhikṣus.
Sā. If there are four or more people, a formal announcement (jñapti) is made. If there are three or two people, they speak to one another until the recitation is finished.
Next, the bhikṣus of the Hīnayāna are sent out. Then, the bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras and bodhisattva upāsakas are summoned to listen together to the recitation of the Bodhisattva Precepts.
Next, the śrāmaṇeras of the Hīnayāna are summoned to be taught the ten precepts. Finally, the upāsakas of the Hīnayāna are summoned to be taught.

Regarding the five precepts: although there is no rule for reciting the ten *śrāmaṇera* precepts or the five *upāsaka* precepts within the Vinaya, Yunqi’s ritual for reciting the precepts first recites them; this does not contradict principle and is beneficial in practice.

Now, following the method of the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) in the Vinaya, only after the *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs* have completed their *pravāraṇā* are the minor assemblies summoned to perform their own *pravāraṇā*.

Taking this as an example, it would perhaps be more appropriate to first complete the recitation of the full precepts (*śīla*), and only thereafter summon the *śrāmaṇera* and the lay attendants (*upāsaka*) to explain the ten precepts and the five precepts to them. Furthermore, regarding the specific dharma of the precepts to be recited:
if one follows this sutra, one should first recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts; if following the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, one should separately recite the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.

One fascicle. This is precisely the root text for the fortnightly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). It enumerates the characteristics of the four grave offenses and the forty-one minor precepts.
As for the fundamental four grave offenses, as well as [the prohibition against] drinking alcohol and so forth, these are already subsumed within the full, ten, and five precepts;
therefore, they are not repeated here. Only the Bodhisattva’s superior discipline (*adhiśīla*) is presented, which truly corresponds to this sutra.

Regarding the correspondence between the two: since those four grave offenses are precisely the latter four grave offenses of this sutra, and although those forty-one minor offenses differ slightly from this sutra in their sequence of expansion and contraction (*ka-ha*), the principles of what is permitted or prohibited and what constitutes observance or violation are explained even more clearly here.
Among the six translations existing in the canon in both earlier and later versions, that translated by Master Kumārajīva is the most excellent; therefore—
This is now compiled in the later collection. Every half-month, one should apparently recite this *śīla-sūtra*. However, one must first perform the *poṣadha* for the bhikṣus;
next, summon the śrāmaṇeras to explain the ten precepts to them; then, summon the upāsakas to explain the five precepts to them;
thereafter, dismiss those who have not yet received the bodhisattva precepts, while the bhikṣus, śrāmaṇeras, and upāsakas [remain] in order.

To sit and listen [to this] is most certainly appropriate. I trust that those of lofty intelligence will consider and put it into practice. Regarding the boundaries used for the Five Sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*):
Bodhisattva-bhikṣus shall still use the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) established according to the rules for bhikṣus; the same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
A śrāmaṇera belongs to a bhikṣu; there is no separate boundary (sīmā) for him. He is permitted to recite along with the bhikṣu and may not recite separately.

It is the same for the other two groups of women, who belong to the bhikṣuṇīs. As for the two groups of lay followers, if there is no specific reason or occasion, [they likewise follow their respective preceptors].
One should go among the Sangha to listen to and recite [the scriptures]. If there are circumstances that prevent this, it is also permissible to recite them by oneself within one's own home.
However, once one has arrived at a monastery (saṃghārāma), one must follow the Sangha in listening to and reciting; one must not recite separately.
Even if the teacher is a bhikṣu of the Hīnayāna and the śrāmaṇera disciple is a bodhisattva, the teacher shall personally perform the duties of a bhikṣu.
The disciple likewise fulfills his duties as a śrāmaṇera. When it comes time to recite the precepts, he first listens to his teacher explain the ten precepts.
Subsequently, moving away from the place where he can see or hear his teacher, he recites the Bodhisattva precepts himself.

If there is someone nearby who is reciting the Bodhisattva precepts, he informs his teacher and goes to listen. Sixth, regarding the detailed and abbreviated rituals: [as compared to] the aforementioned...

The details regarding the breadth and brevity of the Master’s precepts are fully contained within the Vinaya and need not be discussed here further. If the assembly consists solely of Mahāyāna followers, there is no difficulty;

one must then recite the complete *śīla-sūtra* for both bhikṣus and bodhisattvas. Should there be difficult circumstances, the bhikṣu precepts may be recited briefly while the bodhisattva precepts are recited in detail.
If the urgent matter is particularly pressing, both sets of precepts are recited in brief. If [the assembly is] large...
Regarding those who dwell together in small groups: if there are difficult circumstances, one should explain the *bhikṣu* precepts in detail and the bodhisattva precepts in brief.

If the difficulty is urgent, both should be explained in brief. If there are only bodhisattvas, śrāmaṇeras, or lay attendants (*karmadāna*), then one should recite only the bodhisattva precept dharma.
If one encounters urgent difficulty, one may either recite only the heavy precepts, or simply say: "Today is the fifteenth day."
Regarding the recitation of the precepts: each person must rectify their body, speech, and mind accordingly; depending on the circumstances, one may proceed as appropriate.
However, unless there are exceptional obstacles, it is not permitted to abbreviate the recitation in its entirety.
Regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited: if one seeks the Dharma or seeks to deliver sentient beings, it is not an offense to encounter hardships.

Regarding the karmic retribution: encountering hardships frequently creates conditions for retreating from the Path; by not traveling, one is able to cause both body and mind to advance along the Path.
Regarding the contemplative understanding: the afflictions of view, thought, the dust-and-sand [delusions], and ignorance constitute an evil land;
they are also called thieves, water, fire, lions, venomous snakes, tigers, and wolves.

Regarding repentance (*pratideśanā*): if one encounters difficulties regarding the matter, fails to prepare the necessary objects, does not recite the precepts, or recites them improperly, these all constitute formal ritual acts (*dharmakarma*).
If one encounters difficulties regarding the principle, one must realize non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Regarding "cultivation and realization": one who attains the five supernatural powers has no fear of difficult circumstances; one who attains the three types of knowledge has no fear of the three delusions.
One whose nature is evil enters universally into both the difficulties of phenomena and principle in order to deliver sentient beings.
Combined Commentary on the "Bodhisattva Grounds Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Six;
Combined Commentary on the "Bodhisattva Grounds Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Commentary by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Zhixu of Ancient Wu;
Revised by the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Daofang of Wēn-líng. The Thirty-Eighth:
The Precept Regarding Violating the Order of Seniority and Juniority toward the World-Honored One.

If you are a disciple of the Buddha, you should sit according to the proper sequence of the Dharma: those who received the precepts first sit in front, and those who received the precepts later sit behind.
One must not inquire whether they are elder or younger bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, persons of noble rank, kings, princes, or even eunuchs, slaves, or servants;
all should sit such that those who received the precepts first are in front, and those who received the precepts later follow in order.
As for sitting, do not be like the foolish practitioners of external paths, whether old or young, who sit without precedence or sequence, following the manner of soldiers or slaves.
Within my Buddha-dharma, those who come first sit first, and those who come later sit later.
If a Bodhisattva fails to sit according to this sequential order of the Dharma, they commit a minor offense.
Regarding the Dharma, there are two aspects: first, the general discussion concerning the seven classes of practitioners; second, the specific discussion concerning the order of ordination.

Regarding sitting, there are two occasions: first, the time for reciting the precepts; second, ordinary times. In both cases, disorder must not be permitted. The phrase "without regard to old or young" also has two meanings:
first, it refers to the general meaning concerning the seven classes of practitioners; second, it refers to the specific meaning concerning the order of ordination. As for the general discussion:
This means that a bhikṣuṇī with a hundred years of seniority may not sit before a bhikṣu who has entered the summer retreat for the first time.

Even if a bhikṣuṇī has received the bodhisattva precepts and has likewise passed a hundred years of seniority, she still may not sit before a bhikṣu of the Hīnayāna who has entered the summer retreat for the first time;
how much less so in the case of a bodhisattva bhikṣu? This is because the bhikṣu belongs to the superior assembly. [The same applies to] a śikṣamāṇā.
Even if one has lived for a hundred years, or has already completed a hundred *varṣas* since receiving the Bodhisattva precepts,

one must never sit before monks or nuns of the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, because such a person is not yet counted among the ranks of the *saṃgha*. Although a *śrāmaṇera* may have lived for a hundred years,
or has already completed a hundred *varṣas* since receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, they may not even sit before a *śikṣamāṇā* of the Hīnayāna.

The *maṇavaka* (novice) sits in front. Although a *śrāmaṇerī* may have been born for a hundred years, or even if she has observed the Bodhisattva precepts for a hundred *la* (years since ordination), she must not sit in front of a *śrāvaka* *śrāmaṇera*.

Likewise, although an *upāsaka* may have been born for a hundred years, or have received the Bodhisattva precepts for a hundred *la*, he must not sit in front of a *śrāvaka* *kāka-vāyasa* (a novice who drives away crows).
If even a lay follower must sit behind a śrāmaṇera, how much more so for śrāmaṇeras and bhikṣus? Thus, the *Śīla-samudaya-sūtra* states:
"If an upāsaka walks ahead of a bhikṣu or a śrāmaṇera, he incurs the offense of 'loss of intention' (*daśita-āpatti*). One should know that this refers specifically to their conduct."
To form a formal assembly (saṃgha) while sitting also constitutes an offense; this refers to the offense regarding sitting. Walking also constitutes an offense.
Regarding the two distinct categories, such as the assemblies of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, one must always discuss both the major and minor types of precepts in their proper order.
When in a major context, it is major; when in a minor context, it is minor. By no means whatsoever may the major be used to subvert the minor. Thus, Mañjuśrī responded to King Ajātaśatru.

Regarding this request: one must first firmly decline, even before Kāśyapa, and only then temporarily take precedence over him; thus, it is clearly demonstrated that the order of the precepts remains undisturbed during ordinary times.
As for the other five assemblies, they should each discuss the order of the bodhisattva precepts among themselves, without regard for seniority by birth—this is easily understood.
As for the mention of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, persons of noble rank, and so forth, it means that these are listed first.
The relative status of the seven assemblies is fixed; subsequently, each group proceeds according to its own category to enumerate the sequence of their precepts.

Once the bhikṣus have finished enumerating the sequence of their precepts, the bhikṣuṇīs then enumerate the sequence of theirs. The reason the other three assemblies are not mentioned is merely for the sake of brevity.
The term "noble person" (guìrén) refers generally to kings, princes, and the like.

When contrasted with eunuchs, slaves, and the lowly, although these individuals are likewise categorized as the two groups of lay followers, they must still be distinguished according to their respective classes.
For even though a Son of Heaven has received the Bodhisattva precepts, since he has not yet left the household life, he must still not take precedence over his sovereign father. Therefore...

Furthermore, "for one class" and so forth are terms used for abbreviation. The intention is to show that elders, officials, brahmins, lay devotees (*gṛhapati*), and others each constitute a separate class.

Since, within the conventions of the world, there is no fixed rule for ranking these people—whether by title, age, or virtue—it is now appropriate to rank them solely by their precepts (*śīla*). However, in the Western Regions (India)...

There are kings who serve as disciples to Brahmins; this shall be discussed separately. For now, we are speaking generally of those who have not yet left the household life, and thus it is certainly not the case that the designations and positions of ruler and subject may be confused.

It may happen, for instance, that a prince of this country and a king of another country act as teacher and friend to one another, or that a prince who has not yet ascended the throne likewise [serves] a Brahmin.
Gatekeepers, elders, and lay devotees who act as teachers or friends to one another shall all be discussed separately.
Eunuchs and slaves must likewise form their own distinct category and may not be mixed among the ranks of the noble classes.

This is because, within the Dharma of renunciation, eunuchs are classified under the "heavy obstacles" (garuka-antarāya) and are absolutely prohibited from entering the ranks of bhikṣus or śrāmaṇeras. As for slaves... [text ends]

This refers to the inclusion of those whose transgressions are light. If a person receives the precepts of a bhikṣu or śrāmaṇera from one who possesses the [proper] lineage, they immediately enter the rank of bhikṣu or śrāmaṇera and may sit before the king; yet now, although one has received the Bodhisattva Great Precepts...
They have still not escaped the status of slaves; therefore, they must be categorized separately so as not to confuse the distinctions between master and servant, or noble and base.
Regarding "one by one": this refers to the formal ritual for binding the finger, which includes both the general and specific types; both must be performed according to the Dharma.

Furthermore, during both types of assemblies, one must sit according to the proper sequence. Question: Since sovereigns and ministers, fathers and sons, and masters and servants all equally receive the Bodhisattva precepts, why must they still each remain within their respective categories?
For instance, in the Vinaya, if a minister receives full ordination first and a king receives it later, the minister becomes the junior seat-holder;
if a son receives full ordination first and a father receives it later, the son becomes the junior seat-holder.
"If I receive full ordination first and my master receives it later, would I then become a junior seat-holder? He replied, "The dharma of the bhikṣu precepts manifests supramundane characteristics;
it is not subsumed under worldly laws. If a ruler does not permit it, a subject cannot leave the household life.
If parents do not permit it, a child cannot leave the household life. If a master does not permit it, a slave [cannot leave the household life]."

Having gone forth as a renunciant, since one’s sovereign, father, or master has granted permission for this renunciation, at the very moment of going forth, one permanently relinquishes the titles and status of subject, son, or slave.
Therefore, even if the sovereign, father, or master later receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), the renunciant shall be regarded as his *upādhyāya* (preceptor) and senior.
If the sovereign, father, or master remains a householder, he shall likewise be regarded as the venerable field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).

Therefore, in the five regions of India, according to the dharma for those who have left the household life, even if they encounter a sovereign, a master, or a host, they all uniformly address them as *dānapati* (patron).
When such a person encounters subjects, children, or servants who have likewise left the household life, they must invariably perform a prostration with their head to the ground;
those who have left the household life must accept this directly, and there is by no means any ritual of returning the salutation. This is not only...

This has been the case since the time of the Buddha. During the Tang dynasty, masters such as Xuanzang and Yijing traveled personally to the Western Regions (India) and witnessed this practice with their own eyes;
thus, the practice of children bowing to their parents is an established fact beyond any doubt or suspicion.

That Master Lianchi explained it away by claiming it was merely a reciprocal bow is nothing more than a skillful expedient used to dispel slander at the moment; it is not a definitive argument. As for the Bodhi...
The Dharma of the Bodhisattva precepts applies to both the mundane and the supramundane.

Because it does not subvert conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), even though one has received the bodhisattva precepts, a ruler remains a ruler, a minister remains a minister, and the same applies to father and son, or master and servant.
If one were to confuse their names and ranks while arranging the sequence of the precepts, then worldly laws would fail to be established. Question: If one...
When one leaves the household life, one permanently relinquishes the titles of minister, son, slave, or servant; is this not to be without a sovereign and without a father?
This is precisely what is criticized by the Confucians. Answer: One merely relinquishes empty names, but does not relinquish gratitude and righteousness.

Therefore, the Vinaya regulations stipulate that a bhikṣu should serve and support his parents with all his heart and all his strength. If he fails to do so, he incurs a grave offense. Even the Buddha...

When his mother entered *nirvāṇa*, the Buddha personally lifted her coffin with his own hands. Furthermore, as bhikṣus dwell in mountain forests, they do not observe the rituals of serving a sovereign.
Even if they were to receive the offerings of a king or cultivate a close friendship with him, they would still be required to offer loyal counsel according to the circumstances;

thus, they do not neglect worldly filial piety and loyalty. How much more so for those who practice in accordance with the Dharma and propagate the supreme teaching, thereby bringing peace to the heavens?
The dragons rejoice; they protect the state and the people, causing parents of the past and present alike to leave the ocean of suffering behind.

This further accomplishes supramundane loyalty and filial piety. Thus, in matters of great loyalty and great filiality, who surpasses those who have left the household life? Such is the great significance of this.

It must not be permitted to further discuss such trivial, empty fame or empty positions. Question: Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, it is indeed true that they do not subvert conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
As previously stated, "in the great, they are great; in the small, they are small," one may likewise say by analogy, "in the ultimate (*paramārtha*), they are ultimate;
in the conventional, they are conventional. Now, since those who have left the household life have already received the Bodhisattva...
Regarding the precepts: if one encounters a sovereign, a father, or a host, may it not also be permitted to act in accordance with secular customs? Answer:
As previously stated, "in greatness one acts as great; in smallness one acts as small," this is because although the degrees of status differ, they are all collectively termed *bhikṣu*.
Now, regarding your analogy that "if one is in the secular world, one is a secular person": you are no longer a bodhisattva bhikṣu or śrāmaṇera;
have you finally become a bodhisattva upāsaka? If you are indeed a bodhisattva upāsaka, then you no longer belong to the ranks of the śrāmaṇeras and bhikṣus.
How, then, can you claim to be universally equal to both the great and small assemblies?

Regarding the sequence of the precepts: if one wishes to enter the ranks of śrāmaṇeras or bhikṣus while still maintaining the status of an upāsaka, this would utterly destroy the characteristics of the supramundane.
Since the Bodhisattva precepts do not destroy mundane characteristics, how could they conversely destroy the supramundane characteristics?
One must realize that both mundane and supramundane characteristics are established as conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and are both ultimately ungraspable.
Because [the former] is destroyed, an ordained bodhisattva still practices the rituals of the ordained, while a lay bodhisattva follows the rituals of the laity;
this is what is called "pervading both the mundane and the supramundane," meaning that in truth, one is truly so.

If one remains in the secular world, one may likewise attain all these things. Question: The Bodhisattva’s Great Precepts extend in duration to the end of the future and reach their ultimate fulfillment at the fruit of Buddhahood;
they may indeed be called most supreme, most excellent, most wondrous, and most great.
For what reason, then, is it that those who receive these precepts are still not permitted to disrupt worldly status and rank, whereas the monastic precepts do allow for such [renunciation]?

Even if one were to practice for the remainder of one’s life, it would not surpass that of an Arhat. How, then, could one fail to accept with peace of mind the prostrations of sovereigns, parents, and masters?
Answer: If one discusses vastness, nothing compares to the Bodhisattva precepts; if one discusses reverence, nothing compares to the monastic discipline (*vinaya*).
For these are the banner and emblem of the sages and worthies, the fragrant standard of those who have transcended the world, and the very foundation of the Saṃgha wheel. Buddha...

Regarding the matters of the Dharma, such a person is not only worthy of receiving the reverence and honor due to a sovereign, a father, or a master, but is also already worthy of receiving the homage of the Four Heavenly Kings and Śakra;
they are also worthy of receiving the homage of Brahmā, and even worthy of receiving the homage of Maheśvara, the lord of the great trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, this applies not only to bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, but even to śrāmaṇeras.
They may likewise receive the rites of respect due to a sovereign, a father, or a host.

This is because although such persons—sovereigns, fathers, and others—may have received the five precepts and the bodhisattva precepts, they still reside at home and have not yet severed sexual misconduct, unlike śrāmaṇeras who have completely severed all sexual desire.

Because they are forever separated from the causes of the suffering of birth and death. For although rulers, fathers, and others may observe the eightfold precepts for three months or six days, this does not equal a śrāmaṇera’s lifelong abstention from eating at improper times, which serves as a superior condition for forever leaving behind birth and death.
Furthermore, although rulers, fathers, and others may receive the five precepts or the bodhisattva precepts, they are still permitted to wear fragrant flowers and garlands.

Anointing the body with fragrant oils, singing, dancing, performing as entertainers, and engaging in or watching such performances, as well as sitting on high or broad couches—these are only temporarily prohibited on days of fasting (*upoṣadha*).
This is because they are not permanently renounced in the way that *śrāmaṇeras* are.

Therefore, although a ruler or a father may have received the five precepts, the bodhisattva precepts, or even the eightfold fast precepts during the three months and six periods of the year, he is still permitted to keep [such items].

Regarding gold, silver, and precious objects acquired through lawful means for the sake of supporting one's superiors and nourishing one's inferiors— this is not equal to a śrāmaṇera dwelling in reliance upon the Saṃgha,

who remains free from factors obstructing the Path and whose deportment and right livelihood are entirely pure. Therefore, if one merely causes them to leave the household life in accordance with the Dharma and maintain the precepts,
then even if they receive the veneration of sovereigns, parents, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, it is truly [no cause for pride].
This is a transgression. Furthermore, it causes your father and others to increase their accumulation of merit; the benefit is inconceivable.

If one lacks the true virtue of renunciation, then even if one were to reverse one's etiquette toward parents, sovereigns, and celestial deities, what could save one from the sin of breaking the precepts?

It would merely corrupt the majestic deportment of the Buddha-dharma and increase one’s faults and errors. Alas! In this degenerate age, those who have left the household life possess the name but lack the reality.
Whether monastics or laypeople, all cling to what they have seen and heard and remain settled in their base habits. When one preaches the True Dharma to such as these, who would believe it?
I have thus briefly set forth these ancient regulations so that people may come to know, even slightly, the transcendent legacy of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, this transcendent protocol is precisely what emerges from the Bodhisattva Precepts; it is entirely subsumed within the Bodhisattva Precepts.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva precepts can be called "vast" and simultaneously possess the sense of "reverence.
If one were to abolish these fixed positions for the seven classes of followers, there would be neither the ritual of reverence nor the meaning of vastness. Question:

Since the precepts for those who have left the household life are thus so revered, why is it that in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Bhikṣu Never-Disparaging prostrates to all four assemblies and receives a prediction of his future Buddhahood?
Answer: This represents the initial opening of the perfect understanding (*yuanjie*). It is both a cause for celebration and for compassion.
Observing the conditions and timing of those [beings], one should forcefully fortify them with the causal seeds of the Mahāyāna; thus, this practice of the "extraordinary gate" was established.

It is not the standard method for general application. If it were truly suitable for universal practice, then since the World-Honored One attained the purification of the six sense-faculties through this very means in the past, he would have surely taught this dharma to the fourfold assembly; how could there be any stinginess?
Regarding this sense of regret, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Vinaya traditions alike prohibit monks from bowing to laypeople; one should know that this has significant implications.
Furthermore, while the Hīnayāna Vinaya merely states that one "should not return the salutation to a white-robed person," the language remains relatively straightforward.

However, when it comes to the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, they state that if a bodhisattva is seated and sees a king or an elder rise [to greet him], he incurs an offense. If [the bodhisattva] is already...
To sit in the full lotus posture when seeing a king or an elder who is kneeling constitutes an offense.

If one’s robes are disarrayed and one sees a king or an elder correcting their appearance and adjusting their garments, it constitutes an offense. If a king or an elder speaks harsh words and one praises them according to their whim, it constitutes an offense.
Observing its severe language and strict intent, it is even more stringent than the Minor Vinaya; this too should be clearly understood.
In this degenerate age, the habitual tendencies of laypeople lead them to pride, while the demeanor of those in the monastic robes leads them to humility.
Therefore, these prohibitions were established in the hope of effecting even a one-thousandth of a reversal.

Thus, a lay bodhisattva who sincerely accepts the Buddha’s precepts must respect the monastic community of both the Mahayana and Hinayana, even if they have broken the precepts or possess no precepts at all.
One must not be arrogant; one must be like a king of elephants toward a hunter, or like a rākṣasa toward a sinner—only then can it be called "revering the Buddha and revering the precepts.

A renunciant bodhisattva must certainly study and practice the great and small codes of discipline well, so as to receive the veneration of humans and devas, and thereby avoid disgracing the monastic body while becoming worthy of being a field of merit. Indeed...

One must not merely engage in empty displays of humility and courtesy. Even more so, one must not simply rely on the dignified appearance of a monk to harbor an empty stomach and a haughty mind, thereby increasing self-conceit and unworthily claiming the designation of a worthy sage. I fear that this human body may not be long preserved;
once the *kāṣāya* is lost, the suffering will be profound. May you all, therefore, exert yourselves with earnest diligence.

This refers to prohibitive karma (*vārita-karman*). An offense is established through three conditions: first, the non-sequential; this includes both general and specific types. Second, the six permutations regarding the perception of non-sequential [action]:
two cases of gravity, two cases of lightness, and two cases of non-offense. Third, sitting down. Both the one who sits and the one who causes another to sit commit the offense;
the offense is incurred for each individual act of sitting.
This applies equally to the seven assemblies and is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited: as in the case of Mañjuśrī and Kāśyapa responding to King Aśoka’s invitation, or when those of lower rank, such as śrāmaṇeras, preach the Dharma, they ascend the Dharma seat.
Regarding the karmic result: those who do not respect the precepts and distance themselves from the True Dharma will experience no benefit;

whereas by respecting the outward signs of the precepts, one gives rise to superior benefits, as recorded in detail in the Sūtras and Vinaya concerning the past causes and conditions of the young monkey and the elephant.
Regarding "understanding": if the ten modes of contemplation do not manifest in their proper sequence, it is called "deviating from the order of the Dharma.
Regarding "repentance": there is deviation in the ritual procedure (*kriyā*) and deviation in the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

As for those who practice and realize [the truth]: they skillfully uphold the Mahā- and Hīnayāna Vinayas and know the sequence of matters; they skillfully cultivate the contemplative wisdom of the four teachings and know the sequence of principles.

Regarding the nature of evil: since the natures of sentient beings and Buddhas are equal, what sequential order could there be? Thus, Mañjuśrī was the teacher of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, yet he still attended Śākyamuni.
Since the one mind is all minds and the one contemplation is all contemplations, how could there be any further sequence?
Therefore, the *Buddhottama-sūtra* states: "The sacred nature has no obstruction; both following and reversing are skillful means."
○ Thirty-ninth: The Precept Against Failing to Cultivate Merit and Wisdom.
If a Buddha’s disciple, they should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings, establishing monasteries, mountain forests, gardens, and fields;
erecting Buddha stupas; and providing places for winter and summer retreats, for sitting in meditation, and for all practices of the Way—all such sites should be established.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings. In times of illness, national calamity, or the threat of bandits;
on the day of the passing of one's parents, brothers, preceptors (upādhyāya), or teachers (ācārya);
and during the third, fourth, or fifth seven-day periods, up to the seventh seven-day period, they should likewise expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya at all ritual assemblies (pariṣad).
Whether seeking blessings, traveling, or engaging in livelihood; when burned by great fires, swept away by great waters, or when a ship is driven by black winds;

or when facing the perils of rākṣasas upon rivers, lakes, or the great ocean—if one reads, recites, and expounds this sutra and vinaya, then even all karmic retributions for sins—the three evil paths, the eight difficulties, and the seven heinous offenses—as well as being bound to the body by cangues, shackles, pillories, and fetters, or being characterized by excessive lust and excessive anger [shall be extinguished].

There are many who are ignorant and many who are afflicted by illness; all such persons should preach this sutra and its vinaya. If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not do so, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
To establish monasteries and the like is a regulation intended to cultivate merit; to lecture on the Mahāyāna and the like is a regulation intended to cultivate wisdom.

These constitute *pratiṣedha-karman* (prohibitive actions). One should practice them according to one's capacity. If, upon encountering the necessary conditions, one fails to act, one incurs an offense for each instance.
There is no offense for those whose strength is insufficient; this refers to what is called "dwelling in little benefit, doing little work, and having little application" in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
If it is done with a mind of resentment, it is a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*); if it is due to laziness or indolence, it is a non-defiled offense (*akliṣṭāpatti*).

The seven assemblies are the same [in this regard], yet the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not fully coincide. During the summer retreat (*varṣā*), the Śrāvakas should repair their dwellings, though this is not prescribed at other times;
however, for the Mahāsattvas, they should cultivate meritorious deeds at all times.
Regarding the opening and closing [of practices]: one may constantly cultivate all superior activities such as meditation and recitation, having no leisure for other pursuits.
As for the fruit and retribution: if one does not cultivate them, one loses the two kinds of adornment; if one does cultivate them, the provisions for enlightenment will increase spontaneously.

Regarding "understanding": not knowing that the nature is inherently endowed with the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) is called not cultivating merit; not knowing that the nature is inherently endowed with the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) is called not cultivating wisdom.
Regarding "repentance" (*kṣamaṇā*): cultivation itself is repentance.

Regarding those who practice and realize: those who have not regressed in their conduct fulfill the cultivation of phenomena; those who have not regressed in their mindfulness fulfill the cultivation of principle.
As for the inherent evil (xing-è): there are no dharmas of merit or wisdom to be cultivated, nor is there anyone who cultivates merit or wisdom.
These nine precepts should be studied and respectfully upheld; they shall be explained in detail in the Chapter on the Brahma-Altar (Brahmacaryā-vastu).
This concludes the ninth set of precepts in the fourth section.
○ Forty: The Precept on Discernment in Bestowing Ordination.

If, O Sons of the Buddha, when bestowing the precepts upon others, you do not engage in discernment—whether they be kings, princes, ministers, officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, faithful men and women, licentious men and women, or the eighteen Brahmā heavens... the six [heavens]... [you must not reject them].
Desire-devas, those without sexual organs, those with dual organs, eunuchs, slaves, and all spirits may all receive the precepts.
One should instruct them that the robes they wear must all be of discolored hues to correspond with the Way;
they should all be dyed blue, yellow, red, black, or purple. All dyed garments, even down to bedding, must be entirely of discolored hues. As for the robes worn on the body—[one].
All dyed colors. Furthermore, whatever clothing people in all lands wear, a bhikṣu must always differ from their secular attire.

When one wishes to receive the precepts, the master should ask: "In your present body, have you not committed the seven heinous offenses? A Bodhisattva Dharma Master may not confer the precepts upon one who has committed the seven heinous offenses in their present body. The seven heinous offenses are: 1. Killing one’s father. 2. Killing one’s mother. 3. Killing an Arhat. 4. Shedding the blood of a Buddha. 5. Destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha. 6.

Causing a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression to abandon the Great Vehicle and turn toward the Śrāvaka vehicle. 7. Slandering the Tripitaka by claiming it is not the word of the Buddha.
To shed the blood of a Buddha; to kill one's father; to kill one's mother; to kill one's preceptor (upādhyāya); to kill one's teacher (ācārya);

to cause a schism in the Saṃgha that obstructs the turning of the Wheel of Dharma through a formal ritual (karmavācanā); and to kill an arhat—if one possesses these seven heinous offenses (ānantarya), one shall not receive the precepts in this present life.
All other persons may fully receive the precepts. According to the dharma of those who have left the household life, one does not prostrate to kings, nor does one prostrate to parents. Six.

If one does not show respect to their parents and does not offer ritual reverence to spirits and deities, yet understands the Dharma Master’s words, and there are those who come from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek the Dharma,
and the Bodhisattva Dharma Master, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, does not immediately bestow the precepts upon all these sentient beings,
they commit a minor offense of defilement.

Regarding "not being permitted to make distinctions": one should not discriminate among categories—meaning that from kings down to ghosts and spirits, all possess Buddha-nature and are all capable of practicing the Bodhisattva path according to their respective types; therefore, all may receive the precepts.

Nevertheless, there are two matters for which one should make distinctions: first, physical appearance and deportment; second, karmic obstructions. One should instruct them regarding the robes they wear on their bodies...

"Kāṣāya," etc., refers to the instruction to distinguish [the wearer] by their outward appearance. The Sanskrit term *kāṣāya* is translated here as "dyed robe" (*rāñjita-vastra*), also as "discolored robe" (*virāga-varṇa*), and also as "bedding" (*śayanāsana*).
It is the general name for the garments of those who have left the household life. Regarding the colors blue, yellow, red, black, and purple:
the Vinaya prescribes three types of discolored colors, namely blue, black, and mūlāna (wood-brown). The current regulation establishes five types; according to the *Mi...* [text].
The Sarvāstivāda school states: "If one wears blue robes, they should be purified by marking them with black and madder;

black robes should be marked with blue and madder; and madder-colored robes should be marked with blue and black. This is called 'altering the color' (*kaṣāya*). Now, it should also be done in this way.
Monks must all differ from the clothing of laypeople. This clearly explains that the essence of both monks and nuns [is defined by this distinction].
Because they are the Sangha Jewel, three types of field-robes (kṣetra-vastra) are specifically prescribed for them to distinguish them forever from the laity.
As for the five groups beginning with the śikṣamāṇā, they must only wear dyed (prakṛti-varṇa-viparīta) colors and must not be confused with bhikṣus.

Regarding the instruction to ask whether one has committed the seven heinous crimes (*saptānantarya*) in this present life, this is taught to filter out those with karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*). Once the karma of the seven heinous crimes is completed, one will certainly fall into [Avīci Hell].

[The period] in between is precisely what obstructs the category of precepts (*śīla-skandha*). Since it is impossible to know [the karmic conditions] of previous lives, those do not constitute an obstruction to the precepts;

therefore, the question concerns only the present life. As for the "father," this body is his physical legacy; thus, even if he were a stepfather or the like, it would not constitute a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense.
As for the "mother," this body was born from her; thus, even if she were a concubine or the like, it would not constitute an *ānantarya* offense. As for the "preceptor" (*upādhyāya*)... [comparison].
There are two kinds of preceptors (*upādhyāya*): first, the preceptor for the ten precepts; second, the preceptor for full ordination (*upasampadā*).
For bhikṣuṇīs, there are three kinds: first, the bhikṣuṇī preceptor for the ten precepts; second, the bhikṣuṇī preceptor for the *śikṣamāṇā* who receives the six rules;
third, the bhikṣuṇī preceptor for full ordination. In all these cases, a bhikṣu may not serve as the preceptor. There are two kinds of *śikṣamāṇās*.
There are two types of preceptors (*upādhyāyī*): first, the preceptor for the ten precepts; second, the preceptor for the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*).

For both *śrāmaṇera* and *śrāmaṇerī*, there is only one type, namely the one who confers the ten precepts. Regarding *ācāryas*, there are five types for a *bhikṣu*: first, the preceptor for the ten precepts;
second, the preceptor who instructs at the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*); third, the *karmācārya* (preceptor of ritual action) at the time of receiving full ordination.
1. The *upādhyāya* (preceptor). 2. The *ācārya* (instructor). 3. The *niśraya-ācārya* (preceptor for dependence), who provides dependence for even a single night. 4.

The *pāṭha-ācārya* (teacher of recitation), from whom one receives even a single four-line verse (*catuṣpāda-gāthā*) or its meaning. 5. The *bhikṣuṇī-ācārya* (nun-instructor). There are seven types of [nuns]:

adding the *karmakārikā-ācārya* (ceremonial instructor) within the *bhikṣu-saṃgha* at the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), as well as the *ṣaḍ-dharma-ācāryā* (instructor of the six rules) and the *śikṣamāṇā-ācāryā* (instructor of the probationary nun).
There are three types of *upādhyāya*: first, the *upādhyāya* of the ten precepts; second, the *upādhyāya* of the six rules; and third, the *upādhyāya* who teaches recitation.
For *śrāmaṇeras* and *śrāmaṇerīs*, there are two types: first, the [preceptor] of the ten precepts; and second, the [preceptor] who teaches recitation.

For *upāsakas* and *upāsikās*, there are three types: first, the *upādhyāya* for receiving the five precepts; and second, the *upādhyāya* for receiving the eightfold fasting precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*).
The third is the *ācārya* for recitation. Furthermore, if one includes the *ācārya* who confers the Bodhisattva precepts, then each of the seven classes of followers adds one more type.
As for the breaking of the *saṃgha* through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), it requires at least eight persons living together, all of whom must be bhikṣus.

When four persons each form their own faction within a single great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and perform various formal acts (*karmas*) separately while reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, they constitute a schism of the Saṃgha that destroys the turning of the Wheel of Dharma;
this applies even down to nine persons, including one who claims to be a Buddha for himself.
He enticed those four bhikṣus to follow his own teachings separately; the other four bhikṣus maintained the correct path and did not comply. Thus, they were divided into two factions.
Whether within or outside the monastic boundaries, anyone who causes what is non-Dharma to be taught as Dharma—such as Devadatta and others—is said to "break the wheel of the Dharma.
"Sages" refers here to those who have attained the four fruits of the Hīnayāna, or those in the Mahāyāna who have reached the stage of *prayoga* (application) and above.

If one does not prostrate before one’s parents or the king, nor show reverence toward one’s six relations or the spirits, yet merely understands the words of the Dharma Master, how great must be the esteem with which they regard that Master?
Coming from a hundred or a thousand *li*, how fervent must be their quest for the Dharma?
To refuse to transmit it under such circumstances—is this not an excessive betrayal of the opportunity presented? It is born of an evil mind and anger.
"Mind" clarifies that this is not a mind that seeks to benefit sentient beings through expedient means.

"The precepts for all sentient beings" clarifies that this Great Precept is fundamentally that which all sentient beings ought to receive together; it is unlike the precepts of bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras.
One must select the appropriate category before conferring [the precepts].

This constitutes a prohibitive act (*pratiṣedha-karman*). A transgression is established through four conditions: first, being a fit vessel for receiving the precepts, meaning one is not subject to the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) and possesses a physical form and demeanor in accordance with the Dharma;
second, the six permutations regarding the perception of fitness (two heavy, two light, and two cases of non-offense); third, the presence of discrimination.

Discerning the mind: this refers to cases where one despises someone for being lowly or feels anger toward them for being impoverished and so forth; such [attitudes] are precisely the primary obstacle to receiving [the precepts].
One incurs an offense according to the person rejected. However, if one knows that the person is incapable of receiving them, there is no transgression. The *Bodhisattva-śīla-karman* states:
"When a bodhisattva wishes to confer the bodhisattva precepts, they should first explain [the following] to them."
The Bodhisattva Dharma-piṭaka, the Mātṛkā, the bodhisattva training rules, and the characteristics of transgressions—these he causes them to hear and receive.

Through wisdom, they observe their own inclinations; being capable of discernment, they accept the bodhisattva precepts not merely through the exhortation of others, nor for the sake of surpassing others.
Know that such a person is called a firm bodhisattva, capable of receiving the purity of a bodhisattva.
The restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*). Furthermore, it is said: one should not receive [the precepts] from those who lack pure faith (*śraddhā*).
This means that regarding such received pure precepts, they initially lack faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), cannot approach others, and engage in improper reflection (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).

One should not receive them from those who possess stinginess and greed (*matsarya-rāga*), those obscured by stinginess and greed, those with great desire (*mahēcchā*), those lacking contentment (*asaṃtuṣṭi*), or those who have violated the pure precepts.

One should not receive [the precepts] from one who lacks respect for the various points of training (*śikṣāpada*); nor from one who is negligent and lax regarding the restraint of the moral code (*śīla-saṃvara*);
nor from one who possesses anger and resentment, who is largely intolerant, or who is unable to endure the transgressions of others;
nor from one who is indolent, lazy, or largely addicted to sleeping day and night.
One should not receive [the teachings] from one who is addicted to reclining, addicted to lying down, addicted to associating with companions, or addicted to idle chatter.

One should not receive them from one whose mind is distracted, even to the extent that they cannot practice by dwelling on a single object of focus with a virtuous mind for as long as it takes to milk a cow.
One should not receive them from one who is obscure, of a deluded nature, of an extremely inferior mind, or who slanders the bodhisattva lineage.
"One should not receive [the precepts] from a *tāra* or a *mātṛkā*. The explanation says: these all exclude those who are not vessels for the Dharma.

How could one say that there is no discrimination at all? Furthermore, if a person originally does not wish to receive them, yet one forces them to receive the precepts, this also constitutes a minor transgression."
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs incur the full offense. For the other five assemblies, there is no matter of bestowing the precepts;

[the rule] was not yet established for them. Regarding the Great and Small Vehicles, they do not fully coincide. In the Hīnayāna, if one first grants permission and later refuses it, one incurs an offense; if permission was not granted, there is no offense.
In the Mahāyāna, which takes the transformation of beings through reception as its foundation, to refuse to bestow [the precepts] constitutes an offense.

Regarding the opening and closing [of precepts]: For example, when the śramaṇa Daojin sought to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from Dharmakṣema, Dharmakṣema did not grant them, but instead commanded him to repent.
After seven days and seven nights had passed, Daojin went to Dharmakṣema to request the precepts again. Dharmakṣema was greatly incensed and did not respond.

Daojin thought to himself that his karmic obstacles had not yet been eliminated, so he once more exhausted his sincerity in prostrations and repentance for a total of three years. Thereupon, he dreamed of Śākyamuni...
Kāśyapa Buddha conferred the precepts upon him. The next day, he went to Dharmakṣema intending to recount his dream.
Before he had even taken a few steps, Dharmakṣema suddenly rose in alarm and exclaimed, "Excellent! You have already received the precepts. I shall serve as your witness.

Subsequently, before an image of the Buddha, he further explained the characteristics of the precepts. This was an instance of responding to the individual's capacity for benefit; had it not been so, the precepts would not have been conferred beforehand.
Although he displays great anger, it is not born of an evil mind or a mind of hatred.
Regarding the karmic retribution: if one discriminates falsely, one incurs the sin of withholding the Dharma and fails to achieve the two benefits [of self and others].
If one discriminates skillfully, one adorns one’s retinue and brings glory to the Dharma-gate.

Regarding "contemplative understanding" (*guan-jie*): it does not pass through the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), but universally cultivates the samādhi of the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*); this is the meaning of discernment (*pravicaya*).

Regarding "repentance" (*chanhui*): there is the discernment of phenomena (*vastu-pravicaya*) and the discernment of principle (*tattva-pravicaya*), which is the single-mindedness of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Regarding those who practice and realize: from the stage of separate abiding (*pratyekavihāra*) onward, there is no selection by way of phenomena; from the stage of perfect faith (*pariniṣpanna-śraddhā*) upward, there is no selection by way of principle.
As for those of inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*): if every dharma were selected, it would be entirely non-existent, and not a single dharma could be received.
○ The forty-first precept: Acting as a Preceptor for Personal Gain.

If, O Sons of the Buddha, when teaching others to give rise to faith, a Bodhisattva acts as a teacher of instruction for another person, and sees one who wishes to receive the precepts, they should instruct them to request two masters—the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya—and these two masters should then question [the candidate].
He said: "Do you have the seven obstructing offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*)? If, in this present life, one has committed the seven obstructing offenses, the preceptor must not confer the precepts upon them.
If one does not have the seven obstructing offenses, one may confer the precepts. If there are those who have violated the ten precepts, they should be instructed to perform repentance."
Before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts during the six periods of the day and night.

With utmost sincerity, prostrate to the thousand Buddhas of the three periods of time until you behold an auspicious sign. Whether it takes one week, two or three weeks, or even up to a year, you must see such a sign.
An auspicious sign refers to the Buddha coming to stroke your head, or seeing light, flowers, and various other wonders.
If auspicious signs appear, one’s offenses will be extinguished; if no such good signs appear, although one performs repentance, it is of no benefit.

Such a person will not obtain the precepts in this present life, yet they will gain increased merit from receiving them. If one has violated the forty-eight minor precepts, one may repent before another person (pratimukha-vinaya), and the offense will be extinguished.
This is not the same as the case of the seven prohibitions (saptāvaraṇa). Furthermore, the preceptor must understand each point of this dharma thoroughly. If...
They do not understand the characteristics of light or heavy, or right and wrong, within the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas; they do not understand the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
