They do not understand the stages of the developmental lineage (śikṣā-gotra), the nurturing lineage (paripuṣṭi-gotra), the innate lineage (prakṛti-gotra), the indestructible lineage (avināśa-gotra), the lineage of the path-seeds (mārga-bīja-gotra), and the lineage of the true dharma (saddharma-gotra), nor the extent of these categories.

They fail to comprehend, one by one, the entry and exit of contemplative practice (vipaśyanā-śamatha), the ten factors of dhyāna (daśa-dhyānāṅga), and all dharmas of conduct. They do not attain these dharmas.
This is acceptable. However, if a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and fame, seeks and covets excessively, greedily desiring disciples,
and falsely pretends to understand all the sutras and vinayas for the sake of offerings— thus deceiving themselves and deceiving others—
then one who bestows the precepts upon such a person commits a minor offense.
The "instructor-dharma-master" (*śāstṛ-upādhyāya*) is precisely the preceptor (*ācārya*).
Since the *bhikṣu* precepts are received within the Saṃgha, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the ritual master (*karmācārya*) must both be present *bhikṣus*.
Since the Bodhisattva precepts are received before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, a present dharma-master may merely serve as the instructor.

Regarding the instruction on the *ācārya*: "One should be taught to request two masters" means that one requests the primary deity Buddha to be the *upādhyāya*—this refers to Śākyamuni of this world—and requests the Bodhisattva who is next in succession to be the *ācārya*—this refers to Maitreya at this time.
These are called the two masters. In the text, the phrase "the two masters" refers to the *upādhyāya* and the *ācārya*.
Regarding the instruction that "one should ask," this means one should ask the preceptor (*śāstṛ*). This refers to the period prior to requesting the two masters;

first, one must inquire regarding the obstructing impediments (*vighna*) to ensure that the seven types of impediments are absent, and only then should one instruct them to request the two masters. Thus, the Bodhisattva...
The *Śīla-sūtra* states: "May the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Great Virtuous Ones of the ten directions listen.
Now that this person [Name] has recited the three times, they have received the Bodhisattva precepts from the Buddhas and the Sangha of Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
The speaker is I; the recipient is [Name]. I am the witness for [Name]. As for the 'Great Master,' this refers to the immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions."

Saṃghaśī was that person; I myself am the junior disciple. Furthermore, having received the Bodhisattva precepts, I took the original Buddha as my Upādhyāya and the Buddha of the Successive Stage (Maitreya) as my Ācārya;
I likewise took the Buddhas of the ten directions as the honored witnesses for the same ritual platform.

The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions serve as fellow students and virtuous friends. That we do not now request them to bear witness as fellow students is similar to how a *bhikṣu* receives the precepts and requests only two masters.
Although other sutras also provide for the request of five types of holy masters, they differ because they are expanded or abbreviated according to the capacities of beings.
Regarding those who violate the ten precepts, this refers to those who have previously received these bodhisattva [precepts].
One may have violated the Bodhisattva Great Precepts, or perhaps have broken the fundamental roots of the precepts previously received as a bhikṣu, śrāmaṇera, or one who has taken the five precepts;

therefore, it is necessary to behold auspicious signs. If, prior to receiving the precepts, one committed acts such as killing or stealing, these constitute merely worldly natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and are not termed violations of the precepts;
thus, there is no need to inquire about them, except in the case of the seven heinous transgressions (*ānantarya*).
One must ask this: even in one's present body, it may be that one does not obtain the precepts; this refers to the fact that receiving the full precepts (*mahāśīla*) again is not permitted.
However, one may obtain "augmentative" reception of the precepts; this means acting as a superior cause for receiving the precepts in a future life.

Regarding "confession before another" (*pratideśanā*), this means confessing one's transgressions before a pure assembly of Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna practitioners, vowing not to commit them again—this is what is meant by "acting as... [a cause].

This is the Dharma-Confession (*dharmakṣamaṇā*). Regarding the characteristics of faults, whether light or heavy: those that are light are easy to confess, while those that are heavy are difficult to confess.
What is transgressive must be confessed; what is not transgressive need not be confessed. If one describes a light offense as heavy, or a heavy offense as light;
if one calls a transgression a non-transgression, or a non-transgression a transgression, one will be unable to resolve others' doubts or bring them out of their offenses. However...

The single ultimate truth (*ekārtha-satya*) is the very essence of the precepts; it is also the primary cause for the ground of the mind (*citta-bhūmi*), the eternally abiding supreme fruit, and the nature of the cultivated seed (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*).
As for the "nature of growth" (*paripuṣṭi-gotra*), it refers to the gradual increase [of wisdom] through the repeated practice of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

The ten minds of initial aspiration (*daśa-prasthāna-citta*) correspond to the nature of the lineage (*gotra-bhāva*). Regarding their "indestructible nature," this refers to the conventional establishment of the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);

thus, they are indestructible. These are the ten minds of cultivation (*daśa-paripuṣṭi-citta*). The nature of the lineage of the path (*mārga-gotra*) refers to the Middle Way capable of penetration; these are the ten adamantine minds (*vajra-citta*).
The nature of the true dharma (*saddharma-bhāva*) refers to the entry into the stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*); these are the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).

As well as the two types of awakening—Equal and Sublime—and those who engage in the meditative practices of entering and emerging to varying degrees: "entering" refers to departing from the conventional and entering into emptiness;

"nurturing" refers to emerging from emptiness and entering into the conventional; "Vajra-like" refers to turning away from the two extremes and entering the Middle Way; and "the Ten Stages" refers to proceeding from the mundane to the sacred.

Furthermore, in the stage of the *śikṣā-bhūmi* (nature of training), the contemplation of emptiness is still slight; in the stage of the *vardhana-bhūmi* (nature of nurturing), [emptiness is more developed].

In the *darśana-bhāgīya* (nature of seeing), conventional contemplation (*parikalpita-darśana*) is still few, whereas in the *akopya-bhāgīya* (nature of being unshakable), conventional contemplation is many.

In the *mārga-bhāgīya* (nature of the path), middle-level contemplation (*madhya-darśana*) is still few, whereas in the *samyaktva-niyata-bhāgīya* (nature of the fixed determination for the true dharma), middle-level contemplation is many.

Furthermore, if the three types of contemplation are practiced sequentially, they are few; if they are practiced within a single moment of mind (*ekacitta*), they are many. [The ten factors of dhyāna.]

These refer to the ten factors, such as joy and bliss, employed in the four dhyānas. If one does not understand the relative weight, the right and the wrong, one is obscured regarding the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*).
If one does not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one is obscured regarding the principle of the precepts (*śīla-nyāya*).

If one does not understand the nature of the lineage of practice (*abhyāsa-gotra*) and so forth, one is obscured regarding the various distinctions between the meditative concentrations associated with the Path (*mārga-samprayukta-samādhi*) and those associated with the Dhyāna (*dhyāna-samprayukta-samādhi*). Being obscured regarding the characteristics of the precepts, one is unable to...
To resolve doubts and emerge from transgressions while remaining ignorant of the principles of the precepts cannot inspire true faith or authentic understanding;

to be ignorant of the distinctions between the Path and meditative concentration cannot lead others to practice, realize, and enter [the Way]. This may be described as "one blind man leading a multitude of blind men."
This is a prohibitive act (*pratiṣedha-karman*) that severely undermines the transformation of the Dharma. Two conditions constitute the offense: first, the mind of seeking profit;
second, the act of gathering disciples. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "To maintain a retinue out of greed for service and offerings is a defiled transgression (*kliṣṭāpatti*).

This [present rule] also concurrently prohibits this. Whereas the previous case of acting as a teacher without understanding was a fault arising from a desire for reputation, the present case lies precisely in [the pursuit of profit].
The love of profit and the pursuit of fame are both the root of birth and death and constitute great obstacles to Bodhi; their transgressions are equal.
Therefore, it is concluded that those who act for the sake of profit, deceiving themselves and others, possess minds that are increasingly base and inferior.

Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs commit the full offense. For the other five assemblies, there is no matter of receiving the precepts; however, if they accept disciples for the sake of profit, they also commit an offense.
This is prescribed for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The qualities of a teacher in the Hīnayāna are as previously explained.
Only prohibition, not permission. Regarding the retribution: destroying the Dharma-gate is a more grievous offense than the transgressions of the evil precepts (*akuśala-śīla*).

Regarding the understanding of the principle: for the Two Vehicles, it is the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); for the Bodhisattvas who have emerged from the provisional (*upāya*), it is the benefit of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This is the specific orientation.
Is it for the sake of middling benefit? Only those of perfect realization (yuanren) thoroughly understand the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) and have no benefit to pursue.

As for repentance: practicing it through ritual action (*vastu*) constitutes benefit for phenomena; performing it according to the rite constitutes benefit for principle (*tattva*). One must maintain single-mindedness and non-arising.

Regarding "cultivation and realization": from the first fruit (srotāpanna) upward, one does not act for the benefit of phenomena; abiding in the perfect stage of the distinct lands, one does not act for the benefit of principle.

As for "inherently evil," it universally benefits the Dharma-realm, which is precisely benefiting oneself alone. From the provisional names [of the teachings] as benefit, up to the ultimate as benefit.
The forty-second precept: Prohibiting the preaching of the precepts to evil persons.

If a disciple of the Buddha, for the sake of profit or gain, shall not preach these Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas before those who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts, nor before non-Buddhists or evil persons, nor before those with false views; the exception being the King.
It must not be said that all others are so; those evil persons who do not receive the Buddha’s precepts are called "beasts.

In every place where they are born, they do not see the Triple Gem. Like wood or stone, they are without mind and are thus called "heretics" (tīrthika). These people of false views are no different from wooden stumps.
If a Bodhisattva preaches the seven teachings and precepts of the Buddha before such evil persons, they commit a light offense.
"Sin. "Reciting the precepts" refers to the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* every half-month. "Excluding kings" is because the Buddha-dharma is entrusted to kings.
To live in vain and die aimlessly is why they are called "beasts"; to be obstinate and utterly lacking in awakening is why they are like wood or stone.
Turning one's back on awakening and aligning with the sensory dust, one constantly dwells outside the principles; therefore, they are called "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika).
This constitutes a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*). To speak of this in advance to others would cause their subsequent reception [of the precepts] to lack sincerity and gravity;

therefore, during the fortnightly *poṣadha* ceremony, those who have not yet received the full ordination (*mahā-śīla*) must first be sent away. An offense is established through four conditions; the first is: not having received [the full precepts].

Regarding the person who observes the precepts: this refers to one who has not yet received these Bodhisattva precepts. Second, regarding the six permutations concerning the perception of the other person as such:
two are grave offenses, two are light offenses, and two are non-offenses. Third, regarding the intention for which it is spoken: this refers to doing so for the sake of gain, honor, and the like.
Fourth, the other person must hear it; from this point, the offense is established.

The seven classes of disciples all commit offenses equally, yet the major and minor precepts are not entirely shared. At all times, one may not speak of the names of the five categories of offenses to śrāmaṇeras and others;
for if they were to understand the meaning and terminology of these five categories, it would constitute the grave offense of stealing the Dharma.
In the Mahāyāna, when reciting the precepts during the fortnightly *poṣadha*, those who have not yet received them must be sent away; at other times, this is not required.

As the preceding text states, "At all times, one should expound this sutra and vinaya," and as the subsequent text states, "Upon seeing any sentient being, one should encourage them to receive the Three Refuges and the ten precepts. Thus, it is known that this is not the same as the Vinaya-piṭaka. Furthermore,
Bodhisattvas— whether bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs— at all times must not speak of the offenses of the five categories to those who have not yet received full ordination.
Furthermore, bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras and others must not preemptively learn the names and meanings of these five categories of offenses,
lest they incur a grave impediment that would permanently obstruct their receiving full ordination in this life.

Only prohibition is applied, not permission. Regarding the karmic retribution: to speak [of this] would be to treat the True Dharma with irreverence; to refrain from speaking serves as a bulwark for the True Teaching.
As for understanding through realization: the eternally abiding Buddha-nature is called the "True Precept. Until one has awakened to the Perfect Doctrine, all are termed "evil persons."

One should instruct, admonish, benefit, and gladden them by means of other dharmas; one should not merely praise the One Vehicle, which would instead cause sentient beings to sink back into the suffering of birth.

Regarding repentance, there are explanations in terms of phenomena, explanations in terms of ritual procedures, and explanations in terms of principle. Within the non-arising of the single mind, one must skillfully penetrate the four [truths].
All are based on causes and conditions.

Regarding those who practice and realize: the explanation of non-transgression in terms of phenomena refers to the first fruit and the stage of separate dwelling; the explanation of non-transgression in terms of principle refers to possessing the wisdom of the faculty of full knowledge.

Regarding those of an evil nature: it is like a potent poison that delights the senses; one does not lightly bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon them, which is to say, this is spoken for the sake of those heading toward evil.
[This is] the forty-third: the precept against intentionally giving rise to a mind that violates the precepts.

If a son or daughter of the Buddha has left the household life with faith and received the true precepts of the Buddha, yet deliberately conceives the thought to violate these sacred precepts, they shall not receive the offerings of any donors. They shall not walk upon the ground of the king, nor drink the water of the king.
Five thousand great ghosts will constantly block their path, crying out, "Great thief! If such a person enters a dwelling or a city, [the ghosts will likewise obstruct them].
Within his residence, ghosts would constantly sweep away his footprints. All the people of the world reviled him, saying, "He is a thief within the Buddha-dharma who harms all sentient beings;
one whom no one wishes to behold with their eyes. This violator of the precepts is no different from a beast, no different from a block of wood."
If one intentionally violates the right precepts, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).

This means that a renunciant bodhisattva, having originally received the precepts out of faith, is thus worthy of receiving all offerings and worthy of being honored by devas, humans, ghosts, and spirits.
If, having received them, they intentionally violate them, they shall no longer be worthy of receiving any offerings.
If one fails to maintain them, one will be despised by both spirits and the people of the world. One can thus see that the precepts must not be violated.
How could one even give rise to the thought of violating them? Although one has not yet actually broken them, one has already incurred the offense through the mind.
These constitute both natural (prakṛti) and proscribed (pratikṣepaṇa) offenses. Because one holds the precepts in contempt, an offense is established through three conditions:

first, the actual transgression; second, the perception that it is a transgression; and third, the arising of the intention to commit the transgression. Each moment of such thought constitutes a light stain (dūṣaṇa). Furthermore, the *Prātimokṣasūtra* states:
"To give rise to the five hindrances (pañcanīvaraṇa) and fail to cultivate awakening is a defiled transgression (kliṣṭāpatti). This [category] is also subsumed therein.
The seven classes of followers commit the same offenses; however, as renunciants, they serve as fields of merit for the world, and thus their responsibility is doubly heavy.
Both major and minor precepts are established. What is termed a "light offense" in the Hīnayāna entails an additional light offense upon the commission of the primary transgression.
The Mahāyāna should follow this same principle. Furthermore, the resolve of a Bodhisattva is more rigorous than that of a Śrāvaka.
Furthermore, if one’s intention to destroy [the precept] was originally absent, one incurs only the fundamental offense according to the specific act; this additional offense is not added.
If one simply gave rise to this thought without yet committing the act, for a minor case one merely reproaches the mind, while for a major case one should likewise perform repentance.
Only prohibitions are not permitted.

As for karmic retribution, if one allows it to arise as before, it will obstruct superior morality (*adhiśīla*), obstruct superior concentration (*adhicitta*), and obstruct superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), resulting in an offense against the light precepts.
If one can awaken to this, then the root of the precepts will become firm and stable, and meditative concentration and wisdom can be achieved.
Regarding "contemplative understanding": to give rise to a mind that stands outside of principle is itself called violating the precepts.

Regarding "repentance": to give rise to a mind that violates a matter is to perform the ritual procedure; to give rise to a mind that violates principle is to abide in the single-mindedness of non-arising.

Regarding those who have attained realization: one at the stage of non-retrogression from position has no mind that transgresses against phenomena; one at the stage of non-retrogression from thought has no mind that transgresses against principle.
As for those of inherently evil nature: they slander the Buddhas, destroy the Dharma, and do not enter the ranks of the assembly;
they join hands with the various demons to act as their laboring companions.
○ The forty-fourth precept: Not making offerings to the scriptures.

If you, O sons of the Buddha, should always with a single mind receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas—even if you must flay your skin to make paper, draw blood for ink, use marrow as water, and split your bones to make pens to transcribe the Buddha’s precepts; or using the bark of trees, rice paper, or silk—[you must do so].

One should always write them out upon plain bamboo or silk and maintain them. One should constantly use the seven treasures, priceless incense and flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels to create incense bags to hold the scrolls of the sutras and vinaya.
If one fails to make offerings in accordance with the Dharma, one commits a minor offense.
There are five ways of making offerings: first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, transcribing; and fifth, offering incense, flowers, and various jewels.

[The practice of] flaying one's own skin to serve as paper and so forth is cited as an example to illustrate how even the most severe acts are undertaken for the sake of the Dharma, let alone those that are lighter.
This is a prohibitive karma (*vāraṇa-karman*). Because one lacks a mind of reverence for the Dharma, one incurs an offense. This applies equally to all seven classes of followers;

however, the Great and Small Vehicles do not entirely coincide. In the Lesser Vehicle, an offense is established for failing to recite and uphold the Vinaya; in the Great Vehicle, one should cultivate the five [precepts].
Furthermore, failing to make offerings to the Triple Gem also constitutes an offense. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:

"Within a single day and night, whether it be the Buddha being present in the world, or a stupa or temple of the Buddha, or the Dharma, or the scriptural scrolls, or the Bodhisattva-piṭaka (Sūtra-piṭaka) and the Mātṛkā-piṭaka, or the community of bhikṣus, or the great bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions..."
O Assembly: if one does not make offerings, whether many or few; or even fails to perform a single prostration; or even fails to praise the merits of the Triple Gem with a single verse;
or even fails to purify the mind for a single thought-moment; or if one is disrespectful, indolent, or lazy—this constitutes a defiled offense.
If it is due to forgetfulness or error, it is a non-defiled offense. There is no offense in cases where one has entered the stage of the pure mind-ground.
Bodhisattva: Just as a bhikṣu who has attained indestructible purity (*abhedya-prasāda*) constantly performs the ritual offering (*dharma-pūjā*) to the Triple Gem, the *Sujāta-sūtra* states:

"If one obtains new grain, fruits, melons, or vegetables, and does not first offer them to the Triple Gem but consumes them oneself first, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence (*āpatti-kaṣāya*). If one gives such leftover food to a bhikṣu, [the bhikṣu]..."
For a nun, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā, this constitutes an offense of negligence for the upāsaka;
it is strictly prohibited and not permitted.

As for the retribution: one who treats the Dharma with arrogance will distance themselves from the True Dharma and lose the seed of wisdom; one who reveres the Dharma will [attain it] in birth after birth.
Everywhere, one constantly encounters the wondrous Dharma.

For the practitioner who contemplates and understands, if for even a single thought-moment they are not in accord with the Great Dharma of True Purity, it is called "not making offerings. Regarding repentance: in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), there is no offering;
in terms of ritual procedures (*vidhi*), there is no offering; in terms of principle (*tattva*), there is no offering; and in terms of non-arising (*anutpāda*), there is no offering.

Regarding those who have attained realization: those at the stage of the first fruit and those on the Ground of Pure Mind possess no pride regarding phenomena; those whose mindfulness does not regress possess no pride regarding principle.
As for those of inherent evil nature, their own mind is itself the Dharma and the Triple Gem; they should not, with the mind, further offer worship to the mind.
○ The Forty-Fifth Precept: Not Failing to Transform Sentient Beings.
If a Buddha’s disciple constantly gives rise to a heart of great compassion, upon entering any city, town, house, or dwelling, and seeing even a single ordinary sentient being, they should proclaim:
"All you sentient beings, you should all receive the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts. If they see oxen or horses...
Regarding all animals, such as pigs and sheep, one should mentally contemplate and verbally declare: "You are animals; arouse the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva enters any mountain, forest, river, or wilderness, they cause all sentient beings therein to arouse the bodhicitta.
If this Bodhisattva does not give rise to the mind to teach and transform sentient beings, they commit a minor offense.
As for the mind of great compassion: it is the knowledge that all sentient beings and the Buddhas of the three periods of time are non-dual and indistinguishable from one's own body and mind;
it is the desire to extract the suffering inherent in their nature and bestow upon them the bliss inherent in their nature. Mind.
Regarding "mindful verbal expression": this refers to the power of the Dharma-nature of the same essence, intended to bring about resonance and awakening.

This constitutes a prohibited action (*vārya-karman*), as it contravenes one's great vow; therefore, it is regulated. A transgression is established through four conditions: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of that being as a sentient being;

third, the absence of a mind to transform them; and fourth, the failure to provide transformation. To encounter one capable of being transformed and yet fail to transform them—this constitutes [the offense]. Following...

This concludes the section on the faults of worldly affairs. However, when a Great Being transforms and delivers sentient beings, it does not go beyond the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

The first is generosity (*dāna*), which consists of three types: material gifts, the Dharma, and fearlessness. This includes that which is prohibited by the precepts, such as stinginess, anger, killing, and stealing. The second is pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*).

This very precept regulation consists of three aspects: [the basis], benefit, and common purpose. While it is separately formulated in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, this sūtra is likewise subsumed under this same precept.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "If, with a mind of resentment, one does not comply with another..."
This constitutes a defiled offense. Laziness and indolence constitute a non-defiled offense. There is no offense in the following cases:

if one intends to perform an improper act; if one is ill and lacks the strength; if one is observing a monastic regulation; if, although the act would be proper, it would cause many people to engage in an improper act;
if it is for the purpose of subduing non-Buddhists; or if it is by means of a skillful expedient to discipline that person.
I submit this explanation: this refers to the inclusion of benefiting others. Furthermore, it says:

when one observes the activities of sentient beings but does not engage in them as a colleague—namely, in deliberating on various matters, whether traveling on a journey, engaging in legal enterprises for profit, managing agricultural estates, herding cattle, mediating disputes, attending auspicious assemblies, or performing meritorious deeds—to fail to participate in these is due to a mind of resentment.
It is an offense of defilement (*kliṣṭa-āpatti*). It is not an offense of defilement if one is lazy or indolent.

There is no offense if one is ill, if one lacks strength, if the other person is able to manage it themselves, if the other person already has many companions, if the task to be performed is contrary to the Dharma or contrary to what is meaningful, if one employs skillful means to subdue them, if one has previously promised another, if the other person harbors enmity, or if [one is] oneself...

One cultivates wholesome karma and does not wish to abandon it even for a moment. This may be due to being dull-witted by nature, or out of regard for the wishes of many people, or to uphold monastic regulations.
The explanation says: this is the inclusion through "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*).
The seven classes of followers commit these transgressions equally.
In the Hīnayāna, there is no principle of transforming others; therefore, [the precepts] are not established for that purpose.
Regarding the karmic retribution: if one does not transform others, one loses the two benefits; if one transforms others, the two benefits increase.

Regarding contemplative understanding: when one mind transforms and instructs other minds, it is called "transforming sentient beings. If even for a single thought-moment one does not accord with wondrous contemplation, it is called "not transforming sentient beings."
Regarding repentance: when it concerns phenomena (*dharma*), there is no transformation; when it concerns the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), there is no transformation.

Regarding non-arising (*anutpāda*): in practice, there is no retrogression; one constantly practices the transformation of phenomena. In mindfulness, there is no retrogression; one constantly practices the transformation of principle (*li*).
As for those of an inherently evil nature, the Buddhas of the three periods of time swallow them all in a single mouth; what sentient beings are there left to deliver?
The forty-sixth precept: Preaching the Dharma in a manner that does not accord with the Dharma.
If you are a disciple of the Buddha, you should constantly teach and transform others, giving rise to a heart of great compassion.

When entering the homes of wealthy patrons or among any assembly, you must not stand while preaching the Dharma to laypeople; rather, you should sit upon a high seat in front of the assembly of laypeople.
Dharma Master. A bhikṣu may not stand upon the ground while preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly.

When preaching the Dharma, the Dharma Master shall occupy a high seat, honored with offerings of incense and flowers, while the fourfold assembly of listeners sits on lower seats, as if practicing filial piety toward their parents or showing reverent obedience to the instructions of a teacher.
It is like the case of a Brahmin who tends the sacrificial fire. If the one preaching the Dharma speaks contrary to the Dharma, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding "high seat," this refers to speaking with words of superiority and inferiority; regarding "senior seat," this refers to speaking with words of high and low.
To speak contrary to the Dharma means to not accord with the ritual protocols for preaching the Dharma; it does not mean to preach in a perverted or erroneous manner.
This is a prohibitive act (*pratiṣedha-karman*). A transgression is established through three conditions: first, [the teaching] is not in accordance with the Dharma;

second, there is the perception that it is not in accordance with the Dharma; and third, one actually preaches the Dharma. If it is done for the sake of fame or profit, it is a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*);

if it is due to forgetfulness or error, it is a non-defiled violation. Furthermore, this is stated based on the case of sitting; according to the Vinaya, however, if another person is lying down while one is sitting, one must not preach to them. If the person is sitting...
If one is standing while the other is seated; if one is not on a seat while the other is on a high seat; if one is on a lower seat while the other is on a higher seat;
if one is walking ahead while the other follows behind; if one is on a high walking path while the other is on a lower walking path;

if one is on the path while the other is off the path—in all such cases, one must not preach for them. Furthermore, one must not preach to those with a cloth wrapped around their necks or those who have covered their heads.

One must not preach the Dharma to those who have their heads wrapped, those who have their hands on their hips, those wearing leather sandals, those wearing wooden clogs, those riding in vehicles, or those holding staffs, swords, spears, knives, or parasols;
however, there is no offense if one preaches the Dharma to the sick. In all such cases, there is no transgression.
The seven classes of followers commit this offense equally, for it is permitted even for śrāmaṇeras and others to ascend the high seat;

furthermore, since laypeople who explain the meaning of a single line or a single verse must also act in accordance with the Dharma, this rule applies to them as well. Moreover, the *Śrāddhakarman-sūtra* states:

"If the Saṃgha does not permit one to preach the Dharma or offer praise, yet one does so of one's own accord, that upāsaka commits an offense of negligence. This [rule] also concurrently governs such cases.
Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools prohibit [this action].

Regarding the permissions and prohibitions, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu goes before a king or a landowner for the sake of the stūpa or the Saṃgha, and that person says, 'Bhikṣu, preach the Dharma to me;
do not speak so as to make me rise,' he must not speak [to make him rise], for fear of giving rise to suspicion."
If there is a person standing at the edge [of the assembly], and the bhikṣu intentionally speaks for the sake of that standing person, the king may hear it, yet the bhikṣu incurs no offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu suffers from an eye ailment and another person holds a staff while leading him forward, and he speaks for that person's sake, there is no offense.
Moreover, when a bhikṣu is on a perilous path in a place of fear, if a guard says, "Venerable sir, preach the Dharma to me," even if he holds a sword, [there is no offense].
As for the staff, it is taught that there is no offense [in using it].
Regarding the karmic fruit: if it is not in accordance with the Dharma, it causes both parties to incur the offense of treating the Dharma with contempt;
if it is in accordance with the Dharma, it causes both parties to gain the benefit of honoring the Dharma.
Regarding "contemplative understanding": sitting upon the seat of the emptiness of dharmas is what is called "acting in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding "repentance": in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), it is not in accordance with the Dharma; one employs [the practice of] phenomena. In terms of principle (*li*), it is not in accordance with the Dharma; one employs non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Regarding those who cultivate and realize [the Way]: from the first fruit upward, their practice is always in accordance with the Dharma; abiding in the distinct stages or the perfect stage, their principle is always in accordance with the Dharma.

As for the inherent evil [of the nature], it pervades both the primary and secondary worlds and the atoms of dust; since all speak and all listen together, how could there be any distinction of high or low?
○ The forty-seventh precept against unlawful restrictions:
If, O sons of the Buddha, there are kings, crown princes, officials, or disciples of the fourfold assembly who, relying on their own high status and nobility,
destroy the Buddha’s Dharma and its precepts, openly establishing secular laws and regulations to restrict us, the fourfold assembly—

Disciples, you are not permitted to leave the household life to practice the Way, nor are you permitted to fashion images, build stūpas, or establish the monastic regulations and administrative systems for the community.
You must cause the monks to be registered in official records; while the Bodhisattva-bhikṣus stand upon the ground, the laypeople shall occupy high seats.
To extensively practice what is contrary to the Dharma is like a military slave serving its master;
yet a Bodhisattva should properly receive the offerings of all people, yet instead acts as a messenger for officials—this is neither Dharma nor Vinaya.

If kings and their ministers who have sincerely received the Buddha’s precepts commit such an act, they shall not incur the sin of destroying the Triple Gem. If one intentionally destroys the Dharma, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
The four groups are: laymen, laywomen, boys, and girls. If they are not permitted to leave the household life to practice the Way, then the Jewel of the Sangha is severed.

If they are not permitted to create images and Buddha-stūpas, then the Jewel of the Buddha is severed. If they are not permitted to produce the Sūtras and the Vinaya, then the Jewel of the Dharma is severed.

This possesses both the nature of being endowed with [the offense] and the obstruction of the two types of karma, because it hinders wholesome dharmas. Four conditions constitute an offense: first, the object is that of the Triple Gem;

second, there is the perception that the object is that of the Triple Gem; third, there is a restricted intention; and fourth, the restriction is accomplished. The offense is determined according to the specific object.

The two groups of lay followers commit the offense in its entirety. As for the five groups of renunciants, they lack independent authority; yet even if they were to impose illegal restrictions according to their power, they would likewise commit the offense.
Both the great and the small are equally subject to restraint.
Regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited: for example, in the past, Maitreya was a king who provisionally established illegal regulations in order to promote the True Dharma.

Regarding the retribution: if there is restriction, one incurs the great sin of severing the Three Jewels; if there is no restriction, one can bring forth the merit of extensively protecting the Three Jewels.
Regarding the contemplative understanding: not manifesting the essential nature of the Three Jewels within all phenomena is termed "non-Dharma restriction."
Regarding the limits:

the limit of the practice of repentance concerns the matter, which requires one to diligently establish the Triple Gem; the limit of the principle concerns the method, which requires one to skillfully cultivate the threefold contemplation within a single mind.

Regarding those who practice and realize [the truth]: there is no restriction concerning the stages from the first fruit upward; there is no logical restriction regarding the distinct stages of perfect abiding.
As for the inherent evil (prakṛti-pāpa), one does not permit the establishment of a separate Buddha-realm outside of the nine realms.
○ Forty-eighth: Violating the Precept of the Dharma.

If a disciple of the Buddha has left the household life with a sincere heart, yet for the sake of fame and profit, preaches the Buddha’s precepts before kings and officials, and arbitrarily imposes restrictive constraints upon bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or disciples of the bodhisattva precepts.
It is like the law for a prisoner, or the law for a soldier or slave; it is like worms within a lion’s body eating the lion’s own flesh, rather than other external worms.
In this way, it is the sons of the Buddha who destroy the Buddha-dharma themselves, not external paths or celestial Māras who can destroy it.
Those who receive the Buddha-precepts should protect the Buddha-precepts as they would cherish an only son, or serve their parents; they must not violate or break them.

When a bodhisattva hears the sound of non-Buddhists or evil persons slandering and breaking the Buddha’s precepts with wicked words, it is no different from three hundred spears piercing their heart or a thousand swords and ten thousand clubs striking their body; they would rather enter hell themselves.

For a hundred kalpas, one shall not even once hear the sound of an evil person using malicious words to slander and break the Buddha’s precepts, let alone breaking the Buddha’s precepts oneself or teaching others to create the causes and conditions for breaking the Dharma; nor shall one lack a heart of filial piety.
If one intentionally acts otherwise, one commits a minor offense of defilement.
Regarding kings and their officials who have received the Buddha’s precepts: although they are fellow practitioners of the Dharma, one may recite the Bodhisattva precepts before them;
however, one must not arbitrarily inflict illegal punishments upon them.
If a disciple commits a transgression, one should only punish them according to the law and must not subject them to acts of confinement, such as treating them like prisoners or soldiers.

O slave! To do so would violate the monastic code. "Remembering as an only son" is a metaphor for the ultimate limit of love; "serving one's parents" is a metaphor for the ultimate limit of reverence.
Furthermore, remembering the son refers to the mind of compassion, while serving one's parents refers to the mind of filial piety.
This constitutes both the nature of the offense and its prohibition. Because it defiles the Dharma-gate, the offense is established through five conditions:
first, being a disciple of the Buddha—meaning one of the seven assemblies of the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna—who has not committed a pārājika offense and has not renounced the precepts;

second, the six permutations regarding the perception of the person as a disciple of the Buddha (two grave and four light); third, even if they are not disciples of the Buddha, one must still not perform acts of binding them.

This is an exception; however, because such instances are somewhat rare, no specific regulation was established for them. Alternatively, they may be subsumed within the precept against harming through anger (*vyāpādavihiṃsā-śīla*).

Third, regarding the mind of punishment: when one desires to cause another person to suffer humiliation, this is precisely the primary factor (*karmapada*). Fourth, the person who is the object of the action.
This refers to kings, ministers, and others who share the same precepts; therefore, only a light offense is incurred.

If one inflicts punishment upon a person who has not received the precepts, it falls under the sixth heavy precept. Regarding the five types of formal disciplinary actions, the fault is determined according to the specific circumstances.

The five groups of renunciants commit this offense equally; as for the two groups of householders, if one punishes a disciple of the Buddha, it falls under the preceding precept and is subject to its restrictions, yet the gravity of the offense is even greater, as extensively censured in the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra*.
Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna prohibit [the use of weapons].

Regarding permissions and prohibitions: in an age of corruption and turbidity, a bhikṣu who protects and upholds the True Dharma may rely on the power of kings and great ministers to arm himself for self-defense, as clarified in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. However, he must not inflict unlawful punishment upon others.
Regarding the karmic retribution: if one acts [in this way], there is the transgression of violating the Dharma-gate and bringing humiliation upon the Saṃgha;
if one does not act, it will cause the assembly of monks to increase in prosperity and find peace and happiness.
Those who understand [the teaching] do not practice according to what has been taught; this is a cause and condition for destroying the Dharma.
Furthermore, not knowing the causes and conditions of the four *siddhāntas* is a cause and condition for destroying the Dharma.

Regarding repentance: there is the breaking of the matter (*vastu*) and the breaking of the ritual procedure (*vidhi*). One must advance simultaneously in both practice and understanding. Regarding cultivation and realization:

from the first fruit (*phala*) upward, there is no breaking of the matter; at the distinct stages (*bhūmi*) and the stage of perfect abiding (*vimalā*), there is no breaking of the principle (*tattva*).
Regarding "inherently evil": it pervades all phenomena without exception.
Thus, these nine precepts should be studied; one should respectfully uphold them.
This concludes the summary of the nine precepts of the fifth section. The detailed explanation of the forty-eight minor transgressions is finished.
△ Third, the summary:
"O Sons of the Buddha, you must receive and uphold these forty-eight minor precepts. The Bodhisattvas of the past have already recited them;
the Bodhisattvas of the future shall recite them; and the Bodhisattvas of the present are now reciting them."
This concludes the summary of the forty-eight minor precepts. The second major section, the enumeration of the characteristics of the grave and minor precepts, is finished.
△ Third, the exhortation for the great assembly to practice them, in five parts: first, citing the Dharma that has been recited; second, entrusting it to those who shall propagate it;
third, clarifying the benefits of propagation; fourth, a renewed exhortation to practice; fifth, the joy of the assembly at that time. Now, the first part.

Listen, O sons of the Buddha! These ten grave and forty-eight light precepts have been recited by all Buddhas of the three periods of time—those who have recited them in the past, those who shall recite them in the future, and those who are reciting them now. I now likewise recite them.
△ Second, the entrustment to those who propagate [the teaching]:
"All of you in this great assembly— whether kings, princes, officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen,
or laywomen who have received and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts— should receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe the Buddha-nature as it is eternally present."
This volume on Abiding in the Precepts shall circulate through the three periods of time; for all sentient beings, the process of transformation shall continue without end.
In the previous section on "Exhorting to Receive," there was an exhaustive listing of lustful men, lustful women, eunuchs, ghosts, animals, and so forth.
That in this [section] one speaks only of "faithful men and faithful women" precisely demonstrates that once the precepts have been received, they are all termed the foremost purity. Buddha-nature.
Regarding the "Scroll of the Ever-Abiding Precepts": as long as this scroll remains in the world, the principle of the causes and conditions of the Buddha-nature shall not perish.
△ Third, the benefit of its circulation:

one shall behold a thousand Buddhas and receive their hands in guidance; in every lifetime, one shall not fall into the evil realms or the eight difficulties, but shall always be born as a human being.
Regarding the heavenly realms, three benefits are briefly enumerated: first, seeing the Sage; second, being free from suffering; and third, attaining happiness. The *Yishu* (Exegesis) states:

"Extending a hand" clarifies that the person who upholds the precepts is in close proximity to the Buddha, not far from him. From lifetime to lifetime, they shall not fall [into lower realms], but will always be born among humans.
O Celestial One, what is abandoned and what is attained—how could it stop at this alone? I have merely cited what ordinary people delight in and loathe as an exhortation.
△ Fourth: A Repeated Exhortation to Practice.
I am now here beneath this tree briefly expounding the seven dharmas of the Buddha’s precepts. You, the great assembly,
should single-mindedly study the Prātimokṣa and joyfully practice it, as is explained in detail for each point in the "Exhortation to Study" within the *Animitta-devaputra-parivarta*.
△ At that time, the assembly rejoiced.
The three thousand scholars and those present listening to the teaching, hearing the Buddha recite it himself, took it to heart with every thought, receiving and upholding it with joy.
Three thousand. This refers to those within the three-thousandfold world system who equally uphold the Bodhisattva precepts.
Thus ends the second major section, the "Section on the Correct Demonstration of the Dharma Gate.

△ Third, the "Section on Circulation for the Benefit of the World," which is divided into two parts: first, the summary conclusion; second, the verses of praise. Within the first part, there are four sections.
First, the universal binding and exposition of the "Mind-Ground" chapter; second, the brief enumeration of the ten general locations; third, the clarification of the Dharma taught;
fourth, the clarification of the great assembly's practice. Now, the first [section].

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha finished preaching the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Precepts within the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as taught by Vairocana Buddha in the World of the High Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury. The thousands of billions of Śākyamunis likewise preached it in this same manner.
Within this, first the explanation of what was spoken by Śākyamuni is concluded; next, the explanation of what was spoken by the other Śākyas is concluded.
△ Second, a brief enumeration of the ten locations where he taught in total:
from the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara up to this place beneath the Bodhi tree, these constitute the section on the ten dwelling places where the Dharma was preached.
All bodhisattvas and the unspeakably vast assembly likewise receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain its meaning.
This applies to worlds numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, the Lotus Treasury World, and worlds as numerous as motes of dust.
Within this, first the ten locations where Śākyamuni preached the Dharma are concluded; next, the remaining ten locations where Śākyamuni preached the Dharma are also concluded.
Below the phrase "microdust worlds," the four characters [indicating omission] are likewise stated as missing.
△ The Dharma taught by the Three Clarities:

the Treasury of the Mind of all Buddhas, the Treasury of the Earth, the Treasury of Precepts, the Treasury of Immeasurable Vows and Practices, and the Treasury of the Ever-Abiding Buddha-nature of Cause and Effect.
Thus have all Buddhas finished expounding the immeasurable treasuries of all Dharmas.

The first five phrases constitute the specific [analysis], while the final phrase constitutes the general [synthesis]. Within these five specific categories, each further possesses both a general and a specific meaning.
Regarding "the treasury of mind" (*citta-garbha*): generally, all phenomena (*dharma*) belong to the mind; specifically, it refers to the thirty stages of the mind (*triṃśat-citta*).
Regarding "the treasury of earth" (*bhūmi-garbha*): generally, all phenomena are termed "earth"; specifically, it refers to...

The Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). Regarding the "Treasury of Precepts" (*śīlakośa*): in its general sense, all dharmas are termed precepts; specifically, it refers to the ten grave and numerous minor [precepts].

Regarding the "Treasury of Immeasurable Practices and Vows": in its general sense, it likewise encompasses all dharmas; specifically, it refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), the myriad practices, the ten great kings of vows, and so forth.
Regarding the "Treasury of the Ever-Abiding Buddha-Nature of Cause and Effect": Buddha-nature is neither cause nor...
The fruit [is thus realized]. Since cause and effect are not separate from Buddha-nature, it is said: "The Mahāyāna cause is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
the Mahāyāna fruit is likewise the true reality of all phenomena. True reality is simply another name for Buddha-nature.

Now, since both the cause is Buddha-nature and the fruit is Buddha-nature, and since Buddha-nature is eternally abiding, both cause and effect are also eternally abiding. In their ultimate unity, they are one.

All dharmas are collectively termed the "Treasury of the Permanently Abiding Buddha-nature as Cause and Effect. Specifically, this is as explained in the "Chapter on the Source of Buddha-nature" and other sections.
△ Fourth, clarifying the practice and observance by the great assembly.
Throughout the hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds, all sentient beings shall receive, uphold, and joyfully practice it.
If one wishes to extensively open the characteristics of the mind-ground, it is as explained in the "Seven Practices Chapter" of the *Buddhāvatamsaka-rāja-sūtra*.

Regarding the "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa): the ground of the mind is without characteristics, yet it possesses all characteristics; these are layered and inexhaustible, their general and specific aspects being inconceivable.

Part Two: Praise in Verse, in three sections. First, praise for the benefit of upholding the Dharma; second, the sequence of the practice of the Dharma; third, the vow to deliver sentient beings. Now, the first section.
The wise person, strong in patience and wisdom, Is able to uphold such a Dharma as this.
Before attaining the path of Buddhahood, they securely obtain five kinds of benefits: First, the Buddhas of the ten directions Pity them and constantly protect them;
Second, at the time of death, They possess right view and their hearts rejoice; Third, in every place where they are born...
They act as friends to all bodhisattvas; fourth, they are a mass of merit.
Having fully accomplished the perfection of ethical discipline, fifth, in both this life and future lives, their innate morality, merit, and wisdom are complete.
These are the sons of the Buddhas, the wise ones, who are able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata. Although they possess only the physical eye, it is called the Buddha-eye.

Furthermore, "patience" (kṣānti) refers to *anurakṣaṇa-kṣānti* (endurance), which is to say, the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*). It is said that to have wisdom (*prajñā*) without patience is called "wild wisdom" (*unmatta-prajñā*);

to have patience without wisdom is called "foolish concentration" (*bāla-samādhi*). Moreover, those of the Two Vehicles possess much concentration but little wisdom, and thus do not perceive the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Provisional-stage Bodhisattvas possess much wisdom but little concentration; although they perceive the Buddha-nature, they do so without clarity. Therefore, both patience and wisdom are required.
Only those who possess both [strengths] are truly wise persons; only they are able to uphold such a Dharma. As for "those protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas":
all Buddhas emerge from this Dharma, which is like a mother to the Buddhas. Therefore, one who upholds it enters into communion with the Buddha’s own essence (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, if one does not uphold this Dharma, the lineage of the Buddhas is severed; if one can uphold this Dharma, it is continued.
The Buddha’s wisdom-life; therefore, the Buddhas always compassionately regard and protect those who uphold the Dharma.

One who possesses right view and rejoices at the time of death has already attained the Buddha-eye; thus, even if an iron wheel were to spin upon one's head, one’s perfect clarity of concentration and wisdom shall never be lost.
To be a companion to Bodhisattvas in birth after birth means that one’s rank is equal to that of Great Enlightenment—this is truly so.

O Son of the Buddha, all bodhisattvas are my fellow students. Those who have fully accomplished the perfection of merit and ethical discipline—wherein ethical discipline is the accumulation of all merits, just as the earth can produce and nourish all things—I now constantly maintain such faith.
Since the category of ethical discipline is already complete, then the entire accumulation of all merits is likewise complete.

It is the full accomplishment. Regarding "the fulfillment of the nature-precepts (*śīla*), merit (*puṇya*), and wisdom (*prajñā*"): one who penetrates these nature-precepts realizes that cultivation arises entirely from the nature, and cultivation is entirely within the nature.
Because cultivation arises entirely from the nature, merit is fulfilled through wisdom; because cultivation fully manifests the nature, wisdom is fulfilled through merit.
Furthermore, the nature-precepts are the essence of the true cause (*samyak-hetu*), corresponding to the virtue of the *dharmakāya*. To maintain this nature—

Precepts are the causal condition for the virtue of merit and goodness, which leads to the realization of the nature of liberation; they are the conditional cause for wisdom, which constitutes the virtue of *prajñā*.
As for their fulfillment in future lives, it proceeds from the fulfillment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) up to ultimate fulfillment.
Having attained these five benefits, one is truly a son of the Buddha and shall succeed to the Buddha’s position; therefore, it is said, "These are the sons of all Buddhas.
△ Second, the section on the practice of learning the Dharma, which has two parts: first, observing the essence of the Dharma; second, guarding and maintaining the characteristics of the precepts.
Now, first:
The wise one who reflects well understands that those who calculate a self and cling to signs cannot give rise to this Dharma;
nor are those who seek to extinguish their lifespan and attain realization suitable places for sowing the seeds, if one wishes to grow the sprout of Bodhi.
The radiance illuminates the world; one should observe with tranquility:
The true nature of all phenomena is neither born nor extinguished, Neither eternal nor discontinuous, neither identical nor different, Neither coming nor going.
Within this single mind, One should diligently adorn it through skillful means.
What a bodhisattva ought to do should be learned in successive stages;
one should not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding those in training or those beyond training. This is called the foremost path, and it is also called the Mahāyāna.
All evil conceptual proliferations are completely extinguished from this source, as are the *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas.

All of these emerge from the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. The ten inexhaustible precepts are all realized in accordance with reality and cultivated in conformity with the nature of phenomena—namely, the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, free from conceptual proliferation.
Ordinary beings cling to existence, while those of the Two Vehicles realize emptiness; both turn their backs on the Truth.
"Because it is a cause, it is not a seed. "One should observe with stillness": "stillness" (*śamatha*) is a synonym for cessation;
"observation" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the meticulous scrutiny of contemplation. When cessation and contemplation are non-dual, that is true cultivation. Regarding "the true mark of all phenomena":

"all phenomena" refers to the provisional and real dharmas of the ten realms and the ten suchnesses. If one observes that their marks are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described, then...
Delusions are not real; they are false and insubstantial. When one contemplates that their nature is fundamentally true—the original Tathāgatagarbha—then there is neither form nor non-form;
this is called the mark of reality. Because it is pure and primordial, it does not arise; because it manifests according to karma, it does not perish.
Furthermore, because it manifests according to karma, arising is itself non-arising; because it is pure and primordial, ceasing is likewise non-ceasing.
Extinction. Because it does not change while following conditions, it is not eternal; because it follows conditions without changing, it is not annihilated.
Because principle conforms to phenomena, they are not identical; because phenomena conform to principle, they are not different. Because delusion has no point of origin, there is no coming;
because awakening has nothing to be extinguished, there is no going. Such dharmas are precisely this one mind; this one mind is precisely the three [natures].
This concerns the nature of the ten minds, the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the gravity or lightness of the various precepts.

Once one has realized this essential nature, one then employs skillful means (*upāya*) to diligently adorn it. Single-mindedness is the causal factor of the principle-nature; tranquil contemplation is the causal factor of the wisdom-nature;
and skillful means is the causal factor of the goodness-nature. Furthermore, both observation and the upholding of the precepts are termed "skillful means."
Adornment. Contemplation is the skillful means regarding principle; it is called the adornment of wisdom. Upholding the precepts is the skillful means regarding phenomena;

it is called the adornment of merit. Furthermore, the fulfillment of the category of morality depends entirely on deep faith in principle, while the advancement of the mental ground depends entirely on diligent cultivation of phenomena. Therefore, it is said: "Because the precepts are pure, wisdom is pure. Because...
Because wisdom is pure, precepts are pure; it is like two hands washing each other—there is absolutely no sequence of before and after.
Furthermore, if one exerts diligent skillful means without tranquil observation, it will be conditioned and tainted, lacking any adornment.

If one engages in tranquil observation without diligent skillful means, it will be withered and empty, incapable of adornment. Therefore, within a single mind, both skillful means and [observation] must be present.
Adornment: This is that which a bodhisattva ought to do; it should be studied in successive stages.

One must not say, "This is merely a matter of study," thereby falling into the second category [of mere conceptualization] and failing to understand cultivation in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*). Within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), learning itself is non-learning;
yet one should practice and study with fervor. Although this is called "successive," it is directly like a bird in the sky.
The traces [of practice] are not the same as the gradual dharma-gates; yet, they are entirely indistinguishable from the principle of the ultimate, perfect, and sudden.

Therefore, it is cautioned that one must not give rise to discriminative thoughts. The wondrous cultivation of non-action is identical in its entirety to the nature of reality (li-xing), and is called the "Supreme Path.
The wondrous nature of no-more-learning gives rise to true cultivation, and is called Mahāyāna. Mahāyāna is translated here as...
Mahāyāna means that it carries both oneself and others together into the city of Great Nirvāṇa.
Because it is the foremost path, it can extinguish the various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles.

Because it is the Mahāyāna, it can bring forth the fruit of *sarvajñajñāna* (the omniscience of all Buddhas). *Sarvajñajñāna* is translated here as "the wisdom of all-knowledge"; it is the threefold [wisdom] within a single mind.
"Jñāna" (Wisdom) is the general designation for the ultimate, supreme fruit. By means of the first path, one is capable of transporting the Mahāyāna vehicle;

by means of the Mahāyāna, one is capable of reaching the stage of Sarvajñā (Omniscience); and by means of Sarvajñā, one perfectly accords with the principle free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*).
In the "Mind-Ground" of the Brahma Net Sūtra, the fruit penetrates the cause and the cause encompasses the fruit; when the principles reach this point, they are at their ultimate limit.
△ Second, the characteristics of upholding the precepts.
Therefore, all you sons of the Buddha, You should arouse great courage and vigor;
Regarding the pure precepts of all Buddhas, uphold them as if they were bright pearls. All Bodhisattvas of the past Have already trained within these.
Those of the future shall study; those of the present are studying now. This is the sphere of action of the Buddhas, praised by the Holy Lord.
Those who wish to return to the true mark of the single mind must cultivate the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground. Those who wish to cultivate the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground must...

Because one upholds the pure precepts of all Buddhas, the text concludes by exhorting the protection and maintenance of the characteristics of the precepts, establishing them as the foundation for entering the Path and advancing in cultivation.

Regarding "protecting and maintaining [the precepts] like a bright pearl," the *Fayin* (Record of Hidden Meanings) states: first, the sense of purity—protecting and maintaining them so they are not defiled;
second, the sense of perfection—protecting and maintaining them so they are not incomplete; third, the sense of radiance—protecting and maintaining them so that...
It dispels darkness. Now, I shall further explain and establish this: purity is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*); perfection is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
and radiance is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*). However, clarity, purity, and perfection are all merely the characteristics and virtues of the jewel.

Within these characteristics and virtues, the three meanings are perfectly present. If one were to further elaborate upon their manifestation, they would constitute the very substance of the bright pearl.

This is the unsurpassed, supreme treasure. Its marks are perfectly complete, luminous, and pure; its function is able to rain down objects to relieve poverty. Its essence is the *dharmakāya*, its marks are *prajñā*, and its function is *vimukti*.
These correspond to the three clusters of the wondrous precepts (*tri-śīla-rāśi*). The correspondence between the dharma and the metaphor is clear and distinct.
Therefore, that which is studied by all Bodhisattvas of the three periods is precisely the sphere of the Buddha’s practice; cause and effect are identical.
How could [this] talisman not be praised by the Holy Sovereign? The Holy Sovereign is the Sage among Sages.
△ Third, the vow to deliver sentient beings.
I have already explained in accordance with the truth this immeasurable mass of merit;
dedicating it for the sake of all sentient beings, may they together proceed toward omniscience. May all who hear this Dharma attain the path to Buddhahood.
The Buddhas themselves recite these precepts; I now also recite them. This is called "Following" (Anuparivarta). The Buddhas [recite them] every half-month.
The Moon speaks in accordance with the Dharma; I now likewise speak in accordance with the Dharma, which is called "conformity.
Speaking thus in conformity, a mass of merit naturally becomes immeasurable; yet, without making it for oneself, one dedicates it entirely to sentient beings.
Furthermore, so as not to cause sentient beings to fall into the two vehicles or the three realms of existence, one directs them all together toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Moreover...
May those who hear this Dharma, upon its passing once through the faculty of hearing, forever become seeds for the Path. Having heard it, may they be able to contemplate it;
having contemplated it, may they be able to cultivate it, such that all shall attain the Buddha-way. This is because one first receives these precepts by giving rise to the bodhicitta;
now, reciting these precepts, one further dedicates them toward bodhi. To dedicate them to sentient beings is the mind that transforms below, which is named [the Bodhisattva Precepts].
It is compassion (*karuṇā*). To turn toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and fully realize the Buddha-way is what is called the aspiration for the higher goal;
this is termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*). Because of this upward aspiration, one is able to transform others below; because of this downward transformation, it is truly called the upward aspiration.

When compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem, it is termed the bodhicitta. This arises from realizing that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in their threefold nature—just as the mind is, so too is the Buddha.
Therefore, one must seek the higher [enlightenment]; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings, and thus one must transform those below.

Because of giving rise to this mind of seeking the higher and transforming those below, one receives and attains the Great Bodhisattva Precepts. Because of upholding these Great Bodhisattva Precepts, one is able to fulfill the two wheels of compassion and wisdom.
As the ancients said: "One gives rise to the *saṃnāha* (armor) at the initial mind, and brings great compassion to its ultimate fulfillment."
To go forth in order to overcome calamities may be called proceeding directly from the bodhi of names toward ultimate bodhi.

These fourteen lines of verse in praise are not explained in the *Yìshù* (Commentary on the Meaning). Some say they are verses for the summary of vows and aspirations recited after the precepts have been finished.
Now, examining the meaning of the text, although they appear to be a single summary of the ritual for receiving the precepts, they may also be [interpreted as such].
This concludes the section on the superior grade. By means of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts, one is able to traverse the stages of the mental grounds (*citta-bhūmi*).
This is because the thirty minds and ten grounds are precisely the positions traversed from cause to fruit by the person who upholds the precepts.
It is also like the three gradual sequences in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which serve as the means for traversing the fifty-five stages.

These constitute what is traversed; when the subject and object are combined, they are termed the "sixty stages of the sages. Now, if we follow the object by means of the subject, then precepts are the mind-ground;
if we follow the subject by means of the object, then the mind-ground is precepts. Since this applies universally, how can there be any doubt?
The Combined Commentary on the "Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind" Chapter of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, Fascicle Seven (End).
Colophon to the Combined Commentary:

Now, the fundamental ground of the mind is shared by all sentient beings. Yet, though the stainless nature-precepts are present in daily life, they remain unrecognized. It is as if one’s eyes were clouded with cataracts...
Flowers dance in the great void; like dreaming ants seeking the scent beneath the steps, the substance of the clear sky remains as it was, and the body of the Wheel-Turning King is unchanged.
Alas! Through delusion and confusion, one falsely undergoes the cycle of illusions, causing our Compassionate Honored One to manifest in person to share in this suffering.

He demonstrates his attainment tirelessly for eight thousand years, bestowing transformation without partiality across the dust-motes and lands of the universe. Now that the single drop of the mind-ground has been spread abroad...
The long-standing delusions accumulated over kalpas are instantly awakened; yet, as the jade caskets have long been sealed, only half of the jewel has been revealed.

That I, a fool and ignorant one, have been able to explore this complete treasure, exhausting my thoughts and every faculty, is like adding a speck of dust to Mount Tai. Reflecting on how the conditions for encountering the Dharma are so difficult to obtain, my tears flow in torrents.
I pray that my fellow practitioners will contemplate deeply and study diligently, adhering equally to both understanding and practice, so that both self and others may be benefited.
I hope that by this I may repay the Buddha’s kindness and not fail my own nature.
On the birthday of the Great Being Kṣitigarbha, in the Dingchou year of the Chongzhen era, the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Zhixu set down his brush and thus recorded this.
The *Combined Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra* was composed by the Dharma Master Suhua of Lingfeng. It has been in circulation for a long time;
its printing blocks are preserved at Gulina in Jinling. Those from near and far who request to read it have gathered at his gate like a marketplace. The monastics of the southeast...

Not everyone was able to obtain copies of the circulating edition. The Venerable Jianmi, its chief editor, moved by the high value placed on paper in Luoyang, intended to produce a new edition to be sent to Lengyan Monastery in Jiaxing for inclusion in the canon, so that it might be widely disseminated. Upon hearing this, I was deeply moved and took sole responsibility for the undertaking.

As the carving of the blocks was nearing completion, a monk asked with some doubt: "The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is the fundamental code of precepts for the monastic community; why has your honor carved this [new edition]?"
"Though you say this is to propagate the treasure of the Dharma, it is by no means the true vocation of a layman.

Do you have some doctrine to offer regarding this? I rose and replied with a bow: "Yes, indeed; no, indeed. Please allow me to briefly set forth my humble views. In the past, while I was serving in Wusong, I met with misfortune and was subjected to censure.
Amidst such distress and affliction, I had no way to request my retirement from office. I then recalled the joys found among hills and valleys, and gazed upon the clouds and mists..."

Vast and distant. The returning sails on the horizon—when will they reach the shore? I recall that in the year of Guisi (1653), I entered the presence of the Elder of Dinnan in Huashan as his disciple;
my dharma name is Shuzhun. I have followed his instructions in pure cultivation.

The Vinaya is my own discipline. I have made it my daily practice to pay homage to Mahākāruṇika. Even beneath the threat of spears, halberds, swords, and lances, or amidst the turmoil of calamity and distress, I have not dared to slacken for even a moment.
I intended to maintain this until the end of my life; yet, unexpectedly, turbid conditions entangled me, and I did not wish to abandon it abruptly.
Pressed repeatedly by my colleagues, I could not bear to further incur the reproach of being like Feng Fu, and so I have yielded.
Having shaved my head, I vowed to cultivate the Great Hall of Gratitude; yet how could I have expected that I would ultimately be unable to escape [samsara]?
Consequently, I again requested leave from the Elder and left the mountains to abandon the precepts.

Since then, I have wandered through the dust and wind for several more years, during which time matters such as breaking the precepts, violating the fast, and errors regarding causes and effects were largely unavoidable. Now, I am utterly ruined.
I have suffered from asthma for sixty years. It has now been more than five months since the summer of the year Jiayin (1854), during which time I died and returned to life.
Could this not be due to the empowerment of the power of the sages? Furthermore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states that both great ministers and lay devotees may receive the pure precepts.

Recalling my former vows and continuing to observe the Vinaya, I have donated funds to re-engrave this scripture, hoping it may benefit and widely disseminate the Dharma, and likewise serve as a support for spiritual efficacy.

By the Dharma-power of this Peak (Feng), may the transgressions and faults of this humble servant be expiated. May those who read this sutra write "Namo Buddhāya" with proper measure and joyfully offer praise;
perhaps, by such means, they may hope for the extinction of their karmic retribution even by a single chance in ten thousand.
Upon hearing this, the monk praised it as excellent and requested that this colophon be appended to the end of the scroll. Thus, I have written it.
Written with reverence by the Thousand-Flower Bodhisattva and Disciple of the Precepts, the Recluse Guizhou, Shen Bao,
at Xishang Garden in the southern suburbs of Shicheng.
